nature-found-086.title: Kapp's charge: an economy built on cost shifting
nature-found-086.text: Economist Karl William Kapp gave a blunt account of where social costs come from. In his heterodox view, outside the mainstream, they are the share of production costs that businesses shift onto society to raise profits. He blamed capitalist accounting laws that let producers leave these costs unpaid. On this view {{ref:nature-econ-848}} is essentially a system of cost shifting, and legal cost shifting is a main source of profit.

nature-econ-363.title: Competition: the contest for customers
nature-econ-363.text: In 1776 Adam Smith described competition as steering productive resources to their most valued uses and encouraging efficiency. Competition is the contest among firms for customers and limited resources, fought with price, product, promotion and place. It arises from scarcity: there is never enough to satisfy every human want. Classical economists held that it pushes firms to develop new products and technologies, giving consumers more choice and better goods. More choice usually means lower prices than when one or a few firms dominate. How much competition a market has depends on the number of firms, {{ref:nature-econ-863}}, information and access to resources. Share and foreign-exchange markets are usually seen as close to perfect, while real estate is a very imperfect market. For a few goods, having many firms is itself inefficient, because competition duplicates costs that do not vary with output; {{ref:nature-econ-350}} covers these cases. Economists still debate how relevant the textbook ideal of {{ref:nature-econ-353}} is to real markets, and whether it should serve as the benchmark.

nature-econ-557.title: The AD–AS model: where demand meets supply for a whole economy
nature-econ-557.text: A common textbook model finds an economy's price level and real output where two curves cross. One is {{ref:nature-econ-868}}, the total spending on goods and services. The other is aggregate supply, the total output producers offer. The demand curve slopes down, so more output is demanded at lower price levels. Near potential output, the full-employment level, extra demand only raises prices, not output. Modern versions put inflation on the vertical axis, with an upward-sloping supply curve based on the Phillips curve, a link between inflation and unemployment.

nature-eco-353.title: Food chains: who eats whom, in a single line
nature-eco-353.text: A green plant is eaten by a snail, the snail by a frog, the frog by a snake, and the snake by an eagle. That is a food chain: a single linear path through a {{ref:nature-eco-297}}. It usually starts with a producer such as grass or algae and ends with a top predator or an organism that breaks down the dead. It shows who eats whom, level by level. When many food chains interconnect, they form that larger, tangled network. A chain's base is primary producers, which make organic compounds from sunlight or from inorganic chemicals. Every other member is a consumer. In dark places such as hydrothermal vents, bacteria and archaea that use hydrogen sulfide and {{ref:nature-eco-727}} form the base. When organisms die, debris-eating animals and other breakers-down of remains turn them into simple nutrients that return to the soil for plants. Food chains also trace pollution. In ecotoxicology, the study of poisons in ecosystems, they show how contaminants pass along and biomagnify, building up at each step. Removing even one link can push other species toward extinction.

nature-eco-670.title: Coevolution: species shaping each other
nature-eco-670.text: Flowering plants and insects have coevolved for over 100 million years, and the earliest bees appeared in the early Cretaceous. Coevolution is two or more species reciprocally shaping each other's evolution through {{ref:nature-eco-745}}. Hummingbirds and bird-pollinated flowers show it as a mutualism: nectar, colour, shape and blooming time match the birds' diet, vision, bills and breeding season. Hosts and parasites enter an arms race. The Red Queen hypothesis predicts that sexual reproduction lets a host stay just ahead of its parasite. Predators and prey, and herbivores and plants, impose mutual selective pressures that produce arms races and anti-predator adaptations. Coevolution can be pairwise or diffuse among a guild of species, and under the geographic mosaic theory it differs between populations depending on location and community {{ref:nature-nbs-347}}. Humans induce it too. Disease-resistant crop varieties bred since the 1940s favored rapid evolution in pathogens that overcame the plant defences. Norgaard and Gowdy applied it to economics and society, arguing that the economy, society and the environment are linked in a coevolutionary relationship.

nature-eco-675.title: Nitrous oxide: the third greenhouse gas
nature-eco-675.text: Per molecule over 100 years, nitrous oxide traps 265 times as much heat as CO2. Its concentration is under one thousandth of CO2's, so its warming contribution is less than one third that of carbon dioxide. It is a minor atmospheric gas that is an active part of the planetary {{ref:nature-eco-176}} and a long-lived {{ref:nature-eco-162}}. It is the third most important such gas for global warming and has been a major ozone-depleting substance. Atmospheric abundance has grown more than 20% from about 270 ppb in 1750, surpassing 330 ppb in 2017, and is rising about 1 ppb per year. About 40% of emissions are human-caused, with growth chiefly from expanding {{ref:nature-res-257}}. Annual human emissions equal about 3 billion tonnes of CO2 in warming effect. Microbes produce it by {{ref:nature-eco-395}}, {{ref:nature-eco-396}} and nitrifier {{ref:nature-eco-396}}.

nature-econ-450.title: Integer programming: when answers must be whole numbers
nature-econ-450.text: It is not possible to build 3.7 cars. Integer programming handles choices like that: optimization in which some or all of the choice variables must be whole numbers. It usually means integer linear programming, where the objective and other constraints are linear ({{ref:nature-econ-456}}). If only some variables must be whole, it is mixed-integer programming. Integers also code yes-or-no decisions as 0 or 1. A farm can use it to plan yields for several crops that share land, labor, capital, seeds and {{ref:nature-eco-662}}, maximizing production without exceeding resources. Districting problems, including {{ref:nature-eecon-232}} districting, are solved this way while respecting natural boundaries and contiguity. The difficulty is that integer programming is NP-complete, a class of problems with no known fast general method, so many instances are intractable. Exact methods include cutting planes and variants of {{ref:nature-econ-426}}. Heuristic shortcuts such as tabu search handle the rest.

nature-eco-185.title: The phosphorus cycle: the slow loop that skips the sky
nature-eco-185.text: Most of the great element cycles pass through the air. Phosphorus almost never does, because it rarely becomes a gas. The phosphorus cycle is the biogeochemical cycle that moves phosphorus through rocks, water and living things. Life cannot do without it. Phosphorus is part of DNA, RNA and ATP, and in animals it also strengthens bones and teeth. The cycle has four main steps. Rock that contains phosphorus is lifted up, then weathers and erodes. Rivers carry the phosphorus to lakes and the ocean, where it is finally buried in {{ref:nature-eco-682}}. Phosphates, the compounds in which phosphorus usually travels, move quickly through plants and animals but very slowly through soil and ocean. That makes this one of the slowest biogeochemical cycles. On land, the slow release of phosphorus from rock as it breaks down limits how much ecosystems can get. In water, phosphorus can limit the growth of aquatic life, so phosphates from fertilizers, sewage and detergents can pollute lakes and streams. Freshwater {{ref:nature-eco-659}}, a sudden mass growth of algae, is generally caused by excess phosphorus. Saltwater blooms tend to come from excess nitrogen.

nature-eco-245.title: Nutrient pollution: too much of a good thing
nature-eco-245.text: Nitrogen and phosphorus feed crops, but in a lake or a bay they become pollutants. Nutrient pollution is the fouling of water by too many nutrients, usually these two, entering it. It is a main cause of {{ref:nature-eco-216}} in lakes, rivers and coastal waters, where the extra nutrients feed algal growth. Sources include runoff from farms, septic tank waste, feedlots, raw sewage and emissions from burning fuels. Fertilizer that crops do not use is lost from fields and harms air and downstream water. In Europe, {{ref:nature-res-257}} is usually the main source of nitrogen in water, while households and industry often dominate phosphorus. Excess nitrogen brings toxic {{ref:nature-eco-659}}, oxygen-starved water, acidic rain, nitrogen-saturated forests and global warming. The costs are real: dearer water treatment, losses to commercial fishing, fishing for sport and shellfish, and less tourism income. Excess nitrate in {{ref:nature-nbs-326}} can cause blue baby syndrome. Remedies include vegetated buffer strips, artificial wetlands, better wastewater treatment and permits that make the polluter pay.

nature-eco-216.title: Eutrophication: when a lake is fed too well
nature-eco-216.text: The word comes from the Greek eutrophos, meaning well-nourished, and that is exactly the trouble. Eutrophication is the build-up of nutrients in a body of water, causing extra growth of algae and plants that can use up the water's oxygen. It is caused by too much of a nutrient, most often phosphates and nitrates. It can happen naturally, or it can be caused by sewage, industrial wastewater, runoff carrying fertilizer and other human sources. Most of these nutrients arrive as the {{ref:nature-eco-245}} described earlier. The sequence is grimly simple. Extra nutrients feed a boom in phytoplankton. The resulting {{ref:nature-eco-659}} and bacterial growth deplete the oxygen dissolved in the water, causing serious environmental damage. Fish die in larger numbers, and desirable species disappear. The problem is everywhere. Surveys found that 54% of lakes in Asia are eutrophic, along with 53% in Europe, 48% in North America, 41% in South America and 28% in Africa. Along the world's coasts, the {{ref:nature-hist-032}} has identified 375 zones where the water runs dangerously short of oxygen.

nature-eco-235.title: Hypoxia: when water runs short of oxygen
nature-eco-235.text: Most fish cannot live once water falls below 30% of the oxygen it could hold. Environmental hypoxia means low-oxygen conditions like this, usually in natural waters or in the thin air at altitude. Water with 1 to 30% of its possible oxygen saturation is called hypoxic, and water with none at all is anoxic. A healthy water body should seldom fall below 80%. The usual cause is nutrient pollution. Dense masses of algae die and sink, and the bacteria decomposing them use up the oxygen as they respire. Hypoxia can also happen without pollution. In estuaries, lighter river water can layer over seawater and block oxygen from reaching the bottom. Low oxygen is not bad for everything. It harms air-breathing organisms but is essential for many anaerobic ones, which live without oxygen.

nature-eco-663.title: The environmental costs of fertilizer
nature-eco-663.text: Only a fraction of nitrogen fertilizer becomes plant matter. The rest accumulates in soil or is lost as runoff, and runoff from farmland is a major contributor to freshwater eutrophication. Heat-trapping gases from manufacture and use of nitrogen fertilizer are about 5% of anthropogenic emissions, one third from production and two thirds from use. Most synthetic fertilizer depends on fossil fuel, which supplies energy and {{ref:nature-eco-727}} for the hydrogen used in Haber process ammonia. Phosphate fertilizers can add toxic elements to soil: cadmium in monoammonium phosphate ranged from 0.14 to 50.9 mg/kg, and fluoride from fluorapatite has risen in soils. Excess fertilizer may break down symbiosis between plant roots and mycorrhizal fungi, while effects on soil animals are still debated. Overapplication can cause fertilizer burn, damaging or killing the plant.

nature-eco-391.title: Soil degradation: five ways soil loses its power
nature-eco-391.text: Soil can wear out. Soil degradation is the decline of soil's ability to do its jobs, and it happens in five main ways. Soil can become more acidic. It can be contaminated or eroded. It can fill with salt. And dry land can turn to {{ref:nature-eco-703}}, the process covered in {{ref:nature-eco-091}}. That last one is widely misunderstood. Drought alone is a common misconception as its cause. It usually comes from poorly adapted human activities, such as {{ref:nature-eco-761}} or harvesting too much wood for fuel. Erosion, the wearing away of soil, is driven by water, wind, ice and gravity, and several kinds can strike at once. Salination is a build-up of salts that cuts the farming value of soils and the plants growing on them. Contamination has a partial natural remedy. At low levels, soil organisms can treat it, mainly through enzymes made by microbes.

nature-eco-341.title: Decomposition: how the dead feed the living
nature-eco-341.text: Earth's living matter is finite, so it must be used again and again. Decomposition makes that possible. It is the breakdown of dead organic matter into simpler substances such as carbon dioxide, water, simple sugars and mineral salts. It is part of the {{ref:nature-es-084}}. Some decomposition is abiotic, driven by chemical or physical processes. Biotic decomposition, or biodegradation, is carried out by living things, mainly microbes. Plant matter breaks down in stages. First, water leaches out soluble compounds, and the material breaks into fragments. That gives the organisms feeding on it more surface to attack. Vertebrate bodies pass through five stages: fresh, bloat, active decay, advanced decay and dry remains. Where decomposition slows, carbon piles up. Waterlogged soils slow it, so carbon-rich {{ref:nature-eco-682}} builds up and act as a long-term {{ref:nature-eco-169}}. People depend on this process too. Ecosystems that lose biodiversity provide fewer services, including decomposing waste.

nature-eco-621.title: Complex adaptive systems: wholes that learn
nature-eco-621.text: Ant colonies, power grids, markets and the climate share a deep feature. Each is a complex adaptive system: many interacting parts that adapt and learn, whose overall behavior cannot be predicted from the parts alone. Cities, firms, governments and ecosystems qualify too. Sociologist Walter F. Buckley coined the term in 1968. Interactions in such systems are non-linear, so small changes in inputs can cause large changes in outputs, and any interaction can loop back on itself as {{ref:nature-eco-638}}. They often organize themselves rather than following a central hierarchy. They run far from equilibrium and need a constant flow of energy to keep their organization. Their high capacity to adapt gives them resilience against disturbance. Researchers often model them with network models and {{ref:nature-es-061}}. The approach is increasingly used to study {{ref:nature-eco-711}} and institutional change, where outcomes can be influenced but not precisely controlled.

nature-eco-277.title: Urban runoff: rain that never meets the soil
nature-eco-277.text: Rain that falls on a road, a parking lot or a roof cannot soak in. Urban runoff is the surface runoff that hard surfaces like these create, from rain, landscape watering and car washing. Instead of filtering through soil, polluted rainwater flows to storm drains. Most municipal storm sewers then discharge it untreated into streams, rivers and bays. Because more water stays on the surface, the {{ref:nature-eco-742}} drops and {{ref:nature-nbs-329}} become more common. Many towns respond with building codes, such as narrow sidewalks and pavers set in earth, that let more water soak in.

nature-eco-257.title: Frozen ground and a carbon feedback: thaw that feeds warming
nature-eco-257.text: For every 1 °C of global warming, the {{ref:nature-eco-678}} in the upper 3 m of ground is expected to shrink by about 25%. As it thaws, long-stored carbon escapes as carbon dioxide and {{ref:nature-eco-727}}, adding to the warming that caused the thaw. That loop is the carbon feedback of thawing ground. Carbon dioxide from microbes respiring with oxygen makes up the overwhelming majority of the emissions. The other gas forms in waterlogged, oxygen-free places, such as thermokarst lakes left by thawing ice-rich ground. There is a brake. Thawed ground grows more vegetation, which takes up more carbon, and this is the main counteracting feedback. The IPCC Sixth Assessment Report estimates releases of 14–175 billion tonnes per 1 °C of warming, counted in the common yardstick of {{ref:nature-eco-160}}. For comparison, human carbon dioxide emissions were about 40 billion tonnes in 2019. A 2021 assessment estimated that emissions from thawing ground would raise the {{ref:nature-clim-241}} by about 8.4%, though its methods were criticized. Researchers also debate where the rising emissions come from: ancient carbon, or faster breakdown of modern plant litter. Its thaw is listed among the {{ref:nature-eco-607}}.

nature-eco-673.title: Detritivores: the first stage of rot
nature-eco-673.text: Why does a forest floor not bury itself in dead leaves? Part of the answer is a crowd of small animals that eat the debris. A detritivore is a heterotroph that gets its nutrients by eating {{ref:nature-eco-709}}: decomposing plant and animal parts and faeces. Millipedes, springtails, woodlice, dung flies, slugs, earthworms and sea cucumbers all work this way. They swallow lumps of matter. Bacteria, fungi and protists, the {{ref:nature-eco-340}}, instead absorb nutrients at a molecular scale. The animals do the first stage of remineralization by fragmenting dead plant matter, so the microbes can do the second. Together they return carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, calcium and potassium to the soil. The job once went undone. In the Carboniferous, fungi and bacteria had not yet evolved the ability to digest lignin, so large deposits of dead plant tissue built up and later became fossil fuels. Feeding on {{ref:nature-eco-682}} has a cost: some detritivores incidentally concentrate toxic pollutants.

nature-eco-302.title: Primary production: where almost all life's food begins
nature-eco-302.text: Almost every living thing on Earth depends, directly or indirectly, on a single process. Primary production is the making of organic compounds from carbon dioxide in air or water. It happens mainly through {{ref:nature-eco-190}}, the capture of sunlight by plants and algae. The organisms that do it are called primary producers, or autotrophs. They form the base of every feeding chain: mostly plants on land and algae in water. A small share runs on {{ref:nature-eco-696}} instead. It draws energy from chemical reactions of non-living compounds rather than from light. On land, production depends mainly on water and temperature. That is why very dry lands and polar regions produce so little. Satellites now let scientists add up the whole planet. Their estimate is 104.9 petagrams of carbon a year, with 56.4 made on land and 48.5 in the oceans. The sea, worked by drifting algae, nearly matches the land. Human societies are part of this cycle of production. Yet they influence it far out of proportion to their share of it.

nature-eco-613.title: Regime shifts: abrupt, lasting changes in how systems work
nature-eco-613.text: In the 1990s strong evidence arrived from four kinds of places: {{ref:nature-eco-422}}, {{ref:nature-eco-453}}, {{ref:nature-eco-520}} and shallow lakes. All showed regime shifts, large, abrupt and lasting changes in how a complex system is structured and works. The system can be an ecosystem, the climate or a financial system. A regime is its typical behavior, held in place by loops of {{ref:nature-eco-638}} that reinforce one another. Shifts happen when those stabilizing loops weaken, or when an outside shock exceeds what the system can absorb. A small disturbance can produce big effects, so inputs and outputs are not proportional. In {{ref:nature-nbs-347}}, shifts can sharply change flows of food, clean water and {{ref:nature-es-121}}. They are hard to reverse and sometimes irreversible. Deforestation could shift Amazon and East Asian rainforests toward {{ref:nature-eco-681}}, affecting food, fresh water, the climate and biodiversity. Shifts are expected to grow more common as human influence on the planet grows. Yet there is no agreed definition, and how to apply the concept remains contested.

nature-eco-325.title: Chemoautotrophs: life powered by chemistry, not sunlight
nature-eco-325.text: On the deep ocean floor, where no sunlight reaches, whole ecosystems run on chemistry. Their producers are chemoautotrophs: organisms that make food using energy from chemical reactions of inorganic substances instead of light. They are often found at deep-ocean hydrothermal vents, and they include some archaea and bacteria. They draw energy from substances such as hydrogen, iron, nitrogen and sulfur. This process, {{ref:nature-eco-696}}, is how producers make food in vent ecosystems without sunlight.

nature-eco-202.title: Sinks for a warming gas: what clears it from the air
nature-eco-202.text: An average {{ref:nature-eco-727}} molecule lasts about 9.6 years in the air before it is removed. {{ref:nature-eco-727}} sinks are the processes that destroy or remove the gas from the air. The most effective is chemical breakdown as the gas rises through the atmosphere, which removes 90% of it. Soil bacteria of the {{ref:nature-eco-734}} type are another major sink, using the gas for energy and producing carbon dioxide and water. Forest soils are good sinks, but wetland soils with a high {{ref:nature-eco-742}} are often sources instead. One subtlety: a single emission affects the atmosphere for about twelve years.

nature-eco-761.title: Overgrazing
nature-eco-761.text: Plants exposed to intensive grazing for long periods, or without enough time to recover, suffer overgrazing. It reduces the usefulness, productivity and biodiversity of land and is one cause of desertification and erosion. A meta-analysis of 148 studies found most ecosystem functions decline as grazing intensity rises, and greater aridity weakens the benefits of light grazing. In Namibia overgrazing is considered the main cause of {{ref:nature-eco-743}} at the expense of grasses over up to 45 million hectares. Violent herder-farmer conflicts in Nigeria, Mali, Sudan and elsewhere in the Sahel have been worsened by land degradation and overgrazing. Hardin's tragedy of the commons used overgrazing as its example. But his model omitted real practice: English and Welsh commons were regulated and 'stinted', limiting animals per commoner.

nature-eco-632.title: Ecosystem collapse: when a living system loses itself
nature-eco-632.text: Consider the reefs described in {{ref:nature-eco-453}}. Even at 1.5 °C of warming, only 0.2% of the world's reefs could withstand spells of unusually hot sea water, against 84% now. Losses like that are what ecologists mean by ecosystem collapse. An ecosystem loses its defining features, and the ecosystem services it provided, once destabilizing pressures push it past a critical threshold. Collapse does not mean all life disappears. The original ecosystem is replaced by a novel one with greatly altered structure and function. Some have called it the ecosystem version of species extinction. It is usually irreversible, and any recovery is slow and needs active intervention. Human drivers include {{ref:nature-nbs-318}}, overexploitation, pollution, climate change and habitat destruction or fragmentation. Collapse can also occur when an ecosystem shrinks below a minimum viable size or loses key biological processes. The timeline may be short. Under a high-emissions scenario, tropical ocean ecosystems could face abrupt disruption before 2030, with forests in the tropics and polar regions following by 2050. Little is known yet about effective ways to conserve or reverse collapsing ecosystems.

nature-eco-521.title: From sub-humid to hyper-arid: grading drylands
nature-eco-521.text: Arid lands cover about 10% of the world's land and hold 20% of its people. Drylands are graded into four classes by aridity: dry sub-humid, semi-arid, arid and hyper-arid. Dry sub-humid lands produce a large share of the world's crops and livestock. By one rainfall-based measure, semi-arid lands get between 500 and 800mm a year. Arid lands have an {{ref:nature-eco-686}} of ~0.05-0.20 under the UNCCD, the UN treaty on desertification. Hyper-arid lands cover ~8% of the world and get barely more than 100 mm of rain; the UNCCD leaves them out of its dryland definition.

nature-eco-720.title: Hydrology from a distance: watching water from above
nature-eco-720.text: Measuring from a distance gives information on hydrologic processes where in situ sensors are sparse, and over large spatial extents. It can measure surface water storage, soil moisture, precipitation, evapotranspiration, and snow and ice. Sources include land-based, airborne and satellite sensors using microwave, thermal and near-infrared data or laser scanning that times reflected light pulses.

nature-found-074.title: Pecuniary externalities: side effects that work through prices
nature-found-074.text: City-dwellers who buy second homes in the countryside can push up house prices for local young people. That is a pecuniary externality: a side effect that works only by changing market prices, not by changing the real resources available to others. Technological or real externalities, such as factory pollution, harm others directly instead. In complete markets, buyers' losses from a price rise exactly match sellers' gains, so efficiency is kept. Some economists say these are not really externalities. When markets are incomplete or people face borrowing limits, they can matter, which helps justify macroprudential {{ref:nature-val-107}} of the financial system.

nature-econ-497.title: Gross or net, domestic or national: decoding the names
nature-econ-497.text: A French-owned cotton factory in Senegal counts in Senegal's domestic figures but in France's national figures. That example captures half of a naming scheme. 'Domestic' counts everything produced inside a country's borders, while 'national' counts everything produced by its nationals anywhere. The other half is gross versus net. 'Gross' means the total product, while 'net' subtracts the amount needed to offset depreciation of fixed capital. So {{ref:nature-acct-119}} is GDP minus depreciation of capital. Each measure can also be framed as product, income or expenditure.

nature-acct-108.title: Environmental profit and loss: Puma's price tag on nature
nature-acct-108.text: Puma produced the first environmental profit and loss account, on 2010 data. It valued greenhouse gases, water use, other air pollution, land conversion and waste. Such an account is a company's money valuation of its environmental impacts across its own operations and its {{ref:nature-acct-118}}, from raw materials to the factory gate. It internalises externalities, bringing outside costs onto the books, by counting the ecosystem services a business depends on as well as the damage it causes. Its main purpose is to show managers and stakeholders how large the impacts are and where in the chain they occur. The method built on models of how industries buy from one another ({{ref:nature-acct-080}}) and on valuation work in environmental economics, such as the TEEB study. Philips's 2017 annual report used it to put that year's environmental impact at Euro 7.2 billion. Preparing one can be expensive. It is seen as a first step toward prices that reflect the use of environmental goods and services.

nature-acct-044.title: Water footprint: the hidden water in what people consume
nature-acct-044.text: The average person's water footprint is 1,385 cubic metres a year. Arjen Hoekstra coined the concept in 2002 as a consumption-based indicator, modelled on the ecological footprint of the 1990s. A water footprint is the total volume of fresh water used to produce the goods and services that a person, community or business consumes or produces. Water use counts as the volume evaporated or polluted per unit of time. Unlike traditional withdrawal statistics, it shows where water is used and polluted, not only how much. A product's footprint is the sum over all processes in its supply chain, divided by the number of units. Since July 2014, ISO 14046:2014 has given guidance for assessments based on {{ref:nature-acct-050}} principles. Critics note that a footprint means little without regional scarcity. The 140 litres behind a cup of coffee may be harmless in humid areas but damaging in arid ones.

nature-acct-056.title: Sustainability measurement: quantifying a slippery goal
nature-acct-056.text: {{ref:nature-eecon-208}} has no fixed definition, so measuring it is hard, perhaps impossible. Sustainability measurement is the set of frameworks and indicators that try anyway, for a process, product, service or business. Frameworks look at environmental, social and economic domains, with tools such as indicators, benchmarks and audits. A benchmark is a reference point for a measurement; once set, it allows trends and progress to be measured. The toolbox includes {{ref:nature-acct-050}} for resource use, the ecological footprint for consumption, and {{ref:nature-acct-069}} for governance. A UN commission published a list of 140 indicators covering environmental, social, economic and institutional aspects. Because each country uses its own indicators, global comparisons can be misread; common indexes would allow comparison.

nature-eco-038.title: Too many people or too much consumption?
nature-eco-038.text: Is the deeper cause of biodiversity loss the number of people, or how much they consume? Many scientists, and the assessment described in {{ref:nature-eco-123}}, name growing human numbers and excessive consumption as the main underlying drivers. Critics point elsewhere. They say habitat loss comes mainly from growth in export commodities such as soybean and oil palm, much of it for livestock feed or {{ref:nature-pol-303}} in richer economies. Country data add a twist. A country's GDP correlates strongly with its environmental footprint, while its population size correlates negatively with footprint per person. Scholars still disagree on which driver matters most.

nature-eco-041.title: Habitat destruction, the leading cause of species loss
nature-eco-041.text: The tropics once held about 16 million square kilometers of rainforest. Less than 9 million remain. That shrinkage is habitat destruction. A natural home for wildlife, explained in {{ref:nature-eco-294}}, becomes unable to support the species that live there, so they move away or die. It is the leading cause worldwide of lost biodiversity and of species dying out. People cause it through resource use, {{ref:nature-res-257}}, industry, {{ref:nature-pol-311}}, mining, logging and fishing with trawl nets. A habitat need not be bulldozed to fail. Degradation, fragmentation and pollution can collapse it without outright destroying it. When habitat goes, the land can support fewer native animals, and each {{ref:nature-eco-374}} declines, sometimes until it disappears. Endemic species with small ranges suffer most because they live nowhere else. For people, the deepest cost is lost ecosystem services such as regulating climate, pollinating plants and managing water. Poor people suffer most. Wealthier people and countries can pay to keep receiving more than their share of natural resources.

nature-econ-851.title: Progressive tax: rates that rise with income
nature-econ-851.text: Under a progressive tax, the rate climbs as the taxable amount grows, so a taxpayer's average rate stays below the marginal rate. The marginal rate is the one on each extra unit of income. The effective marginal rate is higher still once lost welfare benefits and tax credits are counted. A progressive tax moves the burden toward people with more ability to pay. Its opposite is a {{ref:nature-pol-124}}, such as a sales tax, where the poor pay a larger share of income. It directly reduces {{ref:nature-econ-850}}, especially when it funds transfers and safety nets, though more evasion at higher rates may mute the effect. Brackets that are not indexed to inflation cause bracket creep, an effective tax increase. The effect on growth is disputed. A 2008 OECD report found a weak negative relationship, while the IMF says some advanced economies could raise progressivity without hampering growth. Hayek and Nozick opposed it on principle.

nature-pol-247.title: Auctioning permits: making polluters pay up front
nature-pol-247.text: Businesses tend to oppose auctioning emission permits. Economists almost uniformly recommend it. Under auctioning, firms buy their permits at auction and the government receives their value. That revenue can fund low-carbon investment and cuts in distortionary taxes, the kind that discourage useful work and investment. Auctioning can also be more efficient and fairer than free allocation. And it removes the {{ref:nature-pol-314}} created by {{ref:nature-pol-246}}.

nature-econ-379.title: Laissez-faire: leave prices alone
nature-econ-379.text: Laissez-faire is the principle that prices and wages should be free of non-market pressure, such as government taxes, subsidies, import duties, {{ref:nature-val-107}} or granted monopolies. Hayek argued that its point is to keep the unique information a price carries. Karl Popper called the idea of the free market paradoxical, since it needs interventions to prevent interventions.

nature-econ-399.title: Partial equilibrium: one market at a time
nature-econ-399.text: Alfred Marshall's supply and demand model is the classic partial equilibrium model. It analyzes equilibrium in a single market, holding everything constant except the one change being studied. The prices of substitutes and complements and buyers' incomes are treated as given, which makes it much simpler than general equilibrium. The cost is missed knock-on effects. A {{ref:nature-pol-321}} on French wine raises its price. Partial equilibrium ignores the knock-on rise in demand for domestic wine, which feeds back and pushes the price higher still. Such knock-on effects usually change the size of a price change but not its direction.

nature-econ-836.title: The risk premium: the extra return that pays for risk
nature-econ-836.text: An investor can buy risk-free government {{ref:nature-mkt-153}} paying 3%. To choose a risky share instead, she might demand 8%. The 5% gap is her risk premium: the extra return demanded for accepting more risk, generally the expected risky return minus the risk-free return. The more risk averse a person or firm, the larger the premium they will pay to avoid a risk, and it usually falls as people grow richer. Premiums swell during economic downturns and periods of heightened uncertainty. For a {{ref:nature-mkt-065}} the risk premium is called the credit spread, the extra yield over the risk-free rate. Schroeder estimated share-market risk premiums of 4.83 to 7.75 percent in the UK and EU, mostly between 6.3 and 7.2 percent. The idea reaches farms and ecosystems too. In some models, the value of keeping options open by spending on quarantine or management of an {{ref:nature-eco-026}} is a risk premium. When a wheat variety resistant to several diseases was released in 2000, it sharply cut the risk premium farmers bore against the crop disease Fusarium head blight.

nature-econ-784.title: Cost of capital: the bar every project must clear
nature-econ-784.text: Every new project a company considers has to clear a bar. That bar is the cost of capital: what a company pays for its funds, both borrowed and from shareholders, or the return investors require for providing them. It is the minimum return investors expect, so a project is worthwhile only if its expected return exceeds it. It also equals what the money could earn in the best alternative of similar risk, the opportunity cost of capital. Finding it means estimating both the cost of {{ref:nature-mkt-153}} and the {{ref:nature-econ-786}}, and both must look forward to expected future risk and return. Financial calculations usually set the {{ref:nature-econ-746}} equal to the cost of capital. One caution applies. For projects outside a firm's main business, its usual cost of capital may be the wrong yardstick, since the risks differ.

nature-econ-554.title: Stabilization policy: smoothing out booms and slumps
nature-econ-554.text: Economies boom and slump, and stabilization policy tries to soften the harm. It is short-run policy by governments and central banks, using fiscal and monetary tools. In a recession, policy turns expansive. When the economy overheats, it turns contractive. Economists usually prefer monetary policy for moderate swings, since independent central banks face less political pressure and shorter delays. Fiscal policy matters more after a major shock, under a fixed {{ref:nature-res-274}}, or in a liquidity trap, when cutting interest rates no longer revives spending. Longer-run structural policies are a different matter. They target things like the structural unemployment rate, or how much people save, invest and study.

nature-econ-563.title: Open market operations: creating money by buying bonds
nature-econ-563.text: A central bank can create money by going shopping. When it buys a security such as a government bond, it in effect creates money, expanding the monetary base. Selling securities shrinks the base again. The monetary base is currency in circulation plus the reserves banks hold at the central bank. This buying and selling, called open market operations, lets the bank influence interest rates, the {{ref:nature-res-274}} or the money supply.

nature-eco-714.title: Reading an FSC label: forest audit and chain of custody
nature-eco-714.text: FSC offers two kinds of certification, and only one lets a product carry its label. Certification of how a forest is run is voluntary: an accredited body inspects the forest at the owner's request, and holders pay an annual fee and must stay compliant. Chain of custody tracks certified material from forest to consumer, and only chain of custody holders may use FSC labels. The FSC Mix label, from 2004, lets manufacturers mix certified with uncertified material under controlled conditions. Unacceptable sources are excluded: illegal wood, wood harvested in violation of rights, and wood from HCV forests. FSC wood can earn up to 2 points in the LEED v4.1 credit Sourcing of Raw Materials.

nature-econ-086.title: Factors of production: land, labor and capital
nature-econ-086.text: Every good and service is made from inputs. Economists call them factors of production, and the classic trio is land, labor and capital. How much of each is used determines output, through a relationship explored in {{ref:nature-econ-312}}. One common list adds a fourth basic factor, the entrepreneur. Land, labor and capital are primary factors: they help production without becoming part of the product or being much changed by it. Materials and {{ref:nature-eecon-238}} are secondary, because they come from the primary ones. The list has a history. The 18th-century French physiocrats held that a nation's wealth came only from land and {{ref:nature-res-257}}. Adam Smith and David Ricardo saw the parts of a price as payments for land (rent), labor (wages) and capital. The list still draws fire. Some economists, such as {{ref:nature-hist-071}} and Benjamin Warr, fault orthodox economics for overlooking resources from nature and the decline of resource capital.

nature-eco-268.title: Mud in the water: sediment as a pollutant
nature-eco-268.text: Soil eroded mainly from farmland is considered the leading global cause of diffuse {{ref:nature-res-261}}, the kind that comes from many scattered sources rather than one pipe. The problem is the excess {{ref:nature-eco-682}} it sends into waterways. {{ref:nature-eco-682}} is a pollutant in itself, and it also carries others, such as farm chemicals against pests and heavy metals. Silt can smother fish spawning beds by filling the gaps between gravel on stream beds. Runoff from roads and urban areas adds settled material contaminated with fuel, oil and other chemicals.

nature-eco-266.title: Wind erosion: soil carried off on the air
nature-eco-266.text: Dust blown off distant land has been linked to declining coral reef health in the Caribbean and Florida. Wind erosion is the removal of soil by wind, a major force in arid and semi-arid regions. Wind works in two ways. It lifts and carries loose particles, called deflation, and it wears surfaces down with airborne particles, called abrasion. Wind erosion is a major source of degraded land, spreading {{ref:nature-eco-703}}, harmful dust and crop damage, especially where deforestation, {{ref:nature-res-273}} and farming make it worse. Its dust is a major air pollutant.

nature-econ-402.title: Price controls: when governments set prices
nature-econ-402.text: Diocletian tried to cap the price of every {{ref:nature-res-264}} in the late 3rd century AD, with little success. Price controls are government-enforced limits on the prices that may be charged for goods and services, and they are ancient: the Code of Hammurabi set wages for shipbuilders. There are two main kinds. A ceiling ({{ref:nature-econ-400}}) sets the most that may be charged. A floor ({{ref:nature-econ-405}}) sets the least. Controls on rents and wages are well-known examples. Governments use them to keep goods affordable during shortages, to slow inflation, or to guarantee a minimum income to some providers. Controls are also one of the indirect ways governments subsidize {{ref:nature-eecon-238}}. A cap set low tends to backfire. Keeping prices artificially low raises demand beyond what supply can meet, and shortages feed illegal trading at higher prices. During the 1973–74 Arab oil embargo, a US price cap below the market level led to long queues and gas stations running dry. Most Western economists say consumer price controls do not work, though since the 1990s wage floors have won strong support among some economists.

nature-found-047.title: Failure of competition: when one firm holds the cards
nature-found-047.text: In a failure of market rivalry ({{ref:nature-econ-363}}), a firm or small group gains enough power over a market to block exchanges that would benefit both sides. This kind of market failure takes several forms: a market with a single seller, one with a single buyer, and markets where sellers compete with slightly different products. Such power can last where {{ref:nature-econ-863}} keep other firms out. An extreme case is a natural sole-seller market, a form of what {{ref:nature-econ-349}} describes, sometimes caused by extreme economies of scale, the cost advantages that come with sheer size.

nature-eco-713.title: The Forest Stewardship Council: certifying wood
nature-eco-713.text: Look for the FSC mark on paper or timber and you are seeing a market-based answer to {{ref:nature-eco-053}}. The Forest Stewardship Council is an international non-profit, multistakeholder organization founded in 1993 that promotes responsible care of forests through timber certification. It runs a global certification system for forests and the goods taken from them. Members join one of three chambers: environmental, social and economic. Governments cannot be members and engage only as land owners. FSC does not audit itself. It accredits certification bodies, which then certify forests and companies to its standards. In September 2012 some 165 million hectares in 80 countries were certified, and about 24,000 chain of custody certificates were active in 107 countries. The main competing system is PEFC, criticized for little local or environmental organization influence and lack of transparency.

nature-econ-106.title: Comparative advantage: why the best at everything still gains from exchange
nature-econ-106.text: Even a country that is better at producing everything gains by trading. That is the principle of comparative advantage, and it holds for people and firms as well as countries. Gains are greatest when each party specializes in what it produces at the lowest opportunity cost and swaps for the rest. This differs from absolute advantage, which is about being more productive overall. David Ricardo developed the classical theory in 1817, using the example of Portugal and England producing wine and cloth. He wrote amid the debate over Britain's 1815 Corn Laws, which taxed imported grain to protect landowners. In 1930 Gottfried Haberler restated the idea in terms of opportunity cost, measuring a good's value in forgone units of another good. The principle describes what specialization and {{ref:nature-res-268}} would bring, not a strict prediction of behavior. Critics such as James K. Galbraith argue that countries locked into {{ref:nature-res-257}} stay poor, because farming depends on land, a finite resource. Others dispute that comparative advantage justifies {{ref:nature-res-269}}, pointing to strategic policy toward foreign commerce and global value chains.

nature-pol-003.title: Non-tariff barriers: trade limits beyond taxes
nature-pol-003.text: A 2019 UNCTAD report found that trade costs from non-tariff measures were more than double those of traditional tariffs. Non-tariff barriers are restrictions on imports or exports other than tariffs, such as quotas, licenses, subsidies, customs delays and technical standards. As tariffs fell through GATT and WTO negotiation rounds, {{ref:nature-res-270}} turned to new measures such as technical barriers to trade. They are grouped as protectionist, assistance (such as domestic subsidies) or non-protectionist, the last aimed at health, safety and the environment. Most can be called protectionist unless they address market problems such as externalities or information asymmetries, as safety standards and labels do. Rising consumer demand for safe and environmentally friendly products has made technical barriers more popular. Whether a particular measure protects health and environment or disguises such protection is often disputed.

nature-found-007.title: Regulating services: bees, wetlands and coastal forests at work
nature-found-007.text: Bee pollination is needed for 15–30% of U.S. food production. That is a regulating service: a benefit people get from nature keeping ecosystem processes in check, such as climate, water and pests. Wetlands hold large amounts of water and release it slowly, making flooding less likely. Coastal mangrove forests protect shorelines from erosion. Other examples are locking carbon away from the air, breaking down and detoxifying {{ref:nature-eecon-231}} and controlling pests and diseases.

nature-eco-198.title: How cities, farms and clearing reshape the water cycle
nature-eco-198.text: Pave a meadow, and the rain that once soaked into it runs off instead. Changes in how land is used and what covers it, such as cities, farm expansion and deforestation, alter the water cycle locally and regionally. They affect rainfall, evaporation, flooding, groundwater and how much fresh water is available. Compacted soils and paved surfaces reduce how much water soaks in and increase surface runoff. Clearing forests reduces local soil moisture, evaporation, rain and snow, and across a region it can shift temperatures and rainfall patterns. A {{ref:nature-nbs-319}} can change natural river flows, lower water quality and destroy habitat for aquatic species. The effect can run the other way too. Trees help regulate the water cycle, reduce soil erosion and prevent runoff, so planting new forests can improve water management.

nature-eco-252.title: The ocean's carbon cycle: a source turned sink
nature-eco-252.text: Before the Industrial Revolution, the ocean released carbon dioxide to the air. Today it does the opposite, taking up a net 2.9 billion tonnes of carbon a year on average. The oceanic carbon cycle is the set of processes that move carbon among pools within the ocean, and between the ocean, the atmosphere, Earth's interior and the seafloor. It is central to the global carbon cycle and holds both inorganic carbon and organic carbon, the kind built by living things. Three main pumps carry carbon dioxide from the air into the ocean interior and spread it through the oceans. Altogether, the oceans take up around 25–31% of the carbon dioxide people emit. Temperature matters. Cold water dissolves more carbon dioxide, so warming seas take up less. Carbon also arrives by river: rivers deliver roughly equal amounts, about 0.4 gigatons of carbon a year each, of dissolved inorganic and organic carbon. Since 1970, {{ref:nature-nbs-319}} building has cut that delivery by an estimated 13%. The final exit is burial in {{ref:nature-eco-682}}, the ocean's long-term carbon sink and its largest loss of carbon. About 90% of organic carbon burial happens on deltas, continental shelves and upper slopes.

nature-eco-443.title: How wetlands soak up floods
nature-eco-443.text: Walling a river in can make its {{ref:nature-nbs-329}} worse. Floodplains and other wetlands act as natural storage reservoirs that soak up excess water and so reduce flooding downstream. They work in several ways. River floodplains let floodwater spread over a wide area, which lowers its depth and speed. Headwater wetlands, high in a river's catchment, slow rain runoff and snowmelt so they do not rush straight into rivers, which helps prevent sudden floods. During heavy rain, wetlands hold the extra water, reducing the area, depth and duration of flooding. Remove that storage and the system changes. Draining floodplains or hemming rivers in with embankments forces the same rain through a narrower channel. Flood peaks then get higher and arrive faster. A wetland controls floods by giving water room; take the room away and the peaks rise.

nature-nbs-325.title: Detention basins: storing a storm and releasing it slowly
nature-nbs-325.text: A detention basin is an excavated area on or near a waterway that protects against flooding, and sometimes downstream erosion, by temporarily storing water. It lets large flows in and limits outflow through a small low opening sized to downstream culvert capacity, and it can control events such as a 1-in-100-year storm. Basins are usually built with new developments to handle runoff from impervious surfaces like roads, parking lots and rooftops. A basin with no permanent pool is a dry pond. One designed to hold some water permanently is a {{ref:nature-nbs-172}}, which manages quantity but has limited effect on water quality. Real-time control of outflow makes basins significantly better at retaining suspended solids and associated contaminants. Extended detention dry basins lengthen storage time beyond the 6 to 12 hours of basic ponds, allowing more settling of solids and cleaner water. Parks in cities can serve as dual-purpose basins, acting as sports fields or parkland normally and storing stormwater in big storms; Joynton Park in Sydney is an example.

nature-econ-436.title: Difference equations: change in separate steps
nature-econ-436.text: Not everything changes smoothly. A difference equation relates a quantity's value at one point to its values at nearby points, when time or another variable takes only separate values. Also called recurrence relations, difference equations are the discrete-time counterpart of {{ref:nature-econ-433}} ({{ref:nature-econ-437}}). The two can stand in for each other. Numerical methods such as the Euler method approximate a differential equation by a matching difference equation. An economist can model a price adjusting to excess demand, buyers wanting more than sellers offer, either way. The study of living things has a matched pair too: the Beverton–Holt population model is a discrete-time analogue of Verhulst's continuous-time equation for {{ref:nature-eco-580}}.

nature-eco-580.title: Logistic growth: fast at first, then leveling off
nature-eco-580.text: Malthus described population growing without limit. The Belgian mathematician Pierre François Verhulst read Malthus's Essay on the Principle of Population and adjusted the picture. Logistic growth starts out exponential ({{ref:nature-econ-442}}) but slows as it approaches an upper limit set by external or environmental factors. A population, for instance, may level off because resources run short. Verhulst devised the model between 1838 and 1847 and first proposed it in 1845. It arises when self-limiting effects, the brakes ignored in the exponential model, become significant. In the study of living populations it is a differential equation, dP/dt = rP(1 − P/K), where P is the population, r the growth rate and K the {{ref:nature-eco-593}}. As the population grows, competition for critical resources slows growth until the population stops growing at K. The discrete-time Beverton–Holt population model is its step-by-step analogue.

nature-econ-611.title: Stock and flow: living off a resource's interest
nature-econ-611.text: A field of grass can be grazed a certain amount each year without harm. Overgraze it, and it becomes prone to erosion and less useful. The difference lies between a resource's stock and its flow. A shared resource has a central stock that must be protected and a flow of units, such as fish or grass, that can be harvested. As long as the stock is not harmed, it keeps regrowing the flow, so careful use can continue indefinitely. Taking more than the flow shrinks the stock, which in turn shrinks future flows. Sometimes the loss cannot be undone.

nature-eco-267.title: Erosion by the plow: when the plow moves the soil
nature-eco-267.text: On many hilly fields, the plow moves more soil than rain or wind does. Erosion by the plow is the movement of soil down a field caused by plowing and other working of the soil. In many fields, especially on hilly land, it is a bigger cause of soil loss than erosion by water or wind. Its signature is the eroded hilltop. Water erosion removes soil mainly from middle and lower slopes, so worn-down hilltops point to the plow instead. The damage is costly, because degraded soil can sharply cut crop yields and cause economic losses for farms.

nature-eco-313.title: HIPPO: five threats to biodiversity in one word
nature-eco-313.text: Conservationists sum up the main threats to biodiversity with five letters: HIPPO. They stand for habitat loss, {{ref:nature-nbs-318}} that invade, pollution, human population and overharvesting, with the I covered in {{ref:nature-eco-026}}. Two of them lead the list. The primary threats are the destruction of habitats, through forest clearing and urban growth, and overharvesting, as in the trade in wild animals and plants.

nature-eco-326.title: Weighing all the life on Earth
nature-eco-326.text: By 2020, the mass of everything humans have made was projected to surpass the mass of all life on Earth. That living total is {{ref:nature-clim-284}}: the mass of organisms in a given area or ecosystem at a particular time. It can be weighed wet, dry, or as organic carbon, depending on the purpose. In 2018 Earth's live matter was estimated at about 550 billion tonnes of carbon, mostly in plants. Plants hold 450 billion tonnes of it, and bacteria plus the similar single-celled archaea hold 30. Animals make up less than 0.5% of the total. The sea breaks the pattern. Ocean producers make almost half of each year's new growth, yet they hold only about 0.2% of that total. On land, it falls sharply at each step up the ladder of who eats whom, but in the oceans it can rise. Wild land mammals are believed to weigh seven times less than in prehistoric times, and livestock now outweigh all wild mammals together.

nature-eco-372.title: Phytoplankton: the invisible half of the world's plant work
nature-eco-372.text: At least half of Earth's oxygen comes from organisms too small to see. Phytoplankton are tiny drifting organisms in oceans and lakes that make their own food by capturing sunlight. Because they need light, they live in the sunlit surface layer of the water. They carry out about half of global {{ref:nature-eco-190}}, though they make up only about 1% of global plant {{ref:nature-clim-284}}. Marine phytoplankton fix about 50 Pg, or petagrams, of carbon a year. They are the base of the feeding networks of sea and lake. They also drive the {{ref:nature-eco-204}}, which moves carbon to the deep ocean. They include cyanobacteria and single-celled protists such as diatoms, and about 5,000 marine species are known. They turn over in days rather than decades, so they respond quickly to a changing climate. Warming splits the water into layers that mix less, cutting their nutrient supply and their output. Some studies indicate that their global density has fallen over the past century.

nature-res-258.title: Bioenergy: fuel from living matter
nature-res-258.text: In low-income countries, wood, charcoal, residues or dung burned in open fires or inefficient stoves still cook many meals. This traditional {{ref:nature-clim-284}} is one face of bioenergy: {{ref:nature-eecon-239}} obtained by using living mass as fuel, whether wood, energy crops, harvest residues or organic waste. The IPCC defines it as energy from any form of living mass, meaning organic material excluding fossilised matter, so coal is not living mass here. Wood and wood residues are the largest living mass energy source today. The main waste feedstocks are wood, agricultural, municipal solid and manufacturing waste. Living mass is upgraded by thermal, chemical or biochemical routes; thermal options are torrefaction, {{ref:nature-clim-285}} and gasification. In the EU in 2023 bioenergy was about three-quarters of renewable heating and cooling and nearly one-fifth of all heating and cooling. Its climate benefit is not guaranteed. Over its life cycle bioenergy can emit less or more greenhouse gas than the energy it replaces, depending on how feedstock is grown, harvested and transported. Energy crops can displace natural ecosystems, degrade soils and use water and synthetic fertilisers, and about one-third of wood for traditional tropical heating and cooking is harvested unsustainably.

nature-clim-274.title: Ozone depletion: the thinning of the shield above us
nature-clim-274.text: In 1974 Frank Sherwood Rowland and Mario Molina suggested that long-lived organic halogen compounds such as CFCs could deplete ozone. Ozone depletion is now defined as a lowered total amount of ozone in the upper stratosphere, plus a much larger springtime decrease over the polar regions, observed since the late 1970s. The main causes are manufactured halocarbons used as refrigerants, solvents, propellants and foam-blowing agents, called {{ref:nature-clim-276}}. The ozone layer absorbs UVB light, so depletion raises surface UVB, which could increase skin cancer. That was the reason for the Montreal Protocol. The treaties came early. The Vienna and Montreal conventions were put in place before a scientific consensus existed or key uncertainties were resolved. They seem to have worked: since the Protocol was adopted and strengthened, concentrations of the most significant CFCs have declined. Effective equivalent chlorine peaked in 1994 and had dropped about 10 percent by 2008.

nature-found-079.title: Pollution: nine million deaths and an unpaid bill
nature-found-079.text: In 2019 pollution killed about nine million people, about one in six of all deaths. Roughly three-quarters of them died from air pollution. Pollution is the release into the natural environment of contaminants that cause harm. It can be any substance, solid, liquid or gas, or {{ref:nature-eecon-238}} such as heat, sound, light or radioactivity. The word usually means contaminants from human sources such as manufacturing, mining, poor handling of waste, transport or farming. Pollution can come from a point source, one concentrated site such as a factory, or a nonpoint source, spread out like farm runoff. Economists treat pollution from manufacturing as a negative production externality, imposing health and clean-up costs on all of society. Goods that pollute tend to be overproduced and underpriced, because the harm is not priced into the market. Polluting industries and waste sites are often placed near vulnerable and marginalized communities, a core reason for the movement for environmental fairness explored in {{ref:nature-gov-168}}. Many sources went unregulated during industrialization, until environmental {{ref:nature-val-107}} emerged in the later 20th century.

nature-pol-175.title: Renewable portfolio standards: a quota for clean power
nature-pol-175.text: In 29 of 50 US states, power suppliers must by law get part of their electricity from clean sources. A renewable portfolio standard (RPS) requires electricity suppliers to get a set share of their power from renewable sources. These include wind, solar, {{ref:nature-clim-284}} and geothermal. Certified renewable generators earn a certificate for each unit of electricity. They sell these to suppliers, who hand them to the regulator to prove compliance. Supporters say relying on the market brings competition and innovation that deliver {{ref:nature-eecon-239}} at the lowest cost. RPS-type schemes also exist in the UK, Italy, Poland, Sweden, Belgium and Chile. A US national laboratory credits state standards with 60% of the rise in US renewable electricity since 2000, though their share of new builds is falling. Like subsidies, these standards create protected markets for such power, an alternative to {{ref:nature-pol-224}}.

nature-found-014.title: Should nature carry a price tag
nature-found-014.text: Measuring the parts of natural capital is fairly straightforward. Putting a {{ref:nature-eecon-241}} value on them is not, and the argument over doing so is still open. Columnist George Monbiot derided valuation as comparing things that cannot be compared, and called the resulting figures "marmalade". Critics add that cultural values cannot carry a dollar amount, so valuation leaves parts of nature out. Defenders reply that valuation puts the environment on a fairer footing against commercial pressures. Valuing nature, they say, is not the same as turning it into cash.

nature-eco-368.title: Models of mutualism: partnerships in equations
nature-eco-368.text: Ecologists can describe partnerships with equations. Models of mutualism are equation-based descriptions of how the populations of two mutualist species grow, given the benefit each gets from the other. A simple form adapts the {{ref:nature-eco-583}}, adding a positive term for the benefit from the partner species. That version has a flaw. Without a limit, modeled numbers could grow forever, which {{ref:nature-eco-593}} makes impossible. In 1989 David Hamilton Wright added saturation. Benefits level off at high densities because of handling time, the time spent making use of each benefit.

nature-found-029.title: Managing the planet's land, water and air for the long run
nature-found-029.text: Feeding humanity takes about 38% of Earth's land surface and about 20% of its net primary productivity, the new plant growth its ecosystems produce. Since the Neolithic Revolution, human consumption has cut the world's forest cover by about 47%. {{ref:nature-eecon-208}} and environmental management means running the oceans, fresh water, land and atmosphere at global scale by its principles. How land is split between cities, farms, forest and {{ref:nature-nbs-350}} strongly affects the global cycles of water, carbon and nitrogen. Biodiversity loss stems largely from habitat loss, as natural capital is converted into man-made capital.

nature-val-086.title: The NOAA panel: can surveys be trusted?
nature-val-086.text: Could surveys of willingness to pay be trusted? The US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration convened a panel of leading economists, chaired by Kenneth Arrow and {{ref:nature-eecon-256}}, to judge. It heard 22 expert economists and published its results in 1993. Its verdict was a cautious yes. Well-designed surveys were reliable enough to start a legal damage assessment, including passive-use values. Good design meant personal interviews, a yes-or-no referendum on a specific tax, and detailed information about the resource and its threats. Preferring cautious estimates, the panel advised asking willingness to pay to protect a good, not willingness to accept its loss.

nature-eecon-185.title: Overconsumption: using up faster than nature refills
nature-eecon-185.text: By 1983 China's consumption had already surpassed the biocapacity of its natural resources. Growing economies can drive overconsumption: using goods, services or natural resources faster than they can be replenished or reused. Applied to natural resources harmed by use, it means the same as {{ref:nature-eco-063}}. The drivers are partly built into how business works. Forces such as {{ref:nature-eecon-249}}, {{ref:nature-eecon-188}}, economic materialism and other unsustainable business models push consumption up. It stands in contrast to {{ref:nature-eecon-196}}. Over the long term, overconsumption in a region shrinks natural resources and degrades the environment. Consuming beyond the environment's long-term {{ref:nature-eco-593}} causes {{ref:nature-eecon-173}}, resource depletion and poorer ecosystem health. In 2010 the International Resource Panel found that household consumption for mobility, shelter, food and energy-using products causes most of the life-cycle impacts of consumption. Movements push back: campaigns against over-buying, {{ref:nature-eecon-143}}, frugality, downshifting, {{ref:nature-eecon-254}} and minimalism. Many of them aim at a {{ref:nature-eecon-072}}. Even so, the term itself is controversial and lacks a single agreed definition.

nature-found-004.title: Ecosystem services: the work nature does for people
nature-found-004.text: New York City had two ways to keep its water clean. It could build a filtration plant, estimated at $6–8 billion plus $300 million a year to run. Or it could restore its Catskill watershed, the land whose streams feed the city's supply, for an estimated $1–1.5 billion. The city chose the land, and the land did the plant's job for a fraction of the cost. That job is an ecosystem service: one of the many benefits people get from ecosystems. Others include pollination of crops, clean air, the breakdown of {{ref:nature-eecon-231}} and {{ref:nature-nbs-329}} control. These services are vital for human well-being, giving direct and indirect benefits such as clean water, food and a steady climate. The term "environmental services" appeared in a 1970 report, and "ecosystem services" later became the standard term in science. In the early 2000s a United Nations initiative, covered in {{ref:nature-es-001}}, popularised sorting them into four groups: provisioning, regulating, supporting and cultural. Economists value these services in dollars using methods such as avoided cost, the cost of replacing a service, travel cost and surveys of what people would pay. A 1997 study put the value of the world's ecosystem services and the natural stocks behind them at US$16–54 trillion per year, averaging US$33 trillion. Some schemes now reward farmers or landowners for managing their land so that it keeps providing a service, an approach explored in {{ref:nature-mkt-136}}.

nature-found-055.title: Air pollution: 7 to 8 million deaths a year
nature-found-055.text: Air pollution kills 7 to 8 million people each year. It is the presence in the air of substances that harm people, other living things or the environment. The culprits may be gases, such as ozone or nitrogen oxides, or small particles, such as soot and dust, both outdoors and indoors. Tiny particles are its deadliest form. Outdoor pollution comes from burning coal, oil and gas for power and transport, uncontrolled fires in wild land, industry, waste, demolition and farming. Indoor pollution often comes from burning wood or crop waste for cooking and heating. The World Bank estimates its welfare and productivity losses cost the world economy over $8 trillion per year. Air pollution is a standard example of an externality: neither makers nor users of cars pay its cost to society. Many sources, especially coal, oil and gas, also release the heat-trapping gases that cause global warming. National laws have often worked, such as Britain's clean air law of 1956 and the 1963 US clean air law.

nature-econ-112.title: What is economics? From wealth to scarce means
nature-econ-112.text: Economics began life as {{ref:nature-gov-242}}, stretching the Greek idea of household management to the running of a state. Its definition has kept moving ever since. In 1803 Jean-Baptiste Say called it the science of producing, distributing and consuming wealth. In 1890 Alfred Marshall called it the study of mankind in the ordinary business of life, tied to the material requisites of well-being. In 1932 Lionel Robbins defined it as the study of human behavior as a relationship between ends and scarce means with alternative uses. His version is perhaps the most commonly accepted today.

nature-gov-188.title: Climate refugees and the gap in the law
nature-gov-188.text: Asian and African mega-deltas and small islands face high risks of floods and storms, and possibly displacement on a large scale. People forced to move by climate change fall into a legal gap, because international law does not yet cover such migration. The International Organization for Migration defines an {{ref:nature-gov-240}} as a person obliged or choosing to leave home because environmental change harms their lives. Such migration is one of the most disputed effects of climate change. How many people will move, and who counts as a climate refugee, remain undefined in law.

nature-found-032.title: Negative externalities: the harm nobody pays for
nature-found-032.text: A neighbour's loud late-night music costs someone else a night's sleep. That lost sleep is a negative externality: a harmful side effect of producing or consuming something that lands on an unrelated third party. Its cost is not counted in the market price. It is also called an external cost or external diseconomy. Formally, it is the gap between what an action costs the person taking it and what it costs society. The music is a consumption example, but production causes them too. Air pollution from burning coal, oil and gas damages crops, materials, historic buildings and public health. Negative externalities are treated as more of a problem than positive ones. The reason is that they are inefficient in a strict sense: someone could be made better off without anyone being made worse off. That test of efficiency is explained in {{ref:nature-econ-168}}.

nature-clim-277.title: The Global Environment Facility: a fund for global goods
nature-clim-277.text: The Global Environment Facility is the largest multilateral funder of biodiversity, distributing over $1 billion a year on average. It gives grants and blended finance to developing countries for biodiversity, climate change, international waters, land degradation, pollutants and forests. In all it has provided more than $22 billion in grants and mobilized $120 billion in co-financing for over 5,200 projects. It began in October 1991 as a $1 billion World Bank pilot and became a permanent separate institution at the 1992 Rio {{ref:nature-hist-003}}. The World Bank has been trustee since 1994. It is the financial mechanism for the CBD, UNFCCC, UNCCD, Stockholm Convention and Minamata Convention, and it supports the Montreal Protocol. Donors pledged a record $5.33 billion in June 2022 for the replenishment cycle running to June 2026. Its Small Grants Programme supported nearly 27,000 civil society and community initiatives in 136 countries.

nature-eco-716.title: Governing through the market instead of the state
nature-eco-716.text: No one can be fined or imprisoned for ignoring FSC. Non-state market driven governance is {{ref:nature-gov-117}} outside state {{ref:nature-val-107}} that uses the market to drive sustainable management, and FSC is a leading example. The FSC network lacks the political authority of a state. Its power rests on buyers and sellers choosing to take part.

nature-eco-458.title: What is killing coral reefs
nature-eco-458.text: Coral reefs worldwide declined 14% from 2009 to 2018. They are threatened by nutrient pollution, warming and acidifying oceans, {{ref:nature-res-027}} and destructive uses of land and sea. Some threats are local: coral mining, dragging nets along the seabed, blast fishing, too much fishing and {{ref:nature-gov-237}}, which persist where {{ref:nature-val-107}} is weak. Too much fishing and excess nutrients from land let algae outcompete and kill coral. The global threats are larger. Greenhouse gas emissions warm the sea and raise sea level, causing widespread loss of coral cover as stressed corals turn white. Ocean acidification slows the corals' building of their limestone skeletons and speeds its dissolving, though corals can partly adjust. The outlook is stark: 70–90% of today's warm-water coral reefs will disappear even if warming is kept to 1.5 °C.

nature-econ-039.title: The prisoner's dilemma: when betrayal is rational
nature-econ-039.text: In 1950 Merrill {{ref:nature-nbs-329}} and Melvin Dresher, working at the RAND Corporation, designed a puzzle that still troubles economists. Two players can each cooperate for mutual benefit or betray the other for individual gain. Betrayal is the rational choice for each, yet both would get a higher payoff if both cooperated. This is the prisoner's dilemma, the basic game behind research on social dilemmas, where individual interest pulls against the group's. {{ref:nature-hist-007}} fits the pattern closely. Every country gains from a stable climate, but each hesitates to cut its own CO2 emissions. Real climate politics is worse than the textbook game, because its payoffs are uncertain, which suggests states will cooperate even less. Hardin's tragedy of the commons can be read as a many-player version, in which widespread betrayal destroys a shared resource. The game has been called the E. coli of social psychology, a standard test case for studying oligopoly and {{ref:nature-gov-235}}.

nature-econ-030.title: When acting alone defeats everyone
nature-econ-030.text: In 1738 David Hume described a puzzle through neighbours agreeing to drain a meadow. Economists now call it a {{ref:nature-gov-235}} problem, or social dilemma. Everyone would be better off cooperating, but people fail to, because their individual interests pull against joint action. Trouble comes when too many members chase immediate, personal gain instead of the group's long-term interest. The pattern explains things as different as the running down of resources and low voter turnout. It also describes the environmental crises at the center of this course: {{ref:nature-hist-007}}, {{ref:nature-eco-035}} and the build-up of waste. Without {{ref:nature-val-107}}, people and firms tend to pick the easier, cheaper option rather than the one that cuts emissions or saves resources that cannot be replaced. In a 1965 book, Mancur Olson argued that rational individuals do not automatically add up to a rational group, a claim explored in {{ref:nature-pol-044}}. For a pure {{ref:nature-econ-633}}, he argued, each contributor tends to give less as others give more. The problem is analysed with {{ref:nature-econ-034}} and through the {{ref:nature-econ-617}}, which arises whenever public goods must be paid for.

nature-econ-349.title: Monopoly: the market with one seller
nature-econ-349.text: The word first appears in Aristotle's Politics, describing Thales of Miletus cornering the market in olive presses. A monopoly is a market in which a single person or company is the only supplier of a particular good or service. With no competition and no close substitutes, it can charge a price well above its marginal cost and earn high profits. Size is not what defines it: a small business can still raise prices in a small market. Its power comes from {{ref:nature-econ-863}}, which may be economic, legal or deliberate. A monopolist does not simply charge the highest price. It picks the output where the revenue from one more sale equals the cost of making it, aiming at the largest total profit. Compared with a market of many small competitors it sells less at a higher price. The trades it forgoes are a pure loss to society ({{ref:nature-econ-345}}). Contestable-market theory adds that a monopoly may act as if it faced competition when entry barriers are low. Governments respond by taking monopoly profits, breaking up the firm or changing rules to curb anti-competitive behavior.

nature-econ-409.title: Profit: what is left after every cost
nature-econ-409.text: Economists usually assume firms try to maximize profit, so they define it carefully. Profit is what a business has left from its revenue after paying the total costs of its inputs, counting both explicit and implicit costs. Accounting profit subtracts only the explicit costs on a firm's books. Economic profit also subtracts implicit costs, so it is smaller. The break-even case ({{ref:nature-econ-354}}) is when revenue just equals total costs, so economic profit is zero: the least a firm needs to stay in a competitive industry. Competition erodes anything more. In a perfectly competitive market, economic profit draws in new firms until prices fall and the profit disappears in the long run. Profit lasts only in markets with one or a few dominant sellers. Obstacles to newcomers protect it: patents, rights to land and rules on how land is used. Competition laws aim to stop powerful firms from building artificial barriers to protect their profits. Profit is greatest where the revenue from one more unit equals its marginal cost. A wider measure, social profit, adds or subtracts the externalities, such as pollution, and the gains to buyers that a firm's activity creates.

nature-econ-397.title: Market power: the ability to set your own price
nature-econ-397.text: Some sellers can name their price. Market power is a firm's ability to raise its price above its marginal cost, by controlling supply or demand, without losing all its customers. Firms with none, as in perfect competition, are price takers; firms with it are price makers. How much power firms have depends on market structure. Perfect competition and a lone seller are the extremes. In between sit {{ref:nature-econ-311}} and markets run by a few firms. Power lasts only behind {{ref:nature-econ-863}}, such as control of scarce resources, advantages of size, better technology or government rules; OPEC's rests on oil. The less elastic the demand a firm faces, the more it can raise price above marginal cost. Economists measure it by markups or, more often, by the market shares of the biggest firms ({{ref:nature-econ-398}} and {{ref:nature-econ-384}}). Competition law, such as the US Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890, uses these measures to judge whether a firm has abused its power.
