Jean Tirole won the 2014 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for analyzing market power and {{ref:nature-val-107}}.

nature-econ-509.title: Consumption: spending to meet today's needs
nature-econ-509.text: In most countries, consumption is the largest part of GDP, usually between 45% and 85% of it. Consumption is the use of resources to meet present needs and wants, as opposed to investing for future income. Mainstream economists count only final purchases of newly produced goods and services by individuals for immediate use. In macroeconomics, consumption equals income minus savings. Economists consider income the most important factor affecting it. In microeconomics, the view is individual: consumers are assumed to choose the goods that maximize their utility within their budget. Add up everyone's consumption and you get one component of {{ref:nature-econ-868}}, the total spending in an economy.

nature-eco-288.title: Top-down and bottom-up control of ecosystems
nature-eco-288.text: Is an ecosystem built from below or ruled from above? Both. Trophic dynamics is the transfer of energy and nutrients between organisms. Energy captured by plants passes to herbivores, then carnivores, then top carnivores, and the total shrinks at each higher level. Bottom-up control comes from how much energy plants bring in, top-down control from predators. Correlations in abundance or {{ref:nature-clim-284}} between consumers and resources are the evidence for bottom-up control, as when herbivore and {{ref:nature-eco-673}} living mass rises with primary productivity. Top carnivores keep herbivores in check; without them herbivores could multiply and eat all the plants. If plant populations fall sharply, herbivores decline and then carnivores decline too. An ecosystem need not be one or the other: a marine system may be bottom-up, then come under top-down control during fishing. Predators can dramatically shift which species dominate on land and at sea, and the balance of the two controls is a major research question. Herbivory can also speed the breakdown of litter and nutrient cycling.

nature-econ-458.title: Slack variables: counting what goes unused
nature-econ-458.text: Return to the farmer choosing between wheat and barley ({{ref:nature-econ-456}}). Not every hectare of land or sack of {{ref:nature-eco-662}} has to be used. A slack variable is a non-negative extra variable added to a linear program to turn an inequality constraint into an equality. In the farm example, the slack variables stand for the unused land, unused crop nutrients and unused {{ref:nature-hist-084}}. Rewriting a problem with slack variables puts it in the augmented form used by the {{ref:nature-econ-457}}.

nature-eco-301.title: Keystone species: small numbers, outsized effects
nature-eco-301.text: When the zoologist Robert T. Paine removed ochre starfish from rock pools, mussels took over. The number of clinging species fell from 15 to 8 within three years, and ten years later mussels largely filled the pools. Paine introduced the idea of the keystone species in 1969. It names a species whose effect on its surroundings is far larger than its numbers would suggest. Like the keystone of an arch, it may be a small part of the ecosystem by weight, yet removing it can trigger a dramatic shift. Sea otters are a famous case. When fur hunting cut them to fewer than 1000 in the north Pacific, sea urchins grazed away the kelp, the underwater forests described in {{ref:nature-eco-422}}. Reintroducing otters restored them. In Greater Yellowstone, removing gray wolves led to {{ref:nature-eco-761}} that hurt beavers and streams. After wolves returned, the riverside ecosystem recovered within a few years. Some keystones help rather than hunt: certain seeds will not grow unless they have passed through a cassowary. The concept overlaps with indicator and umbrella species and with {{ref:nature-eco-116}}, and it has helped ecologists talk to conservation policymakers. One researcher listed 230 species called keystones in about 157 studies over the 50 years since Paine's paper. Critics say the term oversimplifies complex ecosystems, has been stretched to many meanings and depends on local context.

nature-eco-164.title: The carbon cycle: life's main ingredient on the move
nature-eco-164.text: The soil underfoot holds about 1,500 gigatons of carbon, a gigaton being a billion tons. All the plants and other organisms above ground hold about 500 gigatons. Carbon is the main ingredient of living matter and a major part of many rocks, such as limestone. The carbon cycle is the exchange of carbon among living things, soils, rocks, water and the air of Earth. It covers both the quick recycling of carbon through living things and its long-term storage in, and release from, the natural stores described in {{ref:nature-eco-169}}. In the air, carbon exists mainly as carbon dioxide and {{ref:nature-eco-727}}. Both gases trap heat and drive part of the warming explained in {{ref:nature-eco-161}}. Carbon dioxide leaves the air mainly through photosynthesis, entering life on land and in the ocean. In 2024 the global average level of carbon dioxide in the air reached a record 422.7 parts per million. The steps of this cycle are key to making Earth able to support life. Antoine Lavoisier and Joseph Priestley first described it, and Humphry Davy popularised it.

nature-eco-258.title: Frozen ground beneath the sea floor
nature-eco-258.text: Beneath the seabed of polar continental shelves lies frozen ground that was dry land in the last ice age and is now flooded. This subsea {{ref:nature-eco-678}} covers about 2 million km2. It holds around 560 GtC, gigatons of carbon, in organic matter and 45 GtC in {{ref:nature-eco-727}}. It responds over millennia, so human-driven warming will affect it mostly hundreds or thousands of years from now. Still, under the high-emissions RCP 8.5 scenario, 43 GtC could be released by 2100 and 190 GtC by 2300.

nature-eco-298.title: Detrital food webs: the economy of the dead
nature-eco-298.text: Leaf litter, dead wood, carrion and dung are all {{ref:nature-eco-709}}: non-living organic matter. A detrital food web starts there. Decomposers break it down and pass it on to detritivores, which carnivores then eat. This web is joined to the grazing web of living plants. Mushrooms from decomposers feed deer, squirrels and mice, and robins eat earthworms that feed on leaves.

nature-eco-320.title: Abiotic components: the non-living rules of life
nature-eco-320.text: A rainforest and a {{ref:nature-eco-703}} differ above all in water, and that one difference limits which species can live in each. Water is an abiotic component of an ecosystem: one of the non-living chemical and physical parts of the environment that affect living things. Others include light, temperature, humidity, acidity, salinity (saltiness), altitude, minerals, tides, dissolved oxygen and soil. Such differences also shape how species compete. Humans now create and change these factors. {{ref:nature-eco-662}} use alters the places species live, and heat-trapping gases ({{ref:nature-eco-162}}) change the ocean's pH, its acidity. Non-living factors can even steer evolution. Salinity, for instance, can give one species an edge over another, and that pressure can lead to new species.

nature-eco-609.title: Amazon dieback: a rainforest that waters itself
nature-eco-609.text: The Amazon makes around half of its own rainfall by cycling moisture back into the air, so forest loss means less rain downwind. Dieback is the risk that enough forest loss pushes much of the Amazon past a threshold into drier degraded forest or {{ref:nature-eco-681}}. Some 17–18% has already been cleared. Modeling suggests warming of 1.5–1.9 °C combined with 22–28% deforestation could trigger the transition across 62–77% of the forest. A 2022 study reported that it has been losing resilience since the early 2000s, recovering more slowly from short shocks.

nature-eco-614.title: Smooth, abrupt or discontinuous: three ways systems change
nature-eco-614.text: Systems prone to {{ref:nature-eco-613}} change in one of three patterns, set by how their fast and slow processes interact. In smooth change, fast variables follow slow ones along a nearly straight line. In abrupt change, the relationship is non-linear. In discontinuous change, the system flips back at a different point from where it flipped forward, which is hysteresis. {{ref:nature-eco-743}} on {{ref:nature-eco-520}}, where small changes in grazing shift grassland to woody {{ref:nature-eco-681}}, is thought to be a case of smooth change.

nature-eco-427.title: What threatens kelp forests
nature-eco-427.text: In the 2010s Northern California lost 95% of its kelp ecosystems to spells of unusually hot sea water. Kelp forests are threatened mainly by too much fishing, pollution, kelp harvesting, invasive species and climate change. The most pressing threat may be {{ref:nature-res-027}}, because removing predators lets the forest collapse into an urchin barren. Heat is the rising one. The 2022 IPCC report says kelp and other seaweeds are suffering mass die-offs and range shifts from extreme heat in most regions. Pollution such as sewage, industrial chemicals, heavy metals and farm runoff has damaged kelp forests in southern California. Managers often limit kelp harvesting and fishing, but that does not protect the whole ecosystem. Marine reserves cover the wider web of interactions. Restoration in California mainly removes sea urchins, using divers and sea otters.

nature-econ-518.title: The capital consumption allowance: running to stand still
nature-econ-518.text: Part of every year's GDP buys no growth at all. It simply keeps the country's productive capacity from shrinking. This is the capital consumption allowance, the part of GDP due to depreciation. It covers wear and tear on physical capital, plus the investment needed to maintain human capital, such as educating workers to replace retirees. GDP equals {{ref:nature-acct-119}} plus the capital consumption allowance.

nature-econ-573.title: Net national product: output after depreciation
nature-econ-573.text: Net national product is gross national product minus depreciation, the loss in value of fixed capital through wear and tear in production. Likewise, {{ref:nature-acct-119}} is GDP minus depreciation. Economics research usually uses the gross measures instead, a choice that has long been disputed. The net measures matter for the environment. Net national product serves as an indicator of {{ref:nature-eecon-208}} in environmental economics and appears in models of resources running out. Research has also studied it as a dynamic welfare indicator.

nature-pol-296.title: Black carbon: the soot that warms and kills
nature-pol-296.text: Black carbon is the light-absorbing form of elemental carbon left by heating material without oxygen or produced by incomplete combustion, as in soot. It forms from incomplete combustion of fossil fuels, {{ref:nature-pol-303}} and {{ref:nature-clim-284}} and is fine {{ref:nature-pol-068}} that causes premature death and disability. About 20% of emissions come from that fuel, 40% from fossil fuels and 40% from open living mass burning. Developed countries were once the main source, but control technologies since the 1950s shifted most emissions to developing countries. Estimates say 640,000 to 4,900,000 premature deaths a year could be prevented with available mitigation measures. In soils black carbon is typically 1 to 6% of organic carbon, and Terra preta soils hold about three times the organic matter of surrounding soils.

nature-pol-246.title: Grandfathering: free permits for past polluters
nature-pol-246.text: Grandfathering gives out emission permits for free, according to how much each firm emitted in the past. It can create incentives that backfire. A firm that cuts its emissions sharply may receive fewer permits later. Firms that get free permits still raise prices to customers, so permits they did not need become windfall profits. The EU's trading scheme gives free permits to industries judged exposed to international competition. Free allocation is complex, and it encourages {{ref:nature-pol-042}}, the pursuit of favors from government, and pressure on officials ({{ref:nature-pol-034}}).

nature-econ-381.title: Gains from trade: why exchange pays
nature-econ-381.text: Gains from trade are the net benefits people or economies get when they can trade more freely with each other. David Ricardo first clearly stated and proved comparative advantage in 1817, and it remains the basic explanation for where they come from. Technically, they are the rise in buyers' and sellers' combined surplus that comes from lower import duties or freer trade. They come from specialization, the larger total output it allows, and selling one kind of output for other goods valued more highly. Prices do the steering. They draw labor and other inputs toward activities where they have a comparative advantage, that is, a low opportunity cost. Freer trade is not always best for everyone. A large economy may use taxes and subsidies to gain at other economies' expense, and market power can let some traders block other mutually beneficial trades.

nature-econ-814.title: What sets the interest rate on a loan
nature-econ-814.text: A loan to a developing country carries a higher interest rate than a loan to the US government. Market interest rates are set in places such as the money market, markets for tradable {{ref:nature-mkt-153}} and banks, and each loan's rate reflects several factors. First is opportunity cost: lenders weigh the other uses of their money, including returns elsewhere. Second is inflation. A lender putting off spending wants at least enough to cover rising prices, so the nominal rate is roughly the real rate plus inflation. Third is a risk premium for the chance of default, which is why loans to developing countries cost more. Fourth is time. Shorter loans usually carry less default and inflation risk, so short-term rates often sit below long-term ones, an upward-sloping yield curve. Fifth is ease of resale: lenders want a higher return on something hard to sell quickly at a fair price than on something easy to sell, or liquid. Finally, a {{ref:nature-econ-561}} strongly influences short-term rates, one of its main tools.

nature-eco-700.title: Fire suppression: a century of putting out the wrong fires
nature-eco-700.text: For decades the American answer to every {{ref:nature-gov-243}} was to put it out. Federal policy in early 20th-century North America aimed to suppress all fires, and it ended the use of {{ref:nature-eco-699}}s. Habitats changed. Oak savannas and canebrakes are now critically endangered, and in the Eastern US fire-sensitive red maple is spreading at the expense of fire-tolerant oaks. Since 1995 the US Forest Service has slowly brought burning back into {{ref:nature-res-092}}. The conflict over burning stems from old campaigns against {{ref:nature-gov-243}} and the later acceptance of fire as a necessary ecological phenomenon.

nature-econ-113.title: Diminishing returns: when more hands add less
nature-econ-113.text: Put more workers on a factory floor with fixed machines and space, and output first more than doubles. Then it rises in proportion. Eventually each new worker adds less and less as people get in each other's way. This is diminishing returns: the fall in extra output gained as more of one input is added while all other inputs stay fixed. It is also called diminishing marginal productivity. Output stays positive, but output per unit of input falls, and so does efficiency. The idea has deep roots in farming. In 1815 Ricardo, Malthus, West and Torrens applied it to land rent, drawing on English {{ref:nature-res-257}} after the Napoleonic Wars. Diminishing returns mean rising costs, both for the next unit and on average. They also explain the bowed-out shape of the limit on what an economy can produce ({{ref:nature-econ-143}}). Technological or managerial innovation can reduce or remove them. Modern versions also hold other outputs equal, since one process can make co-products, such as a factory producing more goods and more CO2.

nature-eco-502.title: Freshwater ecosystems: rich life in scarce water
nature-eco-502.text: Swamps, deltas and rivers make up just 1% of Earth's surface, yet freshwater ecosystems hold 41% of the world's known fish species. A freshwater ecosystem is an aquatic ecosystem of low-salt water: lakes, ponds, rivers, streams, springs, bogs and wetlands. That sets it apart from the sea, whose water is much saltier. The three basic types are lentic (still water such as ponds and lakes), lotic (flowing water such as rivers) and wetlands. Still and flowing water are the two classic forms. Scientists also classify freshwater habitats by temperature, light penetration, nutrients and vegetation. Land-based fresh waters produce about 1.5% of global net primary production, the plant growth left after plants meet their own energy needs. Many freshwater organisms cannot tolerate salt, and irrigation water can pick up harmful levels of it. Five broad threats stand out: overexploitation, {{ref:nature-res-261}}, changed water flows, habitat destruction and invasive species.

nature-eco-053.title: Deforestation: trading forest for farms, ranches and towns
nature-eco-053.text: Forests cover about 31% of Earth's land. That is one-third less than before {{ref:nature-res-257}} spread, and half of that loss came in the last century. Deforestation is the clearing of a forest or stand of trees so the land can serve a non-forest use, such as farms, ranches or towns. It is one of the main forms of {{ref:nature-eco-041}}. Between 2015 and 2020 it ran at an estimated 10 million hectares a year, down from 16 million a year in the 1990s. {{ref:nature-res-257}} is by far the main direct cause. In 2025 the spread of cropland and {{ref:nature-nbs-350}} drove nearly 90% of global deforestation. Logging, {{ref:nature-res-273}}, mining and climate-driven fires in wild land add to it. Clearing destroys habitat, so it brings loss of biodiversity, species dying out, local climate change and the displacement of forest peoples. It also cuts the carbon forests take up, weakening their role in slowing climate change. Cleared regions often suffer soil erosion and the slide toward {{ref:nature-eco-703}} described in {{ref:nature-eco-091}}. The costs can dwarf the gains. In Brazil, economic losses from deforestation could reach around 317 billion dollars a year, about 7 times the value of the commodities it produces.

nature-econ-832.title: Price indexes: tracking the cost of a basket of goods
nature-econ-832.text: If prices rise 5% from a 2010 base, a price index set to 100 in 2010 reads 105 in 2011. A price index tracks the cost of a fixed sample basket of goods, a {{ref:nature-res-264}} bundle, relative to its cost at a base date or place. It is usually set to 100 at the base date, so a one percent rise in the bundle's price in the first period takes it to 101. The inflation rate between two dates is the change in the price index divided by its earlier value. The {{ref:nature-econ-506}} uses a bundle of goods bought by consumers, while {{ref:nature-econ-483}} uses a price index of its own.

nature-found-080.title: Why the best amount of pollution is not zero
nature-found-080.text: Society gets something from pollution: the polluting goods themselves, and lower prices. Otherwise no one would pollute. So the aim is not zero pollution but the socially optimal level, the amount at which society's welfare is greatest. That is where the harm of one more unit equals the benefit of producing it. The free market misses this point, because it ignores pollution's cost to society. The true supply curve sits higher than the market one, and the optimum lies where the curve of marginal social cost meets market demand. At that optimum, output is lower and price higher than in the free market, so the free market outcome is a market failure. A corrective tax proportional to the damage of each extra unit yields the efficient level of pollution reduction. The model is used to compare ways of internalizing the externality, such as import taxes, taxes on the damage like a carbon levy, and cap and {{ref:nature-res-268}}. Accepting some pollution can raise overall wellbeing, though every increase is still a cost that must be counted.

nature-econ-609.title: Solutions to the tragedy of the commons: from owners to communities
nature-econ-609.text: Finding solutions to the tragedy of the commons counts among the main problems of political philosophy. The proposals run from local, self-organized rules to government action. One is {{ref:nature-res-266}}. Turning a common resource into private property gives the new owner a reason to keep it productive, an idea linked to Coase in 1960. It works when the owner pays the full price of using up the resource. Another is a government cap on how much any one person may use, through permits for mining, fishing, hunting, grazing and logging. Governments step in when a community is too large for its social ties to hold it together. A middle way shares ownership between government and community, so that no one or two parties hold all the power. Cooperation can also come from below. Political scientist Robert Axelrod argues that even self-interested people often find ways to cooperate, because restraint serves both them and the group.

nature-eco-715.title: The criticism of FSC certification
nature-eco-715.text: FSC has been criticized since its founding, even by NGOs that once backed it. FERN (2011), Friends of the Earth UK (2008), ROBINWOOD (2009) and the Swedish Society for Nature Conservation (2011) withdrew their support. Critics argue that only large businesses can afford certification, producing a model of a few massive suppliers. FSC responded with a Small and Low Intensity Managed Forests standard. Resolute, the largest manager of FSC-certified forests, was accused of logging on Barriere Lake Algonquin territory. FSC added a Quality Assurance Unit in 2013 and an online claims platform in 2014. It remains disputed whether FSC acts effectively on complaints and whether its model favors large firms.

nature-econ-387.title: The invisible hand: self-interest serving the public
nature-econ-387.text: Adam Smith used the phrase just once in The Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759) and once in The Wealth of Nations. He wrote of "an" invisible hand, never "the." It became his most famous metaphor: the way free markets can lead self-interested people to benefit the public without meaning to. In The Wealth of Nations it appears in a chapter about where merchants invest their capital, not about {{ref:nature-res-269}}. Paul Samuelson's 1948 textbook popularized the phrase and gave it a new meaning: that free markets regulate themselves and reach outcomes government cannot improve. The idea is a central justification for the hands-off thinking behind neoclassical economics. Joseph Stiglitz argues the hand often seems invisible because it is not there. With externalities, markets on their own produce too much pollution, which is why environmental economics deals largely with market failures. Stiglitz, Piketty and others argue that markets often fail to turn self-interest into social good. Scholars also disagree about what Smith himself meant.

nature-found-087.title: Why social costs are so hard to count
nature-found-087.text: Pricing carbon means tracing a ton of heat-trapping gas through rising temperatures to crops, health, flooding and ecosystems. That chain shows why social costs are hard to measure, especially future, environmental and long-range harms. Environmental, social and political harms that span long periods are hard to predict and put numbers on. So they are hard to include when weighing costs against benefits. Distance adds complexity: costs from one firm in China can affect people's health in the United States.

nature-eco-220.title: The economic bill for murky, smelly water
nature-eco-220.text: Murky water costs money to clean. Eutrophication and harmful algal blooms impose economic costs through dearer water treatment, lost fishing and shellfish harvests, and lower tourism income. Plants that treat water for drinking must also deal with colour and smell problems. Tourism suffers because the water looks less attractive and is less safe, thanks to bacteria from decomposition. Could a little extra fertility pay? In principle, controlled eutrophication could raise fishery output and community income. It is not currently recommended, because damage can set in quickly.

nature-nbs-115.title: Habitat fragmentation: when one wild place becomes many islands
nature-nbs-115.text: Keep 10% of a habitat as one unbroken remnant and, as a rough rule, half its biodiversity is lost. Habitat fragmentation is the breaking up of a large, continuous habitat into smaller, isolated patches. It splits populations and degrades ecosystems. Five changes come bundled together. There is less total habitat and less interior compared with edge. Fragments are cut off from each other, one patch splits into several, and patches get smaller on average. People cause it by clearing native vegetation for farms, rural development, cities and hydroelectric reservoirs. {{ref:nature-nbs-319}} building and water diversions do the same to rivers and lakes. Fragmentation consistently reduces biodiversity by 13 to 75%. It also impairs ecosystem functions such as {{ref:nature-clim-284}} production and nutrient cycling. Small, isolated populations are fragile. Minor swings in climate or resources that a large population would absorb can wipe them out. The damage is slow to show, and experiments find biodiversity and ecosystem functioning still declining 20 or more years later. Linking fragments with corridors of native vegetation, bridges or underpasses can ease isolation, as {{ref:nature-eco-152}} explains. It does not restore interior habitat.

nature-nbs-329.title: Floods: when water covers dry land
nature-nbs-329.text: Floods caused agricultural losses above USD 1.5 trillion between 1991 and 2023, the most destructive hazard type for global agriculture. A flood is an overflow of water that submerges land that is usually dry. It can follow prolonged heavy rain, fast snowmelt, high tides, tsunamis, or the failure of {{ref:nature-nbs-319}}, embankments and retention ponds. Impervious surfaces and {{ref:nature-gov-243}} make floods worse. A flash flood rises rapidly with little warning, usually from intense rain over a small area or on already saturated ground. People raise the odds. Human changes such as deforestation, wetland removal, rerouted waterways and embankments often raise the intensity and frequency of flooding. Coincident events, such as warm rain melting snowpack or ice and debris blocking channels, can make extreme floods more frequent than simple rainfall-runoff statistics predict. Flood statistics estimate the 100-year flood from a series of annual maximum flows, and regional data let ungauged reaches be estimated indirectly. Floods are not only a loss. Smaller, more frequent floods can recharge groundwater and make soil more fertile, and periodic flooding was essential to ancient peoples along the Nile, Indus and other rivers.

nature-econ-419.title: Bifurcation theory: when small changes flip a system
nature-econ-419.text: Turn a setting slowly, and at some point a whole system may suddenly behave differently. That switch is a bifurcation. A small, smooth change in a parameter, a fixed setting of the model, causes a sudden qualitative change in how the system behaves. Bifurcation theory studies how the qualitative behavior of a family of equations, such as the solutions of {{ref:nature-econ-433}}, changes as its parameters change. Henri Poincaré introduced the name in 1885. Bifurcations occur both in continuous systems described by differential equations and in discrete systems described by maps. The idea matters for nature. In the study of living things, abrupt shifts linked to a critical or bifurcation point are also called critical transitions. Systems nearing such a point show {{ref:nature-eco-654}}: they recover more and more slowly after being knocked off balance ({{ref:nature-econ-471}}). Catastrophe theory, which influenced research on these shifts, is a branch of bifurcation theory.

nature-eco-091.title: Desertification: how dry land turns to desert
nature-eco-091.text: Dry regions cover about 40–41% of Earth's land and are home to more than 2 billion people, at least 90% of them in developing countries. Desertification is the gradual degradation of fertile land in those regions into {{ref:nature-eco-703}}, through natural processes and human activities. It is the harshest form of {{ref:nature-eco-060}}. The immediate cause is the loss of most vegetation. Drought, climate shifts, {{ref:nature-nbs-342}}, {{ref:nature-eco-761}} and cutting trees for fuel or building all strip it away. Bare dry soil then blows or washes off, leaving infertile layers that bake into unproductive hardpan. Some 10–20% of dry regions are already degraded, and a billion people are threatened by further desertification. Climate change is expected to expand dry regions from 38% of continental land in the late 20th century to 50% or 56% by 2100. Remedies exist: shelter belts and woodlots, planted lines and blocks of trees, fix soil and cut erosion. Yet the economics can work against them. Sustainable practices can cost individual farmers more than they gain, even when they benefit society and the environment.

nature-eco-748.title: Gene flow: genes on the move between populations
nature-eco-748.text: Gene flow, also called migration, is the transfer of genetic material from one population to another. Its power is easy to underrate. If the rate is high enough, two populations share equivalent allele frequencies and count as one effective population. One migrant per generation is enough to prevent divergence driven by {{ref:nature-eco-751}}. High gene flow reduces genetic differentiation and can constrain speciation and range expansion. It can also add novel variants under positive selection, a process called adaptive introgression. Researchers estimate it directly from dispersal and reproductive success, or indirectly by comparing allele frequencies; with one migrant per generation, FST equals 0.2. Barriers stop it. They can be physical, as in allopatric speciation, or reproductive, as in sympatric speciation. The Great Wall of China has hindered gene flow in native plants. Hybridization with {{ref:nature-nbs-318}} can swamp a rare species' gene pool, when introgression replaces its alleles with an invader's. The effects depend on context. Gene flow can enhance a population's fitness or have negative consequences.

nature-eco-383.title: Ecological productivity: how fast an ecosystem grows
nature-eco-383.text: Swamps and marshes are listed as producing 2,500 grams of carbon in new {{ref:nature-clim-284}} on each square meter every year. That figure measures ecological productivity: the rate at which an ecosystem makes new living matter. It is often given in grams per square meter per day. The productivity of plants and other autotrophs is called primary productivity. That of animals and other heterotrophs is secondary productivity. Three things set it: nutrient supply, temperature and water. More is not always better. Nutrients washed in from {{ref:nature-eco-662}} can trigger sudden surges of algae. These raise primary production but leave the ecosystem less stable.

nature-eco-682.title: Sediment: loose material carried somewhere new
nature-eco-682.text: A riverbank, a beach and a sandstone cliff share one origin: sediment. It is solid material made of loose particles that has been transported to a new place and deposited. {{ref:nature-clim-286}} and erosion break material down, and then wind, water, ice or gravity carry it away. Most sediment moves by water, in what are called fluvial processes, but wind carries some, called aeolian sediment, and glaciers carry more. Moraines and till are ice-borne sediments. Scientists classify it by grain size, grain shape and composition, and measure size on the log base 2 Phi scale from colloid to boulder. Buried sand and silt can become sandstone and siltstone through lithification, so deposited sediment is the source of sedimentary rocks.

nature-clim-178.title: Biochar: charcoal that feeds the soil
nature-clim-178.text: Long before Europeans arrived, Amazonians smoldered farm waste into charcoal, creating soils later settlers called terra preta. Biochar is that kind of charcoal: made by heating biomass with little oxygen, and meant for soil and other organic uses. The process, {{ref:nature-clim-285}}, yields solid biochar, liquid bio-oil and syngas. In soil it can improve aeration and fertility, reduce nutrient leaching and acidity, and cut greenhouse gas emissions. It helps degraded tropical soils more than temperate ones. Too much, or the wrong feedstock, can harm soil life, change pH and raise salinity. Biochar is so stable that it can stay in soils for thousands of years, which underlies its use for carbon removal, described in {{ref:nature-clim-180}}. A 1–2% share in concrete also cuts emissions from cement.

nature-found-075.title: Pollutants: when a substance becomes a problem
nature-found-075.text: Oil occurs naturally, yet it can still be a pollutant. A pollutant is a substance or form of {{ref:nature-eecon-238}} put into the environment that has unwanted effects or makes a resource less useful. Some occur naturally; others are made by people, such as manufactured materials and by-products. A pollutant becomes pollution, or a health concern, once its concentration is high enough to do significant harm. It can then damage plant and animal growth, human health, resources people use, or property values. Some pollutants break down naturally. Others, such as the insecticide DDT, break down into products that are themselves pollutants. Measured against the planet's safe limits, mapped in {{ref:nature-eco-597}}, people have released novel entities, new kinds of substance, well beyond safe levels. Because pollutants cross borders, international rules are needed, such as {{ref:nature-found-099}}, signed in 2004.

nature-pol-240.title: Tax or cap: two ways to price carbon
nature-pol-240.text: A {{ref:nature-pol-081}} fixes the price of each tonne emitted and lets the amount adjust. Emissions trading does the reverse: it fixes the total amount emitted and lets the price move. Economists disagree over which is better. A tax is generally favored for its simplicity and price stability. It is also easier to enforce broadly: British Columbia enacted and implemented its carbon tax in five months. A cap can in principle hold emissions to a fixed remaining total. Most cap-and-trade programs lower the cap by a fixed percentage each year, guaranteeing that emissions decline. Permits therefore suit cases where certainty about emissions is needed. Prices under a cap are more volatile, though. That makes them riskier for investors, consumers and governments that auction permits. Both tools can be bent by politics. Industries may lobby their way out of a tax, while freely handed-out permits can invite corrupt behavior. On paper the two are close cousins. Both are efficient, and if permits are auctioned they have the same social cost and effect on profits. A last dispute concerns other climate policies. Some economists say a cap stops measures such as {{ref:nature-eecon-239}} support from cutting emissions further; others say only an enforced cap guarantees cuts ({{ref:nature-pol-242}}).

nature-found-013.title: SEEA: keeping national books on nature
nature-found-013.text: Can a country keep books on its environment as it does on its economy? The System of Environmental-Economic Accounting, or SEEA, is the international statistical standard for doing so. It tracks both the economy's impacts on the environment and the environment's contribution to the economy. The SEEA Central Framework reached its final form in February 2014. In March 2021 the UN Statistical Commission adopted a standard for ecosystem accounting, covering the extent, condition and services of ecosystems in physical and {{ref:nature-eecon-241}} terms. SEEA is a satellite of the UN's main system for measuring economies, described in {{ref:nature-econ-596}}, and shares its definitions, rules and boundaries.

nature-eco-299.title: Are complex food webs more stable?
nature-eco-299.text: Are food webs with more species and more links more stable? Ecologists have not settled the question. Two measures frame it. Connectance is the fraction of all possible feeding links that actually occur in a network. Complexity is sometimes defined as the number of species multiplied by connectance, though that definition has been criticized. Equation-based models challenged the idea that complexity brings stability. Later studies found that it holds in real systems after all.

nature-found-039.title: Two schools: environmental and ecological economics
nature-found-039.text: Two schools study the same planet and often reach different conclusions. Environmental economics applies standard economics to the environment. The other, ecological economics, treats the economy as a part of the ecosystem. The split starts with training: most environmental economists trained as economists, while most ecological economists trained as ecologists. Ecological economists stress a "strong" form of {{ref:nature-eecon-208}}. They reject the idea that human-made capital can stand in for natural capital. Their field is described as more pluralistic, open to many methods, and more focused on long-term viability and the scale of the economy. Environmental economics is seen as idealistic about the price system. The ecological school, by this account, is more realistic about factors outside it. The two schools hold conflicting views that trace back to different philosophical foundations, and the disagreement is unresolved.

nature-eecon-076.title: Entropy pessimism: can technology beat physics?
nature-eecon-076.text: Every technology turns valuable resources into waste and so raises {{ref:nature-eecon-109}}. Entropy pessimism holds that technology therefore cannot escape the laws of physics. Neoclassical production functions treat technology as a factor of production with no mention of natural resource inputs. In ecological economics, technology is simply the way natural resources are transformed. {{ref:nature-eecon-256}} replied in 1997 that "elementary physics" had not by itself prevented growth in industrialized countries. Economists still disagree on whether technology can overcome resource limits.

nature-acct-092.title: Full-cost accounting: costs counted as resources are used
nature-acct-092.text: A vehicle bought once and used for ten years is costed across all ten years, not in the year the cash is spent. That is the logic of environmental full-cost accounting, a cost-accounting method that gathers the possible environmental costs and benefits of each option under consideration. It traces direct costs and allocates indirect ones. It values goods even when no cash changes hands, such as equipment paid for by a state grant. It includes overheads, past costs such as buying equipment, and future ones such as closing a facility. Florida uses it to identify and report the actual costs of solid {{ref:nature-eecon-232}}. A major motive is anticipating market or regulatory problems that come from ignoring the whole outcome of a process. Prices can mislead: subsidies to energy and food keep them artificially low, hiding true costs and the externalities of fossil fuels and mechanised farming. The method is one part of {{ref:nature-acct-103}}, alongside human and social capital. Experts find both 'full' and 'true' troublesome labels, because the words are subjective.

nature-econ-031.title: Three ways out of a social dilemma
nature-econ-031.text: If a {{ref:nature-gov-235}} problem traps people, what frees them? Researchers group the answers into three kinds. Motivational solutions rely on people caring about others, and research finds stable individual preferences for how much people weigh others' outcomes against their own. Strategic solutions work in repeated interactions; the best known is {{ref:nature-econ-737}}, which cooperates first and then copies the partner's last move. Structural solutions change the rules of the game or remove the dilemma, as when money rewards have cut household water and electricity use. Cooperation is likelier when people can monitor each other, sanction defectors, communicate, know one another and manage resources with clear boundaries. Graduated sanctions, which start mild and let violators regain trust, support shared resource management. Yet sanction systems are costly and are themselves public goods, and rewards can crowd out voluntary cooperation.

nature-eco-386.title: Secondary succession: how life returns after fire
nature-eco-386.text: Knobcone pine cones open only when a forest fire heats them. For some species, destruction starts the cycle. Secondary succession is the succession that follows an event such as fire, harvesting or a hurricane. The event knocks back an existing ecosystem but leaves soil and some life in place. That head start makes it usually faster than {{ref:nature-eco-349}}, because soil, seeds, roots and underground plant parts survive. Consider an oak–hickory forest after {{ref:nature-gov-243}}. Annual plants, which live a single season, come first. Grasses and pioneer species follow, then shrubs and young trees. Over about 150 years the forest returns to a stable mature community resembling the one before the fire. The rebuilding reaches underground too. Succession from Imperata grassland to regrown forest raises the carbon stored in the soil.

nature-econ-094.title: The Marginal Revolution: three thinkers, one idea
nature-econ-094.text: In 1871 two economists in different countries published the same new idea. In England, Jevons argued in The Theory of {{ref:nature-gov-242}} that value depends entirely on utility. In Austria, Carl Menger presented the theory in his Principles of Economics. Walras followed in Switzerland in 1874. This spread of marginal utility theory in the 1870s is called the Marginal Revolution. A second generation, including Alfred Marshall, Böhm-Bawerk, Wieser and Pareto, carried the ideas into the mainstream. Over the 20th century a large literature grew on the conflict between marginalism and the labor theory of value.

nature-found-041.title: Environmentally harmful subsidies: paying to use nature up
nature-found-041.text: Some government payments reward companies more for exploiting natural resources than for protecting them. The damage these environmentally harmful subsidies do to nature has been conservatively estimated at $4-$6 trillion U.S. dollars per year. The largest support the {{ref:nature-gov-231}}, farming and water sectors.

nature-eco-201.title: A small gas with a big warming punch
nature-eco-201.text: Since about 1750, {{ref:nature-eco-727}} has made up just 3% of human heat-trapping gas emissions by mass, yet about 23% of their warming push on the climate. In Earth's air it is a powerful heat-trapping gas whose rising level is driving the change described in {{ref:nature-hist-007}}. Its level has risen about 160% since 1750, almost entirely because of human activities. By 2025 the concentration had climbed from 722 parts per billion before industry to 1936 ppb, the highest in at least 800,000 years. It is potent but less persistent than carbon dioxide. Over 20 years it traps about 84 times as much heat as the same mass of carbon dioxide, but over 100 years only 28 times. It is the second largest contributor to human-caused warming. From 2010 to 2019, its emissions caused 0.5 °C, about 30% of the warming seen. Wetlands are the largest natural source, providing roughly 20–30% of it in the air. Cutting it by the end of the century could make a substantial difference to meeting the goals of the Paris climate agreement.

nature-eco-196.title: The water cycle: one supply, endlessly moving
nature-eco-196.text: Earth's total mass of water stays fairly constant. What changes with the climate is how that water is split between ice, fresh water, salt water and air. The water cycle, or hydrologic cycle, is the continuous movement of water on, above and below the Earth's surface, as it changes between liquid, ice and vapour. Energy from the sun powers it. Water rises by evaporation and by transpiration from plants. It condenses into clouds and falls as precipitation, rain or snow. Some ice turns straight to vapour, which is called sublimation. On the ground, water soaks in, flows across the surface or moves underground. The ocean is the source of 86% of global evaporation. Most rain falls back into the ocean or onto land, where much of it flows over the ground as {{ref:nature-eco-275}}. That moving water does heavy work. It carries almost all eroded {{ref:nature-eco-682}} and phosphorus from land to rivers, lakes and seas, and together with groundwater it carries nitrogen too. The cycle is essential to life and plays a large role in the global climate and ocean circulation.

nature-eco-017.title: The effects of climate change, from reefs to economies
nature-eco-017.text: Damage climbs steeply with temperature: one comparison found total damages at 1.5 °C were 90% lower than at 3.66 °C. The effects of climate change are its well-documented and growing impacts on the natural world and on human societies. They include a warming trend, shifting rainfall and more weather extremes, with fiercer fires, thawing {{ref:nature-eco-678}} and spreading {{ref:nature-eco-703}}. Some changes can become irreversible once tipping points are crossed. Oceans and ice sheets absorb most of the extra heat. That delays some effects, which then continue after surface temperatures settle, and makes {{ref:nature-clim-037}} a major long-term concern. Mountains, coral reefs and the Arctic are the most immediately threatened ecosystems. At 2 °C, about 10% of land species would become critically endangered. For people, food and water supplies, health, farming, fisheries and forestry are at risk, and heat stress will limit outdoor work in the tropics. The burden is unequal. Poor people, children and Indigenous peoples are especially at risk, while rich industrialised countries, which emitted most carbon dioxide, have more resources to adapt. Wealthy colder countries have felt little economic harm or even gained, while poor hot countries probably grew less than they would have.

nature-eco-406.title: Terrestrial ecosystems: life on land
nature-eco-406.text: Terrestrial ecosystems cover 144,150,000 km², or 28.26% of Earth's surface. A terrestrial ecosystem is one found on land, such as {{ref:nature-eco-565}}, {{ref:nature-eco-559}}, forest, grassland or {{ref:nature-eco-703}}. It differs from water ecosystems in having soil, not water, at the surface, with plants reaching above it. Water is plentiful in some places and scarce in others. Temperatures also swing more by day and by season than they do in water. The UN goal described in {{ref:nature-gov-030}} targets the conservation, restoration and sustainable use of these ecosystems.

nature-eco-681.title: Savanna: grassland with scattered trees
nature-eco-681.text: A savanna is a mixed woodland-grassland biome whose trees are spaced widely enough that the canopy does not close. The open canopy lets light reach an unbroken grass layer. Savannas have seasonal water, with most rain in one season, and often lie between forest and desert or grassland. Year-to-year rainfall variation and dry-season fires in wild land are common to all of them. Fire shaped many savannas. Fire-stick farming appears to explain much of the savanna in tropical Australia and New Guinea, and Indian savannas result from human fire use. Fires kill or suppress tree seedlings and keep the canopy open. Today less than three percent of savanna ecosystems are estimated to be highly intact. Grazing by livestock changes {{ref:nature-nbs-350}} and promotes {{ref:nature-eco-743}}, since removing grass cuts competition for water and removes fuel that would feed fires. Clearing trees for grazing can raise production two- to fourfold, and about 4,800 km2 of Queensland savanna was cleared annually in the 2000s. Introduced weeds such as buffel grass and prickly acacia can alter savanna structure and composition worldwide.

nature-found-081.title: What it costs to cut pollution
nature-found-081.text: In 2005, US pollution abatement capital and operating costs came to nearly $27 billion. Abatement means cutting pollution, and its cost is what a firm pays to reduce the pollution it produces. Measured per extra unit cut, it is called marginal abatement cost. Firms cut pollution by choice, or because {{ref:nature-val-107}} forces them to.

nature-econ-346.title: Harberger's triangle: the shape of lost surplus
nature-econ-346.text: On a supply and demand graph, the deadweight loss from government intervention in an otherwise perfect market appears as a triangle. It is generally credited to Arnold Harberger. The interventions include price floors, caps, taxes, import duties and quotas. A tax, for example, drives a wedge between what buyers pay and sellers receive, and the triangle's area is the surplus lost for good. The triangle also measures the loss when a government fails to step into a market with externalities. How much it matters is disputed. Martin Feldstein holds these losses can drag down long-run growth, while James Tobin argued their effect on the economy is small.

nature-econ-746.title: The discount rate: how fast the future shrinks
nature-econ-746.text: Start-up firms are judged by a tougher yardstick than established companies. The yardstick is the discount rate: the rate at which the charge for delaying a payment must grow as the delay gets longer. Its yearly version, the discount yield, is the share of the original {{ref:nature-mkt-153}} that must be paid to delay payment for one year. In financial calculations the rate is usually set equal to the cost of capital. It may be raised to allow for the risk that expected cash flows will not arrive. That is why start-ups typically get higher rates, reflecting disadvantages such as hard-to-sell shares and few willing investors. The starting point is the risk-free rate, the return from risk-free securities such as government borrowing. The {{ref:nature-econ-845}} builds a discount rate as that risk-free rate plus beta, a measure of how much a share moves with the market, times the equity market risk premium.

nature-eco-695.title: Stream insects and snails as water-quality witnesses
nature-eco-695.text: Almost every stream holds animals that can tell you how clean it is. Macroinvertebrates are convenient indicators of the ecological health of water bodies and terrestrial ecosystems. They are almost always present, easy to sample and identify, visible to the naked eye, short-lived and generally sedentary. They live in nearly every stream and river, including ones too shallow for fish. Some tolerate {{ref:nature-res-261}} well, others do not. The EU Water Framework Directive, in force from 23 October 2000, requires all surface and groundwater bodies to be in good status. It also requires biological monitoring, which raised the use of biometrics in Europe.

nature-eco-130.title: Indirect drivers: the forces behind the bulldozer
nature-eco-130.text: A bulldozer clearing forest is the visible end of a long chain. Indirect drivers are the political, economic and social forces that give rise to the human activities that harm the environment. They include population, growth of the economy, {{ref:nature-res-273}}, technology and climate change. Direct drivers, such as mining, {{ref:nature-res-257}}, urban infrastructure and transport, result from them. Together they shape {{ref:nature-eco-129}}. Consumption beyond what ecosystems can sustain can be measured with the tool described in {{ref:nature-acct-027}}. Impact depends on lifestyle, affluence and pollution as much as on the raw number of people. Cultural values matter too: how a society views nature shapes how hard it works to preserve it. Blaming growing human numbers for environmental problems is controversial. Critics say it can unfairly blame poor people in the Global South.

nature-econ-604.title: Financial capital: the money that buys the machines
nature-econ-604.text: A tailor's sewing machine is capital you can touch. The money that bought it is capital of a different kind. Financial capital is money, and other resources measured in money, that businesses use to buy what they need to produce goods or services. It comes from a firm's retained earnings, the profits it keeps, or from lenders and investors. Lenders charge a price for it: interest. Firms spend it on real capital, the physical goods that help produce other goods. Fixed capital buys lasting assets, while working capital pays for stock, running expenses and credit. Some ecological economists want natural capital added to the usual analysis of land, labour and financial capital. The link already shows in {{ref:nature-res-264}} markets, which respond to anything that affects natural capital, such as weather that damages food crops.

nature-econ-534.title: Index numbers: one figure that tracks many
nature-econ-534.text: If the price of a {{ref:nature-res-264}} doubles between 1960 and 1970, its index with 1960 as the base reads 200. That is the whole trick of an index number. It compares a value with a base value, usually set at 100. A single number can then track how a group of related figures, such as prices or employment, changes over time. The consumer price index is one example. Others include cost-of-living indexes, stock market indices such as the S&P 500, and indices of raw-goods prices. Some compare places rather than times, as {{ref:nature-econ-583}} does for currencies. Either way, index numbers turn complex data into figures that are easy to compare.

nature-econ-122.title: Goods and services: things and activities
nature-econ-122.text: A restaurant sells both: the food on the plate and the service at the table. Goods are usually tangible items such as pens or pears, while services are activities other people provide, such as teaching or haircuts. Most products fall somewhere between pure goods and pure services. Producing, distributing and consuming them underpins all economic activity and {{ref:nature-res-268}}. Adam Smith drew a sharper line. He counted only work that produced material goods as productive and treated services as unproductive.

nature-econ-208.title: The second best: when fixing one flaw makes things worse
nature-econ-208.text: Letting goods cross borders untaxed is good, says the textbook. Yet liberalizing trade while ignoring an environmental externality can leave welfare lower than doing nothing. Richard Lipsey and Kelvin Lancaster showed why in 1956. Their theory of the second best starts when one condition for an ideal economy cannot be met. The best remaining option may then require moving other conditions away from their ideal values too. If one market distortion cannot be removed, adding another in a linked market may partly offset it and raise efficiency. Fixing a market failure in one sector while an uncorrectable failure remains in a related sector can lower overall efficiency. A common error, the 'fallacy of exhaustive effort', assumes that meeting as many remaining ideal conditions as possible gives the second-best result. Policy on the environment, described in {{ref:nature-pol-018}}, uses the insight directly. When an externality itself cannot be taxed, taxing a related product can be the second-best correction.

nature-econ-156.title: Economic value: what something is worth to someone
nature-econ-156.text: Clean air, pollination and {{ref:nature-nbs-329}} defense have never carried price tags, yet economists increasingly say they have economic value. Economic value measures the benefit a good or service gives a person, firm or other economic agent. It is usually counted in money, as the most a person is willing and able to pay. At root, value is how much of one wanted thing a person would give up to get another. Early economists split it into value in use and value in exchange, and exchange is what links value to price. Beyond that, agreement breaks down. One theory ties value to the labor needed to make something, while another ties it to the extra satisfaction buyers get from one more unit. Rival theories of value are a major source of disagreement between schools of economics. Many neoclassical theories simply equate value with market price, which has a stark consequence: something with no market to set a price has no economic value. That is why biodiversity's growing economic standing rests on ecosystem services such as clean air, food, water, protection from flooding and pollination.

nature-eco-184.title: Nitrate in the water we drink: fertilizer that slips underground
nature-eco-184.text: Nitrate dissolves easily and soil holds it poorly, so it readily escapes down to groundwater. Nitrate pollution is the build-up of nitrate from human activities in groundwater and surface water, where it can harm human health. Heavy use of nitrogen fertilizer in farming is a significant source. Other diffuse sources include livestock feeding, contamination from human and animal waste, and municipal and industrial waste.

nature-eco-221.title: How overfed waters make people sick
nature-eco-221.text: Eutrophication harms human health in two main ways. The first is excess nitrate in {{ref:nature-nbs-326}}. It can cause blue baby syndrome in infants, and it can form disinfection by-products during water treatment. The second is toxic algae. Swimming in water with toxic algae, or swallowing it, can cause rashes, stomach or liver illness, and breathing or nerve problems.

nature-eco-447.title: Wetland loss: two-thirds gone since 1900
nature-eco-447.text: Since 1900, 65–70% of the world's wetlands have been lost. Wetlands are damaged or destroyed by drainage, pollution, damming, taking too many fish and other human activities, as well as by natural disturbances. Drainage is the classic story. People cut dykes and ditches to create farmland and raise economic output, and some of the world's key farming areas were once wetlands. The bill can arrive later: settlements built on drained wetlands become prone to sinking ground and rising {{ref:nature-nbs-329}} risk. Because wetland water barely flows, toxic pollutants concentrate quickly and harm native species. Shrimp farming has wiped out large areas of mangrove, damage that is hard to curb because global demand is strong. In East Asia, up to 65% of coastal wetlands have been destroyed by coastal development. Damage comes in degrees. Minor and moderate disturbances let a wetland recover on its own; severe ones need human help.

nature-econ-270.title: Selection bias: when the sample tells the wrong story
nature-econ-270.text: Volunteers may differ from the people a study means to describe; studies find they tend to come from higher social standing. That is one face of selection bias. It arises when the people, groups or data chosen for analysis are picked in a skewed way. The link between exposure and outcome in the sample then differs from the link among everyone eligible. It typically occurs when researchers filter or adjust on a factor that both the exposure and the outcome influence, creating a false association ({{ref:nature-econ-213}}). The family includes loss to follow-up, volunteer bias, healthy-worker bias and nonresponse bias. In general it cannot be fixed by analyzing existing data alone, though the Heckman correction works in special cases. The study of nature is affected too: researchers' choices of where to study may bias modern estimates of biodiversity.

nature-eco-026.title: Invasive species: newcomers that harm their new home
nature-eco-026.text: An {{ref:nature-nbs-318}} usually starts small. It has to persist at low densities first, and sometimes it takes several introductions before it takes hold. An invasive species is one that people have carried to a new place, where it harms the environment it has entered. Invasive species are the subset of established non-native species that threaten native species and biodiversity. Invasions happen naturally too, but human help has greatly increased their rate, scale and geographic range. Biological invasion is now one of the five top drivers of {{ref:nature-eco-035}} worldwide, and it is growing with tourism and globalization. Successful invaders share common traits: fast growth, rapid reproduction, association with humans and a record of earlier successful invasions. Scientific consensus holds that their effects on biodiversity are mainly negative. Some can still provide habitat or food for other organisms. The label itself is slippery, since "invasive" is poorly defined and often subjective.

nature-eco-384.title: Secondary production: building bodies from food
nature-eco-384.text: Animals, fungi and many bacteria build their bodies from what they eat. Secondary production is the creation of new {{ref:nature-clim-284}} by these consumers from the food they assimilate, or absorb into their tissues. It is driven by organic material passing from one feeding level to the next. Measuring it takes care. Methods include increment summation, removal summation, the instantaneous growth method and the Allen curve method.

nature-es-116.title: Soil formation: the slowest factory on Earth
nature-es-116.text: In Sicily's Mediterranean climate, {{ref:nature-clim-286}} makes new soil at about 1/10 mm per year. Soil formation, or pedogenesis, is the slow making of soil, shaped by place, environment and history. It starts with the breakdown of fresh parent material, the rock or sediment underneath. Microbes feed on the nutrients released and leave residues that become humus, the dark, stable organic part of soil. Over time the soil develops distinct layers called horizons, which differ in color, structure, texture and chemistry. A full profile takes decades to several thousand years to develop. Farming spends this capital far faster than it is made. Erosion from farm fields is estimated at 11 to 20 times the formation rate on fields farmed without {{ref:nature-nbs-342}}, and over 100 times with conventional plowing. Soil formation is a supporting ecosystem service, and the whole business of feeding people depends on it. Vasily Dokuchaev, regarded as the father of soil science, showed in 1883 that soil forms over time under climate, vegetation, topography and parent material.

nature-found-060.title: Ground-level ozone: the smog of hot afternoons
nature-found-060.text: Ozone near the ground peaks on hot summer afternoons. It forms mainly when nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds, carbon-based vapours, react in sunlight. Ground-level ozone is the main gas in {{ref:nature-found-105}}, the haze that sunlight makes from these pollutants. It harms human health, materials, forests and crops, and it slows plants' capture of {{ref:nature-eecon-238}} from sunlight. One study estimated that a 1% rise in ozone concentrations would cause a global economic loss of $10 billion each year.

nature-pol-241.title: Carbon revenue: what to do with the money
nature-pol-241.text: A carbon tax or a permit auction raises money, and governments must decide how to spend it. One standard proposal returns it to the public per person. Richer people with bigger carbon footprints pay more, so poorer people can come out ahead. Per-person refunds would not, however, cover commuters in rural areas or people in poorly insulated houses. Other proposals fund {{ref:nature-eecon-239}} support, research, public transport and car sharing. Revenue could also pay for negative emissions, which remove carbon dioxide and cost about $150–165 per ton depending on the technology.

nature-pol-242.title: Why green-power support adds nothing under a binding cap
nature-pol-242.text: Under a carbon tax, public support for {{ref:nature-eecon-239}} adds to the emission cuts. Under a binding cap, it does not. While the cap applies, renewable support brings no further emission cuts, because the cap has already fixed the total amount emitted. So the choice between a tax and a cap ({{ref:nature-pol-240}}) also decides what other climate policies can achieve.

nature-val-053.title: Bequest value: saving nature for future generations
nature-val-053.text: Part of what people value in nature is what they can hand on. Bequest value is the satisfaction people get from preserving natural or cultural heritage for future generations. Together with existence value, it makes up non-use value. It is often used when estimating the value of an environmental good or service. Attempts to value ecosystems count it as the welfare an ecosystem may give future generations. In some optimization models, equation-based models that search for the best plan, it goes by another name: the 'salvage value' of the system.

nature-econ-099.title: Trade-offs: more of one thing means less of another
nature-econ-099.text: A full container must lose some items before it can take any more. That is a trade-off in its simplest form: a choice in which you accept less of one thing in return for more of another. Limits of many kinds create trade-offs, even simple physics. Investing shows one clearly. Stocks offer higher potential returns with more risk, while bonds are safer but pay less. Economists express a trade-off as the cost of the most preferred alternative given up, explored in {{ref:nature-econ-095}}. They often draw it as a frontier of the best possible combinations, such as the limit on how much of two goods an economy can make. Nature brings its own versions. In environmental management, funding under {{ref:nature-mkt-092}} faces trade-offs among biodiversity conservation, carbon storage and fair distribution, since maximizing one reduces the other two. More broadly, the tension between prosperity for all and environmental conservation makes trade-offs necessary in {{ref:nature-eecon-208}}.

nature-found-020.title: Assimilative capacity: how much nature can absorb
nature-found-020.text: A big, fast river can absorb more {{ref:nature-eecon-231}} than a slow stream, because water lowers contaminant levels mainly by diluting them. That limit has a name. Assimilative capacity is how much pollution an environment can absorb without harm to it or to the people who use it. Nature absorbs pollutants by diluting and dispersing them, and by removing them through chemical or biological processes. A pollutant actually causes pollution only once that capacity is exceeded. Take salt. If an irrigation standard for salt is 450 mg/L, a water body's assimilative capacity is the salt that can be added before that level is passed. Governments use the idea to guide the sustainable growth of city regions and to judge how much pressure a region is under. Critics call its definition vague. They also say it wrongly implies that small amounts of pollution do no harm.

nature-acct-069.title: Environmental Performance Index: ranking countries' green policies
nature-acct-069.text: In 2024 Estonia, Luxembourg, Germany, Finland and the United Kingdom ranked top of the Environmental Performance Index. India, Myanmar, Laos, Pakistan and Vietnam ranked last. The index scores countries on the environmental performance of their policies. The World Economic Forum started it in 2002 with Yale and Columbia University centres, and the report appears every two years. The 2024 report uses 58 indicators to rank 180 countries on cutting climate-warming emissions, ecosystem vitality and environmental health. Scores rise with national wealth, but with diminishing returns. Rule of law and regulatory quality predict performance better than wealth. Wealth cuts both ways: it funds clean water and {{ref:nature-eecon-232}} but also raises consumption, rubbish and emissions. Critics fault its arbitrary choice of metrics and its bias against data-poor countries. India rejected its 176th place in 2024. The index has since added and reweighted indicators.

nature-pol-044.title: The logic of joint action: why small groups win
nature-pol-044.text: In 1965 Mancur Olson's book The Logic of {{ref:nature-gov-235}} argued that small groups with concentrated interests win out over large groups with diffuse interests. The reason is the {{ref:nature-econ-617}}. Members of any group providing a public good are tempted to free ride on others' efforts. Large groups face higher organizing costs, and each member gains less, so they are less able to act. Without selective incentives, joint action is unlikely even among large groups with shared interests. A minority bound by concentrated incentives can therefore dominate the majority. Critics dispute parts of the argument. Susanne Lohmann notes the US quota on sugar imports ({{ref:nature-pol-005}}) created 2,261 jobs while reducing overall welfare, and blames information asymmetry rather than free riding. Gunnar Trumbull counters that diffuse interests such as consumers can win through a 'legitimacy premium' and coalitions.

nature-econ-185.title: Distribution: how output and income are shared out
nature-econ-185.text: An economy's output has to end up in someone's hands. Distribution is the way total output, income or wealth is shared out among people, or among the factors of production such as labor, land and capital. Studies of household income often look at the share going to the top or bottom fifth of households, and at what drives those shares. Distribution has been central to {{ref:nature-gov-242}} since the 19th century, in the work of Adam Smith, David Ricardo and John Stuart Mill. Welfare economics separates how much output is possible from how the resulting income is shared. In neoclassical theory, supply and demand in the markets for labor, land and capital set equilibrium output, income and its distribution. Vilfredo Pareto proposed that income follows a power law, now called the Pareto distribution. The field of {{ref:nature-eecon-059}} treats fair distribution as a goal alongside efficient allocation and a sustainable scale of the economy.

nature-eco-666.title: The Green Revolution
nature-eco-666.text: A period in which technology transfer led to a large rise in crop yields, the Green Revolution spread from developed countries and then globally until the late 1980s. Its package combined high-yielding cereal varieties, especially dwarf wheat and rice, with chemical fertilizers, pest-killing chemicals, controlled irrigation and mechanization. The new seeds need far more fertilizer than traditional varieties. High-yielding varieties absorb more nitrogen, so semi-dwarfing genes were bred in to stop cereals falling over before harvest. The term was first used by USAID administrator William S. Gaud in a speech on 8 March 1968. The CGIAR network of agricultural research centres was founded on 19 May 1971, backed by the World Bank, FAO, IFAD and UNDP. One 2021 estimate says it raised yields by 44% between 1965 and 2010. Cereal output more than doubled in developing nations from 1961 to 1985. Its energy came from fossil fuels: natural gas for fertilizer, oil for those chemicals and hydrocarbon-fuelled irrigation. Efforts to import the model into Africa were generally less successful, owing to corruption, insecurity, weak infrastructure, and scarce irrigation water and varied soils.

nature-eco-287.title: Ecosystems as one system: the living and non-living together
nature-eco-287.text: In Guatemala's western highlands, forest loss has raised the risk of landslides and water shortages. Totonicapán, which kept its forests, is more economically stable. The study of whole ecosystems is the science behind such contrasts. It studies how the living and non-living parts of an ecosystem interact as one integrated system. It focuses on working processes such as primary production, the decay of dead matter, and feeding relationships, which keep ecosystems and their services going. Eugene Odum and {{ref:nature-hist-063}} measured flows of energy and matter through whole ecosystems. Most natural ecosystems are limited by nitrogen. Nutrients recycled from decaying plant litter keep them productive. The field's findings have improved the sustainable production of forage, fiber, fuel and water. They also show the cost of chasing maximum output: intensive {{ref:nature-eco-662}} use in the US Midwest has degraded fisheries in the Gulf of Mexico.

nature-eco-092.title: Grazing or rainfall? The fight over what makes deserts
nature-eco-092.text: Early studies blamed livestock, naming {{ref:nature-eco-761}} as a leading cause of desertification. Later work on the Sahel region of Africa shifted attention to climate. Drought there is now thought to stem mainly from rainfall swings driven by ocean temperatures, aerosols and greenhouse gases. Changing ocean temperatures and lower sulfate emissions re-greened the Sahel, leading some scholars to call vegetation loss from farming a minor factor. Even the word is slippery: by 2005 there were more than 100 formal definitions of desertification. Researchers still disagree on whether local overuse or climate variability is the main recent driver.

nature-eco-607.title: Climate tipping points: thresholds with no easy way back
nature-eco-607.text: Early IPCC work judged climate tipping likely only above 4 °C of warming. By 2021 it was considered significantly probable at just over 1 °C, and highly probable above 2 °C. A tipping point is the climate's version of an {{ref:nature-eco-592}}: a critical threshold that, once crossed, leads to large, accelerating and often irreversible change. The IPCC defines it as a threshold beyond which a system reorganizes, often abruptly or irreversibly. A small disturbance can cause a disproportionately large change, often through self-reinforcing {{ref:nature-eco-638}}. Tipping behavior appears in ice sheets, glaciers, ocean circulation, ecosystems and the atmosphere. Thawing {{ref:nature-eco-678}}, ground that stays frozen, can release {{ref:nature-eco-727}}. Melting ice makes Earth less reflective. Both would speed warming. Crossing tipping points would likely have severe impacts on human society and could accelerate global warming.

nature-eco-304.title: Ocean primary production: growth in the sunlit layer
nature-eco-304.text: In the sea, almost all new organic matter is made by algae. Ocean primary production happens in the photic zone, a sunlit surface layer about 10-100 m thick. That layer faces a constant drain. Sinking particles carry nutrients out of it, and they come back only when deeper water mixes upward or wells up. Some waters lack a single ingredient. Where wind-blown {{ref:nature-eco-703}} dust does not reach, as in the Southern and North Pacific oceans, a shortage of iron limits production. The result is high-nutrient, low-chlorophyll regions: plenty of other nutrients, but little of the green pigment that marks growing algae.

nature-eco-562.title: Tropical forests: half the world's species on a fifth of its land
nature-eco-562.text: Tropical forests cover less than one-fifth of Earth's land yet hold about 50% of the world's species. They also hold about 60 percent of vascular plants, the plants with internal tubes for water. They are the forested regions with tropical climates, roughly between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn. The tropical domain holds the largest share of the world's forests, 45 percent, ahead of boreal, temperate and subtropical forests. The label covers more than steamy jungle. It includes evergreen rainforests, open eucalyptus forest, tropical conifer forest, {{ref:nature-eco-681}} woodland and mountain cloud forests. Because no single scheme defines a forest, estimates of their extent vary between sources. Much current clearing in these biodiversity-rich places is driven by exports of beef, soy, coffee, cacao, palm oil and timber. Putting a value on the forests' ecosystem services is widely held to encourage sustainable policy, but only with clear monitoring of what actually happens.

nature-econ-342.title: Markets: where buyers meet sellers
nature-econ-342.text: Markets range from one building's food market to a city's housing market, a whole country, or worldwide dealings such as diamonds. A market is any arrangement that lets buyers and sellers exchange goods, services and information. Each exchange, with or without money, is called a transaction. Most markets rely on sellers swapping goods or labor for buyers' money rather than on barter. A market can arise more or less on its own or be built on purpose. Economists see it as a coordinating mechanism: it uses prices to pass information among firms, households and individuals, and that use of prices is its defining feature. By letting tradeable things be valued and priced, markets spread resources around a society. Some markets are even created by {{ref:nature-val-107}} to tackle side effects such as pollution, for example markets in pollution permits. Markets can also go wrong. When a market's equilibrium is not efficient, economists say a market failure has occurred, though government fixes can fail too. A seller or buyer with the power to sway prices ({{ref:nature-econ-397}}) can distort them, which lowers welfare and efficiency.

nature-econ-196.title: Market distortions: when prices stop telling the truth
nature-econ-196.text: A tax on wages discourages some people from working. That push is a market distortion. The term covers any departure from perfect competition that makes a market settle at a price clearly different from the competitive one. People pursuing their own good then no longer maximize society's welfare. A distortion can be measured as the gap between a good's market price and its marginal social cost. Sources include {{ref:nature-val-107}}, monopoly, import duties and limits on imports, uncorrected externalities, unequal tax rates, inflation and incomplete information. Each can cause a net loss of social surplus. Not every tax distorts. A proportional tax on wages does, because it discourages work; a fixed charge that nothing can change, explored in {{ref:nature-pol-119}}, does not. Distortions are often responses to market failures, the circumstances that prevent perfect competition. They can also be reduced on purpose. Revenue from {{ref:nature-pol-253}} could be used to cut distorting taxes, making climate policy more efficient.

nature-econ-760.title: Negative interest rates: paying to lend
nature-econ-760.text: In theory, no lender should accept less than 0%, since simply holding cash avoids a guaranteed loss. Yet the European Central Bank from 2014 and the Bank of Japan from early 2016 used negative rates, alongside {{ref:nature-econ-564}}. A negative interest rate charges savers for holding money and has been described as a tax on holding money. Silvio Gesell proposed the idea in the late 19th century. During the European {{ref:nature-mkt-153}} crisis, some countries' government bonds sold at negative yields, so lenders in effect paid governments to borrow.

nature-econ-288.title: Coming to the nuisance: can newcomers complain
nature-econ-288.text: Can someone who moves next to an existing nuisance still complain about it? That is the question of coming to the nuisance.
