In English law, unlike US law, coming to the nuisance is no defense, and the 1879 case Sturges v Bridgman still stands. Coase used that case, a noisy sweet-maker next to a quiet doctor, to illustrate his argument. Many US states limit nuisance claims, for example with right-to-farm rules that protect {{ref:nature-res-257}} from newcomers' complaints about smells.

nature-es-040.title: Nature positive tourism: leaving places better
nature-es-040.text: The World Travel and Tourism Council says 80% of goods and services in the industry are highly dependent on nature. Nature positive tourism aims not just to leave no trace but to leave positive benefits for the natural world. It is a form of regenerative tourism, meant to help reverse nature's decline by 2030 and achieve full recovery by 2050. Actions include supporting tree replanting, making room for nature in city hotels, and cutting light and {{ref:nature-res-261}}.

nature-eco-072.title: Agricultural biodiversity: the living variety behind food
nature-eco-072.text: By a conservative estimate, about 6,000 species are commonly used for food. Agricultural biodiversity is the part of biodiversity that matters for farming. It is the variety of plants, animals and microbes, at gene, species and ecosystem levels, that sustains food and farm production. Farmers, herders, fishers and forest dwellers manage it. It gives rural livelihoods stability, adaptability and resilience, and it is critical for adapting to and slowing climate change. It also earns income, through food and raw materials and through services such as pollinating crops, controlling pests and cycling nutrients. Of the 115 major crop species grown worldwide, 75% rely on pollinators. Spreading cities, deforestation, single-crop farming, abandoned traditional practices and Westernized diets all threaten it. Its loss leads to genetic erosion, including the loss of landraces and breeds adapted to their local area.

nature-hist-023.title: Neoclassical economics: the mainstream's core
nature-hist-023.text: The dominant approach to microeconomics takes its name from Thorstein Veblen, who coined the term in 1900. Neoclassical economics explains production, consumption and prices through {{ref:nature-econ-360}}, driven by people maximizing utility and firms maximizing profit. Three assumptions hold it up. People have rational preferences. Individuals maximize utility and firms maximize profits. And people act independently with full information. In this view a good's value comes from its marginal utility to the user, unlike {{ref:nature-hist-012}} and Marxian economics, which use the labor theory of value. The approach developed in the 1870s and replaced the classical school as the mainstream. Its break with the classical school is often dated to Jevons and Menger in 1871 and Walras in 1874–1877. From the 1950s, combined with Keynes's ideas, it formed the neoclassical synthesis that dominated mainstream economics. Although it favors markets, it accepts that externalities, a form of market failure, can stop markets from producing socially desirable outcomes. Under suitable assumptions, though, flexible prices allow every welfare-improving exchange, so markets left free yield an optimum of social welfare.

nature-econ-633.title: Public goods: shared by all, paid for by few
nature-econ-633.text: No one can be kept from the safety a {{ref:nature-nbs-329}} control system provides, and one more protected house takes nothing from the next. That makes it a public good: a good or service that no one can be kept from using and that one person's use does not reduce for others. Knowledge, official statistics, national security, aids to navigation and street lighting are other examples. So are clean air and many other goods from the environment. Public goods are usually supplied by government and paid for by taxes, for a simple reason. People who do not pay can still use them, so public goods may be under-produced, overused or degraded, the trouble explored in {{ref:nature-econ-617}}. Private firms find them unprofitable, so without government they might be produced only in small amounts or not at all. Paul Samuelson set out the modern theory in his 1954 paper The Pure Theory of Public Expenditure, building on Wicksell and Lindahl. Yet public goods need not come from the public sector. They can occur naturally, or be produced by individuals, firms or community groups. Technology can change a good's status: encryption lets broadcasters sell access, and cheaper ways of charging for roads allow drivers to pay by actual use. Pure public goods are rare. Economists still debate how to define them, whether they form a real category at all, and how serious the problems they cause are.

nature-eco-442.title: What wetlands do for people, and what they are worth
nature-eco-442.text: One analysis valued the storm protection wetlands provide against hurricanes at US$33,000/hectare/year. That is one of many ecosystem services, the benefits people get from nature, that wetlands supply by storing and cleaning water. The {{ref:nature-es-001}} and the {{ref:nature-gov-051}} list a long roster: {{ref:nature-nbs-329}} control, refilling of underground water, storm protection, cleaning of water, biodiversity, products, culture, recreation and a steadier climate. Many wetlands are linked to water stored underground and help refill the porous rock layers that supply much of the world's {{ref:nature-nbs-326}}. Coastal wetlands protect shores by reducing the speed and height of waves and floodwaters. In highly developed areas, wetlands may be the only habitat left for pollinating insects, birds and mammals. Replacing these services would take enormous sums for treatment plants, river barriers and flood banks, and many could not be replaced at all. According to the Ramsar treaty, intact wetlands are often worth much more to society than the gains people expect from converting them to intensive use.

nature-eco-683.title: Sediment transport: how flows move grains
nature-eco-683.text: Sediment transport is the movement of sediment by flowing water, wind or ice, set by the strength of the flow and the particle's size, volume, density and shape. Stronger flows raise lift and drag on a particle, while larger or denser particles tend to fall out of the flow. Water can move larger sediment than air because it is denser and more viscous. Typical rivers carry sand and gravel, and large {{ref:nature-nbs-329}} carry cobbles and boulders. The Exner equation balances sediment in transport against deposition on the bed. A {{ref:nature-nbs-319}} makes a river pool and deposit its whole load, while taking it out or a fall in base level causes erosion.

nature-eco-374.title: Population: one species, one place, one time
nature-eco-374.text: Ecologists rarely count a large population in full. Methods such as the Lincoln index instead estimate the total from the individuals actually seen. In the study of living things, a population is a group of organisms of the same species living in a particular place at a particular time. A description usually names who belongs to it, its size, the area it occupies and the period studied. Ecologists stress individuals interacting and competing in one area. An evolutionary view stresses genes and reproduction instead. Populations of different species living and interacting together make up a {{ref:nature-eco-331}}. Separate populations of one species, spread out in space, can be treated as a larger unit: a {{ref:nature-eco-379}}.

nature-res-146.title: Pastoralism: herding where crops cannot grow
nature-res-146.text: Between 200 million and 500 million people practiced pastoralism as of 2019, and 75% of all countries had pastoral communities. Pastoralism raises livestock by letting animals graze on large open grazing lands, historically by nomads who moved with their herds. It is practiced where dryness, poor soils, extreme temperatures or lack of water make crops difficult or impossible. Pastoralists manage rangelands covering about a third of Earth's land surface, producing food where crops cannot grow. Mobility varies. Some herders make short daily moves, some practice transhumance between seasonal grazing lands, and some are fully nomadic. Fences, harder borders, spreading crop farming and the {{ref:nature-res-191}} of common land have made settled herding more common. One review of many studies found pastoralism 2 to 10 times more productive per unit of land than capital-intensive alternatives. Yet policies often try to replace it. Grazing can help keep savannas and woodlands diverse and stop them turning into dense shrubland or forest. Because they work marginal land, pastoral communities are very vulnerable to global warming.

nature-eco-036.title: HIPPO and the Evil Quartet: naming the drivers of loss
nature-eco-036.text: Edward O. Wilson boiled the problem down to one acronym, HIPPO: Habitat destruction, Invasive species, Pollution, human over-Population and Over-harvesting. Jared Diamond's version is an "Evil Quartet" of habitat destruction, overkill, {{ref:nature-nbs-318}} and secondary extinctions. Both lists name the main human pressures behind {{ref:nature-eco-035}}. Today's fuller list is habitat loss, land-use intensification, pollution, overexploitation, invasive species and climate change. Habitat destruction leads worldwide. At sea, a 2019 report by the panel described in {{ref:nature-gov-020}} found catching too many fish to be the main driver of mass extinction. Invasive species can drive natives extinct by outcompeting them, pushing them out of their role in the ecosystem, or interbreeding with them. The pressures also interact. In 2021 the same panel and the UN's climate science panel issued a joint report. It found that biodiversity loss and climate change must be tackled together, because they are inextricably linked.

nature-eco-348.title: Ecological succession: how communities rebuild over time
nature-eco-348.text: Plow up a grassland and leave it, and it may need at least 100 years, and potentially 1,400 years on average, to regain its earlier biodiversity. That slow rebuilding is ecological succession: the way the mix of species in a community changes over time. It comes in two main kinds. {{ref:nature-eco-349}} starts on newly created ground with no life. {{ref:nature-eco-386}} follows a disturbance, such as a fire, that destroys an existing community. Succession drives itself. Growing plants cast shade, add organic matter to the soil and change the nutrient supply, which opens room for different plants. Early communities are dominated by fast-growing species that spread well. As a community nears its mature end point, or climax, the variety of species, plant {{ref:nature-clim-284}} and stability rise. Net primary productivity and the speed of nutrient cycling fall. Two filters decide who succeeds at a site. One is whether seeds can reach it, called dispersal limitation. The other is whether they can survive there, called environmental filtering. Ecologists still debate how far chance, rather than predictable factors, sets the path of succession.

nature-pol-276.title: Green certificates: trading proof of renewable power
nature-pol-276.text: A green certificate proves that a certain amount of electricity, typically one megawatthour, came from renewable sources. It represents the environmental value of that power and can be traded separately from the electricity itself. Poland, Sweden, the UK, Italy and Belgium use such certificates as a more market-like alternative to {{ref:nature-pol-224}}. There is a catch. Buying a certificate only shifts the claim to renewable power; it does not change how much {{ref:nature-eecon-239}} is generated.

nature-found-021.title: Accommodative capacity: a sharper measure of what water can take
nature-found-021.text: Assimilative capacity proved too slippery for some regulators. Inconsistency in how it was used led NOAA and the EPA, two US government agencies, to restrict the term. Accommodative capacity was proposed as a less ambiguous alternative, because its uses are defined more in numbers. It is the rate at which {{ref:nature-eecon-231}} can be added to a body of water while keeping contaminants below levels that cause unacceptable biological harm.

nature-pol-295.title: The incineration debate
nature-pol-295.text: Few waste plants divide a neighborhood like an incinerator. Using them for {{ref:nature-eecon-232}} weighs the economic appeal of local industry against health and environmental risk. Supporters say {{ref:nature-pol-294}} avoids landfill methane, saves landfill space where land is scarce, and replaces fossil power with partly {{ref:nature-clim-284}}-based energy. They also note that in Europe the highest incineration rates generally go with top recycling performance. Critics say fly ash concentrates ecotoxic heavy metals and needs specialized landfills, and that the {{ref:nature-eecon-022}} prefers prevention, reuse and recycling. In the UK, the EU Landfill Directive led to the {{ref:nature-pol-117}} and the Landfill Allowance Trading Scheme. Business, regulators, activists and residents contest it over health, recycling and lock-in.

nature-res-194.title: Ostrom's IAD framework for studying the commons
nature-res-194.text: Forests and grazing lands share a tricky pair of traits. They are rivalrous, since one person's use reduces what others get, and non-excludable, since keeping people out is impractical. To study how people manage such resources, {{ref:nature-hist-039}} built the Institutional Analysis and Development framework, or IAD. Built on {{ref:nature-econ-098}} assumptions, it explains outcomes by documenting governance structures, the positions of the people involved, called actors, and their formal and informal rules. It breaks complex problems of {{ref:nature-gov-235}} into smaller 'action arenas'. Institutions are studied through seven types of rule: position, boundary, choice, aggregation, information, pay-off and scope.

nature-eco-066.title: Forests and climate: a feedback loop of loss
nature-eco-066.text: Standing forests in the tropics help cool the global average temperature by more than 1 °C. Clearing them works the other way. Changing how land is used, mainly through deforestation, is the second largest human source of carbon dioxide after burning fossil fuels. The emissions come from burning the wood and leaves of forests and from decomposing plant material and soil carbon. As of 2019, deforestation caused about 11% of global greenhouse gas emissions. Growing forests are carbon sinks, taking up roughly 25% of human carbon emissions each year. That service is weakening. In 2019 forests took up a third less carbon than in the 1990s, because of heat, drought and deforestation. The link runs both ways, as a self-amplifying loop. More tree loss means more warming, which brings more fires in wild land, pests and storms, and so more tree loss. Tropical deforestation risks triggering climate tipping points and the collapse of forest ecosystems.

nature-econ-059.title: Homo economicus, the perfectly rational 'economic man'
nature-econ-059.text: Adam Smith wrote that we expect our dinner not from the kindness of the butcher or the baker, but from their regard to their own interest. Economic models turned that remark into a character: homo economicus, or 'economic man'. This imagined person is always rational and narrowly self-interested. As a consumer he maximizes his satisfaction, or {{ref:nature-econ-100}}. As a producer he maximizes profit. And he can think through every possible outcome to pick the best. The name came from his critics, who used it in the late nineteenth century to attack John Stuart Mill's {{ref:nature-gov-242}}. 'Rational' here has a narrow meaning. It only means reaching one's own goals at least cost, and says nothing about whether those goals are wise in an ethical or social sense. Nor must the goals be selfish: a person's utility can include the wellbeing of family members, which fits models that stress cooperation. Two later ideas push against this view: {{ref:nature-econ-021}}, which studies biases, and {{ref:nature-econ-022}}, which stresses limits of mind and time. Advanced theory now often uses modified agents, with limited rationality or even envy, to depict real decisions more realistically.

nature-found-056.title: Air pollution and the body: 8.1 million deaths in a year
nature-found-056.text: Air pollution contributed to 8.1 million deaths in 2021, more than 1 in 8 deaths, according to the 2024 Global Burden of Disease Study. Breathing polluted air raises the risk of COPD, a long-term lung disease, as well as stroke, heart disease, lung cancer and pneumonia. Outdoor fine particles caused the most of these deaths, 4.7 million. Indoor particle pollution followed with 3.1 million, and ozone with 0.5 million. Burning coal, oil and gas is the largest source of air pollution deaths. In 2015, air pollution cut global average life expectancy by 2.9 years, against 0.3 years from all direct violence. Exposure in pregnancy makes stillbirth, miscarriage, birth defects and low birth weight more likely. Estimates differ by source: the World Health Organization puts the toll at 6.7 million deaths a year.

nature-eco-278.title: Agricultural runoff: farm chemicals on the move
nature-eco-278.text: Spray a field just before heavy rain, and the chemicals may end up in the nearest stream. Agricultural runoff is water flowing off farmland that carries chemicals such as nitrates, phosphates, {{ref:nature-hist-084}}s and herbicides. It happens when chemicals are overused or applied just before heavy rain. Either way, farm chemicals are wasted and downstream ecosystems are threatened. Nitrate fertilizer is especially easily lost, because it is highly soluble and is repelled by negatively charged clay. Concentrated runoff from farms can cause dead zones in large water bodies.

nature-eco-399.title: Nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium: the numbers on a bag of plant food
nature-eco-399.text: A bag labeled 10-10-15 contains 10 percent nitrogen, 10 percent available phosphorus (P2O5) and 15 percent water-soluble potassium (K2O). Those three elements are the main plant nutrients added as {{ref:nature-eco-662}}, and they are always listed in its analysis. Phosphorus that plants can actually absorb is the nutrient most often lacking, especially in humid tropical soils. Inorganic kinds are more concentrated than organic ones, and plants can use them immediately.

nature-eco-668.title: Where a heat-trapping gas comes from
nature-eco-668.text: About 60% of the {{ref:nature-eco-727}} released in 2019 came from human activity: roughly 360 million tons from humans and 230 million tons from natural sources. The 2024 total was estimated at 610 million tons, nearly two-thirds human. The 2021 CCAC and UNEP assessment attributes over 50% of global emissions to people: fossil fuels 35%, waste 20% and {{ref:nature-res-257}} 40%. The part made by living things comes from methanogens, which live in warm, moist soils and in the digestive tracts of ruminants, which emit it by burping and defecating. Landfills turn anaerobic within about a year of filling, letting methanogens take over. Rice paddies emitted about 30 of 400 million metric tons of anthropogenic emissions in 2022. {{ref:nature-clim-284}} burning, mostly human-caused, and gas-engine 'slip' of unburned gas also release it. Sinks weaken too. Converting forest to farmland adds soil nitrogen, which inhibits its oxidation and weakens the soil microbes that oxidize it. It mixes through the troposphere in about 1-2 years, and satellite data show over 80% of emission growth in 2010-2019 was tropical and terrestrial. See {{ref:nature-eco-201}} for the gas itself.

nature-econ-083.title: Capital: goods made to make other goods
nature-econ-083.text: A chocolate bar is a consumer good; the machine that makes it is capital. Capital means durable goods that people have produced and then use to make further goods and services, like the machinery in a factory. Unlike raw materials or {{ref:nature-eecon-238}}, it is not used up in one round of production. It gives productive services over many cycles. Economists treat capital as a factor of production alongside labor and land, a classification dating from the classical economists. Unlike land and resources that cannot be renewed, capital can be produced or increased. Producing goods that are not consumed straight away, but used to make other goods, is called investment or capital accumulation. A nation's capital stock includes buildings, equipment, software and inventories, and modern usage also counts non-physical assets.

nature-eco-165.title: Carbon pools: where the planet keeps its carbon
nature-eco-165.text: Most of Earth's carbon is going nowhere. It sits inertly in the rocks of the lithosphere, the planet's rigid outer shell. Scientists usually split the global carbon cycle into major carbon pools, or reservoirs, linked by pathways of exchange. A pool is any part of the Earth system, such as the air, ocean or soil, where carbon is held in some form for a period of time. The pools include the ocean; {{ref:nature-eco-682}}, including fossil fuels; living things on land and their soils; the atmosphere; and the rocks of the geosphere. The deep ocean is the largest pool of actively cycled carbon, holding 50 times more than the atmosphere. Yet it exchanges carbon with the surface only over hundreds of years. About a third of soil carbon is stored in inorganic forms such as calcium carbonate. Pool is the broader term: {{ref:nature-eco-169}} is one particular kind of pool.

nature-eco-608.title: Ice sheets, currents and forests: the climate's tipping elements
nature-eco-608.text: Completely melting the Greenland ice sheet would raise global sea levels by 7.2 metres. That ice sheet is one of the climate's tipping elements: parts of the climate system, such as ice sheets, ocean currents and large forests, that may have {{ref:nature-eco-607}}. As of September 2022, researchers had identified nine global core tipping elements and seven regional impact tipping elements. Several are likely to tip at 1.5 °C of warming. They include the collapse of the Greenland and West Antarctic ice sheets, the die-off of tropical reef corals and abrupt thaw of northern {{ref:nature-eco-678}}. The stakes are large. Around 500 million people depend on reefs, and a sustained ocean temperature rise of 1 °C above average is enough to cause bleaching, the whitening of stressed coral. The Atlantic overturning circulation is a vast system of ocean currents. Its collapse would cool parts of Europe by over 10 °C and threaten crop yields across most world regions. Frozen ground holds carbon from organisms that died over thousands of years.

nature-eco-286.title: Ecosystem diversity: the variety of living systems
nature-eco-286.text: Insects that pollinate crops are worth $14.6 billion a year to the US economy. Doing the job by hand would cost $5,715-$7,135 more per hectare. Services like these depend on ecosystem diversity, the variety of ecosystems in a region or across the whole planet. It covers living features and non-living ones such as water and soil, on land and in water. Globally it spans dry lands, forests, grasslands, wetlands and oceans, which makes it the largest scale of biodiversity. Diverse ecosystems help supply oxygen, purify water and provide plants used as medicines.

nature-econ-648.title: The Environmental Goods Agreement: trade talks that collapsed
nature-econ-648.text: In 2015, 18 members of {{ref:nature-pol-007}} began talks to cut import duties on goods used to protect the environment. In trade usage, 'environmental goods' means such products: {{ref:nature-eecon-239}} technology and pollution control systems, for example. The talks aimed to spread cleaner technologies for air pollution control, waste treatment, power from sources that replenish, monitoring and energy efficiency. They collapsed in 2016.

nature-econ-783.title: The effective annual rate: comparing loans on equal terms
nature-econ-783.text: A {{ref:nature-mkt-153}} that pays interest twice a year has a yearly compounded rate higher than its quoted rate. The effective annual rate captures this. It is the total interest payable over one year divided by the principal, which puts rates with different compounding on a common footing. Many countries require lenders and banks to disclose this annual compound rate so consumers can compare products fairly. It goes by names such as annual equivalent rate (AER), effective annual percentage rate and annual percentage yield.

nature-econ-218.title: Designing experiments that can reveal causes
nature-econ-218.text: Ronald Fisher worked out much of modern experimental method for {{ref:nature-res-257}}. His books The Arrangement of Field Experiments (1926) and The Design of Experiments (1935) set out how to plan a test. Design of experiments means planning procedures that test how changing one part of a system leads to changes in other parts ({{ref:nature-econ-212}}). It decides which parts to change and which to hold fixed, based on hypotheses about what drives variation. The changed inputs are independent variables; the outcomes they should change are dependent variables. Charles S. Peirce had already stressed randomization-based inference in publications of 1877–1878 and 1883. Only when participants are randomly chosen and randomly assigned can differences in outcomes be confidently put down to the different conditions. The main concerns are validity, reliability and replicability, along with enough statistical power to detect an effect. Laws and ethics rule out some well-designed experiments on people, through review boards, informed consent and confidentiality. Valuing nature uses the craft too. Choice experiments that value environmental goods depend on a design that controls which hypothetical scenarios respondents see.

nature-acct-050.title: Life-cycle assessment: from cradle to grave
nature-acct-050.text: Every manufactured product has a life story. It begins when raw materials are extracted, the cradle, and runs through making, distribution and use to recycling or disposal, the grave. Life-cycle assessment, or LCA, adds up the environmental impacts of a product, process or service across every stage of that life. An LCA inventories the energy and materials needed across the supply chain and calculates the resulting emissions. It covers more than greenhouse gases, including {{ref:nature-res-261}}, air pollution and ecotoxicity, harm to living things from toxic substances. At first LCA was used mainly to compare a product with alternatives. Now it informs product design, product labelling ({{ref:nature-pol-186}}), consumer education and government policy. An LCA is only as accurate as its data, which come either as unit process data or as environmental input-output data. Critics note that not every factor can be reduced to a number. Rigid system boundaries, the lines that decide what is counted, also make change hard to capture.

nature-eco-418.title: What threatens the world's forests
nature-eco-418.text: Forests are threatened mainly by clearing for timber, land, mining, cities and farming, and by climate change. Deforestation removes large areas for timber and land development. Clearing also breaks the forest that remains into smaller patches, making it harder for forest species to find food, shelter and mates, which cuts biodiversity. Mining clears native forest, and its logging and smelting cause soil erosion and acidification that slow recovery. Farming turns forest into fields and single-crop plantations and brings fertilizers and {{ref:nature-hist-084}} that harm the soil. Spreading cities split habitats with roads, cities and infrastructure, displacing wildlife. On top of all this, climate change harms forests through fires in wild land, droughts, soil erosion and heat stress.

nature-econ-146.title: The subjective theory of value: worth in the eye of the beholder
nature-econ-146.text: A collectable car or comic book can gain value long after it was made, through age, personal attachment, cultural meaning or scarcity. The subjective theory of value explains why. It holds that a good's value is set by the people buying or selling it. No property of the good, and no labor that went into it, decides it. It broke away from the labor theory of value during the {{ref:nature-econ-094}}. Jevons, Walras and Menger created its modern version independently and almost at the same time in the late 19th century. One consequence is striking. Because exchanges are voluntary, both sides value what they receive more than what they give, so {{ref:nature-res-268}} itself can create value. The theory also helps explain why non-essential goods can be worth more than essential ones. Alfred Marshall combined both views. Prices, he said, depend on objective production costs on the sellers' side and on buyers' subjective utility.

nature-econ-810.title: Insuring crops and homes against nature's hazards
nature-econ-810.text: Weather, hail, drought, frost, pests or disease can all cost a farmer a harvest. Insurance for crops helps farmers manage those losses. It is a special form of property insurance, which protects against risks to property such as fire, theft or weather, with versions for {{ref:nature-nbs-329}}, earthquakes and crops. Another kind, {{ref:nature-clim-035}}, pays farmers when a modeled climate trigger, linked to a high chance of large crop loss, is exceeded and harvest losses occur. Flooding shows the limits of private cover. Many US insurers do not offer cover against flooding in some regions, so a federal program acts as insurer of last resort.

nature-es-103.title: Water purification: nature's filter and the engineer's
nature-es-103.text: When New York City's water fell below EPA standards, the city did something unusual. Rather than rely only on treatment plants, it restored its polluted Catskill Watershed and let the land do the cleaning. Water purification is the removal of unwanted chemicals, germs, suspended solids and gases from water so it is fit for a given use. Nature does a great deal of it. Soil and rock layers filter underground water so well that it often needs only a disinfectant added. In bank filtration, natural riverbank sediments provide the first stage of cleaning. Slow sand filters work through living processes rather than simple straining, and a diverse community of water plants helps purify water for human use. Engineered treatment uses physical steps such as filtration and sedimentation, chemical steps such as chlorination, and biological steps. The need is enormous. A 2007 WHO report said 1.1 billion people lacked an improved {{ref:nature-nbs-326}} supply, and 1.8 million died from diarrheal disease each year.

nature-eco-506.title: The non-living conditions that shape water life
nature-eco-506.text: Dissolved oxygen often decides how much life a body of water holds, and what kind. It is one of the abiotic factors in aquatic ecosystems: the non-living conditions, such as bottom material, depth, nutrients, temperature, salinity and flow, that shape what lives there. Nitrogen and phosphorus levels decide which algae dominate. Too much algae can kill fish as it decays, and in places like the Gulf of Mexico decaying overgrowth creates oxygen-starved dead zones. Changes far upstream matter too. A {{ref:nature-nbs-319}} can reduce spring {{ref:nature-nbs-329}} and sediment, letting salt water push into coastal wetlands.

nature-eco-375.title: Studying populations: births, deaths, arrivals and departures
nature-eco-375.text: A population changes in only four ways: individuals are born, die, arrive or leave. The study of populations looks at those changes, through births, deaths, immigration and emigration, and how populations interact with their environment. Its bookkeeping fits on one line: N1 = N0 + B − D + I − E. The new number is the starting number, plus births, minus deaths, plus immigrants, minus emigrants. Population size is the number of individuals, and population density is how closely packed they are. The largest population an environment's resources can sustain is its {{ref:nature-eco-593}}. The field began with Malthus's model, in which a population in a constant environment grows or declines exponentially. Fisheries and wildlife managers track three rates: {{ref:nature-eco-590}}, growth and mortality, including deaths from harvesting. {{ref:nature-eco-760}} also grew from this field. It predicts a species' long-term chance of persisting in a patch of suitable land, and it matters for conservation.

nature-res-139.title: Illegal logging: timber taken outside the law
nature-res-139.text: More than half of global logging may be illegal. Illegal logging is harvesting, transporting, buying or selling timber in breach of the law. It includes cutting without permission, in {{ref:nature-gov-038}}s, of protected species or beyond agreed limits, often through corruption. In trade, fraudulent customs declarations, tax avoidance and fake certification are called wood laundering. Demand for raw materials, {{ref:nature-res-142}} and demand for cattle {{ref:nature-nbs-350}} drive it. Losses from public land alone exceed US$10 billion a year. Estimates need caution, though: governments tend to underestimate the problem while NGOs publish alarming figures. The damage spreads. Illegal logging drives deforestation and biodiversity loss, fosters corruption and tax evasion, and cuts producer countries' revenue. The EU's 2003 FLEGT Action Plan fights it mainly through Voluntary Partnership Agreements with timber-producing countries.

nature-eco-034.title: Are all invaders villains? Critics of the invasive label
nature-eco-034.text: Not every newcomer is a villain, some scientists argue. They say not all biological invasions are harmful and that the language of invasion misleads. They describe an "effective invasion", in which an alien species fills a vacant niche and joins local food webs without displacing natives. Some urge that species moving to escape a warming climate be treated as refugees rather than invaders. Entomologist Chris D. Thomas goes further, arguing that most {{ref:nature-nbs-318}} are neutral or beneficial. His remains a minority view against the consensus, described in {{ref:nature-eco-026}}, that invaders are mainly harmful.

nature-eco-292.title: Functional diversity: the range of jobs in an ecosystem
nature-eco-292.text: Losing a single top predator can send effects all the way down to the plants, reducing plant {{ref:nature-clim-284}} and the variety of their genes. Functional diversity is the range and value of the traits of species and organisms that influence how an ecosystem works. Traits such as how an organism moves, gathers resources, reproduces or when it is active all add to it. Greater functional diversity raises an ecosystem's ability to regulate flows of energy and matter and to supply air, water and wood to people. It also raises productivity, by letting more niches be filled. Diverse ecosystems better withstand extinctions, invasions, logging, farming and pollution. Neither the benefits nor the losses scale in a straight line. A species can also vanish from its job before it vanishes from the Earth. Functional extinction is the point at which a species no longer performs its historical role, and endangered tigers, tuna and sea otters usually qualify.

nature-nbs-095.title: Meta-analysis: combining many studies into one answer
nature-nbs-095.text: In 1904 Karl Pearson pooled studies of typhoid inoculation. Gene V. Glass gave the practice its name in 1976, calling it 'the analysis of analyses'. Meta-analysis combines the numerical results of many independent studies of the same research question ({{ref:nature-nbs-094}}). Its core step is computing one combined effect size, a measure of how big an effect is, from the studies' effect sizes and variances. Pooling increases statistical power and can settle disagreements between individual studies. A fixed effect model weights studies by the inverse of their variance, so large studies dominate. A random effects model allows true effects to differ between studies. Pooling cannot fix poor design or bias in the original studies, which argues for including only sound ones. The method has delivered pointed verdicts. A 2020 meta-analysis of 180 studies found no evidence of the decoupling of growth from environmental harm needed for ecological {{ref:nature-eecon-208}}. A 2021 meta-analysis of 3186 estimates rejected the {{ref:nature-eecon-225}}.

nature-found-045.title: Market failure: when free markets squander value
nature-found-045.text: Mainstream economics keeps a list of the ways free markets go wrong. Market failure is a situation in which a free market's allocation of goods and services is not efficient, so economic value is lost. The causes on the list include the power of a single dominant seller, externalities, and missing or unequal information. Others are one side's greater power to bargain, irrational behaviour, and unemployment or inflation. Another cause is goods that no one can be kept from enjoying, explored in {{ref:nature-econ-633}}. Economists who study the environment deal mostly with externalities. Governments respond in several ways. They often tax or restrict goods with negative externalities and subsidise goods with positive ones. Other remedies include rules based on weighing costs against benefits, or market tools that change incentives, such as emission fees or redefined rights of ownership. Most mainstream economists think government can sometimes improve the outcome, as with building codes or endangered species laws. But government interventions can themselves misallocate resources, a problem explored in {{ref:nature-found-064}}. Economists first used the term in 1958, though the idea is traced back to John Stuart Mill and Henry Sidgwick.

nature-found-030.title: Environmental economics: weighing what markets leave out
nature-found-030.text: Markets are often trusted to steer resources to good uses with no one in charge, through the combined effect of many self-interested choices. Environmental economists work where that steering cannot be relied on. Environmental economics is the branch of economics that studies environmental problems and the economic effects of policies meant to deal with them. Market failure, where markets do not put resources to their best use, is the idea at its centre. The field weighs the costs and benefits of policies on air pollution, water quality, toxic substances, solid {{ref:nature-eecon-231}} and global warming. Most environmental economists are trained as economists and bring economic tools to these problems. Putting an economic value on the environment is a major topic, because many natural resources carry no market price at all. The name became popular in the 1960s. Yet links between economics and the environment go back to Condorcet, Adam Smith, Malthus and Ricardo. An economic solution to environmental problems proposed by Ronald Coase is credited with settling the field as a sub-field of economics. It was once separate from the economics of natural resources, but the two are now hard to tell apart. Its main professional bodies are the Association of Environmental and Resource Economists and the European Association for Environmental and Resource Economists.

nature-pol-233.title: The Toxics Release Inventory: America's pollution register
nature-pol-233.text: The 1984 Bhopal disaster prompted Congress to create the Toxics Release Inventory in 1986, under the Emergency Planning and Community Right-to-Know Act. It is a public US database of toxic chemical releases and {{ref:nature-eecon-232}} activities reported by industrial and federal facilities. For most listed chemicals, a facility must report if it makes 25,000 pounds, or processes or uses 10,000 pounds, a year. Reports cover releases to air, water and land, and amounts of waste sent off-site.

nature-pol-033.title: Constitutional economics: agreeing on the rules of the game
nature-pol-033.text: Constitutional economics applies public choice and {{ref:nature-gov-242}} to the design of constitutional rules. Buchanan and Tullock argued that for government to benefit everyone, people must agree on the rules, not on every government action. They split decisions into two kinds. Constitutional decisions set lasting rules. Political decisions are made within those rules.

nature-eco-396.title: Denitrification: returning nitrogen to the air
nature-eco-396.text: In waterlogged soil, some bacteria breathe nitrate instead of oxygen. Denitrification covers the processes in oxygen-poor soil that turn nitrates and nitrites back into nitrogen gas or nitrous or nitric oxide, returning nitrogen to the air. It is done mainly by bacteria such as Pseudomonas and Paracoccus, which live without oxygen or can switch to doing so. Too much of it depletes soil nitrogen and fertility, and excess nitrogen {{ref:nature-eco-662}} can cause it. It also has uses. Because it removes nitrate and reduces leaching to groundwater, it can treat sewage and high-nitrogen animal waste.

nature-eco-294.title: Habitat: the place a species can live
nature-eco-294.text: The large blue butterfly lives only in chalk grassland, and only where certain ants live too. Its needs are narrow and exact. That set of needs is its habitat: the resources and the living and non-living conditions in a place that let a species survive and reproduce. Physical factors include soil, moisture, temperature range and light. Living factors include food supply and predators. A habitat can be seen as the physical form of a species' {{ref:nature-eco-281}}, its role in its surroundings. Species differ in how choosy they are. Generalists thrive in many conditions, while specialists like the large blue need a narrow set. Habitats on land include forests, grasslands, wetlands and dry lands. Freshwater ones include rivers, lakes, marshes and the peat wetlands described in {{ref:nature-eco-508}}. Losing its habitat is the single greatest threat to any species. {{ref:nature-eco-041}} is the leading cause of the loss of species and of extinction worldwide. Protecting habitats, through the parks described in {{ref:nature-gov-148}}, reserves or limits on human activity, is a necessary step in keeping biodiversity. Not all tree cover counts. Plantations of a single tree species add trees but fail to provide the varied habitat most woodland creatures need.

nature-econ-350.title: Natural monopoly: when one supplier is cheapest
nature-econ-350.text: In 1848 J.S. Mill first called some monopolies "natural," pointing to gas and water supply, roads, canals and railways. A natural monopoly is a firm whose cost per unit keeps falling across the whole range of market demand. One large supplier is then cheaper than several small ones. Left alone, such markets tend to turn into a monopoly, often after an early entrant expands fast and drives out rivals. Breaking them up is inefficient by definition, so governments mostly use {{ref:nature-val-107}} and public ownership. Regulators often impose average-cost pricing. It removes excess profit but weakens the incentive to cut costs.

nature-econ-865.title: Public utilities: essential services under public control
nature-econ-865.text: A public utility is an organization that maintains the infrastructure for a public service, often also providing the service itself. Utilities supply goods considered essential, such as water, gas, electricity, telephone and waste disposal, and are subject to public control or {{ref:nature-val-107}}. The reason is the cost structure. Utilities are capital-intensive, with large {{ref:nature-econ-303}} and high {{ref:nature-econ-307}} for plants, lines and treatment facilities. Electricity transmission lines and natural gas pipelines have the traits of a {{ref:nature-econ-350}}: where infrastructure exists, competing brings little benefit. In the US, public utilities commissions regulate electric, gas, telecom, water and rail companies, approving or denying rate increases on behalf of ratepayers. In 1996, FERC Order No. 888 required electric utilities to open their transmission systems and unbundle transmission from other operations. That restructured the regulated {{ref:nature-econ-349}} toward competition among bulk sellers. Modern utilities may draw partly or wholly on clean and {{ref:nature-eecon-239}}, mostly wind turbines and solar panels. In OECD countries, wholesale {{ref:nature-clim-282}} has become far more decentralised with solar and wind power, while distribution and transmission networks often stay centralised and need heavy government involvement.

nature-eco-712.title: Free trade versus infant industries: an unsettled dispute
nature-eco-712.text: Should poor countries open their markets, or shield their young industries? Economists disagree. Paul Bairoch argues that liberalism forced on the Global South in the 19th century delayed its industrialization. Joseph Stiglitz notes that the US and Japan built their wealth by protecting infant industries, while the IMF and World Bank demand open markets from vulnerable economies. Ha-Joon Chang adds that import duties were only one tool of now-developed countries, alongside export subsidies, monopoly rights, cartel arrangements and directed credits. The question matters for how {{ref:nature-eco-711}} is judged.

nature-econ-786.title: The cost of equity: what shareholders expect
nature-econ-786.text: Shareholders expect to be paid for the risk they carry. The cost of equity is the return they require, inferred by comparing the shares with others of similar risk. It is commonly computed with the capital asset pricing model: the risk-free rate plus beta times the market's risk premium. Beta measures a security's sensitivity to movements in the market. The market risk premium has averaged around 5% in some developed countries during the twentieth century and up to 7% in emerging markets. The matching cost of {{ref:nature-mkt-153}} takes the risk-free rate on government bonds of the same term and adds a default premium.

nature-pol-075.title: Nonpoint source pollution: contamination with no address
nature-pol-075.text: A single factory pipe is easy to find. A thousand fertilized fields are not. Nonpoint source pollution is diffuse contamination of water or air that does not come from one identifiable source. It is often the combined effect of small amounts of pollutants gathered from a large area. It contrasts with {{ref:nature-pol-170}}, which comes from a single source. Nonpoint pollution travels by {{ref:nature-eco-275}}, rain, deposition from the air, drainage and seepage, which makes it hard to trace back. Paved city surfaces and farms that spread fertilizer and manure are major sources. Even a smokestack, a single source where it stands, acts as nonpoint where its pollution lands after being carried far and mixed with others. In the United States it is the leading cause of {{ref:nature-res-261}}, mainly from farm runoff and altered waterways.

nature-es-066.title: Land change models: forecasting the face of the Earth
nature-es-066.text: In 2011 a study in western Mexico ran two outwardly similar land change models and got considerably different results. That is a fair warning about a powerful tool. Land change models describe, project and explain how land cover and the human uses of land change over time. They help explain how people have changed Earth's surface and will change it, guiding decisions from a single plot to whole regions. The method applies landscape {{ref:nature-nbs-347}} and is a key part of land change science. Approaches include machine-learning models trained on past land cover, cellular models that compare neighboring areas, economic supply-and-demand models, agent-based models and hybrids. The model should fit the goal: agents for questions about policy and actors, machine learning and cellular models for spotting patterns. Practitioners use them to explore the effects of policies on water, food, {{ref:nature-res-273}} and more. All carry irreducible uncertainty, and the further ahead they project, the more uncertain they become.

nature-econ-151.title: Absolute advantage: simply being better at it
nature-econ-151.text: Suppose the UK needs fewer hours to make cloth and Portugal fewer to make wine. By specializing and trading, both end up with more of each good. That is absolute advantage at work: the ability of a person, firm or country to produce a good or service more efficiently than others. Adam Smith first described it in The Wealth of Nations in 1776. Arguing against {{ref:nature-hist-022}}, he said all nations could gain from trading freely and specializing. Yet a party can lack an absolute advantage in anything and still gain from {{ref:nature-res-268}}, through the principle covered in {{ref:nature-econ-106}}.

nature-acct-025.title: Environmental functions: when nature's uses compete
nature-acct-025.text: Water can serve as {{ref:nature-nbs-326}} or as a dumping ground for waste, but once pollution passes a threshold, the two uses compete. Each is an environmental function: a possible use of the physical surroundings people did not make, on which they depend for producing, consuming, breathing and recreation. When one use comes at the expense of another, the functions compete. Competing functions are scarce, and so they are economic goods ({{ref:nature-found-051}}). Most functions that were once free goods, so plentiful that using them cost nothing, have become scarce.

nature-eco-504.title: River ecosystems: water that drains the land
nature-eco-504.text: Fast, turbulent water carries more dissolved oxygen than a slow pool, and it supports more species. A river ecosystem is a flowing-water, or lotic, ecosystem that drains the landscape, with its living things and physical and chemical conditions. Each river is part of a larger watershed, where small headwater streams feed ever larger channels. Food sources change along the way. Streams under a forest canopy get most of their food from trees, while wider, open streams get most from algae. Threats include water loss, damming, chemical pollution and {{ref:nature-nbs-318}}. A {{ref:nature-nbs-319}} cuts spring {{ref:nature-nbs-329}} and traps sediment, harming wetlands downstream.

nature-res-147.title: Hardin, Ostrom and the fate of shared grazing land
nature-res-147.text: In 1968 {{ref:nature-hist-052}} argued that shared grazing land is bound to be overgrazed, a claim at the heart of the {{ref:nature-econ-606}}. He treated pastoralist land use as unstable and a cause of environmental damage, and his paper gave a basis for privatizing land. Many scholars call his assumption that herders cannot talk or make agreements implausible. Yet it shaped development projects that broke up working pastoral governance, often disastrously. {{ref:nature-hist-039}} disputed Hardin's view. She argued that community groups and cooperatives can manage shared grazing land more sustainably than privatization or full state control.

nature-eco-089.title: The insect decline: fewer bugs, uncertain numbers
nature-eco-089.text: In German nature reserves, the seasonal {{ref:nature-clim-284}} of flying insects fell by 76% over 1989–2016. Insects account for up to 90% of all animal species, so their fate matters. Since the 2010s, researchers have reported a widespread fall in insect numbers across many groups, sometimes reaching extinction. Estimates of insect species at risk of extinction range from 10% to 40%. A 2020 meta-analysis, which pooled 166 long-term studies, found land insects declining about 9% per decade, while freshwater insects rose 11% per decade. One study ranked the causes: habitat loss to cities and to farms that push land hard, {{ref:nature-hist-084}} and fertilizer pollution, pathogens and {{ref:nature-nbs-318}}, then climate change. The decline threatens insect-eating birds and mammals, and services such as pollinating crops and disposing of waste. Global trends are hard to judge. Data vary by time, place and species and come mostly from Western Europe and North America. A 2019 review projected that 40% of insect species could go extinct within decades, but that claim was challenged, and global estimates remain uncertain.

nature-eco-346.title: Ecological pyramids: picturing life's levels
nature-eco-346.text: In a pond at any moment, the phytoplankton weigh less than the fish and insects above them. They reproduce fast but live briefly. An ecological pyramid is a diagram showing the {{ref:nature-clim-284}} or productivity at each trophic level of an ecosystem, with producers at the base. It comes in three forms. A pyramid of energy shows the energy kept as new living matter at each level. A pyramid of living mass shows the living matter present. A pyramid of numbers counts individuals. Energy pyramids are normally upright. Their base is narrow to begin with: only 1 to 2 percent of the Sun's energy is absorbed by {{ref:nature-eco-190}} and turned into food. Living-mass pyramids can be inverted in the sea, as the pond shows. Number pyramids can invert too, when many beetles feed on one tree. Charles Elton developed the pyramid of numbers in 1927. Bodenheimer expressed it in living mass in 1938, and the energy pyramid draws on Hutchinson and Lindeman (1942).

nature-econ-087.title: Matter, power and design: an ecological view of production
nature-econ-087.text: Ecological economists replace land, labor and capital with three different factors: matter, {{ref:nature-eecon-238}} and design intelligence. The point is to make production obey physical limits. Matter can be recycled but never created or destroyed, so there is an upper limit on how much can be withdrawn and used. Usable power loses its usefulness over time, as when electricity running a machine turns into heat. Once matter and power are used at their maximum sustainable rates, only better design can raise output per unit. This underlies a central claim of the field: infinite growth is impossible.

nature-econ-088.title: Entrepreneurship: a fourth factor of production?
nature-econ-088.text: Land, labor and capital do not organize themselves. Entrepreneurship, the work of combining them to make a profit, is sometimes counted as a fourth factor of production. Some authors added it in the first half of the 20th century, and it became standard in the post-war neoclassical synthesis. Many economists today instead treat {{ref:nature-econ-531}} as the fourth factor, with entrepreneurship as one form of it. Others have proposed {{ref:nature-eecon-238}}, the value of social ties, or cultural heritage.

nature-eco-635.title: Ecosystem health: a useful metaphor or a value judgment?
nature-eco-635.text: {{ref:nature-hist-051}} wrote of land health and land sickness, and the metaphor goes back at least to the early 1800s. Ecosystem health is that metaphor: a way of describing the overall condition of an {{ref:nature-found-015}}. Fire, drought, invasive species, climate change, mining, fishing, farming and logging can all change that condition. The Great Lakes Basin tracks it with a suite of 80 lake health indicators, including native fish, phosphorus and toxic chemicals. Yet there is no universal benchmark. Judgments depend on the measures chosen and on society's goals. Species in an ecosystem also reshuffle over time, so a healthy state is hard to pin down. Supporters value the idea as a simple way to communicate. Critics argue it is a value judgment passed off as science, and propose neutral terms such as ecosystem status, ecosystem prognosis or ecosystem {{ref:nature-eecon-208}}.

nature-found-046.title: Ecological market failure: when the economy outruns nature
nature-found-046.text: Ecological economists make a bolder claim than most: the market cannot exist without "failing". Firms, they argue, routinely shift social and ecological costs onto others, including future generations. An ecological market failure is one in which economic activity exhausts vital resources that cannot be replaced, damages fragile ecosystems or overloads nature's ability to absorb {{ref:nature-eecon-231}}. Today's prices cannot reflect the wishes of people not yet born, so finite minerals are not shared fairly over time, an issue called intergenerational fairness. Resources that renew themselves but that no one clearly owns get overused, as in too much fishing and grazing, a pattern explored in {{ref:nature-econ-606}}. Climate change is presented as an overwhelming example, with the atmosphere as a global common that no one owns. Growth becomes uneconomic when its ecological costs exceed its social benefits, a case explored in {{ref:nature-eecon-090}}. Herman Daly and Nicholas Georgescu-Roegen called for government limits on the overall level of economic activity. Ecological economists say most mainstream economists overlook these failures, because the standard test of efficiency ignores time.

nature-eco-699.title: Controlled burns: fighting fire with fire
nature-eco-699.text: Managers sometimes light fires on purpose. A controlled or prescribed burn is a fire set deliberately to remove built-up vegetation and decaying organic material from a landscape. Uses include tending forests, restoring ecosystems to health, land clearing and {{ref:nature-gov-243}} fuel management. Burns are usually done in cooler months. Fire can stimulate germination of some trees, and in grassland it shifts species towards natives and removes invasives. Planning stresses safety, preventing escape and limiting smoke. Back burning against the wind gives a slower, controllable fire and a black line. Indigenous peoples use fire worldwide, and it has been used to clear land since the Neolithic. The risk is real: the Calf Canyon/Hermits Peak Fire, New Mexico's largest fire in wild land, began from two US Forest Service controlled burns that got out of control and merged.

nature-pol-036.title: The median voter theorem: why the middle wins
nature-pol-036.text: Line up voters and candidates along one left-right spectrum, and majority-rule voting elects the candidate the middle, or median, voter prefers. That is the median voter theorem. Voters are assumed to rank candidates by closeness, so the candidate nearest the median voter beats every rival by a majority. Duncan Black first derived it in 1948, and Kenneth Arrow independently. With two candidates a simple majority vote satisfies it; with more, any Condorcet method does. In more than one dimension there may be no majority winner, as the McKelvey–Schofield chaos theorem shows. The theorem is popular in {{ref:nature-gov-242}} because it yields testable links between voters and policy. The tests are not kind. Levitt (1996) found senators from the same state but different parties voted only slightly more alike than random pairs, and studies from India also contradict its predictions.

nature-eco-099.title: Endangered species and the bald eagle's comeback
nature-eco-099.text: In 1963 the United States had just 417 nesting pairs of bald eagles. By 2020 it had 71,400, thanks to habitat protection, legal protection and a ban on the {{ref:nature-hist-084}} DDT. An endangered species is one at very high risk of going extinct in the near future, worldwide or in a particular region. On the IUCN's Red List, described in {{ref:nature-eco-087}}, "Endangered" sits between "Vulnerable" and "Critically Endangered". The criteria are specific. One is a population that falls 20% within five years and has fewer than 2,500 mature individuals left. Another is a decline of 50% to 70% over 10 years or three generations, whichever is longer. Species become endangered mainly through habitat loss and loss of genetic variation. In 2026 the Red List named 49,500 species worldwide as threatened with extinction. Many nations respond by banning hunting or harvest, restricting development or setting land aside as reserves.

nature-eco-273.title: The sulfur cycle: an element that trades electrons
nature-eco-273.text: Sulfur is found in many proteins, so every living thing needs it. The sulfur cycle is the biogeochemical cycle that moves sulfur between rocks, waterways and living things. It runs through changes in sulfur's oxidation state, a count of how many electrons an atom has given up or gained. That state ranges from +6 in sulfate to −2 in sulfides. The steps include breaking down organic sulfur to hydrogen sulfide, oxidizing sulfide to sulfate, and reducing sulfate back to sulfide. Microbes that oxidize sulfide often use the energy to fix carbon dioxide, building it into living matter. Sulfur compounds can also serve in cellular respiration. Earth's main sulfur sink is the sulfate dissolved in the oceans. In the seabed, sulfate is used to break down buried organic matter and {{ref:nature-eco-727}}. Deeper down, where the sulfate runs out, its production takes over. Sulfur also takes part in forming fossil fuels and most metal ore deposits.

nature-eco-241.title: Net ecosystem production: the carbon an ecosystem keeps
nature-eco-241.text: Net ecosystem production is the carbon an ecosystem has left after every living thing in it has respired. Formally, it is gross primary production minus all the respiration in an ecosystem, by plants, animals and microbes. It is given as mass of carbon per area per time, such as grams of carbon per square meter per year. The leftover carbon can be stored as {{ref:nature-clim-284}}, buried in {{ref:nature-eco-682}} or soils, or exported to another system. It can also be burned, or broken down by sunlight, and so turned back into carbon dioxide. Net primary production is different: it subtracts only the plants' own respiration, not that of animals and microbes. The measure has practical uses. It is one of the main factors directly linked to {{ref:nature-eco-727}} emissions from wetlands.

nature-val-017.title: Shadow prices: money values where markets are silent
nature-val-017.text: Clean air has no price tag, yet a cost–benefit analysis needs one. A shadow price fills the gap. It is a money value given to something not traded in a market, or a market price corrected for distortions and social effects. Shadow prices are needed for two reasons. Externalities, costs and benefits that fall on people outside a deal, go unpriced. And taxes, subsidies, quotas and import duties distort market prices. Tools for estimating them include contingent valuation, benefit transfer, hedonic pricing and the travel cost method. Lacking reliable data, analysts often build them from assumptions, so they are subjective and somewhat inaccurate. They are still widely used to value intangible costs and benefits, especially for public goods rarely bought and sold. Measures of a nation's total wealth use them as weights on produced, human and natural capital. That use is controversial, because little is known about how life-supporting ecosystems produce their benefits.

nature-econ-785.title: WACC: blending the cost of borrowing and equity
nature-econ-785.text: The weighted average cost of capital, or WACC, blends the cost of {{ref:nature-mkt-153}} and the cost of equity into a single cost of capital. It is the minimum return a firm must earn to satisfy its lenders, owners and other capital providers, or they will put their money elsewhere. It can serve as the discount rate for a project's free cash flows. For profitable firms, it is cheaper than new equity because of tax advantages. Too much of it, though, raises default risk and borrowing costs. Management seeks the financing mix that minimizes the cost of capital and so maximizes the firm's value.

nature-eco-369.title: Parasitism: living on, and off, a host
nature-eco-369.text: Almost every free-living animal hosts at least one parasite species. Vertebrates alone host between 75,000 and 300,000 species of helminths, or parasitic worms. Parasitism is a close relationship in which one organism, the parasite, lives on or in another, the host, and harms it. Parasites range from the protozoans that cause malaria to hookworms, lice, fungi such as honey fungus, and plants such as mistletoe. Parasitic plants make up about one per cent of flowering plants and occur in almost every biome. Unlike organisms that break down dead matter, parasites feed on living hosts. Their burden is lopsided: most hosts carry few parasites, while a few hosts carry the great majority. Farmers put parasites to work. Parasitoid wasps and microbial pathogens serve as biological control agents in {{ref:nature-res-257}}.

nature-pol-076.title: Sediment, nutrients, toxins and germs in runoff
nature-pol-076.text: Four kinds of pollutant dominate runoff: sediment, nutrients, toxic chemicals and disease-causing pathogens. Sediment clouds water, cutting light for underwater plants and for the fish and shellfish that depend on them. Of the nutrients, phosphorus and nitrogen cause the most concern. The toxic chemicals include heavy metals and compounds such as PCBs and DDT, which resist breakdown and persist in the environment. For pathogens, coliform bacteria in runoff serve as an indicator of {{ref:nature-res-261}} rather than as a cause of disease.

nature-pol-311.title: Urban sprawl: cities that spread and spread
nature-pol-311.text: Researchers admit the term lacks precision. Urban sprawl is the rapid spread of cities and towns, often with low-density housing, single-use zoning and heavy reliance on the private car: unrestricted spread of housing, commerce and roads over large areas with little concern for dense urban planning. Single-use development separates homes, work, shops and recreation so far that walking, transit and cycling are impractical and every activity needs a car. It builds on {{ref:nature-pol-177}}. Sprawl often takes fertile farmland next to cities, and in the US a like-kind exchange tax break means the tax code subsidizes it. Environmental effects include land consumption, habitat loss, lower biodiversity and local ecosystem destruction; a review found {{ref:nature-res-273}} endangers more US species than any other human activity. Lost habitat and fragmentation raise contact between wildlife and people, which can raise vector-borne and zoonotic disease risk. Sprawl raises driving, vehicle emissions and air pollution, cuts physical activity, and raises crash risk through greater exposure to driving. Public services cost more in spread-out areas: roads, pipes, sewers and power lines are longer per household, so maintenance costs more.

nature-res-133.title: Groundwater, the planet's buried store of fresh water
nature-res-133.text: About 99% of the world's liquid fresh water lies underground. This groundwater fills the pore spaces of soil and rock, and the cracks in rock, beneath Earth's surface. At a certain depth, called the water table, soil or rock becomes completely saturated. In the {{ref:nature-eco-196}}, water soaking down from the surface recharges it, and it flows back out naturally at springs and seeps. People lean on it heavily. Groundwater supplies about half of the world's {{ref:nature-nbs-326}}, 40% of irrigation water and a third of industrial water. It makes up about 30 percent of readily available fresh water. It also works as natural storage, a buffer when surface water runs short in drought. Some of it is ancient: deep water that soaked in millennia ago is called fossil water. Not all of it is drinkable, because arsenic, fluoride and salt can contaminate it.

nature-eco-534.title: What people have done to estuaries
nature-eco-534.text: Chesapeake Bay's oysters once filtered the whole estuary every three or four days. After years of fishing them too hard, the job takes almost a year. Estuaries are degraded by pollution, taking too many fish, development, damming and diversions. Because they sit at the bottom of rivers, they gather pollutants from far upstream, and long-lived toxins can build up in aquatic life. Fertilizer and waste runoff deplete oxygen and can create dead zones, cutting water quality and fish numbers. {{ref:nature-nbs-319}} building and diversions have shrunk some great desert-river estuaries. The Colorado River Delta is now essentially a salt flat.

nature-eco-331.title: Ecological communities: many species sharing one place
nature-eco-331.text: Two species can share a meadow only if they make their living in different ways. Each species occupies a niche, and having different niches lets species coexist. Together, the populations of different species living in the same area at the same time form a community. It is also called a biocoenosis, a biotic community or an ecological community. The study of communities looks at how these coexisting species interact, and their distribution, structure and abundance. Some species carry outsized weight, among them the kinds described in {{ref:nature-eco-355}}, {{ref:nature-eco-301}} and {{ref:nature-es-086}}. Losing them often destabilizes the whole community. Ecologists often measure a community's structure through networks of who eats whom.

nature-res-183.title: The commons: resources that belong to everyone
nature-res-183.text: Before 1968, academic titles mentioning 'the commons' were very rare. Then an article by {{ref:nature-hist-052}}, 'The Tragedy of the Commons', turned an old English legal term for common land into a general word for shared resources. The commons are the cultural and natural resources open to all members of a society, such as air, water and a habitable Earth. The word can also mean resources a group of users governs for itself, through rules it creates, rather than through the state or the market. How a commons is run makes a large difference. In Mongolia, where herders moved together between grazing lands, grassland degradation was about 9%. Under state or household grazing land it was about 75% in Russia and 33% in China. Nepal handed forest control to communities from the late 1980s, giving locals a financial stake in preventing overuse. Globalization brings new pressures. Fish and timber are sold on world markets, which makes their impacts harder for local communities to monitor.

nature-eco-030.title: Island restoration: clearing out invaders
nature-eco-030.text: Removing invasive animals from just 169 islands would improve survival prospects for 9.4% of the most highly threatened island vertebrates, a 2019 study found. Island restoration repairs island ecosystems, chiefly by removing {{ref:nature-nbs-318}} and bringing back native ones. Islands hold many of the world's endemic species. Their small size also makes them very vulnerable to them.

nature-econ-385.title: Income elasticity of demand: what richer people buy
nature-econ-385.text: As people grow richer, their spending on food grows more slowly than their income, an observation called Engel's law. Income elasticity of demand measures this kind of response: how strongly the quantity of a good people buy responds to a change in their income. It is the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in income. If a 10% rise in income lifts demand by 20%, it is 2.0. Normal goods score positive and inferior goods negative; below 1 marks a necessity and above 1 a luxury. Food as a whole lies between zero and one. Estimates for gasoline in developed economies range from 0.66 to 1.26. Elasticities for food and {{ref:nature-eecon-238}} tend to fall as incomes rise: for cereals, from 0.62 in Tanzania to 0.05 in the United States. As economies get richer, spending shifts toward services, which need fewer commodities to produce. The pattern matters for nature. Most measures of environmental damage rise with income, though with an income elasticity below one.

nature-eco-653.title: Human ecology: people inside their environments
nature-eco-653.text: A city leans on far more land than lies inside its limits: typically at least ten times as much. Human {{ref:nature-nbs-347}} studies ties like these, the ways humans relate to their natural, social and built environments. It emerged from the study of nature and the social sciences in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It examines how populations adapt to environments and how technology and economies shape {{ref:nature-eecon-208}}, extending the study of {{ref:nature-eco-129}}.

nature-eco-743.title: Woody plant encroachment: when shrubs take over grassland
nature-eco-743.text: Open grassland can quietly turn into scrub. Woody plant encroachment is the spread and thickening of native shrubs and bushes at the expense of grasses and forbs. It concerns native plants, not alien invasives, and can shift open grasslands and savannas to closed woodlands. It affects an estimated 500 million hectares on all continents, and the UNCCD names it a key contributor to rangeland loss. Causes include overgrazing, suppressed fires in wild land, fewer wild herbivores, land abandonment, and possibly climate change. Once established, shrubs suppress grass. The result is a form of land degradation harming biodiversity, the refilling of groundwater, carbon storage and herbivore carrying capacity. The cost is economic too: in the western United States, rangeland tree expansion has cost producers an estimated $5 billion since 1990. Encroached grasslands can be a stable state that does not return on its own, and restoring them is difficult.

nature-res-221.title: Hotelling's rule: why oil in the ground should gain value
nature-res-221.text: An owner of oil faces a choice each year: extract now, or leave it in the ground and sell later. In 1931 {{ref:nature-hist-062}} published the classic answer in the Journal of {{ref:nature-gov-242}}. Hotelling's rule describes how the net price of a non-renewable resource should change over time when its owner extracts it to earn the most rent. The net price is the selling price minus costs. With efficient extraction it rises each period by a percentage equal to the discount rate, which maximizes the present value of the resource. The rule also implies that efficient use of a resource that cannot be added to, under stable conditions, ends in its depletion. The largest rent obtainable while emptying the stock is the subject of {{ref:nature-res-252}}. That rent equals the net price, and equals the shadow value of the natural capital still in the ground. L. C. Gray had published a similar result for a single mine owner in 1914.

nature-eco-227.title: How plants change the water a landscape yields
nature-eco-227.text: A dense forest may actually reduce the water that flows out of a landscape. The type and density of vegetation strongly shape evapotranspiration, and so how much water a landscape yields. Dense vegetation such as forest may raise evapotranspiration, sending more water back to the air and less downstream. Rainforests are an exception. While they stand, they raise humidity, cool the ground and slow winds, increasing stream flows and groundwater. Clearing them often turns land toward {{ref:nature-eco-703}} as soils dry out and erode. Deforestation also lowers evapotranspiration and so the moisture in the air, which can reduce rain downwind.

nature-econ-866.title: Utility rate control: three ways to cap a price
nature-econ-866.text: Regulators of a {{ref:nature-econ-865}} have three common tools for setting the price it may charge. Average-cost pricing sets the price equal to average production cost at the break-even point, serving most of the market, but regulated firms then lack incentive to minimise costs. Rate-of-return {{ref:nature-val-107}} lets firms set any price so long as the return on invested capital stays under a cap. It is flexible but can cause overcapitalization, since investing more capital raises the allowed profit. Price cap control directly sets a maximum price, which can result in a loss of service area.

nature-acct-061.title: Embedded emissions: the carbon hidden in trade
nature-acct-061.text: In 2004, 23% of global emissions were embedded in internationally traded goods. They flowed mostly from China and developing countries to the US, Europe and Japan. Embedded emissions, also called embodied emissions or embodied carbon, are the greenhouse gases released in making a good, counted as belonging to whoever consumes it. Emissions are usually counted where they are produced, as countries do when reporting under the UN climate convention ({{ref:nature-clim-053}}). So emissions embedded in imports are attributed to the exporting country. Wang and Watson suggested in 2007 that nearly a quarter of China's CO2 emissions might come from producing exports. In Western Europe, imported emissions make up 20-50% of consumed emissions. Choosing between production and consumption accounting is partly a question of fairness: who is responsible for emissions? One response is {{ref:nature-pol-265}}, a {{ref:nature-pol-321}} on the carbon embedded in imports.

nature-econ-594.title: Stocks and flows: what you have versus what moves
nature-econ-594.text: Michał Kalecki once called economics 'the science of confusing stocks with flows'. The joke rests on a simple distinction. A stock is a quantity that exists at one point in time. A flow is a quantity measured per unit of time. Suppose a country has 20 machines on 1 January 2010 and 23 a year later. The machine count on each date is a stock. The change between them, 3 machines per year, is a flow, the country's net new equipment for 2010. A nation's whole capital stock works the same way: the flow of new machines and buildings adds to it, and the flow of wear and tear drains it. Capital itself is a stock that yields a periodic income, which is a flow. Because stocks and flows have different units, they cannot be added or compared directly. A nation's capital stock is measured in dollars, while its yearly output is measured in dollars per year. Their ratios still make sense. A country's {{ref:nature-mkt-153}} divided by its yearly output gives a figure measured in years. Irving Fisher formalized the distinction in economics in 1896, and it runs through everything that follows in this chapter.

nature-pol-171.title: Regulating and monitoring pollution
nature-pol-171.text: Behind every pollution limit stand an agency and a measurement. Regulation and monitoring of pollution means the laws and agencies that limit pollution and reduce its harm, together with the measuring of pollution levels. Locally, environmental agencies or the public health system usually oversee it. The modern system began with US rules on industrial and mining air pollution and {{ref:nature-res-261}} in the 1960s and 1970s. Because many pollutants cross borders, UN treaties regulate them too, such as the {{ref:nature-clim-094}} of 1987 on ozone-depleting chemicals. Polluters have historically lobbied governments of poorer countries to keep regulation lax.

nature-res-112.title: Aquifers: not underground lakes, but soaked rock
nature-res-112.text: An aquifer is not an underground river or lake. It is a layer of porous, permeable or fractured rock, or of gravel, sand or silt, saturated with groundwater. Porous means full of tiny spaces; permeable means water can move through them. People tap aquifers through wells for {{ref:nature-nbs-326}}, farming and industry. Between aquifers may lie an aquitard, a layer of clay or non-porous rock that restricts groundwater flow. Trouble starts when people take out more water than nature puts back. That exceeds the aquifer's practical sustained yield, the amount it can supply year after year. The results include {{ref:nature-res-137}}, sinking land, creeping salt and polluted groundwater.
