The Ogallala Aquifer shows the scale: in its arid parts, annual recharge is only about 10 percent of annual withdrawals.

nature-eco-545.title: Vegetated coasts: seagrass, mangrove and marsh together
nature-eco-545.text: Seagrass beds, mangrove forests and tidal marshes together cover about 50 million hectares. These plant-dominated shore habitats are known as vegetated coastal ecosystems. They provide fish production, coastline protection, pollution buffering and high carbon storage. Their secret lies below. They sit on organic-rich sediments, sometimes metres deep, whose carbon stocks can be several times those of forests. When they are degraded or converted, that sediment is exposed to oxygen, and microbes release large amounts of greenhouse gases. They are being lost to fish farming, {{ref:nature-res-257}}, damming, dredging, eutrophication, urban development and rising seas.

nature-eco-350.title: The climax community: succession's supposed end point
nature-eco-350.text: Classical thinking about nature held that succession ends in a climax community. Such a community is in steady balance with its environment and persists unless heavily disturbed. It is described as having a wide variety of species and complex feeding links. At climax, gross primary production is balanced by total respiration. Nutrient uptake from the soil is balanced by nutrients returned in falling litter. The intermediate stages on the way are called seral communities. Frederic Clements held that succession converges on a stable climax set by climate. Modern ecologists have largely abandoned that idea for views in which nature does not settle into one fixed balance.

nature-res-191.title: Enclosure: fencing off England's common land
nature-res-191.text: From the 1530s to the 1640s, enclosure riots were the leading form of social protest in England. Enclosure was the practice of fencing off 'waste' or common land and taking it over, stripping commoners of their traditional rights to use it. It merged scattered strips into large fields bounded by hedgerows, walls or fences, for the sole use of owners or their tenants. Parliament passed the first enclosure act in 1604. Its stated aim was more efficient farming, but enclosed land also became much more valuable. In Tudor England, high wool profits led lords to turn common fields into sheep {{ref:nature-nbs-350}}, evicting villagers. The movement probably peaked from 1760 to 1832, and surplus rural workers moved to towns to become industrial workers. The Hammonds said it ruined small farmers, cottagers and squatters. Chambers and Mingay argued it brought more food, more cultivated land and more rural jobs. Many Marxists see it as 'primitive accumulation' that laid the ground for capitalism.

nature-eco-408.title: Are trophic cascades weaker on land?
nature-eco-408.text: The earliest documented trophic cascades were all in water, which led to speculation that cascades are mainly an aquatic phenomenon. The debate over terrestrial trophic cascades asks whether cascades on land are as strong as those in lakes, streams and seas. A 2002 meta-analysis found them generally weaker on land, with smaller changes in plant {{ref:nature-clim-284}}. A 2009 study, however, found many tree species heavily affected by the loss of an apex predator. Critics note that real food webs blur trophic levels through omnivory, diets that change as animals grow, and food arriving from outside. Studies still disagree.

nature-eco-364.title: The upside-down pyramid of life in the sea
nature-eco-364.text: In the sea, consumers can outweigh the producers that feed them. Their total mass can exceed that of the producers, turning the usual {{ref:nature-clim-284}} pyramid upside down. The reason is speed. Ocean producers are tiny, fast-reproducing phytoplankton, so a small mass can sustain a high rate of primary production. Land producers such as mature forests need far more mass for the same output. As a result, zooplankton make up most marine animal mass, and they link phytoplankton to the rest of the food web.

nature-eco-601.title: Planetary integrity: keeping Earth's life support working
nature-eco-601.text: Planetary integrity is the healthy functioning of Earth's life-support systems, the {{ref:nature-found-022}} among them. It is also called ecological integrity. Scholars say it must be maintained for the long term. It belongs to the same family of ideas as {{ref:nature-eco-597}}.

nature-eco-513.title: Boreal ecosystems: the subarctic belt of the north
nature-eco-513.text: Boreal soils hold about 338 Pg of carbon, comparable to the carbon in all the living matter of tropical ecosystems. A petagram (Pg) is a billion tonnes. A boreal ecosystem is a subarctic ecosystem of the Northern Hemisphere, roughly between 50° and 70°N, commonly called taiga. It spans parts of North America, Europe and Asia. Its plants range from black and white spruce to willows, wildflowers and alders, and caribou move in during winter to eat lichen. Boreal systems are less diverse than tropical ones but still hold a variety of species. Disturbance keeps them cycling. Fires in wild land, {{ref:nature-nbs-329}}, mudslides and insect outbreaks clear ground and drive secondary succession, the regrowth of plant communities on disturbed land. Boreal ecosystems are among those most vulnerable to climate change.

nature-res-233.title: Ricardo's law of rent
nature-res-233.text: 'Corn is not high because a rent is paid, but rent is paid because corn is high.' With that line David Ricardo turned an everyday assumption upside down. Around 1809 he formulated the law of rent, set out fully in On the Principles of {{ref:nature-gov-242}} and Taxation. It says the rent of a piece of land equals the extra output it produces compared with the best land available rent-free, using the same labor and capital. Ricardo's example used plots yielding 100, 90 and 80 units of corn. Once the 90-unit plot must be farmed too, the best plot earns a rent of 10 units. The output of the best rent-free land is called the margin of production. The law is the origin of the term Ricardian rent. It applies to urban and rural land alike, and to any natural factor of production that is privately owned. Ricardian rent differs from contract rent, the payments tenants actually make for using others' property.

nature-eco-090.title: Wildflower strips: flowers at the field's edge
nature-eco-090.text: Insects in German nature reserves were found to carry about 16 farm chemicals against pests on average. One response has been to propose buffer zones with reduced {{ref:nature-hist-084}} use around reserves. Wildflower strips work at the farm itself. They are strips of land at field edges, sown with flowering plants that pollinators favor. They aim to sustain local biodiversity, conserve insects, restore farmland birds and offset the harms of agricultural intensification, answering {{ref:nature-eco-089}}.

nature-pol-112.title: Green border taxes: taxing trade to cut pollution
nature-pol-112.text: Should a country tax imports made with dirty processes? A green border tax, also called an environmental {{ref:nature-pol-321}}, is a trade barrier such as an import or export tax used to reduce pollution. It targets goods with a large carbon footprint, or goods from countries with lax environmental rules; a {{ref:nature-pol-265}} is one type. Supporters say it could stop foreign countries gaining an advantage from weak rules and bring partners' standards into line. Critics argue it reduces trade without reaching the main sources of pollution, much of which arises within a country's own borders. Developing countries fear that environmental goals will be used as cover for shielding domestic industry from foreign competition. Import duties alone can also weaken export competitiveness and contribute to deindustrialization. Underneath lies an open question: does freer trade increase pollution, or, by raising incomes, end up reducing it?

nature-pol-265.title: Carbon border charges: pricing the carbon in imports
nature-pol-265.text: If one country prices carbon and its neighbor does not, factories may simply move. A carbon {{ref:nature-pol-321}}, or border carbon adjustment, is a charge on imports according to the carbon emitted in making them ({{ref:nature-acct-061}}). Its usual aim is to prevent {{ref:nature-pol-252}}, the shift of emissions to states that have no carbon price. Likely targets include electricity from coal-fired power stations, iron and steel from blast furnaces, and fertilizer from the Haber process. California has applied one to imported electricity since 2011, and the EU and UK apply them from 2026 and 2027. Border adjustment is considered an economically efficient fix for leakage, but it might disguise trade barriers meant to shield home industry. Current WTO rules may prohibit some types, and the WTO has reached no conclusion.

nature-eco-669.title: Cutting emissions of a heat-trapping gas
nature-eco-669.text: Capturing and using {{ref:nature-eco-727}} can deliver environmental and economic benefits together. The IEA says about 40% of fossil-fuel emissions of the gas, 9% of all human emissions of the gas, could be eliminated at no net cost to firms with existing technology. The US EPA's 1996 Landfill Rule requires large landfills to collect and burn the gas landfills give off, though it excludes 96% of US landfills. Satellites such as Sentinel-5P, at about 50 square kilometre resolution, monitor emissions; MethaneSAT aims for 1 kilometre.

nature-eco-291.title: Functional roles: what species do, not just what they are
nature-eco-291.text: In 1927 Charles Elton proposed sorting the members of an ecosystem into 'guilds' of similar resource users. That idea grew into the study of what species do, the branch of biology that studies the roles, or functions, species play in their community or ecosystem. It emphasizes how species' bodies work, how they are built, and how they grow and breed. From the 1970s guilds were renamed functional groups. From the 1990s biodiversity came to be seen as a diversity of functions, not just of species. Restorations with a wider range of functions have shown lower levels of invasion by other species.

nature-econ-605.title: Leverage: running a business on borrowed money
nature-econ-605.text: Borrowing can magnify a business's profits, and its dangers. Leverage is the ratio between a firm's borrowed capital, its {{ref:nature-mkt-153}}, and its own capital, its equity. Own capital comes from the owners, for example from money they have put aside or inherited. Borrowed capital comes through borrowing and usually must be repaid with interest. High leverage can bring higher profit, but it also raises the risk of insolvency, of being unable to pay what is owed.

nature-eco-217.title: Cultural eutrophication: the human hand in green water
nature-eco-217.text: Cultural eutrophication is eutrophication caused by human activity. It became more visible in the mid-1900s, when the green revolution spread chemical fertilizers through farming. Phosphorus and nitrogen are its two main causes, letting algae grow fast and bloom densely. Laundry detergents were once a major phosphate source. They fed the problem until phosphate detergents were phased out in the 1970s, and since then sewage and {{ref:nature-res-257}} have supplied most of the phosphate. Nitrogen comes mainly from farm runoff of fertilizer and animal waste, from sewage, and from nitrogen that settles out of the air. The label separates these cases from the slow enrichment that lakes undergo on their own, described in {{ref:nature-eco-218}}.

nature-pol-287.title: Water quality trading: cleaner rivers at the lowest cost
nature-pol-287.text: Different polluters in one watershed, the land draining to a river or lake, face very different costs to control the same pollutant. Water quality trading puts that gap to work. Sources that can cut {{ref:nature-res-261}} cheaply sell pollution-reduction credits to sources for whom cuts are costly. Most programs trade nutrients such as phosphorus and nitrogen ({{ref:nature-eco-245}}). The US EPA issued its Water Quality Trading Policy in 2003, and all programs must meet the {{ref:nature-pol-155}}. Funders include watershed beneficiaries, polluters compensating for their impacts and public good payers.

nature-econ-395.title: Market economies: letting prices guide production
nature-econ-395.text: In a market economy, strong demand with limited supply pushes prices up and invites more production. That price system is the heart of the definition. A market economy is one in which decisions about investment, production and distribution are guided by prices set through supply and demand. Prices signal people to adjust what they produce and invest. Market economies range from barely regulated free-market systems to interventionist ones, where governments correct market failures and promote welfare. All of them need clearly defined, enforceable rules of ownership ({{ref:nature-econ-621}}), though these need not be private: co-operatives and state firms can also deal in markets. Governments have several tools. They can set maximum or minimum prices, such as a lowest legal wage, or use taxes on harmful side effects ({{ref:nature-pol-088}}) to deal with externalities. Joseph Stiglitz argues that markets suffer from imperfect information and need government action to fix widespread market failures. A sustainable market economy tries to balance growth with environmental protection, using tax breaks, carbon trading and environmental rules.

nature-res-167.title: The human right to water and sanitation
nature-res-167.text: On 28 July 2010, the UN General Assembly recognized clean {{ref:nature-nbs-326}} and sanitation as a human right. The principle is that every life depends on them. Its clearest definition came in General Comment 15 of the UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, drafted in 2002. Recognition is not the same as enforcement, though. Only a few countries have written the right into enforceable law.

nature-es-120.title: Holding back the sea: defenses against storm surge
nature-es-120.text: After the North Sea {{ref:nature-nbs-329}} of 1953, engineers built storm-surge barriers that stay open for shipping but close when a surge threatens. The Dutch Delta Works, the Thames Barrier and the Saint Petersburg {{ref:nature-nbs-319}} are among the largest. Barriers are hard infrastructure. Communities can also use soft infrastructure such as dunes or mangroves, better building, and social measures. Warnings, education and local evacuation plans reduce the toll on people.

nature-res-192.title: The open-field system before enclosure
nature-res-192.text: Before {{ref:nature-res-191}}, English common land lay under the lord of the manor. A manor was made up of peasant tenants' holdings and the lord's own farm, the demesne. Tenants held rights such as {{ref:nature-nbs-350}}, pannage, the right to let pigs forage, and estovers, the right to gather wood. Landless peasants often farmed narrow 'waste' strips nobody officially used. The system ended with new methods such as the Norfolk four-course rotation, which raised crop and livestock yields by improving soil fertility and cutting fallow periods.

nature-eco-647.title: Biotic resistance: why some invasions fail
nature-eco-647.text: Not every newcomer takes hold. Biotic resistance is the set of ecosystem properties that limit how well {{ref:nature-nbs-318}} can invade. Charles Elton applied the term to them. They include physical conditions such as temperature and drought, and living ones: competition, parasitism, predation and missing mutualists, the partners a species may need. Higher species diversity and lower resource availability can add resistance, extending {{ref:nature-eco-646}} to the problem of invasive species.

nature-eco-677.title: Three ways to draw a food web
nature-eco-677.text: A food web can be drawn as a bare map, a ledger or a web of influence. Topological webs are non-quantitative maps of which organisms eat which, compared by chain length and connectivity. Flow webs add quantitative carbon or nutrient transfer, built from the {{ref:nature-clim-284}} of each functional group, usually in kg carbon per hectare, assuming each group is in equilibrium. Interaction webs show how one group influences another, including indirect effects, such as a predator of root herbivores benefiting the plant roots. Community matrix models describe each link with Lotka-Volterra equations plus living-mass and feeding data, and can show how small changes affect web stability.

nature-eco-345.title: Why energy moves more efficiently in the sea
nature-eco-345.text: Energy passes between trophic levels more efficiently in the sea than on land. Transfer from phytoplankton to herbivorous zooplankton is estimated at about 20%, compared with 10% on land. Phytoplankton mass can turn over 100–300 times a year, while land plants turn over only 0.5 to 2.0 times. The number of levels shapes what the sea can support. Coastal upwelling zones, where deep water rises, may have as few as three trophic levels and support whales. Open oceans can have six and support only small tuna and squid at the top.

nature-econ-317.title: Returns to scale: what happens when you double everything
nature-econ-317.text: Double every worker and machine a firm uses, and what happens to output? Returns to scale is the answer: how much output rises, in proportion, when all inputs grow together in the long run. Constant returns mean output doubles too. Decreasing returns mean it less than doubles, mainly because management and coordination get harder as scale grows. Increasing returns mean it more than doubles, thanks to the efficiency gains of size. One firm can show all three, with increasing returns at low output, constant in between and decreasing at high output. Mainstream theory holds that technology alone sets the pattern, not market conditions. With fixed input prices, constant returns mean flat long-run costs per unit, decreasing returns mean rising ones and increasing returns mean falling ones. For a Cobb–Douglas function, returns are increasing if the exponents sum to more than 1, constant if they sum to 1, and decreasing if less. Increasing returns can also trap whole economies. Path-dependent increasing returns help lock industrial economies into fossil-fuel {{ref:nature-eecon-238}} systems.

nature-eco-711.title: Economic development: improving lives, not only output
nature-eco-711.text: Is a richer country always a better-off one? Economic development is the process by which the economic well-being and quality of life of a nation, region, community or individual are improved. It differs from {{ref:nature-econ-478}}: development is a policy intervention to improve well-being, whereas growth is a market phenomenon of rising productivity and output. Policies historically focused on industrialization and infrastructure, and since the 1960s on poverty reduction. In 1997 the UNDP defined development as increasing people's choices, naming empowerment, equity, productivity and {{ref:nature-eecon-208}} as chief factors. One flaw is that GDP per capita is calculated without deducting depreciation of fabricated assets or depletion and degradation of natural resources. The state's capabilities most often limit a country's goals, so a gradual approach avoids burdensome ones. The definition is itself contested: 20th-century economists stressed growth, while sociologists stress other aspects.

nature-res-002.title: What economists want from a fishery
nature-res-002.text: In 1954 H. Scott Gordon asked why fisheries so often ran down, and in 1955 Anthony D. Scott followed; both articles appeared in the Journal of {{ref:nature-gov-242}}. Economists define the goal of fisheries management as maximizing the present value of all future profits from a fishery. They often treat fisheries as common property resources, which suffer the problems of open access, chiefly overexploitation. Gordon showed that without intervention, fishers keep entering until total value minus costs is zero, so profits vanish. The two papers became foundational for environmental economics, giving the basic case for managing renewable resources. A main remedy for this market failure is to assign property rights, which the broadest economic survey suggests prevents population collapse. Newer models add differing technologies and costs among fishers, uncertainty and the biology of how fish populations grow.

nature-eco-603.title: Ecological resilience: taking a blow and recovering
nature-eco-603.text: A forest can usually recover when lightning or landslides damage up to 10 percent of its area. Beyond that, recovery gets harder. This capacity to resist damage from a disturbance and then recover is called ecological resilience. Canadian ecologist C.S. Holling introduced the idea to describe how natural systems persist through change. The shocks can be natural, such as fires, {{ref:nature-nbs-329}}, windstorms and insect outbreaks. They can also be human: deforestation, {{ref:nature-hist-084}} use and the introduction of exotic species. A large or long enough {{ref:nature-eco-624}} can push an ecosystem past a threshold into a different regime, a new set of processes and structures. Biodiversity loss, resource exploitation, pollution, changes in how land is used, and climate change increasingly cause such shifts, often to degraded states. The IPCC, the international panel that assesses climate science, widened the idea in its Sixth Assessment Report. Besides keeping function, identity and structure, resilience there includes the capacity to transform. The lesson for managers is practical. Using nature's goods and services sustainably requires understanding an ecosystem's resilience and its limits. Interest has shifted away from {{ref:nature-res-013}} toward managing whole ecosystems to build resilience, with management and governance that learn and adjust.

nature-eco-162.title: Greenhouse gases: the trace gases that warm the world
nature-eco-162.text: Nitrogen and oxygen make up 99% of dry air, yet they barely absorb heat radiation. Carbon dioxide, {{ref:nature-eco-727}} and nitrous oxide, under 0.1% of the air, do. A greenhouse gas is a gas in an atmosphere that traps heat and so raises the surface temperature of a planet such as Earth. It absorbs the heat radiation the planet gives off, and that produces the greenhouse effect. Water vapour causes 41–67% of the effect, but human activity does not directly change its global level. Most of the carbon dioxide people add comes from burning fossil fuels, plus cement, fertilizer and land-use change such as deforestation. Emissions reached an all-time high of 53.6±5.2 Gt CO2e per year over 2014–2023. That unit counts every gas by the amount of carbon dioxide that would warm as much, as {{ref:nature-eco-160}} explains. In 2022 the IPCC warned that emissions must peak before 2025 and fall 43% by 2030 for a good chance of limiting warming to 1.5 °C.

nature-eco-256.title: Permafrost: the Arctic's frozen carbon vault
nature-eco-256.text: Frozen soils cover nearly 9% of Earth's land, yet they store between 25 and 50% of the organic carbon in the world's soils. Ground that stays below 0 °C for at least two years in a row is called {{ref:nature-eco-678}}. The Arctic carbon cycle is the part of the global carbon cycle that moves carbon between frozen soils, plants and microbes, the atmosphere and back. The northern circumpolar region alone holds around 1,460–1,600 Pg, or petagrams, of organic carbon in its soils. That is more than double the carbon now in the atmosphere. The carbon is old: radiocarbon dating shows it is often thousands of years old. It got there slowly. Wind and rivers dropped {{ref:nature-eco-682}}, peat built up, and as the ground surface rose, the buried layers froze into the ground with their carbon locked inside. Early research often overlooked this huge store, but attention has grown enormously since the 2000s. What happens when it thaws is the subject of {{ref:nature-eco-257}}.

nature-eco-218.title: Natural eutrophication: lakes grow richer with age
nature-eco-218.text: Lakes naturally grow more productive as they age. Natural eutrophication is this slow enrichment of waters by the gradual build-up of {{ref:nature-eco-682}} and nutrients. It usually comes from dissolved phosphate minerals and dead plant matter collecting in the water. Climate, geology and other outside influences also regulate how productive a lake naturally is.

nature-econ-164.title: Causes of economic inefficiency: why economies fall short
nature-econ-164.text: Economies fall short of Pareto efficiency for many reasons. Imperfect market structures, such as monopoly, monopsony, oligopoly and monopolistic competition, cause inefficiency. So do hidden information, including problems that arise when one party acts for another, and the falling long-run costs of a natural monopoly. Governments add their own: limits on prices and quantities, and {{ref:nature-val-107}} arising from government failure. One inefficiency can offset another. If pollution leads to too many tires being made, a tax on tires might restore the efficient amount.

nature-econ-645.title: The bundle of rights: ownership as a set of sticks
nature-econ-645.text: Owning land is less like holding one thing than holding a bundle of sticks. Each stick is a separate right that can be split off, given to someone else and later put back. The idea began with Wesley Newcomb Hohfeld in 1913, though he never used the phrase. The five traditional rights are possession, control, exclusion, enjoyment, meaning use including resource extraction, and disposition, or transfer. A tenant may live on land while someone else owns the minerals or water beneath it. Governments keep rights such as environmental {{ref:nature-val-107}}, land-use rules and eminent domain, and third parties may hold others, such as {{ref:nature-mkt-126}}.

nature-econ-334.title: Forcing the better-informed side to speak up
nature-econ-334.text: Sometimes the side that knows more will not share it voluntarily. Mandatory information disclosure rules then require it to. In the United States, the Securities and Exchange Commission's {{ref:nature-val-107}} Fair Disclosure requires companies to reveal material information, the facts that could sway an investor, to all investors. The rule narrowed the information gap, and the evidence showed up in lower trading costs.

nature-econ-331.title: Akerlof's lemons: used cars and hidden flaws
nature-econ-331.text: In 1970 George Akerlof published a paper about used cars that brought information problems to the forefront of economic theory. In his model the seller knows a car's exact quality. The buyer knows only the chance that it is a bad car, a 'lemon'. A lemons market needs three things. Buyers cannot judge quality before buying, sellers gain by passing off bad goods as good, and sellers have no credible way to prove quality. A lack of reputation, {{ref:nature-val-107}}, guarantees or warranties helps produce it. Researchers still disagree on whether a lemons market actually exists in used vehicles.

nature-econ-019.title: Menus of contracts that make types sort themselves
nature-econ-019.text: A principal facing an agent with private information about its type can offer a menu of contracts, built so that different types pick different ones. In these screening models the best type usually trades as much as it would with full information, a result called 'no distortion at the top'. Other types trade less. Designing the best {{ref:nature-econ-671}} is a many-agent version of the basic screening model, and Roger Myerson and Eric Maskin pioneered these models. Applications include {{ref:nature-val-107}}, public procurement and price discrimination. The models have been tested in laboratory and field data.

nature-eco-317.title: Anti-environmentalism: the organized opposition
nature-eco-317.text: Environmentalism has organized opponents. Anti-environmentalism covers ideas and actions that oppose environmentalism as a whole or particular environmental policies. It can take the form of an organized countermovement that targets climate science and environmental {{ref:nature-val-107}}. Its actors may include workers in industries threatened by rules to protect the environment. They may also include anti-environmentalist think tanks, research groups that promote these views.

nature-eco-315.title: Free-market environmentalism: property rights as protection
nature-eco-315.text: Could a lawsuit protect a river better than a {{ref:nature-val-107}}? Free-{{ref:nature-res-117}} holds that free markets, property rights and tort law, the law of civil harms, are the best tools for a healthy environment. Its advocates rely on individual and class-action lawsuits to drive out polluters. Clear property rights, they argue, let people bargain for better outcomes and sue to stop harm. They blame environmental problems on laws that blur those rights and on transaction costs too high for bargaining. Critics reply that it cannot handle collective problems: water is hard to privatize and pollution is hard to trace.

nature-eco-417.title: What forests do for the planet and for people
nature-eco-417.text: Forests host 80% of all land-dwelling organisms. They provide many benefits to the planet and to people, from oxygen and carbon storage to water {{ref:nature-val-107}}, soil protection, habitat and products. They produce about 28% of Earth's oxygen and act as crucial carbon sinks. Trees store large amounts of water and help regulate underground water, evaporation and rain and snow patterns. Some researchers describe a 'biotic pump', in which forests help drive the water cycle by drawing moisture in from the ocean. Forests also hold the ground together. Without them, erosion and sediment get worse, and removing or compacting leaf litter worsens erosion and flooding. About 399 million ha of forest are set aside mainly to protect soil and water, 119 million ha more than in 1990. People also rely directly on forests for fuel and wood products; the boreal forest alone supplies much lumber and paper.

nature-eco-438.title: Studying city nature: a young and lopsided field
nature-eco-438.text: A review of 217 papers found most studies of urban ecosystem services were done in Europe, North America and China, at the scale of a single city. The {{ref:nature-nbs-347}} of cities, including the study of what urban nature provides, is a young field whose research is still limited and unevenly spread. Another review found a strong bias toward the northern hemisphere, with case studies mostly in the United States and China. Assessments use biophysical models, digital mapping and valuation, but few findings have been turned into policy on how land is used. Researchers are building better tools to map services such as water {{ref:nature-val-107}}, air cooling and the cleaning of water.

nature-es-004.title: Nature's Services: the 1997 book that framed a field
nature-es-004.text: In 1997 {{ref:nature-hist-053}} edited a book with a plain, insistent title: Nature's Services: Societal Dependence on Natural Ecosystems. It opens with her introduction, 'What are Ecosystem Services', followed by a history of the idea by Harold Mooney and Paul Ehrlich. The book laid out the framework still widely used for understanding nature's benefits to people. With Costanza and colleagues' global valuation, it became one of the two seminal 1990s works on the subject. It served as a model for ecosystem {{ref:nature-val-107}} in several regions and was a catalyst for the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment.

nature-es-012.title: Ecotourism: travel that is supposed to help
nature-es-012.text: In South Africa, 70% of the money the {{ref:nature-gov-148}} system makes comes straight from tourism. That is the promise of ecotourism: travel to natural places that aims to do little harm and to support conservation and environmental education. Some definitions add that it must pay its way for the host community or make conservation financially possible. It counts as one part of sustainable tourism. It differs from plain nature tourism by trying to build tourists' appreciation of habitats and local culture. The possible benefits are real: visitor spending and jobs, money to run and expand {{ref:nature-gov-038}}, and a reason to protect or restore natural land. So are the drawbacks. Visitors can still damage the places they protect, raise local rents and property values, and bring health risks to people and wildlife. Most ecotourism businesses belong to foreign investors, so most profits leave the area instead of returning to the local economy or conservation. The trips usually depend on flying, which adds to climate change, and few operators leave a net-positive mark on the environment. Weak {{ref:nature-val-107}} lets underwater hotels and helicopter tours call themselves ecotourism, a form of {{ref:nature-nbs-075}}. Environmentalists, interest groups and governments define the term differently, and where tourism stops being ecotourism is still disputed.

nature-es-039.title: Responsible tourism: everyone is accountable
nature-es-039.text: Responsible tourism is the set of behaviors and practices, by travelers and providers alike, that can lead to sustainable tourism. It aims to maximize benefits to local communities and minimize social and environmental harm. Both service providers and consumers are held accountable for the tourism they develop or join. Some critics argue it distracts from wider issues that need {{ref:nature-val-107}}, such as visitor numbers and environmental impact.

nature-econ-491.title: Income: what you gain over a period
nature-econ-491.text: Watching a sunset is a joy, but it is not income. Income is the ability to consume and save that a person, household or firm gains over a set period, usually counted in money. Because non-monetary joys are left out, reported income may misstate well-being. Income is also hard to define, and its meaning differs between fields. Economic income can differ from income as the law defines it. US tax law, for example, counts wages, salary, profit, interest, rent and other earnings received in a calendar year as household income. For a firm, gross income can be defined as all revenue minus the cost of goods sold. Some rules hold under every definition. Borrowing or repaying money is never income, but interest and forgiven {{ref:nature-mkt-153}} are. Education raises income by increasing workers' skills and productivity. Economists conventionally write income as Y. Because it is measured over a period, income is a flow, in the sense of {{ref:nature-econ-594}}.

nature-econ-500.title: Wealth versus income: the orchard and its apples
nature-econ-500.text: Picture an orchard. Wealth is like the value of the orchard on December 31, minus the {{ref:nature-mkt-153}} owed on it. Income is like the value of the apples it yields each year. The first is a stock, measured at a point in time. The second is a flow, measured per unit of time. For a nation's wealth in the national accounts, the liabilities that count are those owed to the rest of the world. The two are linked by behaviour. The wealth effect is the rise in total consumption that follows a rise in national wealth.

nature-econ-063.title: The pain of paying
nature-econ-063.text: Watching a taxi meter or a gas pump climb is unpleasant. Researchers call that feeling the pain of paying, a negative response to a financial loss. It depends on the mental account the money comes from. A $30 t-shirt feels like a bigger expense paid from $50 in a wallet than from $500 in a checking account. The feeling has a payoff: consumers who feel more pain of paying for the same goods hold less {{ref:nature-mkt-153}}.

nature-econ-448.title: Transversality conditions: how a plan should end
nature-econ-448.text: A plan over time needs a proper ending as well as a beginning. A transversality condition is an end-point condition needed for optimality when a dynamic problem's final state is left free ({{ref:nature-econ-465}}). With a free terminal value, the costate variable must equal zero at the final time ({{ref:nature-econ-466}}). In a lifetime consumption problem, a transversality condition says the consumer carries no {{ref:nature-mkt-153}} at the end of life. If the end lies infinitely far off, a transversality condition on the {{ref:nature-econ-446}} applies instead.

nature-es-084.title: Nutrient cycles: nature's recycling system
nature-es-084.text: In 1749 Carl Linnaeus wrote about nature's recycling in a book called Oeconomia Naturae, the 'economy of nature'. The phrase fits. A nutrient cycle is the movement of living and non-living matter back into the making of new living matter. Energy and matter behave very differently here. Energy flows one way through an ecosystem and is never reused, while mineral nutrients go round and round. The cycles include carbon, sulfur, nitrogen, water, phosphorus and oxygen, among others. Decomposition, the breakdown of dead matter, largely controls the recycling, and food webs full of different species do the work. Not every ecosystem balances its books. Some run a nutrient {{ref:nature-mkt-153}} and act as sinks, while others carry a surplus and act as sources, depending on climate, landform and geology. Most textbooks treat 'nutrient cycle' and 'biogeochemical cycle' as the same thing, though 'nutrient cycle' usually means cycling within one ecosystem. For people, this natural recycling is one of the ecosystem services that sustain human welfare, a supporting service on which much else depends.

nature-eco-169.title: Carbon sinks: the places that soak up carbon
nature-eco-169.text: A forest or an ocean does something no machine yet does at large scale: it pulls carbon out of the sky faster than it lets carbon go. Such a store is a carbon sink, a carbon pool, natural or artificial, that takes up more carbon from the atmosphere than it releases. Sinks are an important part of the natural carbon cycle. Globally, the two most important are vegetation and the ocean. Soils hold more carbon than all land plants and the atmosphere together, but heavy, industrial farming has severely depleted the carbon in many agricultural soils. For gases other than carbon dioxide, a sink need not store anything. It can break the gas down, as when nitrous oxide is reduced to harmless nitrogen gas. Artificial sinks store carbon in building materials or deep underground. Still, no major artificial system yet removes carbon from the air on a large scale. Meanwhile, deforestation and industrial {{ref:nature-res-257}} have depleted natural sinks, and this change in land use is one cause of global warming. Public awareness of sinks grew after the 1997 treaty described in {{ref:nature-clim-056}} promoted their use to offset emissions.

nature-eco-171.title: Helping forests, soils and seas store more carbon
nature-eco-171.text: Two of the most powerful tools for cutting emissions before 2030 are simple: restoring ecosystems and converting less land. Enhancing natural carbon sinks means managing forests, soils and other ecosystems so they remove more carbon dioxide from the air and store it durably. Preserving and strengthening sinks is an important way to slow global warming. It requires changes in farming and forestry, such as preventing deforestation and restoring ecosystems by replanting trees. The 2022 IPCC report calls these land-based options AFOLU mitigation, short for {{ref:nature-res-257}}, forestry and other land use. Ocean methods such as seaweed farming and fertilising the sea have been proposed, but none has yet been used at large scale.

nature-eco-667.title: The Green Revolution: gains and trade-offs
nature-eco-667.text: Few agricultural changes are praised and blamed so loudly. Its effects on hunger, income, health and the environment are mixed and argued over. A 2012 review found it contributed to widespread poverty reduction, averted hunger for millions and avoided converting thousands of hectares to cultivation. A 2021 study found it substantially raised income: a ten-year delay would have cost 17% of GDP per capita, and no Green Revolution could have halved developing-world GDP per capita. A 2020 study of 37 developing countries found modern crop varieties reduced infant mortality by 2.4-5.3 percentage points from a baseline of 18%. Critics answer that more food is not the same as reliable access to enough food. The shift brought malnutrition such as iron and vitamin-A deficiencies, with crops grown in single-crop fields often exported, fed to animals or made into fuel. Malthusian critics call it unsustainable, yet a 2021 study found it reduced population growth rather than increasing it. Effects on wild biodiversity are disputed. Higher yields may spare land, but worn-out land and nutrient depletion pushed farmers to clear forest to keep production up. Studies indicate it substantially raised CO2 emissions, while a 2021 study found it cut the land used for {{ref:nature-res-257}}. Its yield gains have been declining as social and environmental costs become clearer; the Evergreen Revolution aims at 'productivity in perpetuity without associated ecological harm'. Scholars disagree about the net effects on biodiversity, access to food and the environment.

nature-eco-231.title: The Haber process: feeding billions, at a price
nature-eco-231.text: Nearly 50% of the nitrogen in human tissues came from the Haber process. Synthetic fertilizer from the process greatly raised farm productivity and population, at the cost of energy use and nitrogen pollution. Vaclav Smil estimated that at 1900 yields, the 2000 harvest would have needed nearly four times more land. Called the detonator of the population explosion, the process helped world population grow from 1.6 billion in 1900 to 7.7 billion by 2018. Without it, modern {{ref:nature-res-257}} could not support 8 billion people. The costs are large too. Crops use less than 50% of applied nitrogen, so the process is one of the largest sources of reactive nitrogen build-up, and the runoff harms habitats. Making and using nitrogen fertilizer causes around 5% of all global heat-trapping emissions. Cheap synthetic fertilizer also weakens farmers' incentive to rotate in nitrogen-fixing legumes. Haber-process fertilizer is a typical high-carbon import that a {{ref:nature-pol-265}} might cover.

nature-eco-163.title: Greenhouse gas emissions: who emits, and how much
nature-eco-163.text: Global emissions run at about 50 Gt a year, and the estimate for 2024 was 57.7 Gt CO2eq. Greenhouse gas emissions are releases of greenhouse gases from human activities, which strengthen the greenhouse effect and drive climate change. Carbon dioxide from burning coal, oil and natural gas is the main cause. By sector, the power sector contributes about 27%, transport 15%, and industrial energy and {{ref:nature-res-257}} 11% each. Emissions began rising with fossil-fuelled industry around 1750 and grew rapidly after about 1950. China emits the most each year, followed by the United States, which emits more per person. Average emissions of 4.9 tonnes per person a year are over twice the 2.3 tonnes consistent with the 1.5 °C goal. There is one hopeful sign: 2015 was the first year with both global economic growth and falling carbon emissions.

nature-eco-105.title: Extinction: when the last of a species dies
nature-eco-105.text: More than 99.9% of all the species that have ever lived are gone. The average species lasts 1–10 million years. Extinction is the end of a species, reached when its last member dies. The end can come before that last death, though. A species is functionally extinct once its few survivors can no longer reproduce and recover. The exact moment is hard to pin down over a large range, so extinction is usually declared after the fact. Life on Earth has passed through at least five mass extinctions. Fossil studies confirm that climate change has caused extinctions. A 2003 review predicted that 15–37% of land species would be 'committed to extinction' by 2050 because of climate change. Humans have become an extra cause, both as a new mega-predator and by moving animals and plants around the world. Today the main human cause is habitat degradation, and {{ref:nature-res-257}} is the main cause of habitat degradation worldwide. In 2014 a special edition of the journal Science declared a widespread consensus that humans are driving mass species extinctions.

nature-eco-122.title: Genetic erosion: losing the variety within species
nature-eco-122.text: Keeping at least 90% of the northern quoll's genetic diversity requires conserving at least eight populations across Australia. Genetic erosion is any decrease in genetic diversity, whether natural or caused by people. Each organism's genome, its full set of genes, is unique. When one dies without breeding, any unique genes it carried are lost. Habitat loss and fragmentation, often from farming and infrastructure, speed the process, and so does diversity that is already low. Small populations are most at risk. Low diversity brings inbreeding and weak immunity, which can 'fast-track' a species toward extinction. In crops, the main driver is replacing local varieties of plants and animals with non-local ones, often commercial varieties. Many researchers see modern {{ref:nature-res-257}}'s push toward genetic and ecological uniformity as the main problem in managing farm ecosystems. Science offers some safeguards, but many are still too expensive. Protecting habitat and letting species live naturally in it remains the best defense.

nature-eco-075.title: Livestock genetic resources: 8,800 breeds
nature-eco-075.text: About 8,800 breeds of birds and mammals, within 38 species, are used for food and {{ref:nature-res-257}}. They are the genetic variety, a livestock case of {{ref:nature-gov-046}}, of these species, breeds and populations. The diversity can be held in live animals or in stored material such as frozen semen or embryos, a form of {{ref:nature-eco-074}}.

nature-eco-596.title: How many people can the Earth support?
nature-eco-596.text: In 10,000 BCE between 5 and 10 million people lived on Earth. By 1900 there were 1.5 billion. The agricultural and industrial revolutions had raised human carrying capacity. This is the number of people the Earth or a region can support, and it depends on how people live and the technology they use. Without the Haber-Bosch process for fixing nitrogen, described in {{ref:nature-eco-230}}, modern {{ref:nature-res-257}} could not support 8 billion people. These successes have come at grave cost, from climate change and ocean acidification to dead zones at river mouths. Degrading the ecosystem services people depend on could lower the ceiling again. Measuring it is arbitrary, because what counts as food or water, and trade between regions, change the answer. A 2004 review of 69 studies found an average predicted maximum of 7.7 billion, with bounds of 0.65 and 98 billion. Some argue 8 billion may already be too many. Sources disagree on that, and on how far technology can raise the limit.

nature-eco-567.title: Forests: where most of Earth's plant life stands
nature-eco-567.text: Forests contain 80% of Earth's plant {{ref:nature-clim-284}}, the total weight of living plant matter. They also account for 75% of the biosphere's gross primary production, the plant growth powered by sunlight. A forest is an ecosystem defined by a dense community of trees. Pinning that down is harder than it sounds, and there are hundreds of definitions. The FAO, the Food and {{ref:nature-res-257}} Organization of the United Nations, offers one. It counts land over 0.5 hectares with trees taller than 5 metres and more than 10 percent canopy cover. Land that is mainly farm or urban does not count. By that measure the world has 4.14 billion hectares of forest: 32% of global land area, or 0.50 ha per person. Some 45% of it lies in the tropics. Forests give oxygen, carbon storage, clean water, {{ref:nature-nbs-329}} control, timber, genetic reserves and recreation, regulate climate and rainfall, and support millions who live from them directly. That bounty is shrinking. Global forest area fell by 178 million hectares between 1990 and 2020, about the size of Libya. Most clearing now happens in the tropics, driven mainly by four commodities: wood, beef, soy and palm oil. Loss can flip a forest's role. If its plant diversity, density or area declines, a forest can turn from a carbon sink into a carbon source. Some researchers add a caution: forests can also impose costs, such as taking land from grazing and crops or reducing available water.

nature-eco-465.title: Living with floods on the floodplain
nature-eco-465.text: River {{ref:nature-nbs-329}}, especially on China's Yellow River, have been among the deadliest natural disasters, led by the 1931 China floods. Floodplain flood control covers the rules, maps, insurance and works that limit flood damage to floodplain residents. How far a floodplain floods depends on the size of the flood, expressed as a return period, such as the 100-year flood with a one-in-a-hundred chance each year. In the United States, a national program offers {{ref:nature-clim-039}} for properties in flood-prone areas drawn on risk maps. Yet upstream development such as a large car park can raise flood levels, and the maps are rarely updated. Some towns have been moved off floodplains. Elsewhere annual floods are part of the rural economy, supporting recessional {{ref:nature-res-257}}: planting as the water recedes.

nature-es-112.title: Medicinal plants: a pharmacy grown for defense
nature-es-112.text: Plants cannot run from insects, fungi or grazing animals, so they make hundreds of chemicals to fight back. Those defenses are why plants work as medicine. Medicinal plants are plants used to keep people healthy or treat illness, in traditional medicine since prehistoric times and in modern medicine today. The Food and {{ref:nature-res-257}} Organization estimated in 2002 that over 50,000 are used worldwide. Around a quarter of drugs prescribed in modern medicine come from them. By one 2023 estimate the global market was US$68 billion a year, growing 10–20% annually, with China and India leading production and export. In much of the rural developing world, traditional herbal medicine is people's only health care. Yet wild plants face climate change, habitat loss and over-collection. Caution applies too: as of 2015 most plant-based products had not been tested for safety and effectiveness, and natural does not mean safe.

nature-val-033.title: Accumulation by dispossession: a new enclosure
nature-val-033.text: Alongside mining and {{ref:nature-res-257}}, bioprospecting and ecotourism are now '{{ref:nature-res-264}} frontiers'. David Harvey calls this accumulation by dispossession. It is a new wave of enclosing shared resources, releasing nature's wealth to capital at very low or no cost. In this view commodification 'stretches' across space and time, and 'deepens' into more kinds of goods and services.

nature-acct-104.title: The trillions hidden in the world's food bill
nature-acct-104.text: Feeding the world costs far more than their prices show. Estimates of their hidden environmental, health and social costs, the ones market prices leave out, run to trillions of dollars. FOLU put them at USD 12 trillion in 2019. Hendricks and colleagues, in 2023, estimated USD 19 trillion, within a range of USD 7.2 to 51.8 trillion. The FAO's 2023 State of Food and {{ref:nature-res-257}}, assessing 154 countries one by one, arrived at USD 12.7 trillion. The largest share is not environmental. FAO later found that health costs from unhealthy diets made up 70 percent of all agrifood hidden costs in 2020.

nature-mkt-141.title: The Conservation Reserve Program: paying US farmers not to plow
nature-mkt-141.text: More than 9 billion tons of soil had been kept from eroding by December 1, 2015, thanks to one American program. Run by the US Department of {{ref:nature-res-257}}, the Conservation Reserve Program pays farmers to take cropland out of production. They plant protective cover such as grass, trees or buffer strips. It is a payment for ecosystem services on a national scale. Its aims are to reduce soil erosion, improve water quality and benefit wildlife. It grew out of the Soil Bank of the 1950s and was formally set up by the 1985 Farm Bill, with contracts of 10 to 15 years. Farmers receive rental payments, up to 50% of the cost of establishing cover, and extra incentives. Money is limited, so only the most qualified land is enrolled. The benefits reach beyond the fields. In 2007 it was estimated to have kept 278 million pounds of nitrogen and 59 million pounds of phosphorus from leaving farmland. Ducks in the Prairie Pothole Region rose 30 percent after 1992 with its help.

nature-mkt-091.title: The Gold Standard: credits with development benefits
nature-mkt-091.text: In 2003 WWF and partners created the Gold Standard to make sure carbon credits are real, verifiable and help development that lasts. It is a certification label for emission-reduction projects in the Clean Development Mechanism and the voluntary carbon market. Projects must prove additionality, avoid double certification and contribute to at least three of the UN's {{ref:nature-gov-010}}. Eligible types are {{ref:nature-eecon-239}}, energy efficiency, planting and replanting forests, and {{ref:nature-res-257}}. The {{ref:nature-hist-033}} lists it as eligible for its quality label.

nature-mkt-024.title: Farm biodiversity: the root of every crop
nature-mkt-024.text: Every crop and farm animal began in biodiversity. Agricultural biodiversity is all the parts of biodiversity that matter for food and farming. It earns income through food and raw materials, and through services farms need, such as pollination, pest control, nutrient cycling and climate regulation. Around 25% of the world's people are estimated to work in {{ref:nature-res-257}}, and by 2006 over 3 billion people depended on marine and coastal biodiversity for their livelihoods. Putting a money value on biodiversity in farming and wild food is both hard and controversial.

nature-res-229.title: Dutch disease: when a boom hollows out the rest
nature-res-229.text: In 1959 the Netherlands discovered the Groningen gas field, and Dutch manufacturing then declined. In 1977 The Economist coined a name for the pattern: Dutch disease. It describes the apparent link between a boom in one sector, such as natural resources, and a decline in others such as manufacturing or {{ref:nature-res-257}}. The mechanism runs through the currency. Boom revenues strengthen it, making the country's other exports dearer abroad and imports cheaper, so those sectors lose ground. Any large inflow of foreign currency can do this, including foreign aid and foreign direct investment. Trade theory says resource-rich countries should specialize in extraction, but this backfires when the resource runs down, because manufacturing cannot return as fast as it left. Diagnosis is hard. Still, very large, unexpected oil and gas discoveries do on average seem to raise the currency's price-adjusted value against others and shrink lagging sectors. Remedies include saving boom revenue abroad in a {{ref:nature-res-243}}, running budget surpluses, and investing in education and infrastructure for the lagging sectors.

nature-res-208.title: Underground water that will not refill in time
nature-res-208.text: Less than six percent of the world's water is replenished on a human timescale of 50 years. Much underground water refills far too slowly to be replaced within human lifetimes, so it is effectively non-renewable. Farming leans on it heavily: 16–33% of the underground water used for {{ref:nature-res-257}} is non-renewable. Pumping too much lowers water levels and can dry up streams, harming the ecosystems on the surface. {{ref:nature-res-133}} looks at this hidden store in more depth.

nature-res-081.title: Plant genetic resources: the raw material of every crop
nature-res-081.text: Only about 120 crop species provide around 90% of the world's food needs. They are the variety within plants, a plant case of {{ref:nature-gov-046}}, built up by human and natural selection over millennia, that can be used for food and {{ref:nature-res-257}} now or later. Farmers first drew on them more than 10,000 years ago, selecting wild plants to develop crops. They are conserved on farms, in gene banks, or in the wild. They were once treated as belonging to all humanity, until the {{ref:nature-gov-015}} gave countries sovereignty over them. Whether genetic data separated from the organism fall under the rules on access and benefit-sharing is disputed.

nature-res-082.title: The Plant Treaty: sharing the world's crop genes
nature-res-082.text: Every week, crop genetic material changes hands about 8500 times under one standard contract. The Plant Treaty, an international treaty on crop genetic material for food and {{ref:nature-res-257}}, aims to secure food security. It does so by conserving, exchanging and sustainably using crop genes and sharing their benefits fairly. The FAO adopted it in November 2001, and it came into force in 2004. Its Multilateral System gives free access to 64 of the world's most important crops for research, breeding and training, using a mandatory Standard Material Transfer Agreement. It also recognizes farmers' rights, though critics argue these are weakly and unevenly realized.

nature-pol-018.title: Environmental policy: governments taking on environmental problems
nature-pol-018.text: In 1863, after harmful chemical releases caused health problems, the UK adopted the Alkali Act and created the Alkali Inspectorate. It was an early example of environmental policy: a commitment by a government or organization to adopt laws, rules and other measures that deal with environmental problems. Such policy typically covers air and {{ref:nature-res-261}}, waste, the management of ecosystems, biodiversity, resources from nature and endangered species. Its aim is to steer human activity to prevent harm to the environment and to people. Why should government get involved at all? The usual answer is {{ref:nature-found-045}}, such as the free rider problem and the tragedy of the commons. Some problems spur action faster than others. Pollution of air and water tends to move governments more than global warming does, because it causes immediate health problems. Success is judged by how far a policy reduces or solves environmental problems, and whether policies have done so remains debated.

nature-res-257.title: Agriculture: feeding cities, reshaping the land
nature-res-257.text: Farming covers 4.8 billion ha, about one-third of the Earth's land, and touches land and water more than any other economic sector. Agriculture is the cultivation of soil and the planting and harvesting of food and non-food crops, together with livestock production. Broader definitions also take in forestry and aquaculture, though horticulture and forestry are often left out in practice. Its surpluses let people live in cities and let population grow far beyond what hunting and gathering could sustain. The cost shows up in {{ref:nature-res-107}}. Expansion drives deforestation and degrades carbon-rich ecosystems such as peatlands, and about 40% of agricultural land is seriously degraded. Livestock occupy 70% of that land, which is 30% of the planet's land surface. Farming pushed for maximum output per hectare raised yields by substituting synthetic fertilizers and {{ref:nature-hist-084}} for labour, but it increased {{ref:nature-res-261}} and often relied on subsidies. Agriculture, forestry and land use contribute between 13% and 21% of global greenhouse gas emissions, so it is tied to {{ref:nature-hist-007}}. FAO estimates that farms must produce about 50% more food, feed and fibre by 2050 than in 2012, adding pressure on water, land and soil.

nature-pol-264.title: Water trading: markets for the right to use water
nature-pol-264.text: Chile's 1981 Water Code made the right to use water ({{ref:nature-res-168}}) freely tradable private property, a strongly free-market approach that has been controversial. Water trading is the buying and selling of water access entitlements between willing sellers and buyers. A seller holds rights beyond its current needs, while a buyer short of water is willing to pay for more. Economic theory says trading moves water from less to more productive uses: urban users can pay up to 10 times more than farmers. The older first-in-time system of prior appropriation led to inefficient allocation and less adoption of water-saving technology. Water is a {{ref:nature-econ-610}}, but once rights make its use rival and excludable, it behaves like a private good. It is still no standard {{ref:nature-res-264}}. Supply is uncertain and moves through complex systems, and supply swings can leave markets thin. Trades can also harm or help third parties who are neither buyer nor seller. Schemes exist in the western United States, Chile, South Africa, Australia and elsewhere; some consider Australia's the most sophisticated.

nature-pol-221.title: Fair trade: a better deal for producers in poorer countries
nature-pol-221.text: Coffee is the most established fair trade {{ref:nature-res-264}}, but the movement also covers handicrafts, cocoa, wine, sugar, fruit, flowers and gold. Fair trade is a trade arrangement meant to help producers in developing countries get sustainable and fair conditions, by paying higher prices and raising social and environmental standards. The current movement took shape in Europe in the 1960s. Sales only took off once Fairtrade certification labels arrived. Fairtrade labeling uses independent audits of producers and traders, and its most distinctive feature is a guaranteed minimum price. In 2011 more than 1.2 million farmers and workers in over 60 countries took part in Fairtrade International's system. Some propose direct trade, which skips the overhead of certification, as an alternative.

nature-pol-001.title: International trade: goods, money and pollution across borders
nature-pol-001.text: In 2025 world trade totaled 80,733 billion US dollars, of which merchandise made up 52,865 billion. International trade is the exchange of capital, goods and services across national borders to meet a need or demand. A product sold from one country to another is an export for the seller's country and an import for the buyer's. Trade abroad is usually costlier than trade at home, because of {{ref:nature-pol-321}} and other barriers such as border delays, language and legal differences. It also substitutes for moving inputs. Capital and labor move less easily between countries, so a country can instead import goods that embody them. Mineral fuels and oils were the top traded {{ref:nature-res-264}} by export value in 2022. Organizations such as the {{ref:nature-pol-007}} work to ease and expand trade. Trade also ties countries to distant environments. A 2020 study of 189 countries found most are more exposed to over-exploited water, energy and land resources through trade, mainly from distant sources.

nature-mkt-137.title: Three ways of seeing payments for nature
nature-mkt-137.text: Is paying a farmer to keep a forest a sensible trade, an imperfect tool, or a moral mistake? Thinkers give three broad answers, and they still disagree. Environmental economics sees a payment for ecosystem services as a voluntary, conditional deal between a buyer and a seller of a service, rooted in the {{ref:nature-econ-629}}. Reality is messier than the theory. Transaction costs, the costs of making and policing a deal, are almost always present. Promises of future payments are not time consistent, meaning a payer may later prefer to break them. Financing often runs short. {{ref:nature-eecon-059}} treats natural and manufactured capital as complements: one cannot simply stand in for the other. It judges a scheme by the weight of its incentive, how directly the money reaches providers, and how far the service is turned into a {{ref:nature-res-264}}. Some services, such as tons of carbon stored, are easy to measure; others are hard. The third view rejects the idea of ecosystem services altogether. These critics argue that nature should be valued for its own sake, and that a market framing protects nature only when it is useful to people. Pragmatists accept the problems of putting a value on nature. Still, they argue, in a commodified society 'something is better than nothing'. The split between the first two schools is traced in {{ref:nature-found-039}}.

nature-pol-010.title: Has the WTO delivered? The critics' case
nature-pol-010.text: Ha-Joon Chang notes that developing countries grew faster in 1960–1980 than in 1980–2000, even though their trade policies are now far more liberal. Critics say the gains from WTO-backed {{ref:nature-res-269}} are not shared equally, pointing to widening gaps between rich and poor. They fear early liberalizing traps developing economies in the primary sector, which often needs little skilled labor. Vietnam cut poverty and grew fast while liberalizing slowly with safeguards; El Salvador's growth stayed weak after it removed import barriers and cut tariffs. Studies credit the WTO with boosting trade, but whether liberalizing reliably brings growth and less hardship remains disputed.

nature-pol-009.title: Equal terms for all: the WTO's non-discrimination rule
nature-pol-009.text: The WTO's non-discrimination rule has two parts. Most-favored-nation treatment means the best terms a member gives any WTO member for a product must be given to all members. Exceptions include {{ref:nature-res-269}} agreements and preferential treatment for developing countries. National treatment means imports must be treated no less favorably than domestic goods once inside the market; it targets discriminatory technical standards. The WTO's other key principles are reciprocity, binding and enforceable commitments, transparency and safety valves.

nature-nbs-216.title: Ecological engineering: a small push that steers big natural forces
nature-nbs-216.text: In 1962 Howard Odum gave a name to a powerful trick: using a small input of human energy to steer large natural processes. He called it ecological engineering. The field combines {{ref:nature-nbs-347}} and engineering to design, build or restore, and manage ecosystems that serve both society and nature. Civil engineering focuses on built infrastructure; this field works with natural infrastructure and the bond between people and planet. Projects range from restored wetlands to greenhouses that turn wastewater into fertilizer, flowers and {{ref:nature-nbs-326}}. They work at three scales: mesocosms of about 0.1 to hundreds of meters, ecosystems of about one to tens of km, and whole regions. Mitsch and Jorgensen set out five basic concepts. The field relies on ecosystems designing themselves, tests ecological theory, thinks in whole systems, saves non-{{ref:nature-eecon-239}} and supports {{ref:nature-eco-309}}. Choosing between designs should draw on {{ref:nature-eecon-059}}, guided by values that favor conservation.

nature-val-085.title: Contingent valuation: putting a price on nature by survey
nature-val-085.text: In 1963 Robert K. Davis used a survey to value a wilderness area for hunters and tourists. It was the first application of contingent valuation, an idea S.V. Ciriacy-Wantrup had proposed in theory in 1947. Contingent valuation puts a money value on things not sold in markets, such as a protected environment or the harm done by pollution. A survey usually asks how much people would pay to keep an environmental feature such as biodiversity. Or it asks how much they would need to be paid to accept its loss. That makes it a stated preference method, unlike methods that rely on prices people actually pay. It rose to prominence in the United States in the 1980s. Governments then gained authority to sue for damage to environmental resources held in trust for the public, including non-use values. The {{ref:nature-val-076}} was the first case where its surveys put numbers on damages. US government departments have since used it widely, for example to value river recreation below Glen Canyon {{ref:nature-nbs-319}}. Critics warn of strategic answers, protest answers, response bias and respondents ignoring their income limits. Clive Spash found that many answers behaved like charitable donations rather than trade prices. Many economists therefore doubt that the answers reflect real values. Defenders reply that newer survey designs have fixed the early biases.

nature-nbs-285.title: Three ways to deploy natural enemies
nature-nbs-285.text: Biological control comes in three basic strategies. Importation, or classical control, brings a pest's natural enemies into a new place where they did not live before. Early importations were often unofficial, and some {{ref:nature-nbs-318}} became serious pests themselves. Augmentation adds more predators, parasitoids or microbes when needed. Inoculative release adds a few at intervals to prevent outbreaks. Inundative release adds many at once to knock a pest down fast. The third strategy, conservation, protects the natural enemies already present.

nature-nbs-132.title: Active rewilding: giving nature a hand
nature-nbs-132.text: Not all rewilding means walking away. Active rewilding covers approaches that involve human intervention. It can mean reintroducing or moving species, engineering habitat, and removing man-made structures and troublesome {{ref:nature-nbs-318}}. Across the field, methods range from protecting land and linking habitats to removing infrastructure and bringing species back.

nature-eco-744.title: Bush control: thinning shrubs without wiping them out
nature-eco-744.text: Managing bushes means shaping how dense they are and what they are made of, to cut risks such as {{ref:nature-gov-243}} or to rehabilitate land. The aim for encroaching native woody plants is to reduce them, not eradicate them. Methods are controlled fire, herbicides and mechanical cutting, which is followed by burning or browsing to stop regrowth. Funding is a key constraint. Selling harvested woody {{ref:nature-clim-284}}, such as charcoal in Namibia, can pay for restoration.

nature-nbs-040.title: Managed retreat: moving out of harm's way
nature-nbs-040.text: Kiribati, a low-lying country facing flooding, is planning to relocate its people. Managed retreat is the planned, coordinated movement of people, buildings and infrastructure away from places at risk. It can answer floods, {{ref:nature-gov-243}}, drought and other hazards, and its form depends on the place, the hazard and local policy. Retreating from high-risk areas such as floodplains reduces exposure. Rising seas are now drawing the attention of politicians, insurers and residents of low-lying coasts. Retreat is controversial. Programs have met lawsuits and resistance from residents worried about home values and insurance costs. Yet more communities consider it as the costs of adaptation rise. One New Zealand coastal hazards expert argues retreat is mainly a social and political issue, not a technical one. Whether migration counts as adaptation is itself debated; the IPCC says it may or may not.

nature-nbs-006.title: Pocket forests: dense, fast and disputed
nature-nbs-006.text: A pocket forest is a small forest made by planting many different native trees and shrubs close together, usually to restore native plants quickly. Instead of passing through early growth stages, it is planted densely with mature-stage species that race each other for sunlight. Interest grew largely from Japanese botanist Akira Miyawaki. The claims are disputed. Forestry scholars say claims that Miyawaki forests grow ten times faster are unsubstantiated, and call the method costly and unworkable for large areas. Dense, layered pocket forests can also catch embers and carry fire upward, raising {{ref:nature-gov-243}} risk in cities.

nature-nbs-107.title: Reforestation: growing back the forests that were lost
nature-nbs-107.text: Up to 90% of newly planted seedlings often fail. That sobering figure hangs over reforestation, the work of restoring forests and woodlands that once stood on a site but were destroyed or damaged. The earlier loss may have come from deforestation, clearcutting or {{ref:nature-gov-243}}. Reforestation differs from {{ref:nature-nbs-102}}, which makes new forest on land that was not forest before. Programs have three main purposes: growing wood to harvest, slowing climate change, and restoring ecosystems and habitat. On the climate side, growing forests and cutting deforestation store more carbon in four ways. They enlarge forests, make them denser in carbon, replace fossil fuels with forest products, and avoid the emissions that forest loss releases. Yet new trees take decades to match mature tropical forests. That is why reducing deforestation usually helps the climate more than replanting does. The choice of tree matters as well. Some species, such as Eucalyptus globulus, draw so much water from the soil that other plants cannot grow. And large programs, such as China's Three-North program begun in 1978, blur the line between restoring old forest and creating new.

nature-nbs-131.title: Rewilding: stepping back so nature can run itself
nature-nbs-131.text: In a Guyana forest, going from 5 to 35 mammal species raised the carbon in trees and soil four to five times. Results like that fuel interest in rewilding, a kind of ecological restoration that aims to raise biodiversity and restore natural processes while reducing human influence. Its key move is to replace human management with natural processes. Unlike other restoration, it accepts new mixes of species and interactions, the kind described in {{ref:nature-nbs-150}}. It often brings back large mammals to rebuild food webs, so that ecosystems regulate themselves. A group called Earth First coined the term in 1990. In 1998 Michael Soulé and Reed Noss gave it a scientific basis built on 'cores, corridors and carnivores': large reserves (see {{ref:nature-gov-038}}), links between them, and large predators. Supporters promote it as a natural climate solution through carbon storage, flood management and lower {{ref:nature-gov-243}} risk. It is also controversial. Critics question its evidence and its effect on farming and livelihoods.

nature-found-027.title: Eco-capitalism: putting markets to work for nature
nature-found-027.text: Eco-{{ref:nature-econ-848}}, or green {{ref:nature-econ-848}}, starts from a claim: nature is a form of capital on which all wealth depends. If that is true, markets should be used to solve environmental problems. Its supporters want governments to use market-based tools, such as a tax on carbon. A central aim is to correct a basic flaw in markets, in which polluters do not pay for the pollution they cause. Critics, including eco-socialists, doubt the approach. They argue that growth, and turning nature into a {{ref:nature-res-264}}, cannot easily be reconciled with {{ref:nature-eecon-208}}.

nature-econ-734.title: Subgame perfect equilibrium: ruling out empty threats
nature-econ-734.text: Reinhard Selten proposed a sharper version of the Nash equilibrium in 1965. A subgame perfect equilibrium, for games with moves in sequence, requires the strategies to form a Nash equilibrium in every subgame, from any point onward. This rules out non-{{ref:nature-econ-736}}, ones a player would not actually want to carry out, so strategies stay rational throughout the game. Every finite game with complete information and perfect recall, where players remember all past actions, has one. In finite games it is usually found by backward induction, though that does not work for infinite games or games with hidden moves. The ultimatum game is a classic example with fewer subgame perfect equilibria than Nash equilibria. In a finitely repeated prisoner's dilemma, backward induction makes both players defect in every round. Yet firms in repeated Cournot competition can collude on the monopoly outcome in a subgame perfect equilibrium, if they are patient enough.

nature-econ-678.title: Perfect Bayesian equilibrium: consistent beliefs, optimal moves
nature-econ-678.text: Games with both hidden information and moves in sequence need a sharper tool. A perfect Bayesian equilibrium requires two things. Players' beliefs must be consistent with the strategies being played, and every player must choose optimally given those beliefs. Like subgame perfect equilibrium, it demands optimal play from every information set onward. That rules out non-{{ref:nature-econ-736}} and beliefs.

nature-eco-203.title: Removing a warming gas already in the air
nature-eco-203.text: Atmospheric {{ref:nature-eco-727}} removal is a set of approaches, still under research, to speed up the breakdown of {{ref:nature-eco-727}} already in the air. The appeal is leverage. Because the gas is a stronger heat-trapping gas, removing a smaller amount of it than of carbon dioxide would have a similar climate effect. The catch is scarcity. The gas's background level is about 1.92 ppm, against about 420 ppm for carbon dioxide, which makes it harder to capture.

nature-eco-159.title: Global warming potential: comparing gases with carbon dioxide
nature-eco-159.text: Over 20 years, {{ref:nature-eco-727}} traps 81.2 times as much heat as the same mass of carbon dioxide; over 100 years, only 27.9 times. Global warming potential, or GWP, measures how much heat a greenhouse gas traps over a set period compared with the same mass of carbon dioxide. By definition carbon dioxide has a GWP of 1. A gas's GWP depends on how strongly it absorbs heat radiation, how fast it leaves the air, and the time frame chosen. {{ref:nature-eco-727}}'s two figures differ because it leaves the atmosphere much faster than carbon dioxide. Regulators usually use a 100-year time scale, and international agreements have adopted it as the standard. Since 1997, reporting under the {{ref:nature-clim-056}} has used fixed IPCC values to convert gases into the common unit described in {{ref:nature-eco-160}}. Other metrics include the global temperature change potential and GWP*, which treats short-lived pollutants such as the gas differently.

nature-eco-009.title: The main greenhouse gases and how long they linger
nature-eco-009.text: Water vapour causes about 50% of Earth's natural greenhouse effect and clouds about 25%, yet neither counts as a driver of climate change. The main greenhouse gases are the ones that do most of the heat-trapping in Earth's atmosphere: water vapour, carbon dioxide, ozone, {{ref:nature-eco-727}} and nitrous oxide, plus clouds. Without this natural effect, Earth's surface would average about −18 °C instead of around 15 °C. Water vapour and clouds change with temperature, so scientists treat them as feedbacks. Carbon dioxide, which causes about 20% of the effect, changes independently of temperature. So do ozone in the lower atmosphere, the industrial chemicals called CFCs, and nitrous oxide. These count as external forcings. Human emissions in 2019 equalled 59 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide: 75% was carbon dioxide, 18% {{ref:nature-eco-727}}, 4% nitrous oxide and 2% fluorinated gases.
