The gas comes from livestock, wetlands, rice, landfills, coal mining and oil and gas. Nitrous oxide comes mostly from microbes breaking down fertilizer. Lifetimes differ widely. The gas lasts about 12 years in the air on average, while carbon dioxide lasts much longer. In the IPCC table, nitrous oxide lasts 121 years with a 100-year GWP of 265, and some fluorinated gases are far stronger, such as SF6 at 23,500. By 2022, carbon dioxide had risen about 50% and the gas 164% since 1750.

nature-eco-204.title: The biological pump: how plankton send carbon to the deep
nature-eco-204.text: Without the ocean's living pump, the air would hold about 400 parts per million more carbon dioxide than it does today. The biological pump is the ocean's living process of moving carbon from the air and from land runoff into the deep ocean and seafloor {{ref:nature-eco-682}}. It starts in the sunlit surface layer, where phytoplankton build organic and inorganic carbon compounds. Their reach is enormous: marine phytoplankton perform half of all photosynthesis on Earth. Uneaten phytoplankton clump together and sink quickly out of the well-mixed surface layer. The faecal pellets of zooplankton, tiny drifting animals, sink with them. In this way the pump moves about 11 billion tonnes of carbon into the ocean interior each year. Large animals help. Whales and seals boost surface productivity by releasing nitrogen-rich fecal plumes, a role that was larger before industrial fishing cut their numbers. The pump may weaken in future. As the surface ocean warms and stratifies, separating into layers that mix less, nutrient supply and primary production may fall.

nature-eco-225.title: Reversing eutrophication: why lakes recover slowly
nature-eco-225.text: Stopping the flow of nutrients into a lake does not clean it overnight. Reversing eutrophication starts with reducing nutrient inputs, but recovery can take a long time, mainly because nutrients stored in {{ref:nature-eco-682}} keep being released. Cutting inputs may not be enough. A water body can have several stable but very different states, so restoration may need more. One option is adding phosphate-binding materials such as alum to lock up phosphorus. Removal at the source can be thorough: Finnish phosphorus removal from the mid-1970s reached 90% removal efficiency.

nature-eco-167.title: The deep carbon cycle: carbon's trip into the mantle
nature-eco-167.text: In 2011 a study of rare super-deep diamonds from Brazil showed that carbon cycling reaches all the way to Earth's lower mantle. The deep carbon cycle is the slow movement of carbon between Earth's surface and its deep interior. Carbon mainly enters the mantle in carbonate-rich {{ref:nature-eco-682}} riding on ocean plates, which sink beneath other plates. This return matters for life. Without it, carbon would build up in the atmosphere to extremely high levels, so the deep cycle helps keep conditions fit for life.

nature-eco-517.title: Marine snow: the slow shower that feeds the deep sea
nature-eco-517.text: A constant shower falls through the ocean: dead and dying organisms, faecal matter and mineral particles, sinking from the upper ocean to the deep. This is marine snow. It sinks at approximately 100 meters per day, and only about 1 to 3% of surface production reaches the seabed. Even so, the deep ocean gets most of its nutrients from it, and many deep-sea organisms survive by feeding on it. As clumps of this material form and sink, they drive the biological pump, exporting organic matter to the deep ocean and its {{ref:nature-eco-682}}.

nature-eco-742.title: The water table: where the ground turns wet
nature-eco-742.text: Dig deep enough almost anywhere and the ground turns wet. The water table is the upper surface of the zone of saturation, below which ground pores are filled with groundwater. Above it lies the vadose zone. Below it, permeable rock layers that yield groundwater are described in {{ref:nature-res-112}}. It is not the same as the water level in a confined deeper layer of such rock, which is the potentiometric surface. The table rises and falls seasonally with precipitation and evapotranspiration, and where it reaches the surface, springs, rivers, lakes and oases occur. Groundwater entering rivers and lakes supplies their base-flow water levels. People change it. Fossil water, held for millennia mainly in {{ref:nature-eco-703}}, is not renewed by rainfall, so extraction permanently changes the table. Crops need a minimum depth: cotton in the Nile Delta is sensitive and needs a deep table, while wheat tolerates 45 cm. Near the coast, lower tables from heavier water use have let seawater contaminate groundwater, as in Libya and Israel.

nature-econ-847.title: Quasi-option value: the worth of keeping choices open
nature-econ-847.text: Quasi-{{ref:nature-val-055}} is the extra value of keeping future choices open when a decision's consequences may be irreversible and uncertain. Arrow and Fischer (1974) and Epstein (1980) showed that possible irreversible consequences lead even a risk-neutral society to favor flexible decisions. The idea grew out of {{ref:nature-val-055}}. That value depends on uncertain future need for something, irreversibility or a high cost of replacing it if it is lost, and its not being storable. Climate policy weighs both sides: possible irreversible damage to each {{ref:nature-eco-327}} and ecosystem against the irreversibility of spending on emission cuts. Economists have analyzed the {{ref:nature-pol-201}} as the interaction of irreversibility and uncertainty.

nature-econ-330.title: When one side of a deal knows more
nature-econ-330.text: The person selling a used car usually knows its condition far better than the person buying it. Economists call this information asymmetry: one side of a deal has more or better information than the other. The gap hands the better-informed side extra power, and it can make trades inefficient. Distrust breeds opportunistic behavior, and in the worst case the market breaks down entirely, a form of {{ref:nature-found-045}}. The idea cuts against perfect information, a key assumption of neoclassical economics. {{ref:nature-val-107}} suffers too: firms know better than regulators what they would do without the rules, which can weaken them. The main forms are {{ref:nature-econ-001}}, {{ref:nature-econ-004}} and monopolies of knowledge. George Akerlof, Michael Spence and Joseph Stiglitz shared the 2001 Nobel Prize for analyzing markets with this kind of gap.

nature-econ-081.title: Pro-environmental behavior: choosing to do less harm
nature-econ-081.text: A home whose location forces car dependency can defeat its owners' best intentions. That is one structural barrier to pro-environmental behavior, the behavior people consciously choose to reduce the harm their actions do to the environment. Green consumption, buying in ways that harm the environment as little as possible, is one form of it. Money incentives, costs, {{ref:nature-val-107}} and policy norms all shape it through people's attitudes, as does how much time, money and power people feel they have. Other barriers are psychological, social or cultural, or financial. Some popular assumptions hold up less well than expected. A review pooling many studies confirmed a strong link between feeling connected to nature and acting greenly. But it found the connection causes less of that behavior than assumed. In a 2019 study, climate messages told as stories were better at inspiring it. Environmental psychology studies these factors to help curb {{ref:nature-hist-007}} and the loss of biodiversity.

nature-econ-221.title: Difference in differences: comparing changes, not levels
nature-econ-221.text: When New Jersey raised its minimum wage, Card and Krueger compared fast-food jobs there and in Pennsylvania. Their 1994 study found no fall in employment. It became a famous use of difference in differences, a quasi-experimental technique ({{ref:nature-econ-214}}). The method compares how much a treated group changed over time with how much an untreated control group changed. It needs data on both groups from at least one period before the treatment and one after. Because the groups may start at different levels, it subtracts the 'normal' gap that would exist without treatment. What remains is the treatment effect. It is a special version of {{ref:nature-econ-245}}. Environmental economists use it to assess {{ref:nature-val-107}} on pollution, energy use and climate. In 2012 Richard Hornbeck used it to show that heavily eroded Dust Bowl counties lost 20 to 30 percent of land values and farm revenues. They saw little recovery 10 years later. It can still suffer from biases such as mean regression, reverse causality and omitted variable bias, depending on how the treated group is chosen.

nature-es-002.title: Clean air, fresh water and the work behind them
nature-es-002.text: Clean air and plentiful fresh water are ecological goods. Purifying that air and water is a service, and so are breaking down wastes, pollinating crops, refilling underground water stores and mitigating greenhouse gases. Together they are the economic benefits of ecosystems' natural workings. Biodiversity underlies them all. {{ref:nature-hist-053}}'s original definition kept goods and services apart, but Costanza and colleagues and the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment lumped both together as ecosystem services. They are a kind of public good. They are also being lost at an unsustainable rate, especially where land is converted from its natural state and loses its ecological functions. One remedy is to create a market, in which society demands these goods and services and public and private landowners supply them. Paying farmers to set land aside marks a shift from 'polluter pays' to 'beneficiary pays'. {{ref:nature-val-107}}, land-care programs, eco-labeling, offset credits and tax rebates can secure supply too.

nature-es-121.title: Climate regulation: nature's thermostat
nature-es-121.text: Climate {{ref:nature-val-107}} is among the services thought to have no viable substitute. It is the regulating service by which nature dampens environmental change, for example by storing carbon and moderating local temperatures. A 1970 report that coined 'environmental services' already listed it alongside pollination, fisheries and {{ref:nature-nbs-329}} control. Tropical rainforests are crucial to it because they capture and store carbon. Mangroves sequester carbon too, coastal seas help regulate climate, and urban trees cool microclimates and take up carbon dioxide. The service can falter. Regime shifts, sudden lasting changes, can weaken it. Examples include forest turning into savanna and faster summer loss of Arctic ice. {{ref:nature-acct-109}} is one attempt to put a money value on regulating services such as this one.

nature-pol-213.title: The Common Agricultural Policy: Europe's farm support
nature-pol-213.text: Butter mountains and wine lakes: those were the nicknames for the huge surpluses the EU bought and stored under guaranteed prices. They came from the Common Agricultural Policy, the EU's farm policy, introduced in 1962. It runs a system of agricultural subsidies, risk management tools and other programs. Reforms have cut its share of the budget, from 73% in 1985 to 37% in 2017, and added rural development. The 'Agenda 2000' reforms split it into two pillars: production support and rural development. Many interests have criticized it since its start, and even the European Commission acknowledges its defects. Critics say it creates artificially high food prices, helped by import {{ref:nature-pol-321}} estimated at 18–28%. Because it has rewarded higher output, larger farms have gained far more from subsidies than smaller ones. A 2024 study reported that 80% of its subsidies in 2013 supported emissions-intensive animal products.

nature-pol-224.title: Feed-in tariffs: guaranteed prices for clean power
nature-pol-224.text: As of 2019, more than 50 countries had feed-in {{ref:nature-pol-321}} policies. A feed-in {{ref:nature-pol-321}} speeds up investment in {{ref:nature-eecon-239}} by giving producers long-term contracts at a guaranteed, usually above-market price for the electricity they supply. It usually guarantees access to the grid and pays prices based on generating costs. Contracts typically run 15–25 years, and the price often falls over time to follow and encourage technology cost cuts. Different technologies get different prices; wind and solar PV, for example, get more per kWh than tidal power. A 2008 European Commission analysis found well-designed feed-in import duties the most efficient and effective support for renewable electricity. They have a cost. Funded by a surcharge on bills, they added 6.88 cents/kWh for German households in 2017. Yet renewables can also lower spot market prices through the {{ref:nature-clim-125}}, as happened in Spain, Denmark and Germany.

nature-pol-226.title: Green industrial policy: governments growing clean industries
nature-pol-226.text: German green industrial policy helped build a {{ref:nature-eecon-239}} industry employing over 371,000 people, double the jobs of 2004. Green industrial policy is government strategy to speed the growth of green industries, correcting {{ref:nature-found-045}} and moving toward a {{ref:nature-clim-208}}. The case rests on hard beginnings. Green industries such as green power face high costs and risks, so they need public support until they become commercially viable. New sustainable technologies cannot compete at once with existing ones, because of {{ref:nature-pol-038}}, so governments nurture technological niches. Without government intervention, the market is unlikely to make that shift on its own. Subsidies for a targeted sector are the most common form. Other tools include R&D funding, tax credits, feed-in {{ref:nature-pol-321}}, mandates and green buying by governments.

nature-pol-188.title: Can ecolabels become trade barriers?
nature-pol-188.text: Labels meant to help the planet can also hinder trade. To qualify for a foreign ecolabel, exporters must adjust to each market's production standards, which can cost money, information and expertise. Labeling programs often reflect the importing country's priorities and technologies, and may not fit the exporting country's environment. Hence the concern that ecolabels create obstacles to trade other than {{ref:nature-pol-321}}, the taxes on imports. Since 1995 the agreements of the {{ref:nature-pol-007}} have covered the possible effects of voluntary product standards and labels.

nature-pol-225.title: Grid parity: when clean power matches the grid price
nature-pol-225.text: Grid parity is the point at which electricity from an alternative technology costs the same as the average grid electricity price in an area. It is a moving target: parity can vary over the day, over years and from place to place. In some areas wind, landfill gas and {{ref:nature-clim-284}} power are already cheaper than grid electricity. Parity has been reached in areas that use feed-in {{ref:nature-pol-321}}.

nature-pol-042.title: Rent-seeking: getting richer without creating wealth
nature-pol-042.text: Robert Shiller's classic example is a landowner who chains a river and charges passing boats to lower the chain. The landowner adds no value. That is rent-seeking. It means growing richer by manipulating public policy or economic conditions, without creating new wealth. Here 'rent' means {{ref:nature-res-218}}: income beyond what is needed to keep a factor in its current use. Profit-seeking creates wealth through mutually beneficial trade; rent-seeking only redistributes existing wealth. Typical examples are lobbying for subsidies, {{ref:nature-pol-321}}, quotas or rules that hobble competitors. The costs are broad. Rent-seeking wastes resources, stifles competition, lowers wealth creation and government revenue, and raises inequality and corruption risk. Money spent on lobbyists rather than research or equipment slows growth, and Mancur Olson argued that countries dominated by organized interest groups lose vitality and decline. Critics note it can be hard to tell beneficial profit-seeking from harmful rent-seeking.

nature-econ-501.title: Who owns the world's wealth
nature-econ-501.text: In 2013, 1% of adults were estimated to hold 46% of the world's wealth. In 2008 the estimate had been 40%, or 32% adjusted for purchasing power parity. The distribution of wealth describes how a society's or the world's total wealth is shared among people and regions. At the other end, some adults have negative net worth, with {{ref:nature-mkt-153}} larger than their assets. The pattern described in {{ref:nature-eecon-164}} holds that inequality of wealth and income rises in early development, stabilizes, then falls.

nature-econ-869.title: Debt and aggregate demand: the credit impulse
nature-econ-869.text: Spending equals income plus net new borrowing, so rising {{ref:nature-mkt-153}} makes demand exceed income and falling {{ref:nature-mkt-153}} makes it fall short. This post-Keynesian view treats changes in borrowing as a fundamental part of {{ref:nature-econ-868}}, sometimes called the credit impulse. The effect scales with the borrowing level: a 1% loan loss at a borrowing level of 10% of GDP costs 0.1% of GDP, but at 300% of GDP costs 3%, enough to cause a recession. Write-offs and higher saving in recessions shrink credit, which can deepen the recession in a vicious cycle. The view descends from Irving Fisher's theory of deflation from heavy borrowing.

nature-eco-110.title: Extinction debt: species doomed by losses already made
nature-eco-110.text: In the Azores, over 95% of native forest was destroyed in 600 years. More than half of the islands' arthropods are now thought committed to extinction, still alive but doomed. That is extinction {{ref:nature-mkt-153}}: the future extinction of species already set in motion by past events such as habitat loss. It arises from time lags. Long-lived trees, for example, may survive for years after new trees can no longer be produced. Habitat fragmentation and habitat destruction are its best-known drivers, because they cut off species' ability to recolonize other patches. The {{ref:nature-mkt-153}} is most likely in long-lived species and in specialists with narrow habitat needs. Tilman, May, Lehman and Nowak first used the term in 1994. It is likened to the 'climate commitment' of warming that continues after emissions stop. Modeling suggests that 80–90% of the extinctions due to past Amazon deforestation have yet to happen. Protecting today's habitat may not be enough. Still, the long delay gives time for restoration to prevent losses.

nature-eco-111.title: Detecting extinction debt before it comes due
nature-eco-111.text: In experiments with miniature moss ecosystems, insect species took 6–12 months to die out after habitat was destroyed. In the wild the delay is longer and harder to see. Researchers detect extinction {{ref:nature-mkt-153}} by checking whether today's species match past habitat better than present habitat, or by comparing cleared and intact areas. The size of the {{ref:nature-mkt-153}} can only be estimated if past populations are known as well as present ones. The processes are slow and noisy, and tiny remnant populations are hard to count, so estimates are very uncertain.

nature-eco-037.title: Farming, the largest driver of biodiversity loss on land
nature-eco-037.text: As of 2023, about 38% of Earth's land surface was used for {{ref:nature-res-257}}, the dominant use of land. That reach makes farming the largest single cause of biodiversity decline on land. As farmland expands and intensifies, it converts and degrades natural habitat, the process described in {{ref:nature-eco-041}}. The 2019 global assessment described in {{ref:nature-eco-123}} found industrial {{ref:nature-res-257}} to be the primary driver of biodiversity collapse. A 2014 UN outlook report estimated that farming causes 70% of projected biodiversity loss on land. Animal farming takes the biggest share of space. Livestock systems occupy about 77% of agricultural land but provide less than 20% of the world's calories. The pressure is set to grow. More than 17,000 species risk losing habitat by 2050 as farming expands to meet food needs. Diet is one lever. A global shift toward mostly plant-based diets would free land for restoring ecosystems and biodiversity.

nature-eco-055.title: Cattle, crops and roads: what drives deforestation
nature-eco-055.text: Around 80% of converted land in the Amazon is used to rear cattle, making beef the primary driver there. Drivers of deforestation are the activities and forces that lead people to clear forests: chiefly farming and ranching, but also logging, mining, roads and wider economic pressures. Agricultural expansion remains the main driver of forest loss, fragmentation and loss of forest biodiversity. One breakdown attributes 48% of deforestation to subsistence farming, 32% to commercial {{ref:nature-res-257}}, 14% to logging and 5% to fuel wood. By the 1990s, though, most clearing came from industrial factors such as extractive industries, large-scale ranching and extensive {{ref:nature-res-257}}. Since 2001, {{ref:nature-res-264}}-driven clearing, which is more likely to be permanent, has made up about a quarter of all damage to forests. Roads open the way: about 90% of deforestation in most of the Amazon has occurred within 100 km of one. The role of human numbers is contested. One study found high fertility a primary driver in only 8% of tropical cases, and sources disagree on its weight against {{ref:nature-res-264}} demand.

nature-eco-597.title: Planetary boundaries: nine limits for a livable Earth
nature-eco-597.text: In 2009 scientists led by Johan Rockström of the Stockholm Resilience Centre and Will Steffen of the Australian National University set out limits for the whole planet. Planetary boundaries mark how far human activity can push the Earth system before it may stop regulating itself. Crossing them could push the Earth out of the Holocene, the stable period in which human society developed. Worse, the authors warned, transgressing a boundary risks crossing thresholds that trigger abrupt, non-linear change at continental to planetary scale, the behavior described in {{ref:nature-eco-592}}. There are nine boundaries. They cover climate change, ocean acidification, loss of stratospheric ozone, nitrogen and phosphorus flows, freshwater use, land system change, biosphere integrity, chemical pollution and atmospheric aerosol loading. The count of breaches keeps rising. Three were judged crossed in 2009 and four in the 2015 update. Novel entities, meaning new human-made substances, became the fifth in 2022, freshwater change the sixth in 2023 and ocean acidification the seventh in 2025. {{ref:nature-res-257}} and food help push four of the nine past their limits, with surplus nitrogen and phosphorus flows the most important. Politics followed the science. UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon endorsed the concept in 2012. It was later dropped from the text of {{ref:nature-hist-008}}, because poorer countries worried it would sideline development.

nature-eco-738.title: Self-reinforcing loops in markets and societies
nature-eco-738.text: A Ponzi scheme grows by feeding on its own growth, and that is why it ends in collapse. Positive feedback in socioeconomic systems means loops in which an outcome strengthens its own cause, as in markets, populations and institutions. Real loops are usually limited by some constraint; left unchecked, a positive loop destroys its system, and a negative loop usually steps in sooner or later. Systemic risk is the danger that an amplifying, leveraged loop poses to a whole system. {{ref:nature-res-257}} and human population can be seen as a pair of reinforcing loops that may end in catastrophe as easily available phosphate runs out. Drought works the same way: less rain dries soils, plants transpire less, and evapotranspiration falls.

nature-mkt-029.title: Why the economy keeps eating into biodiversity
nature-mkt-029.text: Failing to halt the loss of biodiversity on land between 2000 and 2010 was estimated to cost the global economy $500 billion. Economic activities often harm biodiversity, and because they make profits, they are usually favored over conservation and restoration. The main causes are habitat loss, changes in land use, pollution and overexploitation, meaning taking too much. BCG estimates that over 90% of human drivers of the loss come from {{ref:nature-res-257}}, infrastructure, fashion and energy. The IUCN estimates that 79% of threatened species are affected by {{ref:nature-res-257}}, infrastructure, energy and mining. Continued loss raises long-term risks such as pandemics, {{ref:nature-nbs-329}} and droughts.

nature-econ-499.title: Wealth: what you own minus what you owe
nature-econ-499.text: For 2018 the World Bank valued the world's produced, natural and human capital at $1,152 trillion. That is wealth counted on the widest scale. In general, wealth means a plentiful store of valuable assets or possessions that can be turned into a form usable in exchange. In economics it is net worth: the value of all assets owned minus all liabilities owed, at a point in time, for a person, household or nation. Adam Smith described wealth as 'the annual produce of the land and labor of the society'. Scarcity is fundamental. A {{ref:nature-res-264}} freely available to everyone gives its owner no potential for wealth. Wealth falls into three main categories: personal property, monetary savings, and income-producing capital such as real estate, stocks and businesses. Global household wealth was estimated at US$418.3 trillion at the end of 2020, excluding human capital. The UN goes further with the measure described in {{ref:nature-acct-012}}, adding up natural, human and physical assets in money terms. Natural capital includes land, forests, energy resources and minerals. Human capital is people's education and skills, and physical capital is machinery, buildings and infrastructure.

nature-val-058.title: Use value: what a thing is good for
nature-val-058.text: Gold can serve as money, as decoration or as an excellent electrical conductor. Each of those is a use, and together they make up its use value: the features that let a thing satisfy a human want or need. The idea comes from classical and Marxist economics. Adam Smith noticed that use and price can part company. Diamonds have little use but fetch a great deal in trade, while water is very useful yet cheap. For Marx, every {{ref:nature-res-264}}, a good made to be traded, is both a use value and an {{ref:nature-val-068}}: the proportion in which it trades for other goods. Not every useful thing can become a {{ref:nature-res-264}}. It must be tradable, its ownership must pass securely from one person to another, and there must be real demand. Later, marginalist economics traced use value to the {{ref:nature-econ-091}} consumers find in a good. Critics of turning nature into commodities still draw on Marx's double idea.

nature-val-068.title: Exchange value: what a thing trades for
nature-val-068.text: Marx gave every {{ref:nature-res-264}} four attributes: use value, exchange value, value and price. Exchange value is the proportion in which a {{ref:nature-res-264}} can be traded for other goods. It is not the same as the money price, which only roughly matches it. Behind both, Marx held, lies value itself, set by the socially necessary labor time needed to produce a good: the work it typically takes. Modern neoclassical economics, the mainstream school, no longer treats exchange value as a separate idea. For it, exchange value is simply the market price, the subject of {{ref:nature-econ-356}}. Before anything can be traded at all, certain conditions must hold: secure, transferable ownership rights, exclusive access and real market demand. Critics of turning nature into commodities see a danger here. Expressing every kind of worth through a single exchange value puts very different things on one scale.

nature-res-243.title: Sovereign wealth funds: saving the windfall
nature-res-243.text: In 1953 Kuwait set up the first sovereign wealth fund for a state, the Kuwait Investment Authority, using oil revenues. A sovereign wealth fund is a state-owned investment fund that buys assets such as stocks, bonds, real estate and precious metals. Most are funded by {{ref:nature-res-264}} export revenues or by central bank foreign currency reserves, and many were set up by oil-rich states. For {{ref:nature-res-264}} exporters, a fund can smooth volatile government revenue and save for the longer term. Assets under management reached $13–15 trillion by 2025; funds built on oil and gas exports held $5.4 trillion as of 2020. In 2008 the IMF led the drafting of the 24 Santiago Principles, standards for transparency, independence and accountability. Many funds have still been exhausted, mainly through political instability rather than economic factors.

nature-pol-322.title: The optimal tariff
nature-pol-322.text: An optimal tariff is one set to maximise the welfare of the country imposing it. {{ref:nature-res-269}} is often the best policy for efficiency, but levying a tariff is sometimes second best.

nature-res-101.title: Water resources: why a wet planet runs short
nature-res-101.text: About 97% of Earth's water is salt water. Only 3% is fresh, and slightly over two-thirds of that is frozen in glaciers and ice caps. Water resources are the natural sources of water that could be useful to people, for drinking, irrigation or other needs. They are one kind of natural resource. Most fresh water that is not frozen lies underground as groundwater, with only a small fraction above ground or in the air. Natural sources include surface water, water flowing beneath rivers, groundwater and ice. People add artificial sources too: reclaimed wastewater, desalinated seawater with the salt removed, harvested rainwater, wells, {{ref:nature-nbs-319}} and reservoirs. A surface water system has only one natural input, the precipitation that falls on the land draining into it, part of the {{ref:nature-eco-196}}. Climate change is shifting that balance. It brings heavier rain and {{ref:nature-nbs-329}}, while droughts can shrink groundwater storage and the recharge that refills it.

nature-res-122.title: Environmental flows: water left for the river
nature-res-122.text: More than half of the world's large rivers are dammed, and {{ref:nature-nbs-319}} change downstream water quality, temperature, sediment, fish and livelihoods. Environmental flow is the amount, timing and quality of river flow needed to sustain freshwater and estuarine ecosystems and the people who depend on them. Estuarine means where a river meets the sea. Managers aim for a flow pattern that serves human uses while keeping rivers healthy, not necessarily restoring pristine flows. The idea grew from 1970s 'minimum flows' for single species such as trout, then 'instream flows'. By the 1990s scientists saw that one minimum flow could not capture how rivers work. The 2007 Brisbane Declaration was endorsed by more than 750 practitioners from more than 50 countries. More than 200 methods now exist; holistic ones include DRIFT, the Building Block Methodology and ELOHA. Gains are possible on both sides. Reoperating {{ref:nature-nbs-319}} alongside {{ref:nature-nbs-187}} has sometimes increased water for hydropower while reducing {{ref:nature-nbs-329}} risk.

nature-nbs-153.title: Passive rewilding: letting abandoned land go wild
nature-nbs-153.text: Wolves, lynxes, boars and brown bears have returned to the Chernobyl Exclusion Zone. No one put them there. Passive rewilding is letting land, usually after it has been abandoned, return to nature with little or no human management. It is also called natural or spontaneous regeneration, and unlike other rewilding, people do not intervene directly. It has three parts: letting wildlife return, reconnecting landscapes so plants and animals can move, and allowing disturbances such as fires, pests and floods. Land is left either on purpose or because of socio-economic change. Forests have been regrowing on abandoned {{ref:nature-nbs-350}} and scrub across Europe and North America. Results vary. In Spain, regrowth on abandoned farmland has raised fire risk, and effects on biodiversity depend on the site. In 1998 Bruce Sterling coined 'involuntary park' for once-inhabited places left to go wild.

nature-nbs-152.title: Anthromes: the biomes people have remade
nature-nbs-152.text: Most land is no longer wild in the old sense. Anthromes are the land's biomes in their modern, human-altered form, mapped by patterns of lasting human land use. Each is a patchwork of uses, often with areas partly reclaimed by nature. Groups include croplands, {{ref:nature-nbs-350}}, plantations and cities, and artificial wetlands such as reservoirs and rice paddies.

nature-eco-400.title: Soil depletion: spending the soil's nutrient bank
nature-eco-400.text: Soil fertility can be spent down like savings. Soil depletion is the loss of fertility when the things that make soil fertile are removed and not replaced. It brings poor crop yields, and it is becoming a global problem. Causes include overly intensive cultivation, over-{{ref:nature-nbs-342}} (too much plowing), salt build-up, and overuse of nutrient inputs that mines the soil's nutrient bank. Fertile soil is being depleted in many African farming regions, especially the Sahel, where population pressure is high.

nature-acct-086.title: Red List Index: watching extinction risk change over time
nature-acct-086.text: Australia's national bird index fell from 0.927 in 1990 to 0.896 in 2020, picking up both the 2019–2020 {{ref:nature-gov-243}} and conservation successes. That is a Red List Index, or RLI. Built from the IUCN Red List, it tracks how the extinction risk of whole groups of species changes over time. Repeating assessments at regular intervals lets changes in threat status reveal trends. The index can be broken down by taxonomic group, biogeographic realm, habitat type or main threat. Assessing every fungus, insect and plant is impractical, so a sampled version, the SRLI, assesses a representative sample. The shark and ray index has fallen 19% since the 1970s because of too much fishing. The RLI is the single indicator for target 15.5 of the {{ref:nature-gov-010}}, and was used for the 2010 global biodiversity target.

nature-pol-046.title: Acid rain: when burning coal sours the sky
nature-pol-046.text: In 1852, in industrial Manchester, Robert Angus Smith first linked acid rain to air pollution. Acid rain is rain, snow or other precipitation that is unusually acidic. Acidity is measured on the pH scale, where lower numbers mean more acid. Most water sits between 6.5 and 8.5, while acid rain averages about 4–5; one definition draws the line below 5. The acid starts as gas. Burning fuels and smelting ores release sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, which reactions in the air turn into sulfuric and nitric acid. Humans now dominate the supply, upsetting the natural {{ref:nature-eco-273}}. Fossil fuels and industry emit 70 Tg (teragrams) of sulfur a year as SO2, far more than {{ref:nature-gov-243}} (2.8 Tg) and volcanoes (7–8 Tg) combined. Power plants alone produce two-thirds of the sulfur dioxide in the air and a quarter of the nitrogen oxides. Coal-fired stations, animal farming, fertilizers, steel mills and vehicles all contribute. The worst-hit regions run from eastern Europe into Scandinavia, across the eastern third of the United States and into southeastern Canada.

nature-nbs-176.title: Flood management: living with water that rises
nature-nbs-176.text: The US Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) estimates that every $1.00 spent on flood mitigation saves $4.00. Flood management, also called flood control, covers the methods used to reduce or prevent the harm floodwaters do. Floods come from a mix of causes. Some are natural, such as extreme weather upstream. Others are human, such as changes to water bodies and to how rain runs off the land. More hard surfaces make flooding worse, and so do {{ref:nature-gov-243}} that strip away vegetation. The methods fall into two families. Structural methods physically hold water back; non-structural methods do not. Wetlands are one of nature's own tools. They hold excess water and, especially on coasts, shield inland communities from storm surges. Protection is not cheap, and its cost rises with the number of people and the amount of property it covers. Yet floods are not simply enemies. Natural seasonal floods renew soil fertility, restore wetlands and support biodiversity.

nature-nbs-062.title: Climate-driven relocation: towns that move away
nature-nbs-062.text: Isle de Jean Charles in Louisiana, about 100 people, became the first total community migration in that state, driven by saltwater intrusion and rising seas. Climate-driven community relocation is the whole or partial abandonment of places, or plans to move their people, because of human-caused climate change. The causes often overlap: rising seas, flooding, land turning into wetland, coastal erosion, cyclones, droughts, water shortages and {{ref:nature-gov-243}}. Vunidogoloa became the first town in Fiji to be relocated, after persistent flooding, saltwater intrusion and erosion. In the Lake Chad Basin, 30,000,000 people are affected by droughts, floods and the lake's shrinking.

nature-clim-224.title: How climate change threatens ecosystems
nature-clim-224.text: Across North America, {{ref:nature-gov-243}} and pest outbreaks driven by climate change caused much of the recent death of trees. That is one face of the risk climate change poses to ecosystems and the services they provide. The main threats are biodiversity loss, changes in ecosystem structure, more tree deaths, more {{ref:nature-gov-243}} and losses of ecosystem carbon. The risks compound, because losing species can raise the risks to ecosystem health.

nature-clim-139.title: How long does removed carbon stay put?
nature-clim-139.text: Removing carbon helps only while it stays stored. Forests, kelp beds and other plants store carbon as they grow, but these stores are volatile, because long-term storage cannot be guaranteed. {{ref:nature-gov-243}}, disease, economic pressure and changing politics can release the carbon again. Injecting CO2 underground, or locking it into insoluble carbonate salts, stores it more securely.

nature-nbs-085.title: Agro-extractivism: farming for export, controlled from abroad
nature-nbs-085.text: More than 46 million hectares of soy have been planted in South America, and over half a million hectares are deforested each year for cultivation. Agro-{{ref:nature-gov-209}} is foreign control over farming, driven by large-scale export commodities often grown as monocultures. These have reduced local and indigenous food sovereignty, food security and access to land and water. Repeated single cropping exhausts soil nutrients and microbes, increasing reliance on synthetic fertilizers.

nature-eco-237.title: Infiltration: how rain soaks into the ground
nature-eco-237.text: Whether a storm waters a field or {{ref:nature-nbs-329}} a street depends largely on one thing: how fast the ground can drink. Infiltration is the movement of water from the ground surface down into the soil. The fastest rate at which water can soak in is called the infiltration capacity, usually measured in meters per day. When rain falls faster than that, the extra water usually runs off over the surface. Texture matters. Soils with small pores, such as clay, take in water more slowly than soils with large pores, such as sand. Compaction squeezes the soil and lowers infiltration further. Wet soil soaks up water more slowly, and fully saturated soil cannot take in any more. Living things help. Plant roots and burrowing animals open cracks that speed water downward, while bare ground can have very low rates, which leads to runoff and erosion. Steeper slopes shed water more readily. Pavement and other impermeable surfaces stop infiltration entirely and send more water across the ground.

nature-eco-275.title: Surface runoff: when water cannot soak in
nature-eco-275.text: A roof or a parking lot lets no rain soak in at all. Every drop that lands becomes surface runoff, or overland flow. This is water flowing freely over the ground when rain, snowmelt or other water cannot soak into the soil fast enough. On natural ground, runoff starts when the soil is already saturated or when rain arrives faster than infiltration can take it in. Runoff is a major part of the water cycle. It is also the main way water wears soil away, the process covered in {{ref:nature-eco-264}}. Its main environmental harm is what it carries. Running water picks up petroleum, herbicides and fertilizers and delivers them into surface water, groundwater and soil. More runoff also means less water seeping down to refill groundwater, so underground water levels drop and droughts hit harder for people who rely on wells. When a stream cannot carry all the runoff flowing downstream, it {{ref:nature-nbs-329}}. The remedies follow from the causes. Limit paved surfaces, control erosion on farms and building sites, build the green networks described in {{ref:nature-nbs-161}}, and control how chemicals are used.

nature-eco-279.title: Taming runoff, from medieval fields to city drains
nature-eco-279.text: Since medieval times, farmers have protected their soil by contour farming, plowing across slopes rather than down them. Runoff mitigation combines controls on how land is used, erosion controls, {{ref:nature-nbs-329}} control and chemical handling rules to reduce the harm runoff causes. Construction sites use straw bales, silt fences and work scheduled for drier months to slow runoff. Holding ponds buffer peak river flows. In the United States, the federal law described in {{ref:nature-pol-155}} requires urban local governments to run programs for managing storm runoff, under discharge permits.

nature-eco-001.title: Extreme weather: the far ends of the range
nature-eco-001.text: Since the 1920s, death tolls from natural disasters have fallen over 90 percent, even as population quadrupled. Extreme weather is unexpected, unusual, severe or unseasonal weather at the far ends of the range a place has seen in the past. The main types are heat waves, cold waves, droughts, and heavy rain or storms such as tropical cyclones. The IPCC counts an event as extreme if it is as rare as or rarer than the 10th or 90th percentile of observed weather. Severe weather, which threatens life and property, is one kind. Natural variability, such as El Niño, explains some extremes, but system-wide changes can raise their frequency or intensity. Warmer air holds more moisture, so storms can drop more rain and cause {{ref:nature-nbs-329}} and landslides. Paving land and destroying wetlands, which store water naturally, can make floods worse. The toll on food is measurable: drought and extreme heat cut national cereal production by 10% over 1964–2007.

nature-eco-060.title: Land degradation: when land loses its power to produce
nature-eco-060.text: Every year around 120,000 km2 of productive land, roughly the size of Greece, is degraded. Land degradation is the process by which land becomes less healthy and productive, through human activity or natural conditions. Unsustainable land management is often the main cause, and over 60% of human-induced degradation occurs on farmland. The UN estimates that about 30% of land is degraded worldwide, with about 3.2 billion people living in degrading areas. A major 2005 global review, {{ref:nature-es-001}}, defined it more narrowly, as the reduction or loss of the biological or economic productivity of dry lands. Its effects spread outward. It lowers crop yields and ecosystem diversity, leaves land more exposed to {{ref:nature-nbs-329}} and droughts, and releases greenhouse gases. Degraded land is also less resilient, so further shocks can drive still more degradation. The flip side is hopeful. Reversing 10% of human-induced cropland degradation could feed an additional 154 million people a year.

nature-eco-042.title: The hidden price of converting a habitat
nature-eco-042.text: Turning forest into row crops can raise a country's food supply. Yet the same land may be worth more left natural, supplying clean water, timber, tourism based on nature, or {{ref:nature-nbs-329}} and drought control. What people give up when a habitat is destroyed is the value the land would have produced if left alone. That forgone value is the opportunity cost of habitat conversion.

nature-eco-128.title: Five kinds of environmental value
nature-eco-128.text: Timber is only the most obvious value of a forest. Pearce and Moran sorted the values of the environment into five classes. Direct extractive uses include timber and food. Indirect uses are ecosystem services such as {{ref:nature-nbs-329}} control, pest control and erosion protection. Option uses are possible future uses, such as unknown medicines from plants. A fourth class, explained in {{ref:nature-val-053}}, is the benefit of knowing others may benefit in future. The last, passive use, is the enjoyment of a species' mere existence.

nature-eco-624.title: Fire, flood and fallen trees: how disturbance shapes ecosystems
nature-eco-624.text: A single tree crashing down counts. So does a mass extinction. Both are disturbances: changes in environmental conditions that cause a marked change in an {{ref:nature-found-015}}. The list includes fires, {{ref:nature-nbs-329}}, storms, insect outbreaks, trampling, earthquakes, plant diseases and volcanic eruptions. Disturbance is not simply damage. Many ecosystems are kept going by it; wetlands, for example, by moving water and periodic fires. Right after a disturbance comes a pulse of regrowth, because competition for space and resources is low. Many shade-intolerant plants need such openings to establish, so biological diversity depends on natural disturbance. In western US ponderosa pine forests, suppressing surface fires lets dense Douglas fir take over, cutting light, plant diversity and the animals that rely on them. How species cope with disturbance may even predict how well they adapt to {{ref:nature-hist-007}}.

nature-eco-637.title: The health paradox: healthier people, sicker ecosystems
nature-eco-637.text: Damming valleys, draining wetlands that breed mosquitoes, diverting water for irrigation, converting wilderness to farmland: each has improved human health by sacrificing the health of wild ecosystems. This trade-off is the health paradox. The utilitarian view treats human welfare as a test of {{ref:nature-eco-635}}. It argues that unhealthy ecosystems bring more disease, fires, {{ref:nature-nbs-329}}, crop failures and collapsing fish catches. The protectionist view sees humans as an invasive species. Conservationists and resource managers remain split over whether to scale back human domination of the biosphere or embrace it.

nature-eco-717.title: Hydrology: following water through the Earth
nature-eco-717.text: Water on Earth never stays put, and hydrology is the study of where it goes. It is the scientific study of the movement, distribution and management of water on Earth and other planets. Its central theme is that water circulates through the Earth by different pathways at different rates, as in the {{ref:nature-eco-196}}. Hydrologists collect and analyse data to solve problems such as environmental preservation, natural disasters and water management. The field divides into surface water hydrology, groundwater hydrology (hydrogeology) and marine hydrology. Applications include calculating runoff and precipitation, determining regional and agricultural water balance, designing riparian restoration, and predicting {{ref:nature-nbs-329}}, landslide and drought risk. The need is old: ancient Egyptians used basin irrigation, and Mesopotamian towns were protected from floods by high earthen walls.

nature-eco-441.title: Wetlands: the ground between water and land
nature-eco-441.text: In 2005 the {{ref:nature-es-001}} found wetlands more threatened by environmental degradation than any other ecosystem. A wetland is a semi-aquatic ecosystem whose ground is flooded or soaked with water, either permanently or for part of the year. It sits between open water and dry land, and its plants have roots adapted to oxygen-poor, waterlogged soils. The single most important factor in making one is hydrology: how long and how often an area {{ref:nature-nbs-329}}. Wetlands exist on every continent except Antarctica, and their water may be fresh, brackish (slightly salty) or salt. They come in several forms. Marshes are dominated by reeds, cattails and sedges, swamps by trees and shrubs, while peat wetlands, among them those described in {{ref:nature-eco-536}}, build up peat. The largest include the Amazon basin, the West Siberian Plain, the Pantanal and the Sundarbans. Wetlands are among the most biologically diverse ecosystems. Their plants improve water quality by removing excess nitrates and phosphorus, two nutrients that pollute rivers. They also purify water, stabilize shorelines, protect against storms and control floods, which makes their loss costly.

nature-eco-475.title: Peatlands: wetlands built from half-rotted plants
nature-eco-475.text: Peatlands cover around 3 million km2, yet they are the largest natural carbon store on land. A peatland is a wetland whose soil is made of layers of peat, partly decayed plant material. Peat builds up because waterlogging cuts off oxygen. Without oxygen, the microbes that break down dead plant litter work slowly, so the litter only partly decomposes and accumulates year after year. The result is staggering. Peat soils store over 600 Gt of carbon, more than all other vegetation types, forests included. Peatlands are most extensive at high northern latitudes. Left intact, they reduce {{ref:nature-nbs-329}} risk and erosion, purify water and help regulate climate. They face three main threats: peat harvesting, drainage for farming, notably for palm oil in the tropics, and fire. Destroying a peatland reverses its gift. The greenhouse gases it locked away escape into the air, worsening climate change.

nature-eco-450.title: Wetlands and climate: carbon store or methane source
nature-eco-450.text: Wetlands are the world's largest natural source of methane, emitting about 20–30% of atmospheric methane, on average 161 Tg a year. A teragram (Tg) is a million tonnes. Wetlands can either store carbon and slow climate change or release greenhouse gases such as methane, depending on the wetland and how it is treated. The reason is in the mud. Waterlogged, oxygen-poor soils favour methane-producing microbes. Drained peat flips the other way and decomposes into carbon dioxide. Peatlands cover only 3% of land, but their degradation produces 7% of all CO2 emissions. Coastal wetlands are strong absorbers. {{ref:nature-eco-428}} and mangroves take up on average 210 g CO2 m−2 y−1, compared with about 20–30 g CO2 m−2 y−1 for peatlands. Even so, restoring coastal wetlands purely to remove CO2, the idea behind {{ref:nature-nbs-034}}, has questionable cost-effectiveness. Their bigger payoff may be adaptation: {{ref:nature-nbs-329}} control, underground water supplies and storm protection help societies cope with the worse floods and droughts of a warming climate.

nature-eco-505.title: What aquatic ecosystems do for us
nature-eco-505.text: A river or lake partly cleans itself. Microorganisms, plankton, plants, invertebrates and fish break down organic matter and filter the water as they feed and grow. That is one of the functions of aquatic ecosystems: the environmental and human services they provide. They recycle nutrients, purify water, reduce {{ref:nature-nbs-329}}, refill underground water and provide wildlife habitat. They also give people places to play. Water-based recreation is very important to tourism, especially on coasts. And they carry meaning beyond money, serving religious and educational uses, from pilgrimage to the Jordan River to the ecological study of lakes.

nature-eco-679.title: Land reclamation: making new land from water
nature-eco-679.text: Land reclamation is the process of creating new land from oceans, seas, riverbeds or lake beds. Methods include infilling with rock and soil, draining submerged wetlands for farming, and deep cement mixing where dredged material may be contaminated. Draining wetlands is habitat destruction: a 2022 analysis attributed 39% of tidal wetland losses between 1999 and 2019 to direct human action, and nearly 65% of Yellow Sea tidal flats are estimated to have been reclaimed. Reclaimed land is prone to soil liquefaction in earthquakes and to subsidence, and drained marshes sink below surrounding water levels, raising {{ref:nature-nbs-329}} danger. Some places now restrict reclamation by law.

nature-eco-445.title: Wetlands that treat a city's sewage
nature-eco-445.text: The East Kolkata Wetlands in India cover 125 square kilometres and treat the city's sewage, and the nutrients in that waste feed fish farms and crops. Natural wetlands and specially built ones ({{ref:nature-nbs-158}}) can be used to treat sewage and other wastewater. Built wetlands use plants, soil and organisms to remove suspended solids, organic matter, nitrogen, phosphorus and disease-causing germs. In cities they do more than clean water. They also reduce {{ref:nature-nbs-329}}, store carbon and provide wildlife habitat.

nature-eco-457.title: Coral reefs as natural breakwaters
nature-eco-457.text: Reefs can cut wave energy by 97%, and many small islands would not exist without them. Coral reefs protect coastlines by absorbing wave energy before it reaches the shore, helping prevent deaths and property damage. They damp waves as well as or better than artificial breakwaters, and in the tropics restoring reefs is much cheaper than building breakwaters. About 197 million people living below 10 m elevation and within 50 km of a reef may get risk reduction from them. The top meter of reef does much of the work. Without it, expected {{ref:nature-nbs-329}} damage would double and costs from frequent storms would triple. For 100-year storms, the kind expected about once a century, flood damage would rise by 91% to $US 272 billion.

nature-eco-433.title: Can salt marshes outrun rising seas
nature-eco-433.text: Mean sea level could rise between 0.6m to 1.1m by 2100. Rising seas threaten to {{ref:nature-nbs-329}} and erode salt marshes, but marshes can sometimes build themselves up fast enough to keep pace. The rule is simple. A marsh survives only if its surface rises faster than the sea; otherwise it drowns. Drowning starts from within. Rising water opens pools inside the marsh, and their edges erode until the marsh can break up into open water. Marshes fight back with their plants. The plants slow currents and calm waves so that sediment settles. That sediment helps the plants grow, and bigger plants trap still more, a self-reinforcing loop scientists call a positive bio-geomorphic feedback. Marshes have one more escape route: moving inland. That needs accommodation space, room to retreat, which is often blocked by coastal roads, sea walls and other development. A marsh squeezed between rising water and a fixed wall has nowhere to go.

nature-eco-462.title: Floodplains: the land a river borrows
nature-eco-462.text: The Nile and Mississippi basins grew farms and cities on land their rivers regularly reclaim. A floodplain is the land beside a river, from its banks to the edges of the valley, that {{ref:nature-nbs-329}} when the river runs high. Regular floods deposit nutrients, so floodplain soils are often very fertile. People have settled there to use that rich soil and fresh water, and the risk of flooding has led to growing efforts to control floods. Floodplains support diverse, productive and often very species-rich ecosystems. Floodplain forests protect waterways from erosion and pollution and soften the impact of floodwaters. Yet the main ways people destroy floodplain ecosystems are flood control itself, reservoirs for hydroelectric power, and conversion to farmland.

nature-eco-464.title: Floodplain ecology: life timed to the flood pulse
nature-eco-464.text: Many river fish spawn just as the {{ref:nature-nbs-329}} begins, using the newly flooded river edge, and their young must grow fast before the water falls. Floodplain {{ref:nature-nbs-347}} centres on this flood pulse: the yearly cycle of flooding and drying that brings nutrients and shapes life on the floodplain. Floods bring in nutrient-rich debris and release nutrients from the soil they cover. Floodplain plants and animals grow and die fast, which lets them colonise shifting ground, and floodplain trees are fast-growing. Away from the river, plant zones follow a gradient of soil moisture, oxygen and flood frequency. Floodplain forests covered 1% of Europe in the 1800s, and because they were cleared less than other forests, they are important refuges for biodiversity. Flood control sharpens the boundary between water and land, which reduces habitat diversity.

nature-eco-483.title: What riverside strips do for people
nature-eco-483.text: A shaded stream stays cool; thin out the trees along its banks and its temperature climbs and swings, sometimes enough to kill fish. Riparian zones provide many such benefits, from slowing {{ref:nature-nbs-329}} and filtering runoff to wildlife habitat and recreation. River bends, plants and roots slow the water, which reduces soil erosion and flood damage. Trapped sediment leaves the water clearer and builds the banks. The strips serve as wildlife corridors, letting aquatic and riverside organisms move along rivers instead of living in isolated groups. They also raise nearby property values through views and amenity, and make room for fishing, swimming and boating.

nature-eco-463.title: How rivers build their floodplains
nature-eco-463.text: A meandering river eats away the outside of each bend and builds a sandbar, a point bar, on the inside, slowly laying down a level floodplain. Most floodplains are built this way, by rivers depositing sediment both inside their bends and when {{ref:nature-nbs-329}} spill over the banks. Water spilling over the banks drops a thin layer of sediment, thickest and coarsest near the channel. Over time this forms low natural ridges along the river's edge. In undisturbed rivers, overbank flow typically happens every one to two years.

nature-eco-429.title: How a mudflat becomes a salt marsh
nature-eco-429.text: A salt marsh begins as bare tidal mud. It forms when that mud builds up with sediment until tides {{ref:nature-nbs-329}} them less often, letting plants take root. Rivers slow down as they reach the flat tidal zone and drop their sediment, helped by the rising tide. Pioneer plants, the first to arrive, catch more sediment around their stems, forming mounds that join into raised terraces bound by roots. As the surface rises, flooding gets shorter and shallower, and a succession of plant communities moves in.

nature-es-005.title: From Plato's springs to a scientific term
nature-es-005.text: Around 400 BC Plato understood that cutting down forests could cause soil erosion and dry up springs. The idea took a very long time to get a name. Modern thinking probably began in 1864, when Marsh challenged the belief that Earth's resources are unlimited by pointing to changing soil fertility around the Mediterranean. In the late 1940s Henry Fairfield Osborn Jr, William Vogt and {{ref:nature-hist-051}} argued that people depend on the environment. In 1956 Paul Sears stressed ecosystems' role in processing wastes and reusing nutrients. By 1970 the warnings were starker: Paul Ehrlich and Rosa Weigert said human activity could destroy the ecological systems our species depends on. That year a report spoke of 'environmental services', listing insects that carry pollen, fisheries, regulating climate and {{ref:nature-nbs-329}} control. {{ref:nature-hist-060}} coined 'natural capital' in his 1973 book, {{ref:nature-hist-019}}. In the 1990s two works became seminal: Daily's {{ref:nature-es-004}} and Costanza and colleagues' first attempt to put a money value on ecosystem services. The Millennium Ecosystem Assessment then popularized the idea, and 'ecosystem services' became the standard term.

nature-es-119.title: Storm surge: when the sea walks inland
nature-es-119.text: In 1970 the Bhola cyclone drove a wall of seawater across the Bay of Bengal, killing up to 500,000 people, the deadliest surge on record. A storm surge is a coastal {{ref:nature-nbs-329}} of rising seawater pushed ashore by a storm, usually a low-pressure system such as a tropical cyclone. It is measured as the rise above the normal tide, not counting waves. Strong winds piling water toward the coast do most of the work. Low air pressure adds more, lifting the sea about 10 mm for every millibar of pressure drop. The damage outlasts the flood: surges wreck roads and buildings, harm soil fertility, push saltwater inland and spread contaminants. With stronger extreme weather and rising seas from climate change, surges are expected to threaten coastal people more. Nature offers a buffer. Tidal marshes protect coastal habitat from storm surge and flooding.

nature-es-122.title: Watershed services: what a healthy catchment gives
nature-es-122.text: A healthy catchment, the land that drains into a river or lake, gives water-related benefits: less soil erosion, lower landslide risk and milder {{ref:nature-nbs-329}} and droughts. These are watershed, or hydrological, services. They are one of the three main kinds of service sold in payment-for-ecosystem-services schemes, with climate mitigation and biodiversity. Costa Rica's payment scheme explicitly counted hydrological services among its four environmental services. Growing markets for them may reward forests managed with low-impact logging.

nature-val-087.title: Ecosystem valuation: putting numbers on nature's services
nature-val-087.text: In 1997 {{ref:nature-hist-048}} and colleagues made the first estimate of what the world's ecosystem services are worth: $33 trillion a year. Ecosystem valuation is the process behind numbers like that. It assigns a value, in money, physical units or other terms, to an ecosystem or the services it provides. The aim is practical. Putting numbers on benefits such as a forest's {{ref:nature-nbs-329}} control and carbon storage helps policy-makers compare policies through {{ref:nature-val-001}}. The tools come in two families. Survey methods, such as {{ref:nature-val-085}}, ask people what they would pay. Revealed preference methods, such as {{ref:nature-val-092}} and {{ref:nature-val-088}}, infer it from behavior. The results vary enormously. TEEB found values from roughly $100 per hectare per year for open ocean to more than $1,000,000 per hectare per year for the richest coral reefs. Valuation is hard because many environmental goods, such as clean air, are not traded. Many are also non-rival and non-excludable: one person's use leaves no less for others, and no one can be kept out. Some programs go on to pay landowners; Costa Rica paid about $42 per hectare to preserve forests. Critics say preference-based valuation avoids deliberation and judgment, and that the money value of services depends on how income is distributed. Behind this lies a philosophical and ethical dispute over whether nature should be priced at all.

nature-val-002.title: From Dupuit's bridges to government policy
nature-val-002.text: In 1848 Jules Dupuit measured the social benefit of a road or bridge by adding up what each user would be willing to pay for it. Alfred Marshall later formalized the idea. In the United States, the Federal Navigation Act of 1936 required it for federal waterway projects, and the {{ref:nature-nbs-329}} Control Act of 1939 made it federal policy. Otto Eckstein gave it a welfare-economics foundation in 1958. In the 1960s it was applied to water quality, recreation and land conservation.

nature-pol-177.title: Zoning: deciding what goes where
nature-pol-177.text: Whether a field can become a factory is usually decided by a town, not a nation. Zoning is a way for a local government to divide land into zones. Each zone has its own rules on what may be built and how land may be used, a limit on {{ref:nature-econ-621}}. Zones may allow a single use, such as housing or industry, or mix compatible uses. Form-based zoning governs building size and shape whatever the use. Single-use zoning separates uses thought incompatible, and in practice it also protects existing uses and a community's character. Overlay zones add rules for a particular concern, such as wetlands or a natural hazard, without rewriting the whole code. Zoning is a key tool for helping cities adapt to climate change and manage {{ref:nature-nbs-329}}. It also draws fire. Environmental activists argue that separating everyday uses forces car ownership and adds traffic. Some economists say it reduces efficiency and raises housing costs; one 2017 study estimated large GDP gains from partial deregulation. Supporters reply that it is essential for keeping harmful uses apart.

nature-pol-314.title: Perverse incentives and the cobra effect
nature-pol-314.text: In Hanoi in 1902, a bounty paid 1 cent per rat tail. Rat catchers cut off the tails and released the rats to breed more. A perverse incentive is a structure that produces undesirable results, especially effects unexpected and contrary to what its designers intended. Horst Siebert coined the name "cobra effect" in 2001 from a British Raj anecdote about a bounty on dead cobras. That anecdote is disputed: a 2025 investigation found no contemporary records of cobra breeding in British India, said the Madras bounty was scaled back over cost, not fraud, and urged retiring the term. Other cases hold up better. At Fort Benning a $40 bounty per feral pig tail coincided with a rising pig population; feed bait raised fertility and survival, and hunters preferred large males over females and juveniles. Endangered Species Act restrictions on landowners can encourage preemptive habitat destruction. A {{ref:nature-mkt-081}} scheme gave one of the highest bounties for destroying the refrigerant byproduct HFC-23, so firms made more refrigerant to earn credits; the EU suspended such credits in 2013. Grandfathered emission permits, offsets, {{ref:nature-mkt-104}} credits and subsidised insurance against {{ref:nature-nbs-329}} damage have all drawn the same criticism.

nature-pol-216.title: The CAP's second pillar: money for the countryside
nature-pol-216.text: Since 2000 the EU farm policy has had a second pillar, which funds the economic, social and environmental development of the countryside. It works through seven-year rural development programs, of which there are 118 in the EU. One of its three axes supports land management that improves the environment and helps fight climate change. Projects can include protecting water quality, sustainable land management and planting trees against erosion and {{ref:nature-nbs-329}}.

nature-mkt-100.title: Markets or funds: the early fight over paying for REDD+
nature-mkt-100.text: Should forests be saved by selling credits or by public money? Early in REDD+, countries and observers split over offset-based versus fund-based designs. Critics of the market route argued that {{ref:nature-nbs-329}} of forest credits could depress carbon prices and weaken incentives to cut emissions at home. The UN settled on a compromise. Since the COP 17 climate conference, its decisions allow REDD+ to be financed by both market and non-market sources.

nature-res-169.title: Water security: enough clean water, risks kept low
nature-res-169.text: About 27% of the world's population lived in water-scarce areas in the mid-2010s, a share likely to reach 42% by 2050. Water security is the goal that trend threatens. It means getting the most benefit from water for people and ecosystems while keeping the risks of {{ref:nature-nbs-329}}, droughts and polluted water acceptably low. People with high water security always have enough water of acceptable quality for health, livelihoods and production. The concept emerged in the 21st century and is broader than the absence of water scarcity, although some organizations use it only for supply. Its main threats are scarcity, pollution, poorer water quality from climate change, poverty, destructive floods and natural disasters. How easily a society stays secure depends on its water environment, its economy and society, and future climate change. The IPCC predicted that 2 °C of global warming would expose roughly 1–4 billion people to water stress. Responses include engineering for more supply or efficiency, financial safety nets for poorer people and caps on demand. There is no standard way to measure it.

nature-res-144.title: Land-use planning: deciding what land is for
nature-res-144.text: Belts of protected countryside and urban growth boundaries ring many cities, holding back development from rural and farm land. They are tools of land-use planning, the process by which a central authority regulates how land may be used. It aims at better social and environmental outcomes and more efficient use of resources. Modern goals include conserving the environment, restraining urban sprawl, cutting transport costs, preventing land-use conflicts and limiting exposure to pollutants. It nearly always relies on {{ref:nature-res-110}}, typically zoning. Zoning controls what may happen on a piece of land and how buildings are placed and shaped. Planning also helps manage {{ref:nature-nbs-329}}, alongside warning systems and {{ref:nature-clim-039}}. Its effects are contested. Planners assume rules change behavior, which is widely accepted. Whether those changes are beneficial is disputed and depends on place and rules. Critics say rules are often too strict, making land supply too slow to respond and pushing prices up sharply. In North America, they argue, planning systems have worsened housing crises.

nature-res-121.title: Catchment factors: why some rivers flood
nature-res-121.text: Rain on roofs, pavements and roads reaches rivers with almost no absorption into the ground. That is one of several catchment factors, the features of a {{ref:nature-res-119}} that determine how likely it is to {{ref:nature-nbs-329}}: topography, shape, size, soil type and land use. Topography and shape set how fast rain reaches the river. Size, soil and development set how much arrives. Sandy soils absorb rain, while clay soils are nearly impermeable and add to flood volumes.

nature-nbs-220.title: Nature-based solutions: hiring ecosystems to do the work
nature-nbs-220.text: A strip of mangrove forest along a tropical coast does four jobs at once. It breaks the force of waves and wind, stores carbon, nurtures fish and holds the shoreline against erosion. That bundle of benefits is the idea behind nature-based solutions, or NBS. They are actions that protect, sustainably manage or restore ecosystems to tackle social challenges, while benefiting both people and biodiversity. The challenges are big ones: slowing climate change and adapting to it, securing water and food, and reducing disaster risk. Cities have their own versions. Roofs covered in plants or built to hold rain, and walls draped in greenery, can cool overheated city centers, capture rainwater, cut pollution and store carbon. The term came from practitioners in the late 2000s. The IUCN and the World Bank took it up to describe working with ecosystems rather than relying purely on engineering. The IUCN now treats NBS as an umbrella over {{ref:nature-nbs-112}}, {{ref:nature-nbs-216}}, {{ref:nature-nbs-218}} and {{ref:nature-nbs-224}}. The European Commission stresses that NBS are cost-effective and deliver environmental, social and economic benefits at once. The {{ref:nature-nbs-329}} evidence is encouraging. A review of 386 cases found NBS as effective as conventional ways of handling floods, or more so, and 66% reported positive ecological outcomes. Politics has followed. Around 130 national climate pledges, known as {{ref:nature-clim-071}} documents, commit to NBS: 65% of signatories. Yet those pledges rarely become measurable action.

nature-nbs-218.title: Ecosystem-based adaptation: living defenses against a changing climate
nature-nbs-218.text: When a storm surge rolls toward a coast, a healthy reef, mangrove stand or marsh can take much of the blow. Using such living defenses on purpose is called ecosystem-based adaptation, or EbA. It uses biodiversity and ecosystem services to help people adapt to the harmful effects of climate change. In practice, EbA conserves, sustainably manages and restores forests, wetlands, mangroves and coral reefs. The goal is less harm from storms, shifting rainfall and temperature extremes. The examples are concrete. Restored reefs, mangroves and marshes soften storm surges. Trees grown among crops, a practice called {{ref:nature-nbs-247}}, help farms ride out drought. Well-managed forests hold slopes in place and prevent flash {{ref:nature-nbs-329}}. EbA can work alone or alongside engineered works such as dykes, hybrid measures such as artificial reefs, and systems that warn people early. Supporters claim a long list of side benefits: better health, food and water security, fewer disasters, stored carbon and conserved biodiversity. The IUCN coined the term in 2008, and the {{ref:nature-gov-015}} defined it officially in 2009. It sits inside the wider family of nature-based solutions. Many countries cite EbA in their climate pledges under the {{ref:nature-clim-074}}. It is increasingly seen as a way to tackle hardship and the climate crisis together in developing countries, where people depend on natural resources.

nature-nbs-222.title: Green plus grey: why hybrids beat either alone
nature-nbs-222.text: Should a city trust concrete or nature? Research suggests the best answer is often both. This hybrid approach combines nature-based solutions with conventional built infrastructure. Studies find NBS improve {{ref:nature-nbs-329}} resilience but cannot act alone; they must be coordinated with grey works. Used together, the benefits reach beyond flood control to better social conditions, more stored carbon and stronger resilience planning. Researchers urge looking for such synergies rather than treating NBS as a rival to engineering.

nature-eco-297.title: Food webs: the tangled network of who eats whom
nature-eco-297.text: Losing one species can harm a whole chain of others, a knock-on loss described in {{ref:nature-eco-106}}. The reason is the food web, the network of linked feeding sequences in a community that shows who eats whom. Organisms are broadly classed as autotrophs, which make their own food, or heterotrophs, which feed on others. Feeding links fall roughly into four kinds: herbivory (plant-eating), carnivory, scavenging and parasitism. Plants form the base. Top predators sit at the summit, where nothing kills them for food. Energy and matter move differently through a web. Energy moves one way, and eventually all of it is lost as heat. Materials such as nutrients cycle round and round. A feeding sequence usually has at most four or five links, and those in water are often longer than those on land. Charles Elton's 1927 book Animal {{ref:nature-nbs-347}} made feeding sequences and food cycles central to the study of nature.

nature-eco-373.title: The Redfield ratio: the ocean's chemical recipe
nature-eco-373.text: Phytoplankton and the deep ocean's dissolved nutrients share one recipe: carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus in the ratio 106:16:1. This is the Redfield ratio. Alfred C. Redfield proposed that phytoplankton needs control the ocean's ratio, since they release nitrogen and phosphorus when they are broken back down into dissolved form. It became a fundamental principle of marine {{ref:nature-nbs-347}} and of biogeochemistry, the study of how chemicals move between living things and their surroundings. It is not universal. {{ref:nature-eco-394}}, {{ref:nature-eco-396}} and changing nutrient inputs can shift it.

nature-eco-758.title: Population pyramids: reading a population's age shape
nature-eco-758.text: A population pyramid is a graph of a population's distribution by age group and sex, usually for a country or region. Males are conventionally on the left and females on the right, with bars in absolute numbers or percentages. In {{ref:nature-nbs-347}} it shows a population's age distribution, hinting at reproductive capability and likelihood of continuation. A broad base signals fertility above replacement, and the shape also reveals the age-dependency ratio of those too young or old to work. Pyramids fall into three types: stationary, with births and deaths roughly balanced; expansive, wide at young ages; and constrictive, narrowed at the bottom. Their shape tracks the {{ref:nature-eecon-250}}: more developed countries sit in stages three to five, least developed in stages one and two.

nature-eco-234.title: The nitrogen cascade: one atom, many harms
nature-eco-234.text: The nitrogen cascade is the passing of the same reactive nitrogen from one ecosystem to the next. It moves through air, water and land until it is turned back into nitrogen gas. Pathways that carry nutrients across system boundaries link one nitrogen problem to the next. Some systems store reactive nitrogen along the way, delaying the cascade and intensifying local effects. In the end, nitrogen that people add is either stored or denitrified, but how much goes each way is still poorly known. Some scientists think the cascade may be as big a problem for Earth's {{ref:nature-nbs-347}} as carbon dioxide.

nature-eco-093.title: Diversity indices: boiling variety down to one number
nature-eco-093.text: Counting species tells only part of the story. A diversity index is a number that measures how many different types, usually species, a dataset or community contains, often weighted by how common each is. Indices summarize parts of biodiversity such as richness, evenness and dominance, so communities or sites are easy to compare. Richness, explained in {{ref:nature-eco-150}}, is a simple count of types. It is popular in {{ref:nature-nbs-347}} because data on abundance are often lacking. Abundance itself can be measured as numbers of individuals, {{ref:nature-clim-284}} or coverage. The Shannon and Simpson indices also account for each type's share of the total. The same measures work outside the study of nature, for demographic groups or even letters of the alphabet.

nature-eco-070.title: Species abundance distributions: a few common, many rare
nature-eco-070.text: In most collections, a few species make up most of the individuals. A species abundance distribution describes how common or rare each species is within an ecosystem. It is one of the most basic and widely used measurements in {{ref:nature-nbs-347}}, with many methods of analysis. Its usual lopsided shape echoes the pattern in {{ref:nature-eco-069}}.

nature-eco-094.title: The Shannon index: how hard is it to guess the next species?
nature-eco-094.text: Claude Shannon proposed this measure in 1948 to quantify the unpredictability of strings of text.
