In {{ref:nature-nbs-347}}, the Shannon index measures the uncertainty in predicting the species of an individual picked at random from a community. The more types there are, and the more evenly they are represented, the harder the prediction and the higher the value. Logarithms to base 2, 10 and e give values in bits, decits and nats respectively. Its exponential is the effective number of species of order 1, the link explained in {{ref:nature-eco-077}}.

nature-eco-593.title: Carrying capacity: how many any place can feed
nature-eco-593.text: Any patch of land or water can feed only so many mouths. Ecologists call that ceiling the carrying capacity: the largest population of a species an environment can keep going over time, given its food, habitat, water and other resources. Below carrying capacity, a {{ref:nature-eco-374}} can grow, as {{ref:nature-eco-376}} describes. Above it, numbers usually shrink for lack of space, food or sunlight. At the ceiling itself, births equal deaths once animals moving in and out are counted, so the population sits in equilibrium. Whatever stops growth is called the limiting factor. It might be food, water or nesting space, or even the amount of waste the environment can absorb. Applied to a whole environment, the idea means resources are not taken faster than they regrow, and wastes stay within what nature can absorb. The term spread through biology in the 1870s. Wildlife and livestock managers developed it in the early 1900s, and it was a staple of {{ref:nature-nbs-347}} by the 1950s. Today it is used to find the maximum population an environment can support in the study of nature, farming and fisheries. Many authors still doubt its value for wild populations, because it can oversimplify how species interact.

nature-eco-628.title: Ecological stability: one word, 167 definitions
nature-eco-628.text: In 1997 Grimm and Wissel counted the meanings of stability in the ecological literature. They found 167 definitions covering 70 different concepts. Broadly, ecological stability is an ecosystem's ability to return to equilibrium after a {{ref:nature-eco-624}}, or to avoid sudden large changes over time. The catch is that an ecosystem can be stable in some properties and not others. A plant community in drought may keep its {{ref:nature-clim-284}} while losing biodiversity. Some ecosystems are not stable at all, as with the wolves and moose of Isle Royale. The concept emerged in the first half of the 20th century and spread with theoretical {{ref:nature-nbs-347}} in the 1970s. Overuse of the term has made its definition a matter of controversy. Grimm and Wissel proposed replacing it with more specific terms such as constancy, resilience and persistence.

nature-eco-640.title: Hysteresis: when a system remembers its past
nature-eco-640.text: A thermostat that turns the heat on below 18 °C but off only above 22 °C uses hysteresis on purpose. Sir James Alfred Ewing coined the word in 1881, from a Greek term meaning 'lagging behind'. It describes a system whose state depends on its history, not just on present conditions. Agar melts at 85 °C but solidifies only at 32 to 40 °C. Between those temperatures, whether it is liquid or solid depends on where it started. Plotted on a graph, such systems often trace a hysteresis loop: one variable takes different values depending on which way another variable is changing. In {{ref:nature-nbs-347}}, this means environmental conditions alone cannot predict a system's equilibrium. Its past matters too, as spruce budworm outbreaks show.

nature-eco-762.title: Earth system science: treating the planet as one system
nature-eco-762.text: Earth system science asks what happens when you study the whole planet as a single, interacting system. It applies systems science to the Earth, studying feedbacks between its spheres and the impact of human societies. It draws on natural and social sciences, including {{ref:nature-nbs-347}} and economics, and takes a holistic view. Its four named features of the Earth System are variability, life, connectivity and non-linearity. Because of strong non-linearities, a small change in a forcing function can push the system across a threshold and cause abrupt change. The field grew partly from a NASA committee formed in 1983, whose reports in 1986 and 1988 stressed human impacts as the reason to join the life and geosciences. It treats the {{ref:nature-found-022}} as part of a {{ref:nature-eco-621}}.

nature-eco-654.title: Critical slowing down: an early warning of tipping
nature-eco-654.text: Since the early 2000s, more than three-quarters of the Amazon rainforest has shown slower recovery from short-term shocks. That sluggishness may be critical slowing down: the increasingly slow recovery from small disturbances shown by a system approaching a tipping point. As recovery slows, the system's autocorrelation, how closely each reading resembles the last, and its variance, how widely readings swing, both rise. Rising values of both in melt rates suggest the Greenland ice sheet is losing resilience. Early warnings need long, good-quality data series, which are rare in {{ref:nature-nbs-347}}. Noise-induced transitions give no warning, and human-driven change may be too fast for signals to appear. How well the signals work for all regime shifts, and whether they leave time to act, is unclear.

nature-eco-655.title: Panarchy: cycles nested inside cycles
nature-eco-655.text: Panarchy views linked human and natural systems as a nested set of adaptive cycles, each running at its own scale of time and space. In resilience theory, it means how much one level of an ecosystem's hierarchy is influenced by the others. C.S. Holling developed the idea, leading to the 2002 book Panarchy: understanding transformations in human and natural systems. It has become an important lens on the resilience of ecological and social-ecological systems. It also reaches beyond {{ref:nature-nbs-347}}, for example linking planetary, political-economic and supply-chain levels.

nature-eco-416.title: Forest ecology: studying the woods as a whole
nature-eco-416.text: Forests cover almost a third of all land, so what happens in them affects the whole biosphere and the human activities it supports. Forest {{ref:nature-nbs-347}} is the scientific study of the living things, patterns and processes found in forest ecosystems. A forest ecosystem is all the plants, animals and microbes of a woodland working together with their non-living surroundings. Forest ecologists usually study whole populations, communities or ecosystems rather than single organisms. Trees vary hugely in size and arrangement, so forests are patchy, varied environments, and that variety supports great biodiversity. Managing forests goes by several names, including {{ref:nature-res-131}} and {{ref:nature-res-156}}. Machine learning now lets forest ecologists process larger and more complex data sets.

nature-eco-437.title: Urban ecosystems: the city as a habitat
nature-eco-437.text: Cities hold more than half of the world's population, and their numbers are expected to keep growing. An urban ecosystem is the ecosystem of a city, town or industrial area: a complex patchwork of buildings, roads, parks and gardens created and maintained by people. It cannot feed itself. Urban ecosystems depend on large imports of water, nutrients, food and other resources. Dense human populations interacting with many kinds of patches produce complex feedbacks among the parts of the system. Social-{{ref:nature-nbs-347}} treats a city as part of a wider system linking its people with the surrounding landscapes. Cities offer jobs, healthcare and education, but urban growth worsens pollution and the loss of green space and biodiversity. Studying urban ecosystems has led to proposals for city design that does less harm to surrounding environments.

nature-eco-739.title: Seascape ecology: reading patterns in the sea
nature-eco-739.text: A seagrass bed in a sand flat is not just a place; it is a pattern. Seascape {{ref:nature-nbs-347}} studies the causes and ecological consequences of spatial pattern in the marine environment, borrowing the frameworks used to study patterns on land. Its central tenet is that patch context matters: surroundings shape local conditions, so the shape, size, arrangement and edges of patches all count. Studies choose scales that fit an organism's movement. Juvenile fish use several habitats as they grow, so ignoring mangrove roots, macroalgae or seagrass can mislead assessments of an estuary. The field has grown since the 1970s, yet in marine systems understanding is still in its infancy.

nature-es-010.title: Deciding what to do with the land
nature-es-010.text: Land-use decisions that touch ecosystem services are messy by nature. They mean weighing {{ref:nature-nbs-347}}, technology, society and the economy together. They are usually spatial, always have several objectives, and rest on uncertain data, models and estimates. Regulators, developers, residents and NGOs all have a say; usually the best science combined with stakeholder values drives the process. Researchers have modeled stakeholders as agents and used repeated random simulations to capture uncertainty in landowner choices. Others have blended uncertain science with stakeholder input in probability models. Images of land taken from above can track the health and extent of the vegetation and ground cover that provide services.

nature-es-046.title: Landscape ecology: seeing nature as a patchwork
nature-es-046.text: In 1939 the German geographer Carl Troll was studying aerial photographs, trying to see how environment and vegetation interact. He coined a name for this view from above: landscape {{ref:nature-nbs-347}}. It is the science of how ecological processes relate to particular ecosystems across whole landscapes, and how to improve those relationships. Landscapes are mixed areas of interacting patches, from forests and lakes to farms and cities. Traditional ecology often assumes places are uniform. Landscape ecology instead studies heterogeneity, the way parts of a landscape differ. Its hallmark is a focus on how pattern, process and scale relate, and on broad-scale environmental problems. Its four main principles concern how this patchiness develops, how things move across it, how it affects living and non-living processes, and how to manage it. The field treats humans explicitly as a force that reshapes landscapes and proposes ways to restore degraded ones. It grew from European planning of human-dominated landscapes and was established by 1980. Its recent growth owes much to GIS and large remotely sensed habitat datasets.

nature-es-061.title: Agent-based models: simple rules, complex worlds
nature-es-061.text: In 1971 Thomas Schelling used coins and graph paper to show how simple choices by individuals could produce segregation that none of them planned. It was an early agent-based model. Such a computer model simulates the actions and interactions of autonomous agents, such as people or organizations, to see how a whole system behaves. In {{ref:nature-nbs-347}} it is called an individual-based model. Its central ideas are agents as objects, emergence and complexity: simple rules for agents can produce complex behavior. The idea dates to the late 1940s but spread only in the 1990s, because it needs heavy computing. In economics, these models drop the assumption of equilibrium and use diverse, interdependent agents, so they can produce booms and crashes. Combined with GIS, the model captures the process while the GIS captures the spatial pattern. Water planners use them to test infrastructure and policy and to value cooperation. Calibration, sensitivity analysis and statistical tests check that a model relates to the real world.

nature-es-073.title: Spatial analysis: asking where
nature-es-073.text: As far back as at least 1,400 BC, Egyptian surveyors measured taxable plots with ropes, an early root of spatial analysis. Today it is the set of formal techniques that study things through their location, shape and geographic arrangement, drawing especially on spatial statistics. In a narrower sense it is geospatial analysis, usually done with GIS software. It was developed for {{ref:nature-nbs-347}}, geology and epidemiology and now reaches forests and water, disaster risk and climate adaptation. Basic operations include stacking maps and buffering, which marks areas within a set distance of features such as roads or rivers. Gravity models estimate flows of people, materials or information between places. Its most fundamental problem is defining where the things being studied are located. Another trap is the ecological fallacy: drawing conclusions about individuals from aggregated data.

nature-val-062.title: Deep ecology: worth beyond usefulness
nature-val-062.text: Rachel Carson's {{ref:nature-hist-006}}, published in 1962, is often seen as the start of the movement. The Norwegian philosopher Arne Næss gave it a name, coining 'deep {{ref:nature-nbs-347}}' in 1972 and first using the phrase in a 1973 article. Deep ecology holds that all living beings have worth regardless of their usefulness to people, and that society should be reshaped to match. Its core principle is that the living environment as a whole has basic moral and legal rights to live and flourish. Næss set it against 'shallow the study of nature', which he criticized as utilitarian, human-centered and consumer-oriented. Deep ecology rejects nature as a resource to exploit. The materialist outlook, including the pursuit of economic growth, must be replaced. Critics push back. Guha and Martínez Alier argue it ignores excessive consumption in the global north, and Murray Bookchin called it misanthropic. Others call it Eurocentric or unscientific, and deep ecologists dispute each charge. Its ideas also feed arguments for valuing ecosystems outside markets.

nature-val-067.title: Social ecology: how people treat nature and each other
nature-val-067.text: 'The ecological crisis is a social crisis,' Murray Bookchin argued. His 1982 philosophy of social {{ref:nature-nbs-347}} links how humans treat nature to how they treat each other. Practices such as monocropping, growing a single crop over and over, and taking too many fish mirror social tendencies to dominate people. Bookchin defined nature itself as a tendency in healthy ecosystems toward more diversity, complementarity and freedom. Social ecology calls for decentralization, interdependence and direct democracy instead of profit extraction.

nature-val-037.title: Environmental ethics: arguments for protecting nature
nature-val-037.text: Should a forest be clear-cut for human consumption? Which species should be valued for their own sake? Environmental ethics asks such questions. It is the branch of practical philosophy that sets out arguments for protecting nature and using resources sustainably. Its main competing views are anthropocentrism, ecocentrism, also called physiocentrism, and theocentrism, which centers value on God. The field grew in response to Rachel Carson, Murray Bookchin and the first {{ref:nature-hist-016}} in 1970. Two papers had a crucial impact: Lynn White's 1967 paper on the roots of the ecological crisis, and {{ref:nature-hist-052}}'s 1968 'Tragedy of the Commons'. Alan Marshall sorts its approaches into three: libertarian extension, {{ref:nature-val-039}} and {{ref:nature-val-040}}. Today it influences law, sociology, ecotheology, {{ref:nature-nbs-347}} and geography. It also has an internal quarrel. Animal ethics and environmental ethics clash over duties to wild animals; some see them as incompatible, others as reconcilable.

nature-val-049.title: The land ethic: citizens, not conquerors
nature-val-049.text: In {{ref:nature-hist-005}}, published in 1949, {{ref:nature-hist-051}} called for an ethic covering humans' relation to land, animals and plants. A land ethic is a framework for how, ethically, people should regard the land. Leopold's basic principle: a thing is right when it tends to preserve the integrity, stability and beauty of the biotic community. Humans become plain members and citizens of the land community, not its conquerors. Leopold saw two flaws in an ethic based on economic self-interest. Most members of an ecosystem have no economic worth, and conservation gets left to government. Other land ethics rest on economics, utilitarianism, libertarianism, egalitarianism or {{ref:nature-nbs-347}}. Leopold's is popular as a moderate view, balancing human interests with a healthy, diverse environment. Critics call it vague, and say it does not clearly explain why it should be adopted. Scholars still debate what it asserts, and whether it rests on human interests or on nature's intrinsic value.

nature-val-031.title: Three objections to commodifying nature
nature-val-031.text: Critics of turning nature into commodities sort their objections into three kinds: practical, moral and consequential. The practical problem is that natural things resist. Fish {{ref:nature-nbs-347}} shapes how fisheries can be privatized, and water's physical properties make it hard to commodify. The moral problem is that a single money value denies nature's many cultural and social values. Livelihoods, territorial rights and sacredness translate poorly into prices. The consequential problem is what markets do once in charge. They handle fairness and equitable distribution poorly, and critics say commodification deepens inequality. Efficiency and profit override other concerns, and market exchange is 'reason-blind' to ecological importance. David Harvey argues there is something 'inherently anti-ecological' about capitalist commodification. These critiques are aimed at {{ref:nature-res-117}}, whose proponents defend pricing nature.

nature-val-040.title: Conservation ethics: protecting nature for people's sake
nature-val-040.text: Protect nature because people need it: that is conservation ethics. It values the environment only for its usefulness to people, and protects it as a means to human welfare. Because it rejects the intrinsic value that deep {{ref:nature-nbs-347}} gives nature, it is often called 'shallow the study of nature'. It may underlie government positions at the 1992 Rio {{ref:nature-hist-003}} and the 1997 Kyoto summit.

nature-val-036.title: Social ecological economics: economies inside society and nature
nature-val-036.text: Economies emerge from society and {{ref:nature-nbs-347}}, and depend on how both are structured and function. That is the starting point of social ecological economics, a proposed paradigm shift in {{ref:nature-eecon-059}} that integrates social, ecological and economic knowledge. It rejects reductionism and builds in value incommensurability and value pluralism. Clive Spash divides the field into social ecological economists, new environmental pragmatists and new resource economists.

nature-acct-040.title: Circles of Sustainability: choosing the right indicators
nature-acct-040.text: Circles of {{ref:nature-eecon-208}} does not prescribe indicators. It is a framework for deciding which are most useful, organized around four domains: economics, {{ref:nature-nbs-347}}, politics and culture. Each domain has seven sub-domains, each linked to indicators. Agencies including the UN Global Compact Cities Programme have used it since 2010.

nature-res-080.title: Marine conservation: managing the seas so they last
nature-res-080.text: Baleen whales were nearing extinction when the International Whaling Commission's global ban on commercial whaling took effect in 1986. Marine conservation is the protection of ocean and sea ecosystems through planned management, so that marine resources are not over-exploited. It aims to limit human damage, restore damaged ecosystems and preserve vulnerable species. It draws on marine biology, {{ref:nature-nbs-347}}, oceanography and the science of fisheries, together with economics, maritime law and policy. Its tools include reserves with seasonal or permanent closures and zoning, sustainable fisheries and fishing quotas. Overfishing is one of the main causes of declining ocean wildlife: the FAO reported sustainable stocks fell from 90% in 1974 to 65.8% in 2017. Researchers suggest blending in customary local management, though past attempts to combine the two have often failed.

nature-res-016.title: Fisheries science: the study behind the catch
nature-res-016.text: Michael Graham's 'Great Law of Fishing' holds that unlimited fisheries become unprofitable. Fisheries science is the academic discipline of understanding and managing fisheries. It draws on oceanography, marine and freshwater biology, {{ref:nature-nbs-347}}, population dynamics, economics, statistics and decision analysis. Research vessels tow nets, sample plankton and water, and carry acoustic fish-finders. Fedor Baranov's 1918 catch equation is perhaps the most used equation in fisheries modeling. New fields have grown out of the discipline, such as bioeconomics and {{ref:nature-res-036}}.

nature-nbs-009.title: Urban green space: country in the city
nature-nbs-009.text: Around the first century C.E., the Romans had a phrase for it: 'rus in urbe', country in the city. In town planning, urban green spaces are open areas set aside for parks and other greenery. The World Health Organization defines them more broadly, as all city land covered by vegetation of any kind. They include plant life and water features, called blue spaces, and range from playing fields to wilder-looking land. Their benefits fall into four groups: recreation, {{ref:nature-nbs-347}}, beauty and health. Green spaces can clean city air, shelter wildlife and lower flood risk by draining rainwater. Homes near urban open spaces tend to be worth more. Quality matters as much as quantity. Visitors gain more from green spaces with more biodiversity, so variety counts, not just greenness.

nature-nbs-028.title: Urban ecology: studying nature among the buildings
nature-nbs-028.text: Ecologists largely turned to cities from the 1970s. Urban {{ref:nature-nbs-347}} is the scientific study of how living things relate to each other and to their surroundings in cities. Dense buildings and paved surfaces create a distinctive landscape. Its goal is a balance between human culture and the natural environment. Researchers use chemical tests, temperature records and heat maps, remote sensing and long-term research sites. Cities disturb nature's chemical cycles. Their demand for chemicals contributes to acid rain, eutrophication and global warming, while paving stops nutrients returning to the soil. Green infrastructure can make cities better homes for wildlife. Because the field is young, many effects of urban growth remain poorly understood.

nature-nbs-112.title: Ecological restoration: repairing ecosystems already damaged
nature-nbs-112.text: Hundreds of thousands of restoration projects now run worldwide, and their number has grown exponentially. Ecological restoration is helping an ecosystem recover after it has been degraded, damaged, destroyed or transformed. That sets it apart from conservation, which tries to prevent damage in the first place. Restoration repairs what is already harmed. The methods are hands-on: controlling erosion, replanting forests, removing weeds and non-native species, reintroducing native species and building wildlife corridors. The reasons vary just as much. Projects aim to restore natural capital such as clean water, help endangered species, adapt to climate change and store carbon. Done well, restoration can help reverse biodiversity loss, keep ecosystem services flowing and support local economies. The field has two halves. Restoration {{ref:nature-nbs-347}} is the scientific study; ecological restoration is the practical work. The record is mixed. Restorations often miss their goals, and their high costs can be seen as a drawback. Public support fades if the costs seem to outweigh the benefits. Even so, the United Nations named 2021–2030 a decade devoted to this work, the {{ref:nature-nbs-137}}.

nature-nbs-116.title: Restoration ecology and conservation biology: sister sciences
nature-nbs-116.text: Two sciences share a love of habitat but look at it differently. Conservation biology studies species populations and often centers on animals. Restoration {{ref:nature-nbs-347}} works at the level of whole communities and centers on plants, because projects usually start by establishing plant communities. It also puts more weight on soils, fungi and microbes, the base of land ecosystems. Both value protecting and restoring habitat. Restoration ecology became a separate field in the late twentieth century.

nature-eco-190.title: Photosynthesis: how sunlight becomes food and oxygen
nature-eco-190.text: The living world captures sunlight at a rate of about 130 terawatts, roughly eight times the power used by human civilization. The machinery doing this is photosynthesis: the process by which plants, algae and cyanobacteria turn light energy, usually from the sun, into chemical energy. These are the autotrophs met in {{ref:nature-eco-324}}, the organisms that make their own food. In its usual form, called oxygenic photosynthesis, the process splits water and releases oxygen. The captured energy is stored in carbon compounds such as sugars, starch and cellulose. Cells later break these compounds down through {{ref:nature-eco-212}} to get the energy back. The scale is immense. Each year photosynthetic organisms turn around 100–115 billion tons of carbon into {{ref:nature-clim-284}}, the stuff of living bodies. The consequences reach far beyond any single leaf. Oxygen released by cyanobacteria long ago filled Earth's air, which made complex life possible. Photosynthesis still produces and maintains that oxygen today, and it supplies most of the energy that complex life runs on. The name is surprisingly recent: Charles Reid Barnes proposed it in 1893.

nature-eco-263.title: Counting soil carbon for climate reporting
nature-eco-263.text: One model puts the organic carbon in the topsoil of EU farmland at 17.63 Gt. Under the UN climate convention, countries must estimate and report changes in stored carbon from land use and forestry, soil carbon included. Five pools are reported: above-ground and below-ground {{ref:nature-clim-284}}, dead wood, litter and soil carbon. Reliable soil carbon estimates are also needed for schemes that pay to cut emissions from the clearing and degrading of forests.

nature-eco-007.title: Carbon dioxide: the gas at the center of the story
nature-eco-007.text: In 2026 the air held 432 ppm of carbon dioxide, or 0.0432%. That is a 54% rise from the 280 ppm of the 10,000 years before the mid-18th century. Carbon dioxide is a trace gas in Earth's air, yet it plays a central part in the greenhouse effect, the carbon cycle and photosynthesis. It is one of the three principal greenhouse gases in Earth's atmosphere, and today's concentration is the highest for 14 million years. The rise is caused by human activity, mainly burning fossil fuels, with cement making, deforestation and {{ref:nature-clim-284}} burning adding more. Human emissions exceed what natural sinks can absorb, so about half of the carbon dioxide from fossil fuels stays in the air. By 2024 humans had emitted an estimated 2,650 gigatonnes since 1850, at 42 gigatonnes a year, and about 1,050 gigatonnes remain in the air. A projected 20–35% of the fossil carbon released so far will keep levels raised for many thousands of years. The rise is tracked at Mauna Loa, where regular measurements began in 1958, building on Dave Keeling's accurate flask samples of the 1950s.

nature-eco-019.title: Climate change and the world's food supply
nature-eco-019.text: Disasters from extreme weather caused food production losses estimated at US$123 billion in 2025, 5% of global agricultural GDP. Climate change threatens people's ability to grow, reach and rely on enough food. The causes include higher carbon dioxide, heat, changed rainfall, more extreme events, and shifting pests and diseases. Climate change is projected to weaken the food supply on every front, affecting how much food exists, its price and quality, and how stable the supply is. The sea is affected too. Ocean {{ref:nature-clim-284}} is expected to fall by about 5% per degree of warming, hitting tropical seas hardest.

nature-eco-123.title: The 2019 global assessment: a million species at risk
nature-eco-123.text: Of an estimated 8 million animal and plant species, 1 million are threatened with extinction. That was the headline of the Global Assessment Report, whose summary for policymakers came out on 6 May 2019. It was produced by the panel described in {{ref:nature-gov-020}}. It reviews 50 years of change, drawing on over 15,000 scientific publications and Indigenous knowledge. It was the UN's first worldwide assessment of biodiversity since the 2005 review covered in {{ref:nature-es-001}}. The threatened include 40% of amphibians and more than a third of marine mammals. Wild mammal {{ref:nature-clim-284}} has fallen by 82%, while humans and their farm animals now make up 96% of all mammal living mass. Over the same 50 years the human population doubled and GDP per person quadrupled. The report ranked the drivers: changes in land and sea use, direct exploitation, climate change, pollution and invasive alien species. Pollinator loss threatens food worth $235 to $577 billion a year. The report urged countries not to fixate on economic growth and to shift government support away from industries that harm nature.

nature-eco-039.title: Only 4 percent of the world's mammals are wild
nature-eco-039.text: Of all mammal {{ref:nature-clim-284}} on Earth today, only 4% is wild mammals. Livestock makes up 60% and humans 36%. That split is the result of a long fall in the total mass of wild mammals over the past 50,000 years, while humans and livestock multiplied. Wild land mammals are believed to weigh seven times less in total than in prehistoric times. The total mass of marine mammals has fallen fivefold.

nature-eco-064.title: Fish stock collapse: the cod that never came back
nature-eco-064.text: Atlantic cod collapsed abruptly in 1992 after heavy exploitation and failed to recover even after fishing stopped. A fish stock collapse is the crash of a fished population, conventionally when its {{ref:nature-clim-284}} falls by more than 95 percent from the highest level recorded. Pushing harvests past the largest catch that can be sustained, explained in {{ref:nature-res-013}}, leads to collapse. That limit usually sits near 30% of pre-harvest living mass, and about 25% of the world's fish populations are already below it. A 2008 study found strong evidence that individual transferable quotas, tradable shares of an allowed catch, help prevent collapses and restore declining fisheries.

nature-eco-096.title: Does variety make ecosystems work better?
nature-eco-096.text: Do more species make an ecosystem work better? Research on the ecological effects of biodiversity asks how the variety of species and genes shapes the way a community functions. It has focused on productivity and stability. Productivity is usually measured as the total aboveground plant {{ref:nature-clim-284}} in an area. More diverse communities appear to produce more living mass and to be more stable when disturbed. Many long-term studies in grassy habitats find that diversity enhances productivity, though results vary. Diversity in species' functional roles may predict productivity better than the number of species. Experiments disagree on whether diversity itself or the particular mix of species drives productivity, and on whether diversity resists invasion. The stakes are real. If diversity stabilizes ecosystems, losing species could feed back into further losses. Habitat fragmentation alters these relationships, and losses can continue two decades after it. Losing species also means losing potential foods, medicines, industrial products and tourism.

nature-eco-051.title: The empty forest: intact trees, missing animals
nature-eco-051.text: A forest can look intact and still be empty. Kent H. Redford named the problem in his 1992 article "The Empty Forest": a forest whose habitat survives but whose large mammals have been lost to human impact. Moderate hunting cuts the {{ref:nature-clim-284}} of mammal game by 80.7%, and heavy hunting by up to 93.7%. Hunted-out species may survive in small numbers yet be ecologically extinct, no longer playing their role. Losing large seed dispersers and predators changes which trees regenerate and how prey species are spread.

nature-eco-097.title: Why mixed plant communities grow more
nature-eco-097.text: Why should a mixed plot of plants produce more {{ref:nature-clim-284}} than a plot of one species? Three explanations are proposed. Complementarity: species with different resource needs together use resources more completely. Facilitation: some species improve conditions for others, as nurse plants or nitrogen-fixing legumes do. The sampling effect: a diverse plot is more likely to include a highly productive species. That last is a composition effect rather than diversity itself, which keeps the debate in {{ref:nature-eco-096}} alive.

nature-eco-703.title: Deserts: dry land that covers a third of Earth
nature-eco-703.text: About one third of Earth's land surface is arid or semi-arid, including much of the polar regions, sometimes called cold deserts. A desert is a landscape with little precipitation, whose dry conditions support distinctive biomes and ecosystems. Deserts generally get less than 250 mm a year. Semi-deserts get 250-500 mm, and grass-clad ones are steppes. Clear skies let heat radiate away at night, so daily temperature ranges can reach 20 to 30 degC. Contrary to the postcard image, around 20% of desert is sand, from 2% in North America to 30% in Australia and over 45% in Central Asia. Plant growth is limited by rainfall, temperature extremes and desiccating winds, so {{ref:nature-clim-284}} and primary productivity are low. Deserts support only a limited human and animal population, and are exploited for minerals and solar energy.

nature-eco-565.title: Tundra: the land too cold for trees
nature-eco-565.text: Arctic tundra is a desert of sorts, with about 150–250 mm of precipitation a year and winter temperatures around −28 °C. Tundra is a biome where freezing temperatures and short growing seasons keep trees from growing. The boundary between tundra and forest is the tree line. There are three types, Arctic, Alpine and Antarctic, and their vegetation is low: dwarf shrubs, sedges, grasses, mosses and lichens. Biodiversity is limited to about 1,700 vascular plant species and 48 land mammal species, though millions of birds migrate there each summer. The frozen soils store {{ref:nature-clim-284}} as carbon, making tundra soil a carbon sink. Beneath it lies another kind of wealth. Arctic tundra is rich in petroleum, natural gas and uranium, and Russia's Yamalo-Nenets region produces 90% of the country's natural gas.

nature-eco-729.title: Methanogenesis: how microbes make methane
nature-eco-729.text: Where oxygen is absent, one group of microbes finishes the job of decay and exhales methane. Methanogenesis is the formation of methane coupled to the capture of energy by microbes called methanogens. It is the final stage of anaerobic digestion and the final step in decomposing {{ref:nature-clim-284}} in anoxic environments. Methanogens come only from the domain Archaea. They respire anaerobically, oxygen inhibits them, and carbon is the terminal electron acceptor. The two best-known pathways use acetic acid or carbon dioxide. Without methanogenesis, a great deal of carbon as fermentation products would accumulate in anaerobic environments. Flooded soils such as rice fields and wetlands are natural methane sources, though aerating them raises sulfates and nitrates that reduce methane production. Methanogenesis is also the main pathway breaking down landfilled organic matter, and the methane can be collected as fuel gas.

nature-eco-543.title: The outwelling hypothesis: mangroves feeding the coast
nature-eco-543.text: A mature mangrove forest reaches its maximum {{ref:nature-clim-284}} after about 20–30 years. After that, the carbon it keeps fixing must be stored in sediment, exported or lost to the air. The outwelling hypothesis holds that much of it is exported as organic matter that feeds detritus-based food webs, which run on dead material, in nearby coastal habitats. Mass-balance studies, which add up carbon going in and out, support the idea. Mangroves usually fix far more carbon than they store, though the amount exported varies a lot between forests.

nature-eco-547.title: Reefs, seagrass and mangroves as one system
nature-eco-547.text: Protecting fish in a mangrove can raise fish numbers on a nearby reef. Coral reefs, seagrasses and mangroves are linked systems that shield one another and exchange fish and invertebrates. Mangroves and seagrasses regulate the sediment, freshwater and nutrients that reach coral reefs. Their ecosystem services reinforce each other: protecting fisheries in one raises fish {{ref:nature-clim-284}} in the others, and tourism gains from both.

nature-eco-723.title: Carbon from outside versus carbon from within
nature-eco-723.text: A lake can feed on its own algae or on what washes in. Allochthonous carbon and nutrients come from outside an aquatic system, while autochthonous carbon comes from within it, such as algae. In streams and small lakes allochthonous sources dominate. In large lakes and the ocean, autochthonous sources dominate. Allochthony is the share of aquatic food web {{ref:nature-clim-284}} derived from allochthonous material.

nature-eco-420.title: Forest biomass: the weight of the woods
nature-eco-420.text: The world's forests hold about 606 gigatonnes of living {{ref:nature-clim-284}} above and below ground, plus 59 gigatonnes of dead wood. Forests build up large amounts of living plant material, and many do so quickly, which makes them highly productive. That store is not permanent. Fires and falling trees can release it suddenly, reshaping the forest's structure.

nature-es-114.title: Nursery habitats: where the next generation of fish grows up
nature-es-114.text: Seagrass meadows give nursery habitat to over a fifth of the world's 25 largest fisheries, including walleye pollock, the most landed species. A nursery habitat is a place where young marine animals live that contributes more young to the adult population, per unit of area, than other places they use. Mangroves, salt marshes and seagrass are typical. Losing them can mean fewer young reaching adulthood, shrinking populations that both biodiversity and fishing need. Counting crowds of juveniles is not proof enough. The best measure is how much {{ref:nature-clim-284}} moves from juvenile to adult populations.

nature-es-068.title: Lidar: measuring the world with laser light
nature-es-068.text: A 2024 lidar study found that England has 390,000 km of hedgerows. Lidar measures distance by shining a laser at a surface and timing how long the reflected light takes to return. As an active sensor, it supplies its own light and uses the speed of light to turn return time into distance. From an aircraft it can map terrain at 30-centimeter resolution or better. In forests it measures tree heights and crown widths and estimates canopy volume, {{ref:nature-clim-284}} and carbon density.

nature-acct-111.title: Material flow accounting: weighing what an economy takes in
nature-acct-111.text: An economy, like a living thing, needs a constant flow of materials and energy through it. Material flow accounting treats the economy as a subsystem inside the environment and measures that flow, an idea called industrial or societal metabolism. It records the materials entering a national or regional economy, the changes in its stocks, and the outputs that leave as exports or as discharges to the environment. It covers all solid, liquid and gaseous materials moved by people or livestock, except bulk water and air, usually in tonnes per year. Materials fall into four groups: {{ref:nature-clim-284}}, fossil energy carriers, metals and non-metallic minerals. It also counts non-market flows such as grazed living mass and mining waste rock, which made up 21% of global extraction in 2010. Direct material input is domestic extraction plus imports. Domestic material consumption is domestic extraction plus imports minus exports. The accounts are a satellite system to the national accounts and are used in SEEA.

nature-acct-072.title: Material footprint: the ore behind the phone
nature-acct-072.text: A phone's metal starts as ore in a mine, and refining it burns coal. A material footprint counts both: all the raw materials needed along the supply chain to make the goods a country consumes, also called raw material equivalents. It is a consumption-based indicator, comparable to carbon and water footprints, and is calculated with environmentally extended input–output analysis. The total sums {{ref:nature-clim-284}}, fossil fuels, metal ores and non-metal ores. It is an indicator for goals 8 and 12 of the {{ref:nature-gov-010}}. Material footprint per person rose 39 per cent from 2000 to 2017, reaching 12.18 tonnes.

nature-pol-308.title: Food versus fuel: crops for cars or for plates
nature-pol-308.text: Should farmland grow fuel or food? Biofuel production can compete with food crops. The text says a 50% cut in grain used for biofuels in the US and Europe would replace all of Ukraine's grain exports. Second- and third-generation biofuels use feedstocks that do not directly compete with food or feed crops, such as wastes and residues, to avoid the dilemma. Yet second-generation fuels raise competition for lignocellulosic {{ref:nature-clim-284}} and so its cost. Responsible policies and economic instruments are needed to make {{ref:nature-pol-303}} production sustainable. Sources flag the food-versus-fuel question as contested.

nature-mkt-114.title: National forest monitoring: watching forests from space and ground
nature-mkt-114.text: Between 2005 and 2020, the number of countries with good satellite monitoring of their forests rose from 55 to 99. Those with good national forest inventories rose from 48 to 102. A national forest monitoring system is a country's institutions and techniques for tracking its forests and producing information for decisions and reporting. REDD+ countries are encouraged to build transparent systems that combine {{ref:nature-es-057}} with ground inventories. The outputs include time series of forest area and change, maps, and estimates of {{ref:nature-clim-284}} or stored carbon with their uncertainty. Having such a system, along with an assessed reference level, is a condition for results-based payments. Steady funding, coordination across agencies and consistent methods over time remain challenges.

nature-res-231.title: Ecological yield: the harvest an ecosystem can spare
nature-res-231.text: A forest can give up some wood each year and still stand. Ecological yield is the amount of an ecosystem's growth that can be harvested while still letting it recover. It is most often measured in forests, where sustainable harvesting takes no more wood in a year than grew that year in a given patch. Take more than is renewed and the ecosystem's carrying capacity shrinks over time. The figure can only be estimated, and it depends on the recovery period chosen: three years' sustainable harvest is not necessarily three times one year's. Firms that borrow to buy rights to land may owe debts that demand more yield than the land can renew. Food chains shrink yield fast. Only about 10% of {{ref:nature-clim-284}} passes from prey to predator, so 100 kg of plants may yield 10 kg of plant-eaters and 1 kg of meat-eaters. In 1986 Vitousek and colleagues estimated that humans use 50 billion tons of photosynthetic living mass a year, 20% to 40% of the Earth's photosynthesis. Measuring ecological footprints accurately requires estimating this yield.

nature-res-027.title: Overfishing: taking fish faster than they breed
nature-res-027.text: Fish and marine mammal {{ref:nature-clim-284}} has fallen by 60% since the 1800s, largely through overfishing. Overfishing is taking fish from a body of water faster than the species can replace itself, so its numbers there keep falling. It can happen anywhere, from ponds and rivers to oceans, and it leaves depleted populations, slower growth and low living mass. The trend is steep. The share of stocks within biologically sustainable levels fell from 90% in 1974 to 66.9% in 2015. The FAO reported 34 percent of marine stocks overfished in 2017. Illegal catch adds an estimated 11 to 26 million tonnes, 14–33% of the world's reported catch. Pushed far enough, a population may no longer sustain itself, a state called critical depensation, and it is wiped out locally or globally. Collapsed stocks may not return. After trout are overfished, carp can take over and stop trout re-establishing. Remedies include regulation, removing subsidies, gentler fishing gear, fish farming and consumer awareness.

nature-res-061.title: How fished populations grow and shrink
nature-res-061.text: In 1838 Pierre Verhulst wrote down an equation in which growth slows as numbers approach a ceiling, the carrying capacity K. Fisheries scientists still use that logistic equation. The population dynamics of fisheries studies how a fished population grows and shrinks over time through births, deaths and migration. Its purpose is practical: to work out sustainable yields and the best harvesting rates. Under logistic growth, maximum sustainable yield sits at exactly half the carrying capacity, where the population grows fastest. Schaefer's catch equation makes the catch proportional to fishing effort, times stock {{ref:nature-clim-284}}, times a catchability factor. The Baranov catch equation of 1918 is perhaps the most used equation in fisheries modeling. And the field's first principle is widely held to be Malthus's exponential law.

nature-res-028.title: Three ways to overfish
nature-res-028.text: Biologists recognize three types of overfishing, each striking a different part of the system. Growth overfishing catches fish too young. They are smaller, on average, than the size that gives the most yield per young fish entering the stock, so total yield is lower than it could be. Recruitment overfishing goes deeper. It depletes the spawning adults until too few remain to replenish the stock with new young fish. Managers treat it with moratoriums, quotas and minimum size limits to rebuild the spawning {{ref:nature-clim-284}}. Ecosystem overfishing works at the largest scale. As large predators decline, the ecosystem shifts toward small forage species.

nature-res-054.title: Fishing down the food web
nature-res-054.text: In pristine oceans, the {{ref:nature-clim-284}} of large predators was 10 to 100 times greater than today. Over the last 50 years alone, cod, swordfish, tuna and other large predators have dropped 90 percent in abundance. In fishing down the food web, fisheries that have used up the big predators turn to smaller species. Finally they take small fish and invertebrates once ignored. Daniel Pauly and colleagues first demonstrated it in a 1998 article in Science. The logic is simple. Bigger fish usually sit higher in the food chain, and fishing tends to take bigger fish, so intense fishing leaves small fish dominating catches. Using {{ref:nature-res-006}} modeling, Pauly found the average trophic level of catches fell by between 0.5 and 1.0 levels over 50 years, globally and in each ocean. Rising prices for small forage fish and invertebrates can be seen as subsidizing the slide. The finding is contested. FAO scientists argued Pauly's team misread the catch statistics. Later studies attribute the falling levels to added low-level fisheries or climate swings rather than predator collapse, and find it is not a global phenomenon.

nature-res-031.title: Fishing capacity: how much a fleet could catch
nature-res-031.text: Half the world's fishing fleet could be scrapped with no change in catch, according to a World Bank and FAO report. Fishing capacity is the most a fishery's boats and gear could catch. It can be measured by the capital fully used, the input view, or by the maximum catch, the output view. Output capacity assumes inputs are fully used, given the stock's {{ref:nature-clim-284}} and age structure and current technology. Capacity utilization compares a fleet's actual catch or inputs with that potential.

nature-res-025.title: The spillover effect: reserves that feed nearby fisheries
nature-res-025.text: Near the edges of fully protected reserves, fish {{ref:nature-clim-284}} was 54% higher than farther away, according to a 2020 meta-analysis of 23 such areas. Inside, commercial species were up to 80% more abundant. Spillover is the net movement of fish, eggs and larvae from a recovering marine reserve into the fishing grounds around it. It sustains nearby fishing without taking anything from inside the reserve, and such benefits are well documented worldwide. Scientists and small-scale fishers increasingly agree that coastal MPAs raise the density and size of commercial species in local waters.

nature-res-076.title: Annual sustainable yield: resetting the catch each year
nature-res-076.text: Carrying capacity is not fixed; it moves from year to year, so the safe catch moves too. Annual sustainable yield is the {{ref:nature-clim-284}} that can be harvested from a fish population each year without causing it to decline. Managers adjust it every year according to population levels and how previous seasons went, so that it tracks a maximum sustainable yield that varies with conditions.

nature-res-070.title: Stock assessment: taking a fish population's pulse
nature-res-070.text: Before managers can set a catch limit, someone has to estimate how many fish there are. A stock assessment gathers biological and fishery data to give managers the information they use to regulate a stock. Biological data include age structure, fecundity, natural and fishing mortality, growth and an estimate of total population or {{ref:nature-clim-284}}. Data come from the fishery itself, such as recorded landings, and from independent surveys using trawls, seines or acoustic and video methods. Common models range from {{ref:nature-res-085}}, which need the least data, to statistical age- or length-structured models and {{ref:nature-res-063}}. Modern methods statistically combine several sources to estimate key quantities and their uncertainty. Managers then predict how stocks will respond to different fishing pressures. Two words matter: a stock is 'overfished' when its living mass is below the level that supports maximum sustainable yield, while 'overfishing' means removing fish too fast.

nature-res-071.title: Biological reference points: the red lines of a fishery
nature-res-071.text: {{ref:nature-clim-284}} at maximum sustainable yield is typically around 40-50% of unfished living mass, though Australia often targets a more cautious 60%. Biological reference points are benchmarks, produced by stock assessments, against which fishing rules are set. If current fishing mortality divided by the mortality giving maximum sustainable yield exceeds one, overfishing is happening. When fishing mortality passes its limit or the spawning stock falls below its threshold, the fishery is shut. Maximum sustainable yield considers only biology; optimum yield also weighs the economics of the harvest.

nature-res-085.title: Surplus production models: the simplest stock assessment
nature-res-085.text: Of the three common kinds of stock assessment model, surplus production models need the least data. Schaefer's version, built on Verhulst's logistic growth, uses the catch equation H = qEX, linking catch to fishing effort and stock {{ref:nature-clim-284}}. Setting catch equal to natural growth gives an equilibrium catch for each long-run level of effort. Because these models estimate maximum sustainable yield directly, they made MSY popular in the 1950s.

nature-res-259.title: First- and second-generation biofuels
nature-res-259.text: Biofuels are classed as first-generation, made from food crops on arable land, or second-generation, made from non-food {{ref:nature-clim-284}}. First-generation fuels come from crops such as sugarcane and maize. Bioethanol is fermented from their sugars or starch and is widely used in the United States and Brazil. Biodiesel comes from oils such as rapeseed and is the most common biofuel in Europe. Second-generation or advanced biofuels use perennial energy crops and agricultural residues, grown as by-products of a main crop or on marginal land.

nature-res-260.title: Surface power density: how much land a watt needs
nature-res-260.text: Power sources differ in how much land they need. Surface power density is the power a generation source delivers per square metre of land, which fixes how much land a given supply needs. One estimate of lifecycle density is 0.30 W/m2 for {{ref:nature-clim-284}}, 1 for wind, 3 for hydro and 5 for solar. Lifecycle density counts land used by supporting infrastructure, manufacturing, mining or harvesting, and decommissioning. Another estimate gives medians of 0.08 W/m2 for living mass, 0.14 hydro, 1.84 wind and 6.63 solar, none above 10 W/m2.

nature-nbs-334.title: Phytoremediation: plants that clean contaminated ground
nature-nbs-334.text: Tobacco plants given bacterial nitroreductase genes removed TNT faster. That is phytoremediation: the use of living plants to clean up soil, air and water contaminated with pollutants. Its main mechanisms are {{ref:nature-nbs-335}}, {{ref:nature-nbs-336}}, {{ref:nature-nbs-338}} and phytofiltration. It is proposed as a sustainable alternative to conventional remediation, though it has never been used at large scales. Microbial bioremediation has so far been more successful. Breeding and genetic engineering can strengthen or add the abilities involved. Plant growth-promoting bacteria in the rhizosphere, the soil zone around roots, improve the results by raising {{ref:nature-clim-284}} and by making heavy metals more mobile.

nature-nbs-335.title: Phytoextraction: harvesting pollutants in plant shoots
nature-nbs-335.text: Phytoextraction is a {{ref:nature-nbs-334}} process in which plants take up contaminants from soil or water and concentrate them in above-ground {{ref:nature-clim-284}}. Non-hyperaccumulators such as poplar and willow take up little pollutant but grow fast enough that they could remove a considerable amount. Heavy metals are often not mobile enough for uptake, which prompted assisted phytoextraction, adding a chelator to raise metal solubility. Metallophytes underpin phytomining, a proposed way to collect valuable metals without excavating.

nature-nbs-121.title: Forest restoration: speeding a forest back toward maturity
nature-nbs-121.text: Active restoration can speed carbon recovery in human-modified tropical forests by as much as 50%. Forest restoration is action that speeds a forest's return toward a climax forest, the end stage of natural succession. Climax forests are fairly stable ecosystems with the most {{ref:nature-clim-284}}, structure and species that climate and soil allow without human disturbance. Forest restoration is a special kind of reforestation. Its main goals are biodiversity recovery and environmental protection, unlike timber plantations. Methods range from protecting leftover vegetation, by preventing fire or keeping out cattle, to planting trees or sowing seeds directly. Success shows up as more biodiversity, living mass, productivity, soil organic matter and water-holding capacity, plus the return of rare and keystone species. It also has a money measure: the value of forest products and of services such as watershed protection and carbon storage. Payments for those services can give local people strong reasons to restore. Climate change complicates the target, because climate shapes climax forests.

nature-nbs-296.title: Paludiculture: farming on wet peat
nature-nbs-296.text: Peatlands cover only 3% of land but store more than 450 gigatonnes of carbon, more than all forests. Paludiculture is farming on drained peatlands after they have been rewetted. Raising the water table gets the carbon store working again, so the land serves as both carbon sink and farm. Crops include berries, herbs, timber and {{ref:nature-clim-284}} for biofuel. Whether a given practice counts as sustainable paludiculture is debated.

nature-nbs-347.title: Ecology: the science of organisms and their surroundings
nature-nbs-347.text: Pull one thread in a living system and the effects may spread far beyond it. Ecology is the natural science that studies the interactions between organisms and their environments. It considers organisms at community, ecosystem and biosphere levels. It overlaps with biogeography, evolutionary biology, genetics and ethology. Ecology is both a biological science and a human science. It is also an applied science of restoration, used to repair disturbed sites. A disturbance is any process that changes or removes {{ref:nature-clim-284}} from a community, such as fire, flood, drought or predation. The structure of an ecosystem is nonlinear. Small changes to critical variables, such as the number of nitrogen fixers, can cause disproportionate and perhaps irreversible changes. Ecologists also study nutrient budgets, and they have found a global feedback between ecosystems and planetary physical parameters such as soil, pH, water and atmospheric gases.

nature-nbs-226.title: Carbon farming: pulling carbon from the air into soil
nature-nbs-226.text: Turning a forest, grassland or savanna into cropland cuts the soil's organic carbon by about 30–40%. Carbon farming tries to run that process in reverse. It is a set of farming and forestry methods meant to store carbon from the air in soil and living plants. The overall goal is a net removal of carbon from the atmosphere, by speeding up how fast carbon is locked away. Methods include changing tillage and grazing, using mulch or compost, adding {{ref:nature-clim-178}} and changing which crops are grown. This charcoal, mixed into soil, locks away roughly 50% of the carbon in the original {{ref:nature-clim-284}}. The potential is large. Carbon farming could offset as much as 20% of 2010 carbon dioxide emissions each year, and by 2016 its variants covered hundreds of millions of hectares. Farmers who store carbon can sell credits to companies that need offsets, as in Australia. But the storage is not permanent. Disturbing the soil or tilling hard turns it back into a source of greenhouse gases. If incentives reward only stored carbon, they could encourage land clearing, single-crop farming and biodiversity loss. The effect on crop yields is unsettled, and critics doubt the practices can spread widely enough to matter.

nature-nbs-259.title: Holistic planned grazing: imitating wild herds
nature-nbs-259.text: In a TED talk, Allan Savory claimed his grazing method could bring carbon dioxide back to pre-industrial levels in 40 years. Critics reject this. Holistic planned grazing moves herds constantly between fields to imitate wild herds. Supporters say trampling restores soil, stimulates regrowth and raises soil carbon and water infiltration. But a meta-analysis of studies from 1972 to 2016 found it did no better than continuous grazing for plant cover and {{ref:nature-clim-284}}. The evidence on its carbon benefits is mixed.

nature-clim-282.title: Electricity generation: turning other energy into power
nature-clim-282.text: Electricity is not freely available in nature. It must be produced by transforming other forms of energy, in power stations, before delivery or storage. Most is made by electromechanical generators driven by heat engines, flowing water or wind. Only photovoltaic solar and fuel cells make commercial-scale electricity without a generator; almost all other commercial power comes from a turbine. World generation in 2024 was 30,850 TWh: coal 34%, gas 22%, hydro 14%, nuclear 9%, wind 8%, solar 7%, oil and other fossil 3%, {{ref:nature-clim-284}} 2%. How clean the supply is depends on where you live. Fossil fuels supply about 10% of electricity in France, 70% in the US and 80% in China. Each source has costs. Coal plants supply about a third of world electricity but cause the most early deaths per unit of energy, mainly from air pollution. Gas plants are more efficient than coal and emit less carbon dioxide, but gas extraction releases significant methane. Hydropower supplied 15% of world electricity in 2023 and, with a dam and reservoir, can change output within seconds or minutes. Grids carry varying loads, and the daily minimum is the base load, often supplied by plants that run continuously.

nature-pol-192.title: Energy subsidies: who pays for cheap power
nature-pol-192.text: In 2020 the International {{ref:nature-eecon-239}} Agency tracked some $634 billion in energy subsidies, around 70% of them for fossil fuels. About 20% went to renewable power, 6% to biofuels and just over 3% to nuclear. An energy subsidy is a government measure that keeps energy prices below market levels for customers, keeps them above market levels for suppliers, or cuts their costs. It can be a direct cash payment or indirect support: tax exemptions, price controls, trade restrictions and limits on market access. Other forms include public research, cheap government services, demand guarantees, and failing to charge for external costs such as pollution. Which source gets the most support can affect the environment. Early support for solar power by the United States and Germany helped bring green power to market and cut emissions worldwide. Because energy policies are interconnected across countries, regulating subsidies at the {{ref:nature-pol-007}} is often seen as necessary.

nature-pol-235.title: Green public procurement: governments buying green
nature-pol-235.text: Rules can steer public bodies to buy efficient computers, recycled paper, electric vehicles and {{ref:nature-eecon-239}}. That is green public procurement, the part of sustainable public procurement that uses government buying power to reach environmental goals. It aims to cut greenhouse gas emissions, improve {{ref:nature-eecon-191}} and grow the market for greener products, which can drive green innovation. It relies heavily on {{ref:nature-eecon-029}}, which counts transport, installation, training, insurance and running costs as well as the purchase price.

nature-pol-228.title: Local content rules: buy local to qualify
nature-pol-228.text: Ontario's 2009 Green Energy and Green Economy Act made wind and solar farms use Ontario-made parts to qualify for subsidies. That is a local content requirement: a rule requiring producers to source a minimum share of goods, labor or services locally. The Ontario law created many jobs, cut emissions and greatly expanded the province's {{ref:nature-eecon-239}} industry.

nature-mkt-144.title: Additionality: would it have happened anyway?
nature-mkt-144.text: Paying someone to do what they were going to do anyway buys nothing. Additionality is the test for that trap. It asks whether an intervention, such as a payment or a credit, actually causes an outcome that would not have happened otherwise. The answer depends on a baseline, a prediction of what people would do without the policy, with everything else held constant. Strictly, additionality is the intervention's impact minus the impact of that reference case. It must also be counted net of side effects such as deadweight, paying for what would happen anyway, and leakage, harm pushed somewhere else. Displacement and substitution can shrink the gain in similar ways. A project is not additional if it would have gone ahead without the credit revenue, for instance because it was profitable anyway. That scenario is called business as usual. Additionality can be checked after the fact, as in program evaluation, or beforehand, as a screen for which projects may issue environmental credits. The stakes are high. Large markets for {{ref:nature-mkt-119}} have shown serious shortcomings on it. Problems with additionality and double counting can also undermine trust in the offsets described in {{ref:nature-mkt-081}}. One industry watchdog, the {{ref:nature-hist-033}}, cited additionality concerns when it excluded several {{ref:nature-eecon-239}} crediting methods. Every payment scheme in this chapter rises or falls on this question.

nature-mkt-087.title: What kinds of projects earn carbon credits
nature-mkt-087.text: Carbon credits come from many kinds of projects, from land use and methane capture to {{ref:nature-eecon-239}} and energy efficiency. Others include replanting forests and switching to fuels that add no net carbon or remove it. Methane, mostly from landfills, livestock and coal mines, can be captured and burned for energy. Industrial gases such as HFCs and PFCs warm far more than carbon dioxide and are easy to destroy at source. Green power projects, by contrast, may not qualify as offsets.

nature-mkt-046.title: Green bonds: borrowing only for green projects
nature-mkt-046.text: The World Bank issued the first labeled green bond in 2008, a year after the European Investment Bank's Climate Awareness Bond. A green bond is a bond whose money is used only for projects with environmental benefits. Like ordinary bonds, they can be issued by governments, development banks or companies, which repay the bond plus interest. Eligible projects include {{ref:nature-eecon-239}}, energy efficiency, pollution control, sustainable land use, biodiversity, clean transport and adapting to climate change. Green bonds raised over $93 billion in 2016, still only around 1% of global bond issuance, and by 2024 total issuance had reached about $700 billion. Legally they barely differ from ordinary bonds: green promises are often not binding in the contract. Critics question some bonds' green credentials, as when the Climate Bonds Initiative refused to list a Repsol bond in 2017. The EU's Green Bonds Regulation, in force from 21 December 2024, created the 'European Green Bond'.

nature-mkt-030.title: Impact investing: profit with a measurable purpose
nature-mkt-030.text: Many impact investors accept expected returns 2-4 percentage points lower in exchange for measurable social impact. Impact investing puts money into companies, organizations and funds meant to produce a measurable social or environmental benefit as well as a financial return. It lines up an investor's values with where the money goes, in fields such as {{ref:nature-eecon-239}}, education and microfinance. It spans private equity, venture capital and debt, and targets returns from below-market to above-market. The term was coined in 2005, and modern impact funds grew prominent soon after the Great Recession. In 2024 about 3,907 organizations managed an estimated $1.571 trillion in impact assets, far smaller than the $78 trillion global stock market. The UN development goals need an estimated $5-7 trillion of investment a year, mostly expected from private capital, and impact investors linked their funds to them.

nature-mkt-077.title: Eco-investing: betting on clean technology
nature-mkt-077.text: One tracker estimated that over $1.248 trillion has been invested in solar, wind, geothermal, ocean and other green sectors since 2007. Eco-investing, or green investing, is investing by values focused on companies that offer environmentally friendly products and practices. Unlike the broader field, it narrows to environmental issues, especially {{ref:nature-eecon-239}} and clean technology. New green technologies carry high up-front costs, which are harder to justify to investors.

nature-res-212.title: Renewable resources: the stock that regrows, if allowed
nature-res-212.text: A forest can regrow and a fish population can breed back, but only if people let them. A renewable resource, also called a flow resource, replaces what is used through natural reproduction or other recurring processes within a human time scale. Some sources, such as sun, wind, moving water and geothermal heat, are practically infinite and cannot be depleted. Resources whose recovery will probably never outlast a human time scale get a name of their own, {{ref:nature-res-215}}. Water, forests, plants and animals stay renewable only as long as they are monitored, protected and conserved. Water shows the catch. It is renewable only when its use is carefully controlled, and underground water pumped far faster than it recharges counts as non-renewable. Overuse is not new: deforestation, overgrazing and fishing too hard were already large problems in early modern times. Unregulated industrial growth endangers these resources, which must be managed so use does not exceed nature's capacity to replenish them. Fisheries show how far it can go, since an unregulated industry can wipe a renewable resource out completely. Even clean energy has a hidden draw: building {{ref:nature-eecon-239}} devices uses mined metals and land.

nature-res-237.title: Marine resources: what the oceans offer
nature-res-237.text: The oceans hold far more than fish. Marine resources are the physical and biological things in the oceans that are useful to people. They include marine biodiversity, ecosystem services from coasts and coral reefs, minerals from deep sea mining, and marine {{ref:nature-eecon-239}}. The term spread through the UN goal set in 2015 to conserve and sustainably use the oceans, seas and marine resources, {{ref:nature-gov-027}}. Sustainable fisheries contributed around 0.1% of global GDP per year.

nature-res-245.title: The blue economy: making a living from water
nature-res-245.text: In 2023 the European Union's blue economy employed nearly 4.9 million people and added €263 billion in gross value added. The blue economy is the economic use of oceans, lakes, rivers and coasts, generally with an emphasis on using their resources sustainably. There is no agreed definition. The World Bank calls it sustainable use of ocean resources for growth, livelihoods and jobs while preserving the health of ocean ecosystems. It spans fisheries, fish farming, shipping and tourism, plus newer activities such as offshore {{ref:nature-eecon-239}}, {{ref:nature-nbs-034}} and seabed mining. It also covers unpriced ocean services such as storing carbon, coastal protection and biodiversity. Mangrove forests show what is at stake. They support more than 4 million fishers and protect coasts, yet 0.5% have been lost each year on average since the 2000s. The term spread after a UN conference on sustainable growth in 2012, {{ref:nature-hist-008}}. Misleading claims about effects on waters have their own label, {{ref:nature-nbs-080}}.

nature-res-246.title: Blue finance: money for healthier oceans
nature-res-246.text: The World Economic Forum estimates that meeting SDG 14, the UN goal for the oceans, needs US$175 billion a year. It is the most underfunded of all 17 goals. Blue finance is finance that cuts the carbon footprint of ocean-related activities and benefits the marine environment. It is part of {{ref:nature-mkt-018}} and overlaps with funding for climate action. It pays for offshore wind and other marine {{ref:nature-eecon-239}}, zero-emission shipping, and the restoration of mangroves and seagrass meadows.

nature-res-149.title: Backstop water sources: the expensive last resort
nature-res-149.text: Desalination cost US$0.53 per cubic metre in Israel in 2005 and US$0.49 in Singapore in 2006. Turning seawater fresh is the classic backstop water source: a supply abundant enough to replace unsustainable or non-renewable water use, usually at a higher {{ref:nature-econ-347}}. A backstop plays the role {{ref:nature-eecon-239}} plays for fossil fuels. Transfers between river basins and trucked water are others, and all are expensive last resorts. Desalination is limited by its energy needs, brine disposal, high capital and water costs, and the cost of moving water.

nature-clim-130.title: Variable renewables: power that follows the weather
nature-clim-130.text: In 2024 wind and solar supplied 15% of the world's electricity and together overtook hydropower for the first time. They are variable {{ref:nature-eecon-239}}: their output rises and falls with the weather and cannot be adjusted on demand. Their traits, unpredictability, variability and low operating costs, make matching supply and demand harder. Small amounts barely affect the grid, but large amounts may require redesigning it. Options include storage, demand response, overcapacity, interconnected grids and linking power with heat, transport and industry. Spreading wind farms widely helps, because distant turbines' outputs are imperfectly correlated. Combined wind and solar could reach 70% to 90% of supply without such help, and up to 94% with 12 hours of storage. How much variability adds to costs is debated. The extra costs are small at low shares and expected to rise as shares grow.

nature-clim-284.title: Biomass: energy and carbon stored in living matter
nature-clim-284.text: Biomass is material produced by the growth of microorganisms, plants or animals. The main types are woody, herbaceous and agricultural, aquatic, animal-derived, microbial and waste-derived. It is a {{ref:nature-eecon-239}} source and a chemical feedstock, though its energy content is low relative to coal and petroleum and its oxygen content high. The crops matter. First-generation biofuels and plant-based plastics come from energy-dense crops such as rapeseed, sugarcane or corn, and they raise crop prices and take arable land from food. Second-generation biomass, such as wood chippings, grass or solid waste, is far harder to convert because of its varied mixture of compounds. Research continues because it can reuse waste. Ecologists use the word differently, for the total mass of organisms in an ecosystem, usually expressed as carbon. A 2017 estimate for the whole biosphere is about 550 Gt C, with about 450 Gt C of it in terrestrial plants. Remote sensing such as NDVI is commonly used to estimate biomass over large areas.

nature-clim-216.title: Renewable energy sources
nature-clim-216.text: Hydropower is the largest renewable source of electricity, supplying 17% of the world's power in 2020. {{ref:nature-eecon-239}} sources are those naturally replenished: solar, wind, hydro, geothermal, bioenergy and marine energy. They generally strengthen energy security and emit far fewer greenhouse gases than fossil fuels. Wind is catching up fast. It provided well over 10% of global electricity in 2024, and onshore wind is often cheaper than existing coal plants. Solar PV is expected to have the largest installed capacity of any electricity source by 2027. Renewables are not harmless, though. Projects can threaten biodiversity when high-value areas become bioenergy, wind or solar farms.

nature-clim-173.title: 100% renewable energy
nature-clim-173.text: Could every bit of energy come from renewable resources? That is the goal of 100% {{ref:nature-eecon-239}}. It is motivated by emissions, pollution, and economic and energy security concerns. The research is fairly young, with few studies before 2009.

nature-clim-086.title: Fossil fuel divestment: pulling money out of oil and coal
nature-clim-086.text: It began on US university campuses in 2011. By 2015 fossil fuel divestment was reportedly the fastest-growing divestment movement in history. Divestment means pressuring institutions to sell their stocks, bonds and other investments in fossil fuel extraction companies, as a way to fight climate change. As of July 2023, more than 1593 institutions with over $40.5 trillion in assets had begun or committed to some form of it. Divesters have three kinds of reason: to align investments with values, to fight the fossil fuel industry, or to protect portfolios from climate-related financial risk. One financial motive is stranded assets, the 'carbon bubble': reserves that cannot be burned safely and would have to be written off. The aim is to speed the shift to {{ref:nature-eecon-239}} by stigmatising fossil fuel companies. Those companies have partly blamed divestment pressure for the rising cost of raising money.

nature-clim-043.title: Mitigation finance: the bulk of climate money
nature-clim-043.text: Mitigation finance is investment that aims to reduce global greenhouse gas emissions. It dominates, accounting for over 90% of worldwide investment in climate finance. Around 70% of mitigation money has gone to {{ref:nature-eecon-239}}; energy efficiency and transport are the other key sectors. Of the estimated US$83.3 billion provided to developing countries in 2020, US$48.6 billion, or 58%, targeted mitigation. The needs are far larger. The 2018 Biennial Assessment put mitigation financing needs for 2020 to 2030 at US$1.7-2.4 trillion per year. The IEA estimates that keeping warming below 2 Celsius needs an average of $3.5 trillion a year of energy-sector investment until 2050.

nature-clim-049.title: Debt-for-climate swaps: turning repayments into projects
nature-clim-049.text: Seychelles redirected $27 million of debt to marine parks, ocean conservation and ecotourism. A debt-for-climate swap works this way. A country's debt is repaid on new, discounted terms, and the repayments, in local currency, go to domestic climate projects instead of foreign lenders. Projects can include carbon sequestration, {{ref:nature-eecon-239}} and protecting biodiversity and oceans. In one Argentine swap, $38,100,000 of debt was addressed and $3,100,000 went to biodiversity, forest and other climate work. The Seychelles deal was a similar debt-for-nature swap.

nature-clim-090.title: The first global stocktake: a verdict delivered in Dubai
nature-clim-090.text: On 13 December 2023, COP 28 in Dubai concluded the first {{ref:nature-clim-089}}, part of the UAE Consensus. Its verdict was blunt. A 43 percent emissions cut by 2030 was needed, but only a 5 percent cut was expected. It set 2030 targets to triple {{ref:nature-eecon-239}} capacity and double global energy efficiency. For the first time at a UN climate conference, it called on all countries to transition away from fossil fuels to reach climate neutrality by 2050. It also set up the loss and damage fund, with $700 million in start-up capital, to be run by the World Bank.

nature-es-109.title: The four pillars of food security
nature-es-109.text: Food security is usually broken into pillars. Availability is the supply of food through production, distribution and exchange. Access covers whether food is affordable and how it is shared out, along with people's preferences. Utilization is how well people use the food they get. Stability is the ability to get food over time, since food insecurity can be passing, seasonal or chronic. A further pillar, {{ref:nature-eecon-208}}, asks that the ways people grow and supply food feed them now without undermining the bases for feeding future generations.

nature-val-057.title: Good as a means, or good in itself
nature-val-057.text: A hammer and a washing machine are valuable for what they do. Their value is instrumental: they are good as a means to an end. Happiness and pleasure are different.
