They are usually thought valuable for their own sake, the kind of worth explored in {{ref:nature-val-056}}. The sociologist Max Weber coined the terms. Not everyone accepts the split. John Dewey thought belief in value for its own sake was a mistake, and treated instrumental judgment as the only way to coordinate behavior well. J. Fagg Foster treated {{ref:nature-eecon-208}} as a synonym for instrumental value, since success must never be short term.

nature-val-011.title: Multiple-criteria decision analysis: juggling conflicting goals
nature-val-011.text: Whether and where to build a nuclear power plant is a decision with very high stakes. Multiple-criteria decision analysis exists for choices like that. It is a field of decision science that weighs several conflicting criteria explicitly when choosing among options. Cost is usually one criterion and some measure of quality another, and the two often pull in opposite directions. When stakes are high, structuring the problem and its criteria explicitly leads to better decisions. There is usually no single best answer, so the decision-maker's preferences are needed to tell solutions apart. Ecological economists favor it as an alternative to standard cost–benefit reasoning. It has been applied to {{ref:nature-eecon-208}} assessment, desertification risk and wind farm siting.

nature-acct-021.title: Human development: growth as a means, not the goal
nature-acct-021.text: Aristotle noted that wealth is merely useful for something else, not the good being sought. Human development takes that idea seriously. It is a view of progress that widens economic development to include social, political and even ethical dimensions. The UN Development Programme defines it as enlarging people's choices. These include the chance to live a long, healthy life, to be educated, to have a decent standard of living and to enjoy freedom and self-respect. On this view economic growth ({{ref:nature-econ-478}}) is only a means of enlarging those choices, not the goal itself. The idea grew in the 1980s from Amartya Sen's capabilities perspective ({{ref:nature-econ-182}}), with Mahbub ul Haq among its key early figures. Its six pillars are equity, {{ref:nature-eecon-208}}, productivity, empowerment, cooperation and security. The UN's Human Development Reports carry several indices built on it, including gender indices and {{ref:nature-acct-003}}, which stems directly from this work.

nature-acct-003.title: Human Development Index: ranking countries by people's lives
nature-acct-003.text: Since 1990 the UN's Human Development Reports have tried to move development economics away from national income accounting and towards people-centred policies. Their best-known tool is the Human Development Index, or HDI. It is a single score combining life expectancy, schooling and income per person, used to sort countries into four tiers of human development. It rests on Amartya Sen's capability idea: whether people are able to 'be' and 'do' desirable things, such as being healthy or taking part in community life. Since 2010 it has combined life expectancy at birth, mean and expected years of schooling, and gross national income per person at purchasing power parity. Each dimension is scaled to an index between 0 and 1. The HDI is their geometric mean, found by multiplying the three scores and taking the cube root. Critics fault it for neglecting {{ref:nature-eecon-208}}, inequality and democracy. In response came {{ref:nature-acct-005}} and a planetary pressures-adjusted HDI. One study found 11%, 21% and 34% of countries could be misclassified by data updates, formula revisions and arbitrary thresholds.

nature-acct-010.title: Green GDP: subtracting the damage from growth
nature-acct-010.text: Fell a forest for timber and GDP records the output, not the loss. GDP measures output alone and ignores the running down or replenishment of the wealth behind it, so it cannot tell whether income is sustainable. Green GDP is a measure of growth that subtracts the environmental consequences of that growth from ordinary GDP. In simple form, green GDP equals GDP minus environmental costs minus social costs. Environmental costs include the using up of resources such as oil and timber, ecological damage such as topsoil erosion, and restoration costs such as restoring wetlands. Benefits from forests, wetlands and farmland stay hidden in GDP because they are hard to measure and price. The UN's system for environmental accounts, SEEA ({{ref:nature-found-013}}), makes it possible to build full accounts from which green GDP can be derived and compared between countries. In the US, early green accounts in 1994 showed GDP overstated mining's contribution to national wealth, and a 1995 amendment halted the work. Experts still disagree on whether to adjust the existing national accounts or redefine income. They also dispute whether non-market goods such as ecosystem services can be reliably valued. Stiglitz, Sen and Fitoussi argued that green GDP does not measure {{ref:nature-eecon-208}} itself.

nature-acct-015.title: Stiglitz-Sen-Fitoussi Commission: France asks what to measure
nature-acct-015.text: In 2008 the French government set up an inquiry into how a nation's wealth and social progress could be measured without relying on the one-dimensional GDP figure. Its formal name was the Commission on the Measurement of Economic Performance and Social Progress, but it became known by its three leading figures. Joseph Stiglitz chaired it, Amartya Sen was economic adviser and Jean-Paul Fitoussi was coordinator. The final report came out in September 2009. It proposed a well-being framework covering health, environment, work, physical safety, economic safety and political freedom. It also took aim at green GDP ({{ref:nature-acct-010}}) and similar indices. These only charge GDP for environmental damage, the report argued, and do not measure {{ref:nature-eecon-208}} as such.

nature-acct-026.title: Adjusted net saving: is a nation getting richer or poorer?
nature-acct-026.text: Ordinary saving figures miss what a country uses up. Adjusted net saving, also called {{ref:nature-eecon-220}}, corrects for that. It takes ordinary net saving ({{ref:nature-econ-587}}), subtracts the value of resources used up and environmental damage, and adds investment in human capital. The result is the net change in a nation's produced, natural and human capital, valued in money. The idea grew from {{ref:nature-eecon-223}}, as Pearce, Atkinson and Hamilton set out a measure of net investment across kinds of capital. A positive value is linked to the possibility of long-run {{ref:nature-eecon-208}}, so policy should aim to keep it at or above zero. The World Bank publishes these estimates for over 150 countries as 'adjusted savings' and suggests them as an alternative to GDP. Along with accounts of humanity's demand on nature ({{ref:nature-acct-027}}), it is an example of an index focused on consuming more than nature can sustain ({{ref:nature-eecon-185}}).

nature-acct-024.title: Sustainable national income: what nature could support for ever
nature-acct-024.text: What if an economy produced only as much as nature could support for ever? Sustainable national income, or SNI, puts a number on that. It estimates the highest production level at which, with that year's technology, vital environmental functions stay available for ever. Economist Roefie Hueting developed the framework, working with a multidisciplinary team at Statistics Netherlands for nearly forty years. Ordinary national income leaves out the loss of environmental functions, so it is always higher than the SNI. The gap between the two shows how far production is from {{ref:nature-eecon-208}}: a shrinking gap means progress, a growing one means drifting away. Following the rule of erring on the side of caution ({{ref:nature-pol-201}}), the SNI assumes no technological progress during the shift to sustainability. The estimates are stark. Tinbergen and Hueting's rough 1991 world estimate put sustainable income at 50 percent of world production. A 2001 estimate for the Netherlands also came to around 50 percent of national income, about the production level of the early 1970s. Between 1990 and 2000 the Dutch gap grew by about 10 billion euros.

nature-acct-002.title: Genuine progress indicator: counting pollution as a loss
nature-acct-002.text: GDP counts pollution twice as a gain: once when it is made and again when it is cleaned up. The genuine progress indicator, or GPI, counts it as a loss, roughly equal to its clean-up and damage costs. The GPI is a measure proposed to replace or supplement GDP by counting the environmental and social factors GDP leaves out ({{ref:nature-found-031}}). It grew out of later work extending the ISEW, with extra emphasis on welfare and the ecological {{ref:nature-eecon-208}} of the economy. Its foundation is John Hicks's idea of sustainable income: what can be consumed in one period without reducing consumption in the next. In simplified form, it takes consumption weighted by income, adds non-market services, subtracts defensive costs and nature's deterioration, and adds capital growth and the trade balance. As of 2014, Vermont, Maryland, Washington and Hawaii had passed state initiatives to consider it in budgeting. Statistics Finland's series from 1945 to 2011 showed GDP and GPI rising together in the 1970s and 1980s, then diverging after the early-1990s recession. Critics say it is harder to measure, rests on a contested definition of well-being and invites political manipulation. Whether growth in money terms hides lost well-being is called a main issue between green and neoclassical economists.

nature-acct-114.title: Triple bottom line: people, planet and profit
nature-acct-114.text: In ordinary accounting the 'bottom line' is profit or loss. The triple bottom line adds two more, judging an organisation on social, environmental and economic results. Freer Spreckley first set out the framework in 1981. John Elkington says he coined the phrase in 1994 and developed it in his 1997 book Cannibals with Forks. His slogan 'people, planet, and profit' titled Shell's first {{ref:nature-eecon-208}} report in 1997. The planet line asks firms to shrink the nature they use ({{ref:nature-acct-027}}), often tallying a product's true environmental cost from raw materials to disposal ({{ref:nature-acct-050}}). The profit line means economic value created after deducting all input costs, including capital, which differs from accounting profit. Measuring the people line is relatively new, problematic and often subjective. Since a 2007 UN and ICLEI standard, it has been the dominant approach to public-sector full cost accounting. Many disagree that it is the right way to improve social and environmental conditions. Critics say it treats the environment as a background externality and is hard to apply in practice.

nature-acct-099.title: Sustainability accounting: reporting beyond the balance sheet
nature-acct-099.text: In most countries, governments do not require companies to prepare and publish {{ref:nature-eecon-208}} reports. Sustainability accounting, also called non-financial reporting, is how firms that do so tell outsiders such as investors and creditors about their social and environmental performance. It began in the 1970s, when environmental matters were part of a broad movement to account for firms' social effects ({{ref:nature-gov-073}}). By 1991–1995 environmental accounting almost completely dominated that movement. It is treated as a branch of financial accounting. Inside the firm, in management accounting, it supports decisions about the triple bottom line of people, planet and profit. Company sustainability reports and triple bottom line accounting are its best-known measures. The Global Reporting Initiative was set up to give organisations guidelines so that social and environmental reports are consistent. The Sustainability Accounting Standards Board standardises some metrics so investors can judge corporate risk.

nature-acct-110.title: Integrated reporting: one report for money and nature
nature-acct-110.text: From 2010 the Johannesburg Stock Exchange required listed companies to issue an integrated report or explain why not. Integrated reporting produces a periodic report on how a firm's strategy, governance, performance and prospects create value over time. It presents financial and other value-relevant information together, aimed mainly at those who allocate financial capital. Backers argue that firms must preserve value from non-financial resources such as people, intellectual property and nature, not just investors' money. So it calls for ecological data, such as greenhouse gas emissions, alongside financial figures. A 2009 meeting convened by the Prince of Wales set up the International Integrated Reporting Committee, or IIRC, to create a global framework. It was renamed a Council in November 2011. In 2021 the IIRC and the {{ref:nature-eecon-208}} Accounting Standards Board merged into the Value Reporting Foundation. By June 2022 the IFRS Foundation had folded that into its International Sustainability Standards Board.

nature-acct-091.title: Environmental reporting: telling stakeholders about impacts
nature-acct-091.text: A company's annual report, its {{ref:nature-eecon-208}} report and its website may all carry the same kind of news: how the company affects the environment. Environmental reporting is the disclosure of an organisation's environmental impacts and performance. It may cover environmental risks and liabilities, energy and waste costs, emissions and pollution controls. It reaches stakeholders through annual reports, sustainability reports, integrated reports and websites.

nature-acct-097.title: WAVES: helping countries put nature in their accounts
nature-acct-097.text: In October 2010 the World Bank launched a global partnership called Wealth Accounting and Valuation of Ecosystem Services, or WAVES. The launch came at the COP-10 meeting of the UN biodiversity treaty ({{ref:nature-gov-015}}) in Japan. It helps countries put the value of natural capital into their national accounts. Its projects in countries such as Botswana, Colombia and Madagascar built the capacity to apply SEEA. The World Bank now runs a successor, the Global Program for {{ref:nature-eecon-208}}.

nature-acct-037.title: Sustainability metrics and indices: many yardsticks, no standard
nature-acct-037.text: There is no universal standard for measuring {{ref:nature-eecon-208}}, so disciplines and international organizations have proposed many different indicators. Sustainability metrics and indices are numerical measures that try to quantify sustainability's environmental, social and economic sides. Examples include the ecological footprint, the Human Development Index, the Genuine Progress Index and {{ref:nature-acct-042}}. Such aggregate measures give a more detailed view of development than traditional indicators such as GDP. Interest in index systems has expanded since the 2010s, more in industrialized than developing countries. Yet for all their popularity, these measures often have limited effect on actual policy and practice.

nature-acct-057.title: Sustainability indicators: simple questions for policy
nature-acct-057.text: Indicator sets answer simple questions. What is happening? Are targets being reached? Are things improving? A {{ref:nature-eecon-208}} indicator tracks some part of the interplay between the environment and social and economic activity. Descriptive indicators say what is happening; performance indicators say whether targets are being met. They are scientific constructs whose principal purpose is to inform public policy-making. They can cover the environment, society or the economy, but there is no fixed definition of a sustainability indicator.

nature-acct-075.title: Happy Planet Index: long, happy lives on a small footprint
nature-acct-075.text: The United States has high life satisfaction, yet on the Happy Planet Index it ranked 108th. The index, introduced by the New Economics Foundation in 2006, is not a ranking of the happiest countries. It measures how efficiently countries turn environmental impact into long, satisfied lives. Roughly, it multiplies life satisfaction by life expectancy and divides by the ecological footprint per person. It was designed to challenge GDP and the Human Development Index, which are seen as ignoring {{ref:nature-eecon-208}}. Costa Rica led the 2009, 2012 and 2016 rankings, and the 2019 ranking with a score of 62.1. Critics say it weights the footprint so heavily that the US would have needed a life expectancy of 439 years to match Vanuatu in 2006. Data gaps also forced estimates of footprint and life satisfaction for several countries.

nature-acct-038.title: Daly's three rules for living within nature's means
nature-acct-038.text: {{ref:nature-hist-040}} set out three operating rules for ecological {{ref:nature-eecon-208}}. First, renewable resources such as fish, soil and groundwater must be used no faster than they regenerate. Second, nonrenewable resources such as minerals and fossil fuels must be used no faster than renewable substitutes can be put in place. Third, pollution and wastes must be released no faster than natural systems can absorb, recycle or neutralize them ({{ref:nature-found-020}}). Daly built on theory from a 1971 book by {{ref:nature-hist-044}} on the economic process. Some see the rules as the physical counterpart of the definition from {{ref:nature-eecon-222}}, which supplies the ethical goal of not depleting natural capital.

nature-acct-042.title: Environmental Sustainability Index: Davos, 2005
nature-acct-042.text: On 28 January 2005, at the World Economic Forum in Davos, the Environmental {{ref:nature-eecon-208}} Index was formally released. Yale and Columbia University centres built the country index with the Forum. Its report compared it with other indicators such as the ecological footprint.

nature-acct-039.title: Natural Step framework: conditions for a sustainable society
nature-acct-039.text: After the report of {{ref:nature-eecon-222}}, Swedish cancer scientist Karl-Henrik Robèrt coordinated a consensus process to define {{ref:nature-eecon-208}} scientifically. The result was the Natural Step framework, which sets out system conditions a sustainable society must meet. Such a society does not keep raising concentrations of substances taken from the Earth's crust or made by society. It does not degrade the environment. And it lets people meet their needs.

nature-pol-145.title: Strategic environmental assessment: judging plans, not just projects
nature-pol-145.text: By the time a single road is assessed, the bigger choice may already have been made. Strategic environmental assessment (SEA) is a systematic process for making sure environmental, and sometimes wider {{ref:nature-eecon-208}}, effects are considered when policies, plans and programs are drawn up. It grew from a weakness of project-level {{ref:nature-pol-132}}: many damaging choices are made earlier, such as building new infrastructure that generates more travel. An SEA usually comes before the related project assessments, so its findings cascade down and reduce later work. The EU's SEA Directive 2001/42/EC made it legally required for many regional, local, development, waste and transport plans. Its phases are screening, scoping, a baseline of the environment, estimating likely impacts, influencing the decision and monitoring afterwards. The UNECE Protocol on SEA, in force since July 2010, goes further: it can be applied to policies and legislation. Aid donors use SEA too, so that strategic-level aid considers the environment.

nature-pol-184.title: Sustainability standards: voluntary rules for good practice
nature-pol-184.text: About 40% of global coffee production is certified, and about 15–20% of cocoa and tea production meets major {{ref:nature-eecon-208}} standards. These standards are voluntary guidelines that producers, traders and retailers follow to show good environmental, social, ethical and food-safety practices. More than 400 exist around the world. A standard is usually written by stakeholders and experts in a sector and lists practices, such as how a crop should be grown sustainably. Certification checks that a business meets it. Traceability then follows certified goods along the supply chain, often ending in a label for shoppers. The standards grew up where national and global laws were weak but consumers and campaign groups demanded action. Some set a high bar and work with top performers; others aim to remove the worst practices across most of an industry. They also differ in whether a first, second or third party does the checking, and whether certified and uncertified material may be mixed. Researchers still debate how effective these schemes are and how they are governed.

nature-pol-185.title: Who writes the rules: consensus standards and private ones
nature-pol-185.text: {{ref:nature-eecon-208}} standards fall into two groups. Voluntary consensus standards come out of an agreed process, as at the International Organization for Standardization. Private standards are written by individual companies for themselves, such as Starbucks' C.A.F.E. Practices and Nespresso AAA. Some standards were launched by coalitions of firms, NGOs and development agencies to harmonize the rules. The Marine Stewardship Council standard is one.

nature-mkt-055.title: Environmental finance: making investment less harmful to nature
nature-mkt-055.text: In 1992 Richard Sandor proposed a course on emission markets at the University of Chicago, later called Environmental Finance. The field it named is a branch of finance that uses market-based environmental policy tools, such as pricing and trading schemes, to make investment less harmful to nature. It seeks to move business resources toward sustainable investments while keeping profits. Inspired by the idea of social cost, Sandor focused on cap-and-trade along with taxes and subsidies. Under cap-and-trade, a total emissions cap is set, and firms receive permits they can buy or sell, rewarding cuts and penalizing excess. Investors gained new yardsticks too: the Dow Jones {{ref:nature-eecon-208}} Index, launched in 1999, rates the ecological and social impact of stocks. Money for climate is one part of the field. It splits into finance for cutting emissions, which takes over 90% of climate spending, and finance for adapting to change.

nature-mkt-018.title: Sustainable finance: seeking returns while weighing the planet
nature-mkt-018.text: Green and other {{ref:nature-eecon-208}}-labeled bonds together reached $170 billion in 2018 and $653.5 billion in 2025. They are among the products of sustainable finance: the practices, standards, rules and products that seek financial returns while weighing environmental, social and governance concerns. The term is often used as a synonym for ESG investing. The wider field also includes {{ref:nature-mkt-030}}, {{ref:nature-mkt-060}} and ethical investing. Its reach is global. The {{ref:nature-clim-074}} asks countries to make finance flows consistent with low greenhouse gas emissions and development that can withstand climate change. Sustainable finance is also described as a cornerstone for reaching the UN's {{ref:nature-gov-010}}, adopted in 2015 with 17 goals and 169 targets. Public money stays important. Much of the money for climate goals, though, is expected to come from the private sector. Over two decades, sustainable finance grew from a niche topic into a recognized field of research and university teaching.

nature-mkt-023.title: Aggregate confusion: why ESG scores disagree
nature-mkt-023.text: Credit ratings from the largest agencies agree 99% of the time. One paper found that ESG ratings agree only 60% of the time. This spread is called the ESG ratings gap, or 'aggregate confusion'. Sustainable finance lacks a single accepted standard for measuring and reporting {{ref:nature-eecon-208}}, so companies and funds are hard to compare. Many bodies write standards independently, including the GRI, the IFRS Foundation and the Carbon Disclosure Project, which has confused companies and investors. Because standards vary and change, some funds labeled ESG still hold oil and coal shares.

nature-mkt-021.title: Disclosure rules: making companies report climate risk
nature-mkt-021.text: In 2015 the Financial Stability Board launched a climate disclosure taskforce. Its job was to push firms to report the risks climate change poses them and how they govern those risks. {{ref:nature-eecon-208}} disclosure rules ask companies to report climate and other sustainability risks and impacts so investors can judge them. Voluntary rules have limited effect, research shows. An EU reporting directive adopted in October 2022 makes reporting compulsory for more firms, widening coverage from about 11,700 companies to about 50,000.

nature-mkt-062.title: Sustainability bonds: green and social at once
nature-mkt-062.text: Green, social and {{ref:nature-eecon-208}} bonds differ in which projects their money may fund. A sustainability bond must fund a mix of both green and social projects. The ICMA principles, from the International Capital Market Association, are the most widely accepted framework for issuing all three kinds. Critics still warn of misleading claims, because no single definition says what makes a bond sustainable.

nature-mkt-032.title: Environmental investing: impact investing for the planet
nature-mkt-032.text: By 2024 green bonds had reached about $700 billion of total issuance, and all {{ref:nature-eecon-208}}-related bonds nearly $8 trillion. Environmental investing is the branch of impact investing aimed at a measurable positive effect on the environment alongside financial returns. It funds projects such as clean energy, public transport and sustainable water management. It arose from the recognition that tackling climate change needs huge private sums.

nature-mkt-063.title: Sustainability-linked bonds: interest tied to targets
nature-mkt-063.text: In September 2019 the Italian utility Enel issued the first {{ref:nature-eecon-208}}-linked bond, promising a 25 basis point penalty on its interest if it missed its target. The terms of such a bond, such as its interest rate, change depending on whether the issuer meets set sustainability targets, tracked with key performance indicators. Unlike green, social or sustainability bonds, the money raised can be used for any purpose. Issuance was around $5 billion in 2019 and $10.6 billion in 2020. Over 85% were tied to environmental measures, most often cutting emissions.

nature-res-213.title: Natural resource economics: running an economy within nature's limits
nature-res-213.text: Fish, trees and ore: for decades, those three made up the core of the subject. Natural resource economics is the branch of economics that studies the supply, demand and sharing out of the Earth's natural resources. It began when researchers mainly wanted to know how to exploit stocks of resources commercially in the best way. Its traditional curriculum centered on models of fisheries, forests and mineral extraction. Its classic topics include welfare theory, how land is used, pollution control, resource extraction, valuing what markets do not price, exhaustibility and {{ref:nature-eecon-208}}. Environmental economics was once a separate subject. More recently air, water, the global climate and environmental resources in general have become important to policy, and interest has moved beyond commercial exploitation alone. The field's main aim now is to understand nature's role in the economy, so resources can be managed sustainably and stay available to future generations. Put simply, it asks how to run an economy within the ecological limits of the Earth's resources. Not everyone is satisfied. {{ref:nature-eecon-059}} criticizes the field for focusing mainly on efficient allocation, and less on fair distribution and on the scale of the economy.

nature-res-236.title: Neo-Malthusianism: the old fear in modern form
nature-res-236.text: After the Second World War, crop gains were followed by rapid growth in human numbers. Paul R. Ehrlich and others then predicted an imminent Malthusian catastrophe. Neo-Malthusianism is the concern that too many people consuming too much will exhaust resources. The fear is that the environment then degrades until ecosystems collapse. {{ref:nature-hist-040}} and Jeremy Rifkin raised such concerns about modern mechanized farming. The emphasis has shifted, though. A 2004 study including Kenneth Arrow and Paul Ehrlich found that {{ref:nature-eecon-208}} worries had moved from the number of people to the balance between consumption and saving.

nature-res-005.title: Managing the whole ecosystem, not one fish
nature-res-005.text: A 2007 set of 'ten commandments' urged managers to keep big old females, natural stock boundaries, seafloor habitats and food-web links. That is the spirit of ecosystem-based fisheries management, which manages fishing for the health and productivity of the whole ecosystem rather than single target species. It is organized around ecosystem services. Current scientific consensus favors it as the most workable way to balance human needs, keep those services and limit ecological harm. It also asks managers to adapt to climate change, account for evolution driven by fishing, and include human social and economic systems. Pitcher and Pauly go further. Harvesting simplifies ecosystems toward small, low-level species, they argue, so the goal should be rebuilding ecosystems, not {{ref:nature-eecon-208}} as such.

nature-res-086.title: Too many boats chasing too few fish
nature-res-086.text: Global landings peaked in the late 1980s and have declined even as fishing effort kept rising. Fishing effort is the human work put into catching fish. A good measure tracks the catch, for example a trawl fleet's engine power times days at sea, kW × days. Excess effort and overcapacity in fleets threaten the {{ref:nature-eecon-208}} of stocks. Schaefer assumed that in an unregulated fishery effort rises until no more profit can be made. Some subsidies push effort higher, and WTO members agreed to ban certain of them.

nature-res-264.title: Commodities: goods the market treats as interchangeable
nature-res-264.text: A bushel of wheat is a bushel of wheat, whoever grew it. That is the idea of a commodity: an economic good, usually a resource, whose instances the market treats as equivalent regardless of who produced them. Economists call this fungibility. Most commodities are raw materials, agricultural or mining products such as iron ore, sugar, rice and wheat. Crude oil, corn and gold are popular ones. Price is set by the whole market, and established physical commodities have actively traded spot and derivative markets. On an exchange the contract's underlying standard defines the commodity, not any quality of a particular producer's product. Wide availability means smaller profit margins and makes factors other than price, such as brand, matter less. Soft commodities are grown goods like wheat or rice; hard ones include gold, silver and oil; energy commodities include electricity, gas, coal and oil. Commoditization is a spectrum. Even electricity can be differentiated by generation method where buyers can pay more for renewables, and some customers pay for {{ref:nature-eecon-208}} or animal welfare, so organic, cage-free or Forest Stewardship Council labels separate otherwise commodity goods.

nature-res-103.title: Water resource management: who gets the water
nature-res-103.text: Many rivers and lakes are shared across national or internal borders, which makes fair management hard. Water resource management is the planning, development, distribution and management of the best use of water. Ideally it allocates water fairly among all competing demands. In practice decision-makers must put {{ref:nature-eecon-208}}, equity and optimization first, in that order. Climate change adds uncertainty, so managers increasingly involve the people affected and build the ability to adapt. The sixth of the UN's sustainable-development goals aims to implement {{ref:nature-res-104}} at all levels by 2030.

nature-res-104.title: Integrated water resources management (IWRM)
nature-res-104.text: Water, land and the resources tied to them cannot be managed in separate boxes. Integrated water resources management, or IWRM, is a process that coordinates their development and management. It aims to maximize economic and social welfare fairly without harming vital ecosystems. It rests on three principles: social equity, economic efficiency and ecological {{ref:nature-eecon-208}}. It emerged at international conferences in the late 1900s and early 2000s and was recommended in the 1992 Dublin Statement. Scholars see {{ref:nature-res-169}} as the goal and IWRM as the process to reach it. It is evolving to include the nexus approach, which recognizes that water, energy and food are closely linked. There is no single correct administrative model; practice depends on context.

nature-res-153.title: Reduced-impact logging: cutting with care
nature-res-153.text: Selective logging touches an estimated 1 billion hectares of forest worldwide, including 680 million hectares of tropical forest. It removes only a few species of trees above a minimum size and leaves the rest standing, unlike {{ref:nature-res-115}}. Done badly, by untrained crews cutting too often or too heavily, it ruins the stand, its water functions and its biodiversity. Reduced-impact logging is the answer: carefully planned and controlled harvesting by trained workers. The term arose in the late 1990s, after mechanized logging was seen to threaten long-term {{ref:nature-eecon-208}}. The FAO's model code calls for a cutting cycle of at least 20 years, removing no more than one-third of the stand's trunk area, and directional felling. It damages fewer trees and less soil, but in Southeast Asia logging more than 8 trees per hectare cancels its benefits. It can earn rewards for keeping carbon in the forest and is an eligible REDD+ activity. Whether it costs loggers money is disputed. Some studies find losses, while others find gains from wasting less timber.

nature-res-181.title: Integrated natural resource management
nature-res-181.text: Conflicts over resources are cheaper to prevent than to settle. Integrated natural resource management brings all stakeholders in from the planning stage to reduce later conflict. It manages resources systematically, balancing biophysical, political and economic sides to meet both users' production goals and wider community goals. {{ref:nature-eecon-208}} is its focus. It grew out of research on sustainable land use, participatory planning, integrated watershed management and {{ref:nature-nbs-146}}.

nature-nbs-341.title: Monitoring and evaluation: checking that a project works
nature-nbs-341.text: Impact assessment after a project ends is rare, because of its cost and the difficulty of showing the project caused the results. Monitoring and evaluation are management processes that organizations use to improve their outputs, outcomes and impact. Monitoring is continuous assessment giving early information on progress or delay, so deficiencies can be corrected quickly. Evaluation is a systematic, objective examination of relevance, effectiveness, efficiency, impact and {{ref:nature-eecon-208}} against objectives, and it also checks that funds are well managed. Indicators must be chosen before implementation; an outcome indicator has a baseline and a target. The credibility of reports depends heavily on the independence of the evaluators.

nature-nbs-235.title: Sustainable agriculture: farming that can last
nature-nbs-235.text: Food systems cause one third of human greenhouse gas emissions. Agriculture's footprint is huge, and sustainable agriculture tries to shrink it. It is farming that reduces harm to the environment, maintains and builds up natural resources, and uses non-renewable resources productively. The aim is to produce crops or livestock without damaging soil, water, biodiversity, or the people on and near the farm. Its toolkit can include {{ref:nature-nbs-297}}, growing trees among crops, mixed farming, multiple cropping and rotating crops from season to season. In 1977 the USDA defined it as long-term practices that meet food needs and improve the environment. They should also use resources efficiently, keep farms viable and improve farmers' lives. Economics explains part of the problem. Environmental costs left out of a farmer's ordinary accounts are externalities, so the market does not punish them. Investment in sustainable farming is said to be four times more cost-effective than direct food aid. Yet it gets only three percent of humanitarian funds. Many certification systems exist, including organic labels, Rainforest Alliance and Fair Trade. People still disagree on what {{ref:nature-eecon-208}} means here. An ecocentric view favors low growth and organic methods. A technocentric view relies on technology and modified industry.

nature-nbs-246.title: Agroecology: ecology applied to the farm
nature-nbs-246.text: Organics is practiced in 188 countries, and it is one of three certified forms of agroecology. Agroecology is the study and practice of applying ecological processes to farming, looking at links between plants, animals, people and the environment. The term can mean a science, a set of practices, or a social movement. It draws on agronomy, ecology, sociology, economics and history. It studies farm ecosystems' productivity, stability, {{ref:nature-eecon-208}} and fairness, at scales from a gene to the globe. Unlike in natural ecology, human activity and economics are the main forces at work. Biodynamic farming, organics and China's Green Food are its certified varieties. Movements such as La Via Campesina use it to pursue {{ref:nature-nbs-317}}. Researchers heatedly debate which model of farming policy should support.

nature-nbs-231.title: Scoring how well farms can weather climate change
nature-nbs-231.text: How ready is a country's farming for a hotter, less predictable climate? The Climate-Resilient Agriculture Index tries to put a number on it. The global version benchmarks countries with nine indicators in three dimensions: productivity and efficient use of resources, environmental {{ref:nature-eecon-208}} and climate impact, and socio-economic resilience. It sorts nations into four levels, from Highly Resilient to Very Low Resilience. A version for India uses 26 indicators to compare its agro-climatic zones.

nature-clim-267.title: Five possible worlds: the Shared Socioeconomic Pathways
nature-clim-267.text: Will the world of 2100 be cooperative or divided, green or fossil-fueled? The Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) offer five answers. They are scenarios of how global society and the economy might change up to 2100, used in the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report. Each pairs a storyline of socio-economic development with data on population, urbanization and GDP per person. The five are SSP1 {{ref:nature-eecon-208}}, SSP2 Middle of the road, SSP3 Regional rivalry, SSP4 Inequality and SSP5 Fossil-fueled development. On their own they describe societies, not emissions. Run through integrated assessment models, they yield emissions scenarios under different climate policies. IPCC scenario names combine the pathway with the forcing, the extra warming push on the planet, in 2100. SSP2-4.5 is one example. The spread of outcomes is wide. Projected warming for 2081–2100 runs from 1.4 °C under SSP1-1.9 to 4.4 °C under SSP5-8.5. A 2025 assessment put median warming under current policies at about 2.7 °C by 2100. That is closest to SSP2-4.5, the middle of the road.

nature-eecon-129.title: Sustainability science: a field built around problems
nature-eecon-129.text: Most fields are defined by their methods. {{ref:nature-eecon-208}} science, says William C. Clark, is defined by the problems it tackles. This applied discipline, emerging in the 1980s, studies sustainability and {{ref:nature-eecon-209}} and links knowledge to action. It grew from publications such as the World Conservation Strategy (1980) and the Brundtland report of 1987, {{ref:nature-hist-004}}. It was launched as an international field at a 2001 world congress in Amsterdam. At its core is the recognition of humanity's epochal impact in the Anthropocene.

nature-eecon-124.title: Post-normal science: when facts are uncertain and stakes are high
nature-eecon-124.text: Some decisions cannot wait for certainty. Post-normal science is a problem-solving approach for science used in policy when "facts are uncertain, values in dispute, stakes high and decisions urgent". Silvio Funtowicz and Jerome Ravetz developed it in the 1990s. In such cases it sets aside the traditional ideal of truth and focuses on quality, checked by internal and extended peer communities. Its diagram plots system uncertainties against decision stakes, separating applied science, professional consultancy and post-normal science. It complements risk analysis and {{ref:nature-val-001}} rather than replacing them. It is meant for pandemics, ecosystem collapse, biodiversity loss and the shift to {{ref:nature-eecon-208}}. In modeling it favors "models to map our ignorance about the future" over models to predict it. Critics say it adds nothing new, turns climate scientists into "stealth advocates" and undermines empiricism.

nature-eecon-101.title: Emergy ratios: judging how a process uses resources
nature-eecon-101.text: {{ref:nature-eecon-099}} accounting produces ratios that judge how a process uses local, renewable and purchased resources. The emergy yield ratio (EYR) measures how far an investment lets a process exploit local resources. The environmental loading ratio (ELR) compares non-renewable and imported emergy with renewable emergy, signaling stress on ecosystems. The emergy {{ref:nature-eecon-208}} index (ESI) is EYR divided by ELR.

nature-eco-644.title: Will population outrun food? The neo-Malthusian debate
nature-eco-644.text: In 1798 Malthus forecast that a growing population would deplete the world's food. Ehrlich revived the argument in 1968. Economist Julian Simon countered that the Green Revolution, a jump in farm output, had prevented famine: grain production rose over 250% between 1950 and 1984. Neo-Malthusians reply that those gains depend on fossil-fuel fertilizers, {{ref:nature-hist-084}} and irrigation. In 2009 the FAO, the UN food agency, said the world would need 70% more food by 2050. The two sides still disagree on whether technology can keep resources ahead of population.

nature-eco-689.title: Bioaccumulation: how poisons build up in a body
nature-eco-689.text: A chemical present at low levels in the environment can still poison an animal slowly. Bioaccumulation is the gradual build-up of substances such as {{ref:nature-hist-084}} or other chemicals in an organism. It occurs when an organism takes in a substance faster than it can lose it by catabolism and excretion. The longer a toxic substance's biological half-life, the greater the risk of chronic poisoning, even when environmental levels are low. Two related ideas help. Bioconcentration is a higher chemical concentration inside an organism than in the surrounding air or water. Biotransformation, the body's chemical alteration of a substance, can strongly change how much of it accumulates. Because the build-up matters at each step of the {{ref:nature-eco-305}} chain, understanding bioaccumulation helps in the assessment and control of chemicals and their use.

nature-eco-693.title: Plants and animals as pollution gauges
nature-eco-693.text: Some living things report pollution without any instrument. Plants and animals serve as biomonitors because their tissues or populations change measurably with pollution. Plant biomonitors include mosses, lichens, tree bark, tree rings and leaves, and tree bark can be analyzed for the pollutants it absorbed. In animals, sub-lethal effects on physiology, morphology and behavior appear long before population changes and act as early warning signals. Frogs and toads absorb toxic chemicals through permeable skin and poorly detoxify {{ref:nature-hist-084}}, so residues accumulate and they are used as bioindicators.

nature-es-088.title: Biological pest control: hiring a pest's enemies
nature-es-088.text: Around 304 AD, citrus growers in China bought nests of predatory ants to guard their fruit, the first known record of biological pest control. The idea is to use living organisms against pests, whether animals, weeds or disease-causing organisms. It works through predation, parasitism and plant-eating, usually with people actively managing it, and it can form part of {{ref:nature-nbs-283}}. Modern biological control began in the US in the 1870s. State entomologists started handing out parasitoids, insects whose young develop inside or on a host and kill it. Today's agents include lady beetles, parasitoid wasps and flies, and disease organisms such as bacteria, fungi and viruses. Bacillus thuringiensis, a soil bacterium, is the most widely used bacterial agent, and its genes have been put into transgenic crops. The payoff is economic and ecological. Biological control can cut losses from pests, disease carriers and invasive species, and natural enemies used instead of {{ref:nature-hist-084}} mean less farm pollution.

nature-es-099.title: What is killing the pollinators
nature-es-099.text: Synthetic {{ref:nature-hist-084}}, above all neonicotinoids, are a primary driver of pollinator decline, damaging the nerves and immune systems of bees and other pollinators. Other proposed causes include parasites and diseases, habitat destruction, climate change, market forces and competition with invasive species. Some effects are subtle. Air pollution breaks down flower scents so they travel shorter distances, forcing pollinators to fly farther. Climate change can make bees emerge when no plants are flowering. A 2021 global assessment said policy should focus on land-cover change, land management and pesticides.

nature-pol-050.title: Brownfield land: the polluted leftovers of industry
nature-pol-050.text: The word was first used on June 28, 1992, at a US congressional field hearing. Brownfield land is previously developed land, abandoned or underused, that may be polluted from past industrial use. Countries define it differently, mainly over whether contamination must actually be present. Examples include abandoned factories, ash ponds, old landfills, dry cleaners and gas stations. Their ground may hold spilled hydrocarbons, solvents, {{ref:nature-hist-084}}, asbestos and heavy metals such as lead. The United States alone is estimated to have over 500,000 brownfield sites contaminated below the level that triggers {{ref:nature-pol-176}}. Not all of this land is dead ground. Industrial brownfields can be valuable ecosystems that support rare plants, animals and invertebrates. Redeveloping them has become a key part of large urban greening projects.

nature-pol-215.title: Hedgerows and birds: the farm policy's environmental record
nature-pol-215.text: Between 1980 and 2009 the farmland bird population fell from 600 million to 300 million, a loss of 50%. Critics blame EU farm subsidies, which drove a large expansion of production using fertilizers and {{ref:nature-hist-084}}. Removing hedgerows and plowing meadows made farming more efficient but cut farmland bird habitat. Reforms since 2004 claim to put the environment at the center of farm policy. In 2010 the EU said 31% of €5 billion for new agricultural challenges would go to protecting biodiversity in the countryside. Yet in 2024 the European Court of Auditors warned the policy was not aligned with the EU's Green Deal climate goals.

nature-mkt-025.title: Natural pest control and the cane toad warning
nature-mkt-025.text: Biological pest control uses natural enemies to keep pests down, an ecosystem function that depends on biodiversity. Control species can cut crop losses without the harms of chemical {{ref:nature-hist-084}}, which brings economic benefits. Done carelessly, it backfires. Cane toads brought to Queensland in 1935 to eat cane beetles became an invasive species.

nature-res-150.title: Precision agriculture: farming field by field, row by row
nature-res-150.text: Precision agriculture treats a field as many small patches rather than one. It is a farm management strategy that collects and analyzes data on fields, plants and animals to fit decisions to local variation. It applies precise amounts of water, fertilizer and {{ref:nature-hist-084}} at the right time, cutting inputs while raising yields. It relies on GPS, mapping software, variable-rate machinery, grid sampling and {{ref:nature-es-057}}. Farmers earn back their investment by saving on inputs, and targeting them also benefits soils and groundwater. The idea first emerged in the United States in the early 1980s.

nature-nbs-195.title: Beaver dams: flood control built by rodents
nature-nbs-195.text: The largest known beaver dam is 775 metres long. Most run from a few metres to about 100 metres. A beaver dam creates a pond that protects its builders from predators and stores food for winter. By reshaping their surroundings, beavers act as a {{ref:nature-eco-301}} and as an {{ref:nature-es-086}}. In their native range, the dams reduce downstream flooding, clean water, maintain wetlands and act as firebreaks. A dam stores floodwater and releases it gradually, lowering the flood wave and keeping streams flowing in dry spells. Bacteria in the debris behind it turn nitrates into nitrogen gas and break down some {{ref:nature-hist-084}}. In Alberta, beaver ponds held 5.7 times more young wood frogs than nearby free-flowing streams. Dams can also flood farmland, roads and railways. In Tierra del Fuego, introduced beavers are considered a plague. When dams are abandoned, their wetlands become meadows and then forest, slowly building up the valley floor.

nature-nbs-267.title: Agricultural pollution: farming's spillover
nature-nbs-267.text: Runoff from farms, gathered in large water bodies, creates dead zones downstream. Agricultural pollution is contamination or damage to the environment, people or their livelihoods from the by-products of farming. Some comes from single discharge points. More often it comes from diffuse non-point sources spread across the landscape, and from air pollution. The list of pollutants is long: sediments, nutrients, pathogens, {{ref:nature-hist-084}}, metals and salts. They reach lakes, rivers, wetlands, estuaries and groundwater. Poor management drives much of it, such as overgrazing, plowing and badly timed pesticide use. Animal agriculture has an outsized impact on the pollutants entering the environment. Economists see the problem as an externality, a cost the farmer does not pay. So agricultural economists design incentives to control it, for example to curb water pollution from farms.

nature-nbs-305.title: Soil conservation: keeping topsoil and fertility
nature-nbs-305.text: Each one percent increase in soil organic matter lets soil hold 20,000 gallons more water per acre. Soil conservation protects that capacity. It means preventing the loss of topsoil to erosion and the loss of fertility from overuse, acidification, salinization or contamination. Deforestation typically causes large-scale erosion, nutrient loss and sometimes desertification. Farmers have practiced conservation for millennia. Techniques include rotating crops, growing plants to cover bare soil, tilling less and planting tree rows against the wind. The EU's Common Agricultural Policy promotes reduced tillage, winter cover, plant residues and grass margins. Farming methods alone are not enough. Solving erosion also needs political and economic action, including changing how land is valued. Taxing {{ref:nature-hist-084}} at different rates is one option studied.

nature-nbs-260.title: Riparian buffers: green strips that guard streams
nature-nbs-260.text: A nine-year University of Georgia study found streamside buffers removed at least 60% of nitrogen and 65% of phosphorus from fertilizer washing off fields. A riparian buffer is a strip of vegetation, usually trees, along a stream that shades it and shields it from nearby land use. Buffers catch sediment, nutrients and {{ref:nature-hist-084}} before they reach the water. They counter eutrophication downstream and stabilize banks. They also provide habitat and wildlife corridors in farm country. Buffers can raise land value and grow profitable crops such as black walnut and hazelnut. Programs such as the US Conservation Reserve Program pay farmers for the land taken out of production. They have limits: a 2017 study found little ability to stop glyphosate leaching to streams.

nature-nbs-274.title: Biodiversity on farmland
nature-nbs-274.text: The FAO estimates more than 40% of Earth's land surface is used for agriculture, which makes habitat loss the main driver of biodiversity loss. Biodiversity in agriculture is the variety of living things on farmland. It falls as varied landscapes are lost and native plants give way to crops. Fallow land, grass margins and scrub strips add habitat variety, and smaller fields have been linked to more species. Diversity pays. In Asian rice, flowering strips beside fields cut insecticide spraying by 70% and raised yields by 5%, an economic advantage of 7.5%. Low crop diversity can increase pests and {{ref:nature-hist-084}} resistance.

nature-nbs-292.title: Organic farming: natural inputs, fewer synthetics
nature-nbs-292.text: By 2022, 4.5 million farmers in 188 countries were farming about 96,000,000 hectares organically, and the market reached $150 billion. Organic farming relies on natural inputs such as compost, manure and green manure, and on methods like crop rotation. It largely bans synthetic {{ref:nature-hist-084}} and fertilizers, and prohibits genetically modified organisms, sewage sludge, growth hormones and routine antibiotics. It began early in the 20th century as a reaction to fast-changing farming. Its environmental record is disputed. On average 30% more species live on organic farms. But a 2012 meta-analysis found organic farming needs 84% more land for the same harvest. Emissions per hectare are lower, yet nitrogen leaching per unit of food is higher. There is not enough evidence that organic food is safer or healthier.

nature-nbs-272.title: The risks of using living things against pests
nature-nbs-272.text: Releasing predators, parasites or pathogens to fight farm pests can cut pollution from {{ref:nature-hist-084}}. But the method carries its own risk. Once released, an agent may be impossible to recall. It may spread into the wild or switch to native hosts. The merits of introducing non-native control agents remain widely debated.

nature-nbs-269.title: Pesticides that linger for years
nature-nbs-269.text: Without pest control, crop losses before harvest would typically reach 40 percent. That is why {{ref:nature-hist-084}} are used, but some do not go away. Persistent pesticides stay in the environment for many years. 2,4-D and atrazine can last up to 20 years, and DDT and dieldrin are also long-lived.

nature-nbs-355.title: Mixed cropping: all the seeds sown together
nature-nbs-355.text: Mixed cropping is a polyculture in which all the seeds are mixed and sown together. The result mimics natural plant diversity and is simple to handle. The costs are that crops can compete, and any {{ref:nature-hist-084}} or fertilizer goes on all of them.

nature-nbs-283.title: Integrated pest management: control, not eradication
nature-nbs-283.text: In 1986 Indonesia banned 57 {{ref:nature-hist-084}} and stopped subsidizing them. It was a bet on integrated pest management, which combines non-chemical and chemical methods to control pests economically while relying less on pesticides. The FAO describes it as mixing biological, chemical, physical and cultural methods to grow healthy crops with minimal pesticide use. Its aim is control, not eradication, since wiping out a pest is often impossible, costly and unsafe. Prevention comes first: resistant varieties, crop rotation and intercropping. Alternating between classes of control helps stop pests becoming resistant. The method runs as six repeated steps: sample, identify, learn the pest's biology, set an action threshold, choose tactics and evaluate. It reduces risks such as pest resurgence, resistance and residues on food.

nature-nbs-082.title: Monoculture: one crop, one field, short-term gains
nature-nbs-082.text: Over 600 million liters of {{ref:nature-hist-084}} are sprayed each year after pest outbreaks. Many of those outbreaks trace back to monoculture, growing a single crop species in a field at a time. In the short term it is easy and efficient: uniform planting, care and harvest often give higher yields and lower costs. With synthetic fertilizers, it has reduced the extra land needed for food, which is called land sparing. Over the long term, though, monocultures are more prone to disease and pests, because local biodiversity falls and nutrients run down. Perennial monocultures such as oil palm, sugarcane, tea and pines can acidify and degrade soils. Declining soil health leads to more fertilizer, whose excess nitrogen can contaminate drinking water and feed algal blooms. Diversity can be added through crop rotation, intercropping, agroecology, silvopasture and {{ref:nature-nbs-086}}.

nature-eecon-139.title: Coevolutionary economics: pests, pesticides and the rules between
nature-eecon-139.text: Pests evolve resistance to {{ref:nature-hist-084}}, pesticides change, and the institutions regulating them change too. Richard Norgaard used that story to bring coevolution into ecological economics. The idea began in biology for two species evolving together, then grew into gene-culture coevolution. Coevolutionary economics studies change as mutual feedback and selection among social, environmental and economic systems. Ecological economics itself is defined by this coevolution of economies and ecosystems. Norgaard and Giorgos Kallis applied it to water development, urbanization and rural communities.

nature-eecon-026.title: Biorefineries: an oil refinery for plants
nature-eecon-026.text: The pulp and paper industry is considered the first industrialized biorefinery system. A biorefinery is a facility that converts biomass, material from living things, into energy and other useful products such as chemicals. The IEA defines biorefining as sustainable processing of biomass into food, feed, chemicals, materials and bioenergy, the full product range of the {{ref:nature-eecon-009}}. It works like an oil refinery. Biomass is split into intermediates such as carbohydrates, proteins and fats. Each refining step is called a cascading phase. Systems are classified by platform, product, feedstock and conversion process, which may be mechanical, biochemical, chemical or thermochemical. The goals are broad: supplying fuels and chemicals, creating rural jobs, getting value from waste and reducing greenhouse gas emissions. Biobased does not automatically mean harmless. Growing the biomass can still cause land-use change, {{ref:nature-hist-084}} pollution and eutrophication, the overloading of water with nutrients. So life cycle assessment is used to compare biobased products with conventional ones.

nature-hist-006.title: Silent Spring: the book that turned the US against DDT
nature-hist-006.text: Rachel Carson thought the word {{ref:nature-hist-084}} was too kind. In Silent Spring, her 1962 book, she argued that these chemicals should be called 'biocides', because their effects rarely stop at the target pests. The book documented the harm done by indiscriminate use of the pesticide DDT and its spread through the wider environment as {{ref:nature-found-079}}. Carson accused the chemical industry of spreading disinformation and officials of accepting its claims without question. Chemical companies fought back hard. They lost the argument with the public. Silent Spring shifted opinion, reversed US pesticide policy and led to a national ban on DDT for farm use. It also fed the movement that created the US Environmental Protection Agency. The book became a rallying point for the new social movement of the 1960s and is seen as the start of the deep ecology movement. As one scholar put it, after Carson no one could so easily sell pollution as the necessary underside of progress. A dispute still clings to it. Some anti-environmentalist groups blame Carson for malaria deaths after DDT was restricted. Scientists and journalists have dismissed that claim as a myth, but it has not gone away.

nature-econ-494.title: Income inequality: how unevenly income is shared
nature-econ-494.text: UN Sustainable Development Goal 10 aims to reduce inequality. Income inequality is the extent to which income is spread unevenly across a population. It can be measured with tools such as the {{ref:nature-econ-873}} and the {{ref:nature-econ-527}}. Many economists argue that some inequality is necessary, but that excessive inequality causes efficiency problems and social injustice. Globalization complicates matters. It tends to raise a country's average income, but unequally.

reviews.nature-as-the-economy-s-foundation: Ecosystems, joined together in the biosphere, make up the stock called natural capital. That stock yields ecosystem services, sorted into provisioning, regulating, cultural and supporting groups, and a rich variety of life often helps keep them steady. Yet people have altered about 70% of Earth's land, fresh water is running short, and pollution, climate change and biodiversity loss feed one another. Efforts to count nature, from the Natural Capital Protocol to national environmental accounts, run into a hard question: whether nature should carry a money value at all. Short-term thinking makes the long-term goal of {{ref:nature-eecon-208}} harder still.
reviews.managing-the-commons: Who holds the rights to a resource shapes how it fares, and open-access resources that no one owns tend to be the most exploited. Hardin's 1968 article made the commons sound doomed, yet Ostrom found farmers in the Swiss Alps running grazing land for hundreds of years with clear boundaries, monitoring and graduated sanctions. Mongolia's shared grazing lands and Nepal's community forests showed the same pattern. England's enclosure moved the other way, turning common land into private fields and stripping commoners of their rights. At every scale, from customary land and urban commons to the atmosphere, the lesson is that rules made and enforced by users can keep a shared resource alive.

nature-eco-257.q: By how much is the volume of permanently frozen ground in the upper 3 m expected to fall per 1 °C of global warming?

nature-eco-720.q: Which water-cycle quantities can be measured from a distance, without sensors on the spot?
nature-eco-720.a: Surface water storage, soil moisture, precipitation, evapotranspiration, and snow and ice.

nature-eco-220.q: How does eutrophication affect the treatment of water for drinking?
nature-eco-220.a: Murkier water raises water treatment costs, and colour and smell problems arise.

nature-econ-134.q: Why is biodiversity increasingly seen as having economic value?
nature-econ-134.a: Because of ecosystem services such as clean air, food, water, protection from flooding and pollination.

nature-eco-092.q: What is now thought to mainly cause drought in the Sahel?
nature-eco-092.a: Rainfall variability driven by ocean temperatures, aerosols and greenhouse gases, rather than too many grazing animals as early studies claimed.

nature-eco-668.q: How much of this gas came from human activities and from natural sources in 2019?
nature-eco-668.a: About 360 million tons came from human activities and 230 million tons from natural sources.

nature-econ-083.q: How does capital differ from raw materials or the power that drives machines?
nature-econ-083.a: It is not used up in one round of production but keeps giving services over many rounds.

nature-eco-681.q: What do all savannas share in terms of rainfall and fire?
nature-eco-681.a: Year-to-year rainfall variation and dry-season fires in wild land.

nature-val-017.a: Because of externalities and because taxes, subsidies, quotas and import duties distort market prices.

nature-eco-601.q: According to scholars, what must be maintained for the long term?
